Figure 2: Process of the Precinct transforming to an employment generating precinct 
Consistent with this policy direction, the 
Department and Council have undertaken master 
planning informed by technical studies to support 
the coordinated transformation of the former mine 
site to alternative, employment-generating land 
uses in the Precinct (Figure 2). The draft Master 
Plan establishes the design framework to realise 
this opportunity, providing the certainty needed 
by investors, industry partners and the 
community, demonstrating a transferable model 
for productive post mining land use across NSW.
Relationship to other  
planning instruments
State Environmental Planning Policy (Precincts – 
Regional) 2021
A new chapter will be prepared for the Macquarie 
Coal Complex Precinct in the State Environmental 
Planning Policy (Precincts – Regional) 2021 
(Precincts – Regional SEPP). The chapter will:
•
Provide zoning and land use controls
•
Determine permissible and prohibited land
uses
•
Set general and site-specific provisions
•
Present the role and requirements of the draft
Master Plan
•
Excise pilot project sites from relevant Local
Environmental Plans.
Existing planning pathways will be utilised.
Macquarie Coal Complex Post-Mining 
Land Use Master Plan 
Prepared by the Department and approved by the 
Minister of Planning and Public Spaces, the draft 
Master Plan is a statutory document that 
supports the Precincts – Regional SEPP and: 
•
Provides the strategic vision, guiding principles, 
strategic context and describes overarching 
Precinct opportunities and constraints
•
Provides an overarching structure plan and aims 
and performance criteria to make sure 
objectives are met
•
Must be considered by the consent authority 
when determining an application for consent
•
Identifies environmental, transport and utility 
infrastructure to support future development 
within the Precinct.
The Lake Macquarie Local Environment Plan 2014 
and Lake Macquarie Development Control Plan 2014 
do not apply to the Precinct.

1  Introduction

--- MP Page 6 ---
Purpose and how to  
use this draft Master Plan
The purpose of this draft Master Plan is to provide 
a hierarchy of Precinct-wide aims and establish 
performance criteria to support the delivery of a 
diverse range of land uses that support regional 
economic diversification, attract investment and 
create local jobs and protect high value biodiversity 
(Figure 4). It is intended to establish a broad 
framework for implementation where detailed 
design, operational and market feasibility must be 
balanced to achieve the vision. The draft Master 
Plan is to be applied with flexibility and the consent 
authority may allow for alternate viable solutions 
so that otherwise permissible development can be 
carried out. 
This draft Master Plan details the overall planning 
direction for the Precinct and is not prescriptive with 
regards to built form design solutions, rather sets 
outcomes to be achieved through flexible solutions, 
such as adaptive reuse and staged delivery. 
Development applications must:
•
Consider the relevant aims and performance
criteria
•
Provide site-specific technical assessments
(such as access, flooding, drainage,
water quality, tree preservation, utilities,
contamination and acoustic separation) as
required
•
Demonstrate the development’s proposed use is
consistent with this draft Master Plan
•
Demonstrate built form suitability for the
Precinct.
Future planning considerations: 
Addendum to Master Plan
The Precincts - Regional SEPP, Chapter 7 requires 
that a Master Plan apply to the Macquarie Coal 
Complex Precinct and that the Master Plan is to be 
considered in the assessment of any development 
application within the Precinct.
To provide for the orderly and economic 
development of the Precinct, some development 
will require an addendum to the Master Plan to be 
prepared before a development application can be 
lodged through the Planning Portal.
Figure 4: Master Plan Precinct-wide 
planning hierarchy
When is an addendum required?
You must prepare an addendum to the Master Plan 
before lodging a development application if:
•
The proposal is located on land identified as
environmentally constrained on the Structure
Plan (Figure 9).
•
The proposal is located on land identified as
requiring further investigation on the Structure
Plan (Figure 9).
What should the addendum include?
•
A map showing proposed land uses within the
sub-precinct(s).

2	 Strategic context
Precinct location and strategic fit
The Precinct comprises approximately 1160 
hectares within the Lake Macquarie Local 
Government Area on the southern periphery of 
greater Newcastle. Macquarie Coal Complex is a 
former mining operation comprising West Wallsend 
Colliery, Teralba Colliery, Westside Mine, the 
Macquarie Coal Preparation Plant (MCPP), Tailings 
Storage Facility (TSF) and associated 
infrastructure. 
Coal mining has been a defining land use in the 
area since the early 19th Century, shaping both the 
physical landscape and the economic profile of 
surrounding communities. The mining operations in 
the Precinct are currently closed and undergoing 
rehabilitation, presenting a large, consolidated 
landholding with significant potential for new 
employment-generating uses.
The Precinct is characterised by a diverse post 
mining landscape that includes rehabilitating 
landforms, residual industrial infrastructure, water 
management features and areas of ecological 
regeneration. These attributes create a complex 
but opportunity-rich setting. Extensive brownfield 
areas with existing access and servicing potential 
are complemented by areas of environmental value 
requiring protection and integration into future 
land use outcomes. 
Transforming the Macquarie Coal Complex aligns 
with the strategic directions of the Hunter Regional 
Plan 2041, which seeks to diversify the regional 
economy, leverage existing infrastructure and 
repurpose former mining land to support long-term 
employment growth. At a local level, the Precinct 
supports the Lake Macquarie Local Strategic 
Planning Statement 2025–2045, particularly in 
relation to growing and diversifying the economy, 
protecting environmental assets and delivering 
infrastructure that supports productivity and 
sustainable growth.
Figure 5 illustrates the Precinct’s location and 
regional context.
Regionally significant  
employment opportunity
The Hunter region is undergoing a structural 
economic diversification. Driven by decarbonisation 
and shifting global energy markets, the region 
is forecast to lose around 14,000 coal-related 
industrial jobs by 2035 (Aurecon, 2026). Total 
employment is expected to grow by 40,000 
to 75,000 jobs over the next decade through 
expansion in healthcare, education, professional 
services and emerging clean economy sectors 
(Aurecon, 2026). The Hunter’s established energy 
and industrial infrastructure, strategic port and 
freight networks, skilled workforce and research 
institutions position it strongly to capture this 
growth. Realising this potential depends on 
supporting changing workforce, delivering 
strategic infrastructure and providing well-located 
investment-ready employment land. 
Lake Macquarie is at the centre of this 
transformation. With an aging population that is 
forecast to grow by 26% to 2046, together with 
high regional immigration, the city is under 
sustained pressure to deliver new jobs and 
services. Population growth is currently not 
matched by the supply of well-located 
employment land, generating a shortfall in 
serviced employment land by 2046 (Aurecon, 
2026). At 
the same time, the Lower Hunter currently lacks 
purpose-built, large-scale industrial precincts 
capable of accommodating renewable energy, 
advanced manufacturing, circular economy models 
and regional logistics uses.
The Precinct’s location, scale and infrastructure 
position it to deliver new employment land, 
support workforce transformation and attract 
emerging industries in the Hunter.

--- MP Page 11 ---
Precinct constraints
The Precinct presents a range of environmental, physical and infrastructure 
constraints that are managed through the structure plan and addressed 
progressively through staged development and site-specific assessment at the 
development application stage.
Geotechnical stability and risk management – Development on the TSF and the 
land located in the dam break inundation zone to the north is currently limited. 
Soft alluvial soils located around the coastal wetlands in the north of the site 
influence construction methods.
Environmental – Existing areas of high biodiversity values, high bush fire risk 
and flood affected areas require further investigation to inform development 
siting and design.
Sensitive uses – Interfaces between existing land uses, including residential 
receivers and potential future industrial land uses will need to be managed to 
mitigate negative noise, odour and visual impacts.
Infrastructure – Heavy vehicle access to parts of the site is currently limited 
due to steep gradients, access through local residential areas and existing rail 
crossings. The location of the existing oil pipeline, electrical transmission lines 
and their associated easements, setbacks and design measures will need to be 
considered. 
Utility infrastructure – Viability and sequencing of the provision of utilities, 
particularly to the West Lake sub-precinct, will need further investigation.

Structure plan
The structure plan (Figure 9) is the principal 
spatial framework for the draft Master Plan. It 
identifies the arrangement of developable areas, 
environmentally constrained areas, recreational 
areas, movement networks and key constraints 
across the Precinct to guide development. 
The structure plan outlines the spatial logic for 
future development at a precinct scale, providing 
a framework within which detailed design, 
subdivision and development assessment will 
occur. The structure plan is supported by technical 
studies.
The following categories are used to describe land 
within the structure plan:
•
Developable areas – Land that is potentially
suitable for development, subject to further
technical investigation and site-specific
assessment at the development application
stage.
•
Environmentally constrained areas – Land
identified as having biodiversity values or where
natural features (watercourses, wetlands, steep
slope, flooding) constrain development.
•
Recreation areas – Land potentially suitable for
active and passive recreation facilities,
balanced with protecting biodiversity and
cultural values.
•
Further investigation – Potentially developable
land that is constrained in the short to medium
term by geotechnical, dam safety, biodiversity
or flood risk factors, requiring resolution before
development can proceed. Development of this
land is contingent upon the completion
of relevant technical investigations and the
achievement of applicable staging triggers.

4  Structure plan and sub-precinct framework

--- MP Page 18 ---
Sub-precinct framework
The structure plan organises the Precinct into 
five development sub-precincts (Figure 10), set 
within a connected network of environmentally 
constrained areas that define the Precinct’s 
landscape framework. Each sub-precinct presents 
a distinctive opportunity, shaped by its topography, 
legacy mining features, environmental values, 
access and proximity to existing communities and 
infrastructure. 
Together the sub-precincts enable a coordinated, 
staged transformation of the Precinct that 
responds to physical setting while delivering 
a diverse range of employment, recreation 
and community outcomes. Each sub-precinct 
description presents key characteristics, land use 
intent and opportunities for future planning and 
development, against which development proposals 
will be assessed.
Figure 10: Sub-precincts

Land use intent
Future development will be anchored by 
employment-generating activity that supports 
regional economic diversification, attracts 
investment and creates local jobs. Complementary 
commercial, recreation, community and visitor land 
uses will support the workforce, deliver community 
benefit and contribute to the broader public value 
of the post mining tranformation.

4  Structure plan and sub-precinct framework

--- MP Page 20 ---
Cockle Creek
Characteristics
Cockle Creek sub-precinct is located in the eastern 
portion of the Precinct and encompasses the 
former MCPP, TSF, mine rail loop and associated 
operational infrastructure. Its direct interface 
with the Main Northern Railway, together with 
established access from Racecourse Road, 
Railway Street and The Weir Road, positions the 
sub-precinct as a strategically connected gateway 
within the broader Precinct. 
Historic industrial use has shaped a substantially 
modified landscape of previously disturbed land 
and legacy infrastructure. These attributes provide 
a strong foundation for early activation and support 
the efficient reuse of land.
Key opportunities
The following attributes shape the sub-precinct’s 
development context and inform a flexible, 
opportunity-led planning response:
•
Reuse of legacy industrial assets – The former 
coal preparation plant, mine rail loop and 
existing rail interface with the Main Northern 
railway provide a platform for new industrial, 
manufacturing, energy and rail-related uses that 
leverage available infrastructure. 
•
Early activation of available land – Areas outside 
the TSF and dam break inundation zone are well-
positioned for near-term development, with 
further land progressively released as TSF 
rehabilitation advances.
•
Enhanced connectivity – A potential new bridge 
crossing of Cockle Creek is identified for 
investigation to strengthen road access and 
unlock additional development opportunities 
across the sub-precinct.
•
Improved internal movement networks – New 
internal road links will support integrated 
movement across the sub-precinct, enabled by 
revocation of the TSF dam declaration or 
delivery of bridge infrastructure above the 
inundation level.
•
Supporting industries that would facilitate rail 
manufacturing, including workshops with skilled 
trades.
•
Established access for short term activity
– Existing connections from Railway Street,
Racecourse Road, The Weir Road and Rhondda
Road provide immediate access to developable
land beyond the dam break inundation zone,
supporting early-stage uses.
•
Integration of environmental values – High value
biodiversity, fauna habitat and wetland areas to
north and east of the sub-precinct are retained
and integrated into the land use pattern,
supporting a considered balance between
development and environmental outcomes.

Killingworth
Characteristics
Killingworth sub-precinct is located in the north-
western portion of the Precinct, near established 
residential areas of Killingworth and Barnsley. 
Accessible topography, established road 
connections via Wakefield Road and The Broadway, 
and a direct interface with environmentally 
constrained areas and biodiversity corridors to the 
south and east define its place-based setting.
Its proximity to existing communities and the 
prevalence of previously disturbed land from 
former mining operations position the sub-precinct 
as a strong candidate for early activation. These 
attributes provide a practical platform for short-
term development opportunities, aligned with 
rehabilitation outcomes and sequenced provision of 
servicing.
Key opportunities
The following attributes shape the sub-precinct’s 
development context and inform an opportunity-led 
planning response:
•
Compatible community interface – Interface 
with established residential areas of 
Killingworth and Barnsley is managed through 
appropriate buffers, setbacks and acoustic 
treatments to make sure land use compatibility 
and protect amenity.
•
Efficient access and movement – Accessible 
topography and established connections 
through Wakefield Road and The Broadway 
enable efficient site access, with heavy vehicle 
routing strategy that directs freight to approved 
routes and reinforces the sub-precinct’s 
logistics advantages.
•
Energy-enabled employment opportunity –
Proximity to the Transgrid substation positions 
Killingworth to attract energy-intensive and 
data-driven industries seeking reliable grid 
access, supporting the Precinct’s role in the 
Hunter’s energy and digital economy 
transformation.
•
Local jobs – The sub-precinct’s location 
adjoining established communities provides for 
accessible local employment that supports 
workforce participation and liveability across the 
surrounding area.
•
Integration of environmental values – Interfaces
with environmentally constrained areas and
biodiversity corridors inform a considered land
use pattern that retains ecological connectivity
while enabling productive use of previously
disturbed land.
•
Evidence-based sequencing – Geotechnical,
water quality, utilities and access investigations
will inform the staged delivery of development.

Key opportunities
The following attributes shape the sub-precinct’s 
development context and inform an opportunity-
led, planning response:
•
A landscape-led destination – West Lake will 
evolve as the Precinct’s landscape, community 
and visitor heart, where rehabilitated land, water 
and bushland frame a curated employment, 
tourism, recreation and interpretation concept 
that supports economic diversification and long-
term adaptability.
•
Signature landscape setting and visitor 
experience – The lake and distinctive landscape 
identity that supports nature-based tourism, 
recreation and visitor infrastructure, including 
walking and cycling trails, lookouts, water-based 
facilities and heritage interpretation.
•
Integrated landscape and environmental values 
– Rehabilitation areas, habitat corridors and 
interfaces with rural landscapes and 
environmentally constrained areas inform a 
considered land use pattern, with buffer zones 
and edge treatments that protect surrounding 
values and reinforce ecological connectivity 
across the Precinct.
•
Evidence-based sequencing – Geotechnical, 
water quality, utilities and access investigations 
will inform the staged delivery of development.
West Lake
Characteristics
West Lake sub-precinct occupies the south-
western portion of the Precinct and encompasses 
the former Westside void, now a 
water-filled lake, together with the surrounding 
rehabilitation areas. The sub-precinct’s distinctive 
landscape identity is shaped by the interplay of 
water, remnant bushland, rehabilitated landforms 
and elevated topography, with expansive views 
across the Precinct and towards Lake Macquarie.
The lake is a signature landscape asset that 
anchors a unique sense of place. It provides 
the foundation for nature-based experiences, 
recreation and visitor infrastructure that enhance 
the Precinct’s broader attractiveness as an 
employment and lifestyle destination. The sub-
precinct enables an active waterfront approach 
to commercial, tourism and recreation around the 
foreshore, with development carefully integrated 
to retain and showcase the area’s biodiversity and 
landscape values.
Further investigation areas on the eastern side of 
the lake offer additional opportunity for low-impact, 
sensitive development that responds to the desired 
future character of West Lake and complements its 
biodiversity and landscape setting.

4  Structure plan and sub-precinct framework

Barnsley West
Characteristics
Barnsley West sub-precinct is in the north-western 
portion of the Precinct, comprising separate parcels 
of land associated with the former Wakefield 
Colliery. Accessed via Wakefield Road and Charlton 
Street, the sub-precinct sits within a distinctive 
landscape setting shaped by its interface with 
adjoining residential areas, environmentally 
constrained lands and established transmission 
infrastructure. High biodiversity land between 
Barnsley West and the Killingworth sub-precinct 
reinforces its discrete identity.
Key opportunities
The following attributes shape the sub-precinct’s 
development context and inform an opportunity-
led, planning response:
•
Small-scale urban services and light industry
– The sub-precinct’s compact scale and
adjacency to residential areas provide for a
curated mix of small-scale urban services, light
industrial and complementary employment
uses that meet local needs while supporting the
Precinct’s broader economic diversification.
•
Amenity-led interface with Barnsley village –
The residential interface informs a high-quality
edge response, including built form transitions,
landscape buffers, acoustic treatments and
operational controls, that protect the amenity
and character of the existing community.
•
Coordinated infrastructure interface – Existing
transmission easements are integrated into
the land use pattern, informing layout, access
and development footprints that align with
infrastructure outcomes and unlock practical
development areas.

4  Structure plan and sub-precinct framework

--- MP Page 24 ---
Teralba
Characteristics
The Teralba sub-precinct is located approximately 
two kilometres south-east of the main Precinct, 
adjoining the established Teralba local centre. The 
sub-precinct is defined by its direct proximity to 
two rail stations, its interface with the heritage-
listed Teralba Conservation Area, and its integration 
with the established residential and commercial 
fabric of the Teralba village.
Together, these attributes position Teralba as the 
Precinct’s mixed use sub-precinct, a compact, 
well-serviced setting where new housing and 
complementary uses can support the ongoing 
vitality of the local centre and contribute to the 
broader regional transformation envisaged by the 
Master Plan.
Key opportunities
The following attributes shape the sub-precinct’s 
development context and inform an opportunity-led 
planning response:
•
Conveniently connected and serviced –
Positioned approximately 300 metres from
Booragul Station and 400 metres from Teralba
Station, the sub-precinct enables direct access
to the regional passenger rail network and
supports a walkable, low-car neighbourhood
model.
•
Reinforcement of the Teralba local centre –
Proximity to established retail, community and
commercial services provides the foundation
for residential and complementary uses that
strengthen the centre’s economic base, activate
the public realm and support day-to-day
amenity for residents and workers.
•
Heritage-informed place-making – The setting
of the Teralba Conservation Area and local
heritage items, including the Miner’s Cottages
and Teralba Public School, informs a considered
design response that respects established
character, scale and views, and integrates
heritage interpretation as a defining element of
local identity.
•
Landscape-led response to Cockle Creek – The
Cockle Creek corridor informs a considered
land use pattern that balances development
opportunity with waterway health, riparian
amenity and flood conveyance, delivering
a high-quality blue-green edge to the sub-
precinct.
•
Enhanced pedestrian and cycling connectivity
– New and upgraded active transport links
to Teralba Station and across the railway
strengthen the sub-precinct’s transit-oriented
potential and improve everyday connections
between the neighbourhood, the local centre
and surrounding communities.
•
Early activation potential – Progress in mine
closure and rehabilitation, together with
established servicing connections, proximity to
existing urban areas and direct public transport
access, positions the sub-precinct as a strong
candidate for early activation and near-term
delivery.

Environmentally constrained areas
Characteristics
Environmentally constrained areas form an integral 
and defining element of the Precinct’s structure, 
comprising tracts of remnant native vegetation, 
rehabilitation areas, riparian corridors, waterways 
and ecological networks distributed across 
the Precinct. Together, these areas establish a 
connected environmental framework that supports 
biodiversity, water cycle management, landscape 
identity and Connecting with Country outcomes.
Environmentally constrained areas anchor the 
structure plan in a high-quality landscape setting 
and reinforce ecological connectivity across the 
region. The intent of these lands is to protect and 
enhance environmental, hydrological, cultural and 
landscape values over the long-term, while 
enabling sensitive land use where suitable.
Key opportunities
The following attributes shape the sub-precinct’s 
development context and inform an opportunity-
led, planning response:
•
Anchoring the Precinct’s ecological framework
– High biodiversity areas, key fish habitat
and terrestrial corridors provide north–south and 
east–west ecological connectivity across the 
Precinct. Biodiversity corridors, coastal 
wetlands, mapped waterways and areas subject 
to Voluntary Conservation Agreements 
informing a clear protection framework aligned 
with statutory requirements.
•
Considered, evidence-based approach to 
compatible use – Where supported by detailed 
biodiversity assessment, low-impact, compatible 
uses may be accommodated within these lands, 
guided by the recognised hierarchy of avoid first, 
minimise where avoidance is not practicable, and 
offset residual impacts. This approach makes 
sure that future use is sensitively located, 
limited in scale, and consistent with the 
retention and enhancement of biodiversity, 
hydrological and landscape values.
•
Water cycle and landscape performance –
Riparian corridors along mapped waterways
provide for flood conveyance, stormwater 
treatment and waterway health, contributing to 
a resilient water cycle framework that supports 
development outcomes elsewhere in the 
Precinct.
•
Compatible low-impact recreation and visitor
experience – Walking trails, lookouts, nature-
based education and interpretation position the
environmentally constrained areas as part of a
layered land use framework that complements
community benefit and economic diversification
across the Precinct.

Implementation and sequencing
Implementation
The implementation and delivery of the entire 
Precinct vision is intended to be sequenced over 
several decades, reflecting the need to manage 
mine closure and rehabilitation responsibilities and 
to allow the future land uses to evolve in alignment 
with development uptake. Delivery of supporting 
infrastructure is intended to be staged to correlate 
with the development as it is implemented over 
time.
Development sequencing provides for 
infrastructure delivery that is proactive but demand 
led and enables early activation while supporting 
long-term, efficient and resilient precinct 
development. Infrastructure delivery is to be 
adaptive, demand driven and coordinated, ensuring 
that development does not outpace enabling 
infrastructure while maintaining flexibility for 
market led uptake. Development is to be staged in 
accordance with available infrastructure capacity, 
with priority given to feasibility of connecting 
with existing utilities and transport networks. 
Infrastructure delivery should adopt an integrated 
and coordinated approach across utilities and 
transport to minimise disruption and duplication.

4  Structure plan and sub-precinct framework

Short-term activation
Areas identified as being capable of early release 
for post mining land use development share 
common characteristics, including land where 
rehabilitation is at or near completion, existing 
road access is available, servicing connections are 
feasible and the risk profile is manageable without 
requiring major investigations or infrastructure 
upgrades.
Early phases are expected to leverage available 
capacity within the Argenton Substation, existing 
potable water connections and established regional 
freight corridors, minimising the need for major 
upfront augmentation. These areas also align with 
transport accessibility and heavy vehicle routing 
capability, supporting early industrial and logistics 
uses.
These short-term activation areas provide the 
opportunity to demonstrate viability of post mining 
land use shift, generate investment confidence and 
deliver tangible employment and community 
outcomes.
Cockle Creek
Previously disturbed areas outside the TSF and 
dam break inundation zone with existing access to 
the regional road network. Early activation within 
this sub-precinct could leverage the existing rail 
loop with opportunities for related manufacturing 
facilities.
This sub-precinct benefits from the strategic role 
of freight and logistics in this area, leveraging 
proximity to supporting flexible, freight-adjacent 
land uses as infrastructure staging evolves.
Development in this sub-precinct is staged to align 
with infrastructure delivery. A graduated approach 
to the staging model is proposed, transitioning 
from lighter industry near Cockle Creek to heavier 
industrial and warehousing uses further within the 
sub-precinct. 
Early activation 
is subject to geotechnical investigation and 
confirmation that development will not 
compromise TSF rehabilitation or increase societal 
risk within the dam break inundation zone.
Killingworth
The northwest area near Killingworth presents 
a strategic opportunity for land uses such as 
advanced manufacturing, data-driven uses and 
business parks, which take advantage of the 
Transgrid substation and existing electricity 
capacity. The area offers opportunity for local 
uplift and diversification through enabling light 
infrastructure, business parks, technology and 
data-driven employment to support local jobs and 
complement existing residential areas.
The sub-precinct is well-suited for activation given 
its previously disturbed land provides a strong 
foundation for redevelopment, complemented by 
its proximity to existing high-voltage transmission 
infrastructure and the Transgrid substation. 
Additionally, road access is available via the 
existing local road network, with potential for 
future upgrades to support new land uses.
Water and wastewater servicing requires further 
investigation. Bush fire and biodiversity interface 
management will be required along the western 
edge.
Barnsley West 
Development of previously undisturbed areas 
adjacent to existing residential in Barnsley is 
contingent upon assessment of transmission 
easements, servicing viability and biodiversity 
values.
West Lake
The West Lake area offers excellent water quality 
suitable for recreational use (subject to ongoing 
monitoring). Rehabilitation around the lake has 
been progressively signed off, with approximately 
one-third approved and the balance targeted 
for completion in 2026, indicating suitability for 
recreational contact. 
Existing walking tracks and connection 
opportunities to Sugarloaf State Conservation 
Area further enhance the Precinct’s potential for 
tourism and recreation uses that are compatible 
with the ecological and landscape values of the 
area. Basic servicing for visitor amenities would be 
required, while the western edge of the lake area 
presents ecological constraints including 
biodiversity corridors and remnant vegetation that 
define the extent of any development boundaries. 
Future development around the lake must 
maintain water quality through appropriate 
catchment management measures.
29
4  Structure plan and sub-precinct framework

--- MP Page 30 ---
Teralba
Teralba sub-precinct is strategically located 
between the Teralba and Booragul train stations. 
Proximity to existing utility networks reduces 
servicing lead times and upfront infrastructure 
costs. Established road access and adjacency 
to nearby rail stations, residential communities 
and employment areas provide a ready platform 
for early development. Together, these attributes 
present a compelling opportunity to deliver 
residential outcomes that complement the 
surrounding context and contribute to the 
Precinct’s early activation and investment 
momentum.
Medium-term activation
Medium-term activation areas require the delivery 
of enabling infrastructure, resolution of key 
transport and access constraints and progressive 
risk reduction through ongoing rehabilitation and 
technical investigations. These areas represent the 
core employment-generating lands of the Precinct 
and will require coordinated investment in roads, 
utilities and potentially rail infrastructure.
Progressive development toward the southern and 
more constrained areas will require coordinated 
upgrades to transport, utilities and Precinct scale 
water cycle management. This includes delivery of 
wastewater infrastructure (currently absent across 
much of the Precinct), expansion of water networks 
and potential major electricity augmentation or 
new substations where demand thresholds are 
exceeded. Concurrently, transport upgrades, 
including intersection capacity improvements, 
new internal road links and potential additional 
crossings of Cockle Creek, must be staged 
alongside development to maintain network 
performance and resilience.
Cockle Creek and Killingworth 
residual land
Previously undisturbed areas outside the TSF and 
dam break inundation zone with existing access to 
the regional road network. Medium term activation 
is subject to biodiversity investigations, geotechnical 
investigation and flood risk assessment. 
Medium term activation in Cockle Creek sub-
precinct requires confirmation that development 
will not compromise TSF rehabilitation or increase 
risk within the dam break inundation zone. 
Long-term activation
Release of areas identified for long-term 
development potential for productive use is 
contingent upon the completion of critical 
investigations, successful risk reduction through 
ongoing rehabilitation and potentially major 
infrastructure interventions. 
Cockle Creek (TSF and dam break 
inundation zone)
Development of the TSF area is contingent upon 
several key prerequisites, including the completion 
and regulatory acceptance of long-term dewatering 
and stabilisation, together with an updated dam 
break failure impact assessment reflecting current 
capped conditions. 
As a declared dam, development in both the TSF 
and dam break inundation zone remain limited to 
land uses that do not increase the risk to life or 
undermine the structural stability of the TSF and 
associated structures. The downstream dam break 
inundation zone may be reduced in size over time 
as rehabilitation progresses, potentially to the 
point of revoking its declaration as a dam. Once 
the TSF dam declaration is revoked, development 
downstream of the dam can be achieved, subject to 
other constraints. 
Re-purposing and use of the TSF and associated 
structures can occur provided detailed structural, 
geotechnical and hydrological investigations occur 
in parallel to each development application.
Until these prerequisites are met, the TSF and its 
associated inundation zone may support interim 
or ‘meanwhile’ uses that maintain a low population 
level. Such interim uses could include solar energy 
installations, for which international precedents on 
tailings dams exist, as well as biodiversity corridor 
functions, landscape rehabilitation and other low 
occupancy uses.
Development within the further investigation areas 
associated with the TSF and dam break inundation 
areas may be brought forward to medium 
horizon, either as a whole or in part, depending on 
rehabilitation and ongoing monitoring.

4  Structure plan and sub-precinct framework

Staging triggers
The progressive release of developable land across 
the Precinct is linked to the completion of key 
technical investigations and the achievement of 
rehabilitation milestones. The following staging 
triggers apply as relevant across the Precinct:
•
Dam safety and Geotech – Geotechnical
monitoring and assessment of TSF, with the view
to de-declaring the dam. Updated dam break
and consequence assessments demonstrating
a reduction in the dam break inundation zone.
Refer to Section 9 Sustainability and resilience
on page 51 for detailed dam safety aims and
performance criteria.
•
Contamination – Completion of staged
contamination investigations and, where
required, remediation or management
measures appropriate to the proposed land
use, in accordance with the Contaminated Land
Management Act 1997 and State Environmental
Planning Policy (Resilience and Hazards) 2021.
•
Geotechnical stability – Geotechnical
assessments confirming the suitability of land
for the proposed development type, particularly
rehabilitated landforms.
•
Flooding – Detailed flood modelling confirming
flood planning levels, developable areas
and appropriate mitigation measures for
development within or adjacent to flood-
affected land, including climate change and
dam break interaction scenarios.
•
Infrastructure and servicing – Confirmation of
utility servicing capacity (water, wastewater,
electricity, telecommunications) and delivery
of enabling infrastructure to support
staged development. Refer to Section 10
Infrastructure, utilities and servicing on page
58 for detailed infrastructure and servicing
aims and performance criteria.
•
Biodiversity – Completion of detailed
environmental surveys to verify biodiversity
values and confirm environmentally constrained
area boundaries.
•
Take-up and market demand – Progressive
development is informed by demonstrated
market take-up across the Precinct.
The sequencing of development is to be 
coordinated with the delivery of supporting 
infrastructure to make sure that the transport 
network, utilities and community facilities can 
accommodate incremental growth. Development 
staging should also be coordinated with mine 
closure and rehabilitation activities so that land 
use transformation proceeds in an orderly manner. 
An indicative description of the staging triggers 
according to sub-precincts is provided in Table 2.

4  Structure plan and sub-precinct framework

--- MP Page 34 ---
 The following character principles guide Precinct development.
Built form
The Precinct supports employment generating development responsive to its 
landscape context setting. Building orientation, scale and siting is carefully 
considered to integrate with the site’s natural features. 
Landscape
Building on existing high environmental value, the Precinct protects and 
enhances its natural landscape, with remnant vegetation and waterways 
treated as defining landscape elements that shape the Precinct’s character. 
Biodiversity can be protected near development areas through the 
establishment of green corridors, landscape buffers and setbacks that 
respond to topography and ecological systems. 
Place and identity
The Precinct offers the opportunity to create a distinctive identity that 
reflects its natural qualities, cultural values and industrial history. 
Public realm and mobility
Well-connected to surrounding networks, the site supports safe, clear 
and legible movement systems that connect sub-precincts, support active 
transport and prioritise pedestrian amenity and landscape integration at key 
interfaces. Access and circulation are designed to respond to the scale of 
employment uses.
Sustainability and resilience
Built form and landscape design embed water sensitive urban design 
(WSUD), ecological restoration, efficient resource use and climate resilience, 
delivering a precinct that performs as a productive landscape.
Interface and transition
Development at precinct edges manages the transition to environmentally 
constrained areas and surrounding communities through graduated built 
form, generous setbacks and landscape buffers that protect amenity and 
maintain natural character.
Flexibility and staged activation
Built form and subdivision patterns accommodate staged delivery and 
evolving uses over time, ensuring that interim conditions and early activation 
areas contribute positively to precinct character without compromising long-
term outcomes.
34
5  Built form and landscape

--- MP Page 36 ---
Sub-precinct interface consideration
The Precinct incorporates a range of contextual 
interfaces, including environmentally constrained 
areas, open space and recreation areas, and 
external sensitive receivers such as established 
residential communities. Three interface typologies 
guide the design of the Precinct’s edges, each 
shaped by the values of the adjoining land and 
the role of the interface in protecting amenity, 
biodiversity and bushfire safety outcomes:
•
Typology 1 – Development adjoining
environmentally constrained areas (including
heavily vegetated and bushfire-prone areas)
•
Typology 2 – Developable area to open space
and recreation areas
•
Typology 3 – Precinct boundary to external
context (including adjoining residential and
other sensitive receivers).
Each typology is illustrated separately in Figure 25 
to Figure 27. Together, these treatments establish 
high-quality, well-managed edges that retain 
the values of adjoining land while supporting the 
Precinct’s long-term productive use.
Aims
•
Establish clear, durable transitions between 
developable areas, environmentally constrained 
areas, open space and surrounding 
communities.
•
Protect biodiversity values, ecological corridors, 
waterways and cultural heritage from the 
indirect effects of adjacent development, 
including noise, light, dust, stormwater runoff, 
weed invasion and uncontrolled access.
•
Provide that interface built form responds to the 
scale, character and amenity of adjoining land.
•
Maintain permeability and connectivity
for people while managing access to 
environmentally constrained areas.
Performance criteria
Typology 1 - Development adjoining 
environmentally constrained areas
A. Development adjoining environmentally
constrained areas protects ecological values,
manages edge effects, accommodates bushfire
asset protection requirements and supports a
clear, maintainable boundary between urban and 
conservation land.
B. A vegetated buffer planted with locally endemic
species must be provided to the environmentally
constrained areas, with a baseline width of 30
metres. This width may be reduced where a site-
specific ecological assessment demonstrates
that a narrower buffer will achieve equivalent or
improved ecological outcomes, having regard to
the sensitivity of the adjoining environmentally
constrained area.
C. Where a perimeter road provides the interface
between developable land and environmentally
constrained area, the road reserve may form part
of the buffer function.
D. The bushland side of any perimeter road must
be managed through bush regeneration to retain
endemic vegetation and ecological values. The
development side of the road must incorporate
low-maintenance bushfire asset protection
zones (e.g. wide road verges, managed grassed
verges) that integrate with the urban edge.
E. Buildings, hardstand, storage and operational
activities must not be located within the
ecological buffer or asset protection zone.
F.	 Development intensity at sensitive environmentally
constrained area interfaces is to be reduced
through setbacks, lower built form scale where
appropriate, and landscape screening to minimise
visual and ecological edge effects.
G. Lighting adjacent to environmentally constrained
areas is to be designed to minimise light spill,
glare and ecological disturbance to habitat areas.
H. Fencing at environmentally constrained
area interfaces must be in the form of a
maintainable barrier that controls access to the
environmentally constrained area while retaining
visual permeability where appropriate.
I.
Stormwater treatment measures must be located
within the developable area and outside riparian
buffers and environmentally constrained areas.
J.
Edge treatments must be designed to prevent
ongoing weed invasion into adjacent native
vegetation, including through selection of
non-invasive landscape species, ongoing
36
5  Built form and landscape

--- MP Page 37 ---
maintenance arrangements and clear physical 
demarcation.
Typology 2 – Developable area to open space and 
recreation areas
A.	 Development adjoining open space or recreation 
areas must provide a positive, legible and active 
interface to the public realm.
B.	 Pedestrian access points and landscape 
treatments are to integrate seamlessly with 
adjoining open space.
C.	 Buildings must be oriented to support Crime 
Prevention Through Environmental Design 
(CPTED) principles and provide passive 
surveillance of public open space, where 
appropriate to the proposed use.
D.	 Open space at sub-precinct interfaces are 
to function as a connected system that links 
environmentally constrained areas, walking and 
cycling routes, significant vegetation and natural 
landforms.
E.	 Lighting at open space interfaces must support 
safe pedestrian movement while applying 
CPTED and wildlife-friendly lighting principles 
where the open space adjoins or connects to 
environmentally constrained areas.
Typology 3 – Precinct boundary to external context
A.	 Development adjoining residential areas or other 
sensitive receivers must provide setbacks and 
landscape buffers informed by detailed land use 
compatibility and acoustic assessment.
B.	 Buildings at sensitive interfaces must be 
sited and designed to minimise overlooking, 
overshadowing and visual dominance.
C.	 Acoustic, air quality and operational mitigation 
measures must be incorporated where required 
to manage amenity impacts.
D.	 Heavy vehicle access, loading and servicing 
areas are not to be located at residential 
interfaces unless no feasible alternative 
is available and mitigation measures are 
implemented to minimise noise, air quality and 
amenity impacts.
E.	 Landscape screening must use locally 
endemic species and contribute to amenity and 
biodiversity outcomes.
F.	 Boundary interface treatments must respond 
to the characteristics of the adjoining land, 
including bushfire, ecological, riparian and 
residential contexts.

Road network, freight and access
Road network and access is influenced by 
the Precinct’s legacy as former coal mine 
operations. Historic mining operations have shaped 
both the physical terrain and created a framework 
that continues to inform movement and access in 
the post mining context. Former haul routes and 
access tracks, originally designed to support 
extraction, processing and transport activities, 
establish a foundational spatial logic for the post 
mining land use movement network. 
The approach to managing transport and mobility is 
multi-layered, combining infrastructure planning 
and staging through demand management and 
integration with land use outcomes. To facilitate 
efficient movement within and around the Precinct, 
the road network of sub-arterial, collector and local 
roads is structured as a clear hierarchy, linking 
developable land to the broader regional network 
to minimise reliance on the external local network. 
Subject to further investigation, a potential new 
east–west crossing of Cockle Creek is identified as 
an opportunity to strengthen network resilience, 
unlock alternative freight access that bypasses 
constrained local roads (Racecourse Road, Railway 
Street and Rhondda Road) and improve 
connectivity to Cockle Creek Station.
Teralba is directly serviced by Teralba and 
Booragul Stations and forms a natural anchor for 
enhanced pedestrian and cycling connectivity to 
the wider Precinct via the Main Northern railway 
corridor and the future active transport network.
Aims
•
Provide an efficient, legible and resilient road
network that supports sequenced Precinct
development.
•
Support safe and efficient freight, workforce
and visitor access to and within the Precinct.
•
Align freight and access planning with the
regional road and freight network, including
future strategic corridors.
•
Improve access across existing infrastructure
barriers, including the Main Northern Railway.
•
Integrate flood and bush fire resilience,
emergency access and network safety into road
planning.
•
Deliver complete streets that support walking,
cycling, buses and future transport upgrades.
Performance criteria
A. The Precinct road network must connect
to the regional road network and provide a
legible hierarchy of sub-arterial, collector and
local roads consistent with applicable design
standards.
B. Road network and intersection upgrades must
be delivered ahead of, or concurrently with, the
development stages they are intended to serve.
C. Internal road networks must be delivered
progressively to support sequenced
development and reduce reliance on external
local roads.
D. Development applications must demonstrate,
through detailed traffic assessment, that the
surrounding network and relevant intersections
can operate at an acceptable level of service for
the proposed stage of development.
E. Freight access routes and approved restricted
access vehicle (RAV) connections must be
established before freight-generating land uses
commence.
F.	 Heavy vehicle and freight movements must
avoid residential streets unless no feasible
alternative exists and acceptable mitigation is
demonstrated.
G. Former haul routes and access tracks should
be prioritised for long-term heavy vehicle
movements within and through the Precinct.
H. A freight management plan must be prepared
for freight-generating development and must
address internal freight circulation, last-mile
movements and community impact mitigation.
I.
Roads, intersections and bus facilities must be
designed to provide safe pedestrian access and
support public transport integration.
J.
Internal roads are to be located on developable
land and, where practical, within existing

connectivity

Active transport and connectivity
The Precinct provides a rare opportunity to 
plan a connected, safe and direct walking and 
cycling network, with preferred active transport 
alignments established with vehicle routes for 
optimal directness, legibility and separation from 
traffic. The active transport network will connect 
employment sub-precincts to Cockle Creek, Teralba 
and Booragul stations, surrounding residential 
communities, existing residential areas and the 
broader regional shared-path network. 
Aims
	•
Establish a connected and practical active 
transport network linking the Precinct to 
surrounding communities, centres and stations.
	•
Improve active transport access across key 
barriers including Five Islands Road and the 
Main Northern Railway.
	•
Integrate active transport with heritage, 
topographic and environmental constraints.
	•
Provide end-of-trip facilities and safe walking 
and cycling infrastructure as part of staged 
precinct delivery.
Performance criteria
A.	 Pedestrian and cycling infrastructure must 
be delivered early to support activation and 
establish sustainable travel behaviour.
B.	 Pedestrian and cycle connections must align 
with the indicative active transport network and 
connect sub-precincts, public transport nodes 
and open space.
C.	 Active transport infrastructure must be designed 
in accordance with CPTED principles, universal 
access requirements and passive surveillance 
principles.
D.	 Pedestrian and cycle links must be coordinated 
with road infrastructure delivery and 
incorporated into road reserves where practical.
E.	 Active transport routes must connect to 
the wider regional shared path network at 
appropriate locations.
F.	 Active transport infrastructure must respond 
sensitively to heritage streetscapes, steep 
terrain and environmental constraints.
G.	 Development must provide end-of-trip facilities 
at a scale appropriate to the proposed use and 
intensity of development.

The Precinct is primarily employment-led and 
will not generate a significant residential 
population. Social infrastructure planning 
therefore focuses on supporting the daily needs 
of the Precinct’s workforce and visitors, 
delivering community benefit to surrounding 
communities and ensuring that facilities are 
staged in alignment with development.
Community facilities
Aims
•
Provide community facilities that support 
workers, visitors and surrounding communities.
•
Locate community facilities and worker amenity 
hubs to activate key nodes and open space.
•
Encourage adaptive reuse of suitable existing 
structures for community, cultural or training 
purposes.
•
Make sure community facilities are accessible, 
appropriately sited and responsive to amenity 
and landscape context.
•
Support opportunities for cultural and
creative industries, including mining heritage 
interpretation and Aboriginal cultural 
enterprise.
Performance criteria
A. Community facilities must provide flexible,
publicly accessible multi-purpose space and
must be co-located with employment areas or
open space where feasible.
B. Community facilities must be sited and designed
to maintain solar access to adjoining public
spaces, retain significant vegetation where
feasible and provide safe, legible pedestrian
access.
C. Development that exceeds a workforce
threshold identified through the social

amenity hub incorporating food and beverage,
convenience services and end-of-trip facilities.
D. Community facilities must provide affordable
or low-cost access options for community use,
including not-for-profit and local organisations.

Bush fire resilience
Bush fire resilience is a key design parameter 
shaping the structure and long-term function of the 
precinct. The draft Master Plan adopts a precinct 
approach to bush fire planning, responding to 
the site’s classification as bush fire prone land 
and the complex interaction between vegetation, 
topography and development. The draft Master 
Plan prioritises consolidated development 
footprints, clearly defined edges and integrated 
interface treatments that support both bush fire 
resilience and biodiversity outcomes.
Aims
•
Protect life and property from bush fire risk
while responding to development potential,
constraints, operational requirements,
rehabilitation outcomes and the protection of
biodiversity and habitat corridors.
•
Enable ongoing land management practices
that concurrently support bush fire resilience,
protection of high value biodiversity, and the
long-term health and diversity of rehabilitated
and retained landscapes.
•
Integrate road hierarchy, access, egress and
emergency response to support operations,
firefighting and evacuation.
•
Enable suppression, staged responses and
long-term resilient precinct activation through
strategic separation, managed land and
services, including compliant water supply.
Performance criteria
A. Development must be located only where an
integrated and appropriate level of bush fire
protection can be achieved having regard to
high value biodiversity, vegetation, topography,
fire run potential, rehabilitation outcomes and
access.
B. Higher-vulnerability and higher-consequence
land uses must be located in areas of
comparatively lower bush fire exposure,
with increased separation from unmanaged
vegetation and hazard areas.
C. Development must not create isolated pockets
of development, rely on a single access route, or
result in layouts that increase bushland–urban
interface exposure or limit emergency response
capability.
D. Development interfaces exposed to unmanaged 
bush fire hazard must be minimised in both 
length and complexity, with preference given to 
consolidated development footprints and 
regular, defensible edges.
E. Vegetation corridors that may facilitate bush 
fire spread towards development areas must be 
appropriately configured and managed.
F. Rehabilitation and vegetation management 
outcomes must be integrated into long-term 
bush fire management arrangements, making 
sure that future vegetation growth does not 
compromise asset protection zones or interface 
performance over time.
G. Development must be designed to minimise the 
total extent of bushland–urban interface and 
avoid fragmented or elongated hazard edges.
H. All interfaces must incorporate clearly defined 
and continuous edge treatments that support 
both bushfire protection and biodiversity 
outcomes.
Geotechnical
The Precinct is characterised by a highly variable 
post mining landscape, where geological 
conditions, legacy mining impacts and 
anthropogenic landforms generate a range of 
geotechnical constraints influencing development 
feasibility. Development will require a risk-based 
and sequenced approach with consideration of 
landform suitability and engineered earthworks 
solutions, including cut and fill, batter stabilisation 
and retaining structures. Site-specific geotechnical 
investigation would be required to confirm 
conditions and inform design.
Key geotechnical considerations include:
•
Possible subsidence from former mining 
operations
•
Presence of soft and potentially saturated 
alluvial sediments around waterways
•
Steep topography
•
Underlying coal seams
•
Potential tuffaceous materials

.

at

-coal -complex .

, please follow the steps below:
 
1) Read our Privacy Statement and decide whether to include your personal information in your 
submission. 
2) Fill in the online submission form. Your submission can either be typed or uploaded as a PDF 
and should include:
 
a) the name of the proposal 
Post Mining Land Use Pilot Project 
– Macquarie Coal 
Complex 
b) a brief statement on whether you support or object to the proposal
 
c) the reasons why you support or object to the proposal.
 
3) You must disclose reportable political donations and gifts. Anyone lodging submissions must 
declare reportable political donations and gifts (including donations of $1,000 or more) made 
in the previous 2 years.
 
4) Agree to our online statement and lodge your submission.
 
 
You may also lodge your submission via post by sending it to:
 
 
Executive Director, State Rezoning
 
Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure
 
Locked Bag 5022
 
Parramatta NSW 2124
 
All submissions will be made public in line with our objective to promote an open and transparent 
planning system. If you do not want your name or other personal identifying details published, 
please state this clearly at the top of your submission.

1 
Introduction 
1.1 
Purpose 
This Explanation of Intended Effect (EIE) sets out proposed amendments to the 
Lake Macquarie 
Local Environmental Plan 2014, State Environmental Planning Policy (Precincts
-Regional) 2021 and 
State Environmental Planning Policy (Planning Systems) 2021
 to rezone land in Post Mining Land Use 
Pilot Project – Macquarie Coal Complex
 for employment generating land uses
. 
The Rezoning Proposal will facilitate the delivery of:
 
• 
At least 500 hectares of 
developable land 
• 
up to 1,130 new jobs 
• 
around 36 hectares of new open space
 
The Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (the Department) has prepared this EIE to 
outline the proposed planning control changes, considerations and intent of the draft Rezoning 
Proposal. 
The changes to planning controls 
proposed under this Rezoning Proposal will be 
implemented 
through amendments to 
State Environmental Planning Policy (Precincts
-Regional) 2021 (Precincts 
Regional SEPP) made under Section 3.29(1) of the 
Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979
 
(EP&A Act). 
The public is invited to comment on all the matters in this EIE and supporting document which can 
be viewed online on the 
NSW Planning Portal
. 
1.2 
Intent of rezoning Macquarie Coal Complex
 
This Explanation of Intended Effects (EIE) sets out the proposed planning framework , including a 
draft Master Plan for future development within the Macquarie Coal Complex (the Precinct ). A 
stage d approach is proposed , with final zoning and permissibility for the Precinct to be informed by 
submissions and ongoing investigations. 
The proposed draft Master Plan and rezoning is in response to the NSW Parliamentary Inquiry into 
Beneficial and productive post mining land use. The proposed rezoning of Macquarie Coal Complex 
has been prepared in collaboration with Glencore, Lake Macquarie City Council (Council) , 
Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, and Australian Government through 
Net Zero Economy Authority (NZEA) as a whole of government approach to beneficial post mining 
land use.   
This EIE seeks to propose amendments to facilitate productive land uses at the Macquarie Coal 
Complex. The rezoning proposal is an ongoing and iterative process to support 
transformation from 
mining to productive, employment generating land uses. Investigations will continue to 
make sure 
the full extent of redevelopment of the site can be realised.
  
This EIE is publicly exhibited and invites feedback from key stakeholders
 and the community on the 
proposed rezoning. Submissions
 received during public exhibition on the rezoning proposal will be 
considered ahead of finalisation of the rezoning proposal and may be amended prior to finalisation.

1.3 
Rezoning pathway 
The Department’s State Significant Rezoning Policy includes a State Led Rezoning (SLR) pathway 
which seeks to identify and delivery strategically important rezonings that can contribute to the 
housing and employment needs of NSW’s growing population, where
 sites meet certain criteria. 
 
The Rezoning Proposal h
as been identified as a project to proceed 
as a State -led rezoning under the 
State Significant Rezoning Policy
. 
In accordance with the 
State Significant Rezoning Policy
 the Rezoning Proposal was considered to 
meet the eligibility criteria as it will:
 
• 
create up to 1,130 direct jobs  
• 
deliver beneficial uses for post mining land 
 
• 
benefit from a State rezoning pathway due to the complexity of the post mining nature of the 
site, and coordination with key agency stakeholders. 
 
1.4 
Site location and description  
The Rezoning Proposal applies to 
1,160 hectares o f land and includes land
 at Macquarie Coal 
Complex and Teralba Southgate 
(the Precinct) across the following areas:
 
• 
West Wallsend (ceased mining in 2016)
 
• 
Westside (ceased mining in 2012)
 
• 
Macquarie Coal Preparation Plant (ceased production in 2016)
 
• 
Teralba Southgate (ceased mining in 2001)
 
This area will be referred to in this document as 
the Precinct and is shown in the
 Macquarie Coal 
Complex location plan in Figure 1.  
The Precinct is on the land of the Awabakal people
 and is ( approximately 28 allotments
) currently 
owned by Macquarie Coal Joint Venture
. Mining operations on the site
 has ceased, with the site
 
advancing through rehabilitation works
 in accordance with the 
Macquarie Coal Rehabilitation 
management Plan ( 2022). The Precinct is well located in 
the Lake Macquarie Local Government 
Area (LGA), approximately 20 kilometres south
-west of Newcastle and approximately 110 kilometres 
north of the Sydney CBD.
 
1.4.1 
Macquarie Coal Complex 
(the Precinct)
 
The Precinct is currently zoned SP1 Special Activities (Mining), C2 Environmental Conservation, C3
 
Environmental Management, and RU2 Rural Landscape. 
The Precinct includes a
 number of existing 
roads, both public and private as well as utility easements bisect the site
. It is characterised by 
significant portions of remnant native vegetation as well as areas subject to rehabilitation 
obligations and cleared land associated historical mine uses.
 
The Precinct sits adjacent to the Lake Macquarie North West Catalyst Area and is bounded by the 
suburb of Barnsley to the north, Cockle Creek and the Central
-Coast Newcastle main passenger and 
freight train line to the east, Teralba and Wakefield to the south and Kill
ingworth to the west. The M1 
Pacific Motorway and Sugarloaf State Conservation Area are also located within in close proximity.

1.5 
Strategic context
 
In 2024, the NSW Government launched an inquiry to investigate new and innovative approaches to 
post mining land use to 
make sure  mining sites continue to bring economic investment to regional 
communities after mines close.
 The findings of the
 inquiry  ‘Report No. 53 Beneficial and productive 
post mining land use’
 were published including the NSW’s response to the inquiry. The NSW 
Government  supported  all of  the recommendations in the inquiry.
  
Specifically, the following recommendations
 are relevant to this project:
   
• 
Recommendation 1
 – Review of existing
 legislation relating to post mining rehabilitation, 
mining  closure  and future land use, to
 facilitate  the transformation  of former mining sites.
   
• 
Recommendation 6
 – Focus  exploring immediate opportunities for two
 pilot projects (Mt 
Arthur  Mine and  Macquarie  Coal  Complex)  to identify  practical  impediments  and  necessary 
legislative and regulatory changes
 to enable land use change, and to
 establish  a State -wide 
model for post mining land use pathway.
   
The Rezoning Proposal was progressed by the Department in partnership with Australian 
Government through NZEA, Council, other NSW Government agencies and Glencore.
 
Following the exhibition of the rezoning proposal, a recommendations
 report will be prepared. The 
report will make recommendations
 on further amendments to the Environmental Planning and 
Assessment Act 1979 (EP&A Act) and the Mining Act 1992. The recommendations
 will be focussed on 
enabling the post mining land use at the Macquarie Coal Complex, and more broadly across the 
State as the energy transformation continues. The recommendations
 will inform regulatory reform 
to create a more streamlined planning pathway for redevelopment of post mining land. The refined 
regulatory framework may still require additional technical studies to satisfy suitability of the land, 
however, it is intended that there will be a clear pathway to undertake development consent on post 
mining land. 
The proposed amendments set out in this EIE can occur independently of the recommended 
amendments to the EP&A Act and Mining Act. 
1.5.1 
Hunter Regional Plan 2041
 
The Hunter Regional Plan 2041 establishes the strategic land use plan for the Hunter region. A key 
component of the plan is managing the Hunter’s shift from coal mining and other alternative 
industries by supporting local communities by planning for these 
mine closures early. 
See m ine and 
power stations located in the Hunter
 in Figure 2. 
The Rezoning Proposal will 
provide economic and employment opportunity and sustainability which 
is a priority in the Hunter Regional Plan 2041.  
 
1.5.2 
Lake Macquarie Local Strategic Planning Statement
 
The Lake Macquarie Local Strategic Planning Statement (LSPS) establishes a 20
-year vision for 
Local Government Area (LGA) and guides Council’s local decision making and future developments. 
The Lake Macquarie LSPS emphasises the importance of supporting a 
diverse local economy to 
increase job opportunities, facilitate economic growth and investment and encourage innovation and 
future emerging industries. The LSPS recognises the strategic value of reusing former mine 
industrial land in the LGA to be utilised
 for these emerging industries. 
Figure 3 shows the site’s 
location within the
 regionally significant growth area on the Lake Macquarie City Structure map.

long -term local jobs. 
 
1.5.3 
Lake Macquarie City Council 
Draft Employment Land Use Strategy 
 
The Lake Macquarie City Council 
draft Employment Land Use Strategy establishes a framework to 
support the shift from historically dominant uses such as mining and manufacturing to maintain an 
ongoing supply of employment land across the LGA. 
It provides sufficient, well
-located and serviced 
land is available to support local jobs, attract investment and foster a resilient economy while 
also 
balancing environmental stewardship
.  
The Rezoning Proposal aligns with the priorities of the strategy by facilitating 
the adaptive re -use of 
post -mining land for employment land
 that is accompanied by existing and planned infrastructure
 
(refer to Figure 3). The introduction of the 
Precincts Regional SEPP
 and precinct master plan will 
create a clear 
planning framework for employment land
 and balance the needs of local job creation 
with environmental protection.

2 Proposed planning control amendments
 
2.1 
Objectives and intended outcomes
 
This section sets out the proposed amendments to planning controls to realise the 
intent of the 
Rezoning Proposal
.  
The key objectives and intended outcomes
 of th e Rezoning Proposal are
 to: 
• 
deliver a diverse range of land uses that support regional economic diversification, attract 
investment and create local jobs
 
• 
facilitate the orderly 
transformation from mining to productive post
-mining uses through a 
coordinated, staged approach that aligns land use planning with mine closure, rehabilitation and 
infrastructure delivery. 
 
• 
establish a flexible and adaptive planning framework that responds to changing environmental, 
economic and market conditions over the long
-term delivery of the Precinct
 
• 
protect environmental values, including remnant native vegetation, threatened ecological 
communities, coastal wetlands, riparian corridors and habitat linkages
 
• 
leverage existing transport connections and infrastructure to establish an efficient, well
-
serviced Precinct
 
Any development application lodged within the Precinct before the commencement of the new 
Precincts -Regional SEPP chapter will be assessed under the existing LMLEP 2014 development 
controls. Any agreement, covenant, or other similar instrument that restric
ts the carrying out of that 
development on the land in which the Precinct is located will also be suspended.
 
The propose d amendments to the State Environmental Planning Policy (Precincts
— Regional) 2021 
(Precincts -Regional SEPP), 
Lake Macquarie Local Environmental Plan 2014 
(LMLEP 2014) and 
State 
Environmental Planning Policy (Planning Systems) 2021
 (Planning Systems SEPP) 
to facilitate the se 
outcomes are outlined below in Sections 2.2 and 2.3 . 
2.2 
Proposed changes to planning instruments
 
The proposed amendment seeks to remove the Precinct from the LMLEP 2014 and amend the 
Precincts -Regional SEPP to include a new chapter that will apply to land within the Precinct (
refer 
to Figure 4 Land application Map
). The new chapter will apply to the Precinct and will set out:
 
• 
aims 
• 
consent authority requirements for development
 
• 
relationship to other environmental planning instruments
 
• 
land use table and development permissibility 
 
• 
exempt and complying development
 
• 
role and requirements for Master plans
 
• 
general provisions
.

Land use zoning 
 
The Precinct is currently zoned 
SP1 – Special Activities (Mining), C2

C3 – Environmental Management, and RU2 
– Rural Landscape under the LMLEP 2014
 (see Figure 6 ). 
It is proposed to rezone the Precinct 
to a zone that will enable land uses to
 facilitate a wide range of
 
productive land uses.
  
Exhibition is primarily seeking feedback on 
the master plan framework and redevelopment
 approach 
with final zoning 
and permissibility to be informed by submissions and ongoing investigations.

2.2.1.1 
Consent authority
 
The Minister for Planning (or 
delegate) will be the consent authority for 
all development within the 
Precinct.  
2.2.1.2 
Exempt and complying development
 
Exempt and complying development is to be enabled in the 
Precinct via the State Environmental 
Planning Policy (Exempt and Complying Development Codes) 2008 
(Codes SEPP).  
 
A provision will be included within the Precincts
-Regional SEPP to identify
 the precinct as a 
prescribed zone. 
 
2.2.1.3 
Subdivision and demolition requirements
 
Subdivision and demolition within the 
Precinct are to be only carried out with development consent.
 
2.2.1.4 
Temporary land use
 
Land in the Precinct can be used for temporary development (for a 
maximum period of 182 days
) 
provided it does not prevent the su
bsequent carrying out of development 
in accordance with the 
objectives of the Precinct. 
 
2.2.1.5 
State significant development
 
The proposed amendment will insert in Schedule 2 of the Planning Systems SEPP the 
Precinct as an 
identified site for State significant development
. 
2.2.1.6 
Master Plan 
The Rezoning Proposal is supported by a draft Macquarie Coal Complex Master Plan (draft Master 
Plan) prepared by the Department and informed by technical and environmental analysis. 
The 
following technical reports were prepared to inform
 the draft Master Plan
: 
• 
Contamination and geotechnical reports
 
• 
Flood ing and water cycle management 
 
• 
Traffic and transport
 report 
• 
Dam report 
• 
Biodiversity and bushfire assessment reports
 
The draft Master Plan is a strategic planning tool designed to guide the long
-term transformation of 
the Precinct. It 
makes sure that development occurs in a coordinated and infrastructure
-ready 
manner, aligned with land use constraints and environmental protection that support the Precinct’s 
vision for a dynamic, employment
-led precinct which stimulates investment
 in the region .  
It is proposed to include a provision within the Precincts 
– Reginal SEPP that a Master Plan applies 
to the Precinct
 and contains the following information:
 
• 
the strategic vision and general objectives for the Precinct
 
• 
the objectives and performance criteria for development
 
• 
heritage items or places of heritage significance
 

--- EIE Page 17 ---
 
Explanation of Intended Effect 
- Post Mining Land Use Pilot Project 
– Macquarie Coal Complex 
| 13 
• 
limitations on development on certain land, including environmentally sensitive areas, land prone 
to flooding and cultural heritage areas
 
• 
and any further matters requested by the Minister.
 
Development consent 
within the Precinct 
must not be granted 
to development unless the consent 
authority has considered the Master Plan, with the Minister also having the power to amend or 
replace the Master Plan. 
 
All future development will be guided by the Master Plan, which will 
direct the long -term 
transformation of the Precinct
, ensuring that development is well
-coordinated, supported by 
necessary infrastructure, and aligned with land use constraints.
 
Following exhibition, the Department will finalise a Master Plan for the Precinct and provide 
additional design guidance for future development within the Precinct. The final Master Plan will be 
published on the planning portal website at finalisation.
 
A provision is proposed to be included in the Master Plan to require an addendum for 
development 
proposed on land mapped as environmentally constrained under the Structure Plan
. There may be 
one addendum that applies to the whole site, or several for different stages. 
 
2.2.2 
Miscellaneous provisions
  
The following additional controls 
will manage certain types of development 
and are compulsory 
under the Standard Instrument
— Principal Local Environmental Plan (2006 EPI 155a)
. 
2.2.2.1 
Flood planning and risk management 
 
To set out controls to 
make sure development considers flooding impacts and compatibility
 as well 
as provide development can provide for safe occupation and evacuation. 
 
2.2.2.2 
Controls relating to miscellaneous permissible uses
 
To set out controls to 
make sure development for the purpose of 
miscellaneous permissible uses
. 
2.2.2.3 
Conversion of fire alarms 
 
To regulate fire alarm systems compatible with Fire and Rescue NSW or private monitoring services.
 
2.2.2.4 
Bush fire hazard reduction 
 
To identify that authorised bushfire hazard reduction work may be carried out without development 
consent. 
2.2.2.5 
Infrastructure development and use of existing buildings of the Crown 
 
To identify that this chapter 
within the Precincts 
– Reginal SEPP 
does not restrict the carry
ing out of 
development on, or behalf of a public authority as outlined under
 the State Environmental Planning 
Policy (Transport and Infrastructure) 2021
.  
2.2.2.6 
Proximity to rail and gas infrastructure  
 
Development near rail corridors and gas pipelines must maintain appropriate setbacks and involve 
consultation with the relevant authorities.

2.3 
Other amendments 
2.3.1 
State Environmental Planning Policy (Planning Systems) 2021
 
The Planning Systems SEPP declares certain kinds of development as State Significant 
Development (SSD).  
 
It is proposed to amend Schedule 2 ‘State significant development
— identified sites’ of the Planning 
Systems SEPP to include the Precinct and identify the following types of development as SSD on 
land within the Precinct: 
 
• 
development that has an estimated development cost (EDC) of more than $
30 million on land 
identified as being within the Precinct. 
 
The proposed amendment will be reflected through the introduction of a map identifying the 
Precinct. The reasons for supporting this SSD pathway within the Precinct include:
 
• 
Regional significance
 – the proposal will deliver on State Government objectives in the Hunter 
Regional Plan 2041, and will increase local jobs and provide recreational opportunities
 
• 
Public Benefits
 – the rezoning proposal will deliver up to 1,130 ongoing jobs to assist in the 
region’s economic transformation
 
• 
Economic benefits – the proposal will deliver economic benefits to the Lake Macquarie region 
by creating a new precinct to support up to 1,130 ongoing jobs
 
• 
Complex and unique
 – there is a role for the State Government in the delivery of the Precinct. 
this will support the orderly and efficient development of the Precinct and benefit the 
community.

3 Considerations
 
In addition to proposed changes outlined in 
Section 2, the Department has also considered other 
specific matters that are relevant to this draft Rezoning Proposal.
 Other relevant State 
Environmental Planning Policies (SEPPs) will continue to apply to the precinct
. These considerations 
are explained below.
 
3.1 
State Environmental Planning Policy (Hazards and 
Resilience) 2021
 
State Environmental Planning Policy (Hazards and Resilience) 2021
 (Hazards and Resilience SEPP) sets 
out provisions for coastal management, hazardous and offensive development and remediation of 
land. The Rezoning Proposal is supported with a suite of technical studies which demonstrate 
compliance with Hazards and Resilience SEPP. A Biodiversity Assessment Report has been prepared 
by SLR to support the proposed rezoning and master plan. The draft struct
ure plan has been 
prepared with consideration to biodiv
ersity, including coastal wetlands mapped under the Hazards 
and Resilience SEPP. 
 
A Contamination Technical Assessment was prepared by Aurecon, providing a land use compatibility 
assessment
 to support the proposed rezoning. The assessment makes recommendations for the 
master plan and notes that all future development will be subject the requirements of the Hazards 
and Resilience SEPP. 
 
3.2 
State Environmental Planning Policy (Biodiversity and 
Conservation) 2021
 
State Environmental Planning Policy (Biodiversity and Conservation) 2021 
(Biodiversity and 
Conservation SEPP) sets out provisions for koala habitat protection. The Rezoning Proposal is 
supported with a suite of technical studies which demonstrate compliance with Biodiversity and 
Conservation SEPP, specifically Chapter 4 
- Koala Habitat Protection 2021
.  
It is noted that future development is required to be assessed
 under the Biodiversity and 
Conservation SEPP 
to assess potential impacts to koalas and koala habitat.
