1 
Executive summary 
This Geotechnical Engineering Report has been prepared to support the State-led rezoning of the Macquarie 
Coal Complex (MCC) (the Precinct), and Teralba Southgate for post-mining land use. The report provides a 
precinct-scale assessment of geotechnical conditions, constraints and risks, and establishes a risk-informed 
framework to guide land use planning, infrastructure provision, and staging. 
The Precinct and Teralba Southgate comprises a highly modified post-mining landscape characterised by 
variable topography, anthropogenic ground conditions, and legacy mining impacts, including mine 
subsidence risk, disturbed terrains, a Tailings Storage Facility (TSF) and areas of potentially deep alluvium. 
These conditions result in spatially variable development constraints across the Precinct and Teralba 
Southgate. 
A multi-criteria geotechnical assessment has been undertaken, considering slope, geology, regolith depth, 
soil landscapes, groundwater, salinity and acid sulfate soils. The assessment identifies a range of 
constraints, from low to high, across the Precinct and Teralba Southgate and confirms that development 
feasibility will depend on location, land use intensity and staging.  
1.1 
Key geotechnical constraints 
The principal geotechnical constraints affecting the Precinct and Teralba Southgate include: 
 Mine subsidence: all the sub-precincts are underlain by historic underground coal workings, resulting in 
potential subsidence risk that must be considered in land use planning and foundation design. Potential 
subsidence risks are not currently quantified as further studies are required. Development in these areas 
must include geotechnical assessments to characterise the risk and potentially solutions such as grouting 
of the former workings, if settlement has not already occurred. 
 Tailings Storage Facility: the TSF comprises hydraulically placed tailings and fill materials with high 
variability, uncertain composition, and long-term settlement potential. The area is currently undergoing 
rehabilitation and remains a declared dam. It represents a high-risk area for development, with settlement 
potentially occurring over decades. 
 Alluvial and low-lying areas: land adjacent to Cockle Creek and its tributaries is characterised by deep, 
compressible soils, shallow groundwater, flooding and acid sulfate soil risk, presenting significant 
constraints to structural development. 
 Disturbed and anthropogenic terrains: areas of fill and disturbed ground exhibit variable and uncertain 
geotechnical properties, reducing bearing capacity and increasing settlement risk. 
 Salinity and reactive soils: much of the Precinct and Taralba Southgate are affected by moderate to very 
high salinity hazard and reactive clay soils, with implications for durability of infrastructure and long-term 
maintenance. 
1.2 
Structure Plan sub-precincts and Teralba Southgate 
 Lower constraint areas (e.g. Killingworth, West Lake, Teralba Southgate, Barnsley West and more 
broadly the eastern portion of Cockle Creek) are suitable for early-stage development. 
 Moderate constraint areas (e.g. environmentally constrained areas) require targeted investigation and 
design responses prior to development, subject to subsidence risk investigation. 
 Higher constrained areas, including the TSF within the Cockle Creek sub-precinct and floodplain 
environments, are subject to long-term considerations for development potential. 
Given that all the sub-precincts are likely underlain by historic underground mine workings and the entirety of 
the Precinct and Terlaba Southgate is mapped as a declared Mine Subsidence District, all future 
development will require approval from Subsidence Advisory NSW (SA) and may entail further site specific 
mine subsidence investigations and assessments. 

--- Geo Page 8 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Geotechnical Engineering Report Rev B_Clean.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
3 
 
 
 
 
 
1.3 
Infrastructure and constructability 
The Report identifies several implications for infrastructure design: 
 Flood-prone areas require resilient design and scour protection 
 Ground improvement (e.g. preloading, wick drains) may be required in soft or compressible soils 
 Excavation in coal-bearing strata may require selective removal and treatment 
 Utilities may require specialised trenching, dewatering, and corrosion protection 
These factors will influence development cost, timing and feasibility across the Precinct and Teralba 
Southgate. 
1.4 
Data gaps and further investigations 
The assessment identifies data limitations, including: 
 Limited and dated geotechnical investigations 
 Incomplete understanding of TSF material properties and depth 
 Uncertainty in mine subsidence risks in details and condition of historic fill areas as well as groundwater 
behaviour. 
To address these uncertainties, following rezoning, further site-specific investigations are required to: 
 Confirm ground conditions and groundwater regimes 
 Refine geotechnical risk mapping 
 Support detailed design and future development approvals. 
Development at later stages must be supported by intrusive investigations, modelling, and engineering 
validation. 
In general, from a geotechnical perspective, the majority of the Precinct  is considered to be suitable for the 
purposes of commercial and industrial use, with varying levels of localised mitigation measures based on 
geographically specific constraints.  
Referral to Subsidence Advisory NSW (SA NSW) will be required to confirm site specific requirements and 
more detailed subsidence modelling may be required. It is expected that many of the site constraints can be 
managed through engineering intervention such as ground improvement and consideration of mine 
subsidence in structural design or ground stabilisation by means such as grouting of former workings.

2 
Introduction 
This Geotechnical Engineering Report (this Report) has been prepared by Aurecon on behalf of the 
Department Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) to support the State-led rezoning of the Macquarie 
Coal Complex for Post Mining Land Use. The Macquarie Coal Complex Land Transformation Precinct (the 
Precinct) and Teralba Southgate form part of the NSW Government’s investigation into future land use 
pathways for mining affected land. 
This Report provides a desktop based geotechnical assessment to support the rezoning, planning and 
staged redevelopment of the Precinct and Teralba Southgate sub-precinct. It establishes an evidence base 
to identify, assess and manage geotechnical constraints, and to guide investigation, earthworks and 
foundation design requirements across in these areas. 
The Report is intended to inform: 
 State-led rezoning processes 
 Structure planning and sub‑precinct development strategies 
 Infrastructure planning and delivery 
 Future development applications and site-specific investigations. 
The Precinct and Teralba Southgate are characterised by a highly variable ground environment, shaped by: 
 Underground mining (West Wallsend Colliery) 
 Open cut mining and backfilled voids 
 Coal processing infrastructure and tailings deposition 
 Progressive rehabilitation and landform recontouring  
These legacy conditions result in a range of geotechnical challenges, including: 
 Mine subsidence risk 
 Variable and uncontrolled fill 
 Soft and compressible alluvial soils 
 Groundwater variability 
 Stability and settlement considerations associated with the Tailings Storage Facility (TSF). 
A strategic, risk-informed framework to manage constraints associated with the geotechnical conditions of 
the Precinct and Teralba Southgate should therefore be adopted.  
2.1 
Background 
Open cut and underground mining operations have all ceased and current activities are focused on 
rehabilitation, closure planning, and long-term environmental management.  
The Macquarie Coal Complex is a decommissioned mining operation previously operated by Glencore, 
which processed coal sourced from the nearby underground West Wallsend Colliery and the Westside open-
cut mining operations. Mining activities at West Wallsend Colliery, Westside open-cut mining operation and 
Teralba Southgate respectively ceased in 2016, 2012 and 2001. 
The Structure Plan has divided the Precinct and Teralba Southgate into three post mining land use land 
categories for conservation, development and recreation purposes, further divided into six sub-precinct areas 
as shown Figure 2-1 and listed in Table 2-1.

2.2 
Purpose of this report 
This Report provides an assessment of the geological and geotechnical setting across the Precinct and 
Teralba Southgate including site conditions, mining and rehabilitation history, engineered landforms, and 
subsidence constraints. It identifies key opportunities and constraints to inform the and Structure Plan and 
supports the development of Master Plan performance and staging triggers.  
1 
6F 

--- Geo Page 11 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Geotechnical Engineering Report Rev B_Clean.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B

This Report has been prepared using publicly available information together with existing project data, 
including previous geotechnical investigations, borehole logs, laboratory testing records, mine rehabilitation 
documentation, and available topographic and subsidence information. 
Specifically, the Report aims to: 
 Provide a rezoning/master plan level geotechnical evidence base to verify developable land and inform 
land use compatibility, built form intensity and infrastructure feasibility 
 Translate Enquiry by Design (EbD) identified constraints, including soils, steep terrain constraints and 
mine subsidence district considerations, into Master Plan mapping, performance criteria and staging 
triggers 
 Provide a clear pathway for later-phase investigations (intrusive testing, stability modelling, settlement 
monitoring) without duplicating Development Application (DA) stage work. 
2.3 
Assumptions and limitations 
This Report has been prepared to inform a Master Plan for post mining land use at the rezoning stage.  The 
assessment is based on existing available information and does not constitute a DA level geotechnical 
design assessment.  
The following limitations apply to this assessment: 
 This assessment has been limited to publicly accessible data available to Aurecon and that provided by 
DPHI, and Glencore 
 No geotechnical or hydrogeological modelling has been undertaken for the purpose of this assessment 
 No detailed development analysis has been undertaken as part of geotechnical assessment 
 No geotechnical investigations were carried out for this assessment. 
The following items are specifically excluded from, or deferred beyond, the scope of this assessment: 
 Comprehensive intrusive site investigation campaigns across the full Precinct and Teralba Southgate 
 Detailed stability modelling, settlement predictions and foundation design 
 DA stage geotechnical design certification and construction-phase verification 
 Detailed data gaps identified for the geotechnical constraint assessment are further outlined in Section 
5.2 
 Mine subsidence is assumed to apply across the entire Precinct and Teralba Southgate, and is treated as 
a site-wide constraint rather than a differentiating factor between sub-precincts.

3.2.2 
TSF landform 
The central portion of the Cockle Creek sub-precinct comprises the TSF landform. The TSF was used for the 
disposal of fine coal processing residues, which were hydraulically placed and retained by earth fill 
embankments. Reference to the West Wallsend Tailings Dam Report indicates this TSF is currently 
undergoing rehabilitation works, including capping, regrading and revegetation. The landform consists of 
tailings with associated mine waste materials and should therefore be considered as an area of variable 
anthropogenic ground conditions and topography. The area is still under final construction with placement of 
fill and final capping in progress at the time of the preparation of this report. The TSF is a declared dam and 
the critical failure section is assessed as being the northern embankment, primarily due to the greater 
thickness of the eastern embankment. The eastern embankment is sufficiently large that this is the area 
where capping materials are being sourced for the final landform. 
Reference to Figure 3-4 indicates that the final landform average slopes are designed to be 1V:8H for the 
area of borrow (or 7 degrees), 1V:100 H for the upper tailings capping area (or 0.5 degrees) and 1V:4H for 
the contour bank stripping area (or 14 degrees) following rehabilitation works (WSP, 2025). Surface drainage 
design has also been included in the final landform design. 
 
Figure 3-4 Visual representation of the final planned landform slopes, with the area of borrow in orange, upper 
tailings capping area in yellow, and contour bank stripping area in red (WSP, 2025) 
3.3 
Regional geology and geomorphology 
Reference to the Seamless Geology layer via MinView (Colquhoun et al., 2019) indicates that the Precinct 
and Teralba Southgate are predominantly underlain by alluvial deposits (Q_ab, Q_af, Q_ap, Q_at and Q_av) 
along Cockle Creek and its tributaries in low-lying areas, potentially including soft to firm clays, silts and 
loose cohesionless materials.  
The rock units of the Newcastle Coal Measures (Pnb, Pnmc and Pnme) are expected in relatively higher 
elevation areas. The Narrabeen Group (Tnc) and anthropogenic deposits are also present locally to the 
southwest and northeast of the site, respectively, with anthropogenic deposits occurring west of Cockle 
Creek around Black Swan Lake and its surrounds.  

--- Geo Page 21 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Geotechnical Engineering Report Rev B_Clean.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
16 
 
 
 
 
 
In structural geological terms, the area lies close to the northern margin of the Sydney Basin and at the edge 
of the relatively undisturbed central region and closer to the more disturbed and deformed northern marginal 
region of the basin. The Precinct and Teralba Southgate are well mapped due to the local mining history and 
a number of north-west to south-east trending structural features are recorded including: 
 The Macquarie Syncline, which extends approximately 50km from Wyong to Buttai with the axial trace 
running less than 1 km to the west of the TSF site 
 The Lochinvar Anticline, located to the northwest of the site 
 Unnamed thrust fault mapped to the south of the rail loop 
 Faulting, including thrust and normal faults, predominantly trending NW–SE 
 Igneous intrusions, comprising a dominant NW–SE dyke trending series aligned with the Macquarie 
Syncline to the west, and an additional E–W trending dyke set to the north of the site 
 Surface exposures of named coal seams (e.g. Fassifern coal seam and Great Northern coal seam). 
These structural features only affect the Newcastle Coal Measures rock units in the Precinct and Teralba 
Southgate and will be more relevant once certain development types become known. Especially where new 
development will be above former mine workings, and the structural details will affect settlement predictions. 
Refer to Figure 3-5 for the geological setting. A higher-resolution version of this figure is provided in Figure 
A4 of Appendix A – Figures.

3.5 
Seismicity 
In accordance with the Australian Standard AS 1170.4-2007, the site has a hazard design factor (Z) of 0.11. 
The following sub-soil classes are likely to be encountered: 
 Class Ce – Shallow soil site (likely across most of the sub-precincts) 
 Class De – Deep or soft soil site (potentially towards Cockle Creek and Diega Creek within sub-precinct 
No.6). 
Further investigation is required to confirm the indicative sub-soil classification. The hazard factor indicates 
that the MCC site is located within a low seismicity risk area. 
3.6 
Slope stability geo zones  
Lake Macquarie City Council host a web portal “Development in geotechnical areas” that provides zoning 
against 6 geotechnical risk categories based on slope and ground conditions criteria, including the presence 
of coal, claystone and degree of induration of quaternary sediments, as outlined in Table 3-6. The geology 
appears to be derived from the NSW Seamless Geology dataset; however, the source and date of the 
slope/topographic data are not specified. As the mapping was developed in 2019, the slope stability geo 
zone classifications may not reflect areas where significant earthworks have since modified landforms, 
including parts of the West Lake and TSF areas and should be treated as indicative in these areas.

3.7.3 
Open cut lake site 
This site is well revegetated and the lake apparently stocked with fish. The uppermost portion of the original 
open cut slopes are still visible above the lake edge on the western side. Glencore Staff mentioned ongoing 
water testing and that the bathymetry of the open cut was partly backfilled prior to allowing water levels to 
rise. Some areas of fill material could be seen around the lake edge and in the access road material 
including limited man-made material.   
3.8 
Soil landscapes 
According to the eSPADE 2.2 tool from the NSW Department of Planning, Industry and Environment 
(Department of Planning and Environment, 2024), the Precinct and Teralba Southgate include various soil 
landscapes, predominantly Killingworth (9232ki) (~ 34 %) in higher areas and Cockle Creek (9232cc) (~ 35 
%) along Cockle Creek and its tributaries in low-lying areas. This is followed by Doyalson (9232do) (~ 11 %), 
Disturbed Terrain (9232xx) (~ 10 %), and more localised occurrences of Warners Bay (9232wa), Gateshead 
(9232ga), and Stockrington (9232sn) (each ≤ 5 %). 
Upland areas (Killingworth soil landscape) are constrained by erosion susceptibility, steep slope, and mine 
subsidence risk. Alluvial areas (Cockle Creek) are constrained by flooding, waterlogging, elevated water 
tables, run-on effects, and dispersive soils. Disturbed Terrain presents the greatest uncertainty due to highly 
variable ground conditions, potential uncontrolled fill, and thus severe geotechnical constraints (e.g. low 
bearing capacity, compressible or loose materials, potential buried obstructions and voids, etc.). The 
remaining soil landscapes contribute to localised constraints including steeper slopes, shallow soils, and 
variable foundation conditions.  
Refer to Figure 3-8 for the soil landscapes across the site. A higher-resolution version of this figure is 
provided in Figure A5 of Appendix A – Figures.

landscape 
Topography 
Soil characteristics

Killingworth (9232ki) 
The Killingworth soil landscape is an erosional landscape 
comprising undulating to rolling and low hills developed on 
the Newcastle Coal Measures of the Awaba Hills region. 
Elevation ranges from 50 to 160 m, with local relief of 30 to 
100 m and slopes of 3 -20%. The area is predominantly 
covered by uncleared tall open forest. 
The landscape variant, Killingworth (9232kia), comprises 
steeper slopes (20-25%). 
Soils are generally shallow (<0.6 m) to moderately deep (<1.5 m), 
typically well to imperfectly drained. Profiles commonly comprise 
loamy to sandy loam topsoils overlying clay loam to clay subsoils. 
Soil types include Yellow Podzolic soils and Soloths on crests and 
hillslopes, with Gleyed variants in lower or poorly drained areas. 
Shallow structured and bleached loams, as well as lithosols, occur 
locally on crests. 
Soil erodibility is generally high. Other limitations include 
shallow soils (localised), seasonal waterlogging, and the 
presence of sodic/dispersible soils with low wet strength. 
Soils are typically strongly acidic with low fertility, with 
localised foundation hazard (high shrink swell subsoils) and 
subsidence hazard (Mine Subsidence District).  
Overall limitations for urban development are moderate. The 
landscape variant, Killingworth (9232kia), comprises steeper 
slopes (20–25%), with associated high limitations for urban 
development. 
Cockle Creek 
(9232cc) 
Alluvial flats, alluvial fans, and drainage plains, with slopes of 
0–2% on floodplains and <5% on fans and plains. Elevation 
ranges from <1 to 50 m with minimal relief (<1 m). Landforms 
include moderately broad (<500 m) alluvial flats and broad 
(up to 1,000 m) deltaic deposits along lower Cockle Creek, 
with localised terraces, levees, and point bars (relief up to 3 
m), and alluvial fans (<500 m) in upper reaches and 
tributaries. 
Soils are generally deep (>2 m). Imperfectly to poorly drained 
Yellow Soloths and Yellow Podzolic Soils occur on floodplains. 
Moderately well to poorly drained Yellow Earths and Grey Earths 
occur on delta and fan deposits, with imperfectly to well-drained 
Yellow Podzolic Soils also present. 
Flood hazard and high water erosion hazard, with localised 
areas of permanently high watertables and periodic to 
permanent waterlogging. High run-on conditions are 
present, with acid, infertile, sodic/dispersible soils of low wet 
strength. 
 
Doyalson (9232do) 
The Doyalson soil landscape is characterised by generally 
undulating rises with local relief of up to 30 m and gentle 
slope gradients. 
Variable profiles reflecting sandstone/conglomerate and local finer-
grained lenses. Typically, up to 0.1 m of loamy sand overlies 0.1–
0.3 m of hardsetting sandy clay, underlain by 0.3–0.6 m of sandy 
clay loam grading to pale grey or strongly pedal clay. Total soil 
depth generally ranges from 0.5–1.5 m, with mainly gradational 
boundaries. 
I In finer-grained areas, shallow sandy soils overlie >1 m of clay 
(total depth ~0.75–2 m) with sharper boundaries. In drainage lines, 
loamy sand overlies sandy clay and >1 m of grey clay. 
Erosion hazard with localised seasonal waterlogging and 
high run-on in footslope areas. The site is within a Mine 
Subsidence District, with generally low but localised high 
foundation hazard linked to clay-rich subsoils, high shrink–
swell, low wet bearing strength, and high erodibility. Soils 
are strongly acidic, very low fertility, and may be stony, with 
localised dispersion, sodicity, and aluminium toxicity.  
Overall, moderate constraints for urban development with 
localised high to severe limitations. 
Disturbed Terrain 
(9232xx) 
The Disturbed Terrain landscape comprises plains to 
hummocky ground extensively modified by human activity, 
including complete removal, disturbance, or burial of original 
soils. Local relief and slope are highly variable. Areas include 
landfill consisting of soil, rock, building, and waste materials. 
Original vegetation has been fully cleared and replaced with 
turf or grassland. 
Highly variable, with original soils removed, buried, or heavily 
disturbed. Bedrock may be exposed in quarries and pits, while 
landfill areas contain transported soils, sediments, and industrial or 
household waste. Surfaces may be artificially topsoiled or covered 
with concrete or bitumen. 
Highly variable, including erosion, mass movement/rockfall, 
steep slopes, seasonal waterlogging, shallow or 
unconsolidated materials, rock outcrop, and Mine 
Subsidence District constraints. 
Soils may be low fertility, acidic, dispersive, stony, and 
highly variable in permeability, water-holding capacity, 
erodibility, and shrink–swell behaviour. 
Urban development is often severely constrained, with high 
to severe limitations for agricultural use.

Soil 
landscape 
Topography 
Soil characteristics 
Limitations 
Warners Bay 
(9232wa) 
The Warners Bay soil landscape comprises undulating to 
rolling low hills and rises developed on fine-grained 
sediments of the Newcastle Coal Measures in the Awaba 
Hills. Elevation ranges from 40–80 m, with local relief of 30–
80 m and slopes of 3–20%. Crests are broad (200–300 m), 
with long, gently convex slopes (500–1,200 m) and broad 
drainage lines. Rock outcrop is rare. The area is 
predominantly cleared tall open forest. 
Soils are moderately deep to deep, typically 1–>1.5 m, and 
imperfectly to poorly drained. Moderately well-drained podzolic and 
soloth soils occur across slopes, with poorly drained structured 
loams in drainage lines. 
Limitations include high water erosion hazard and Mine 
Subsidence District constraints, with localised steep slopes 
and mass movement hazard. Seasonal waterlogging and 
high run-on occur on lower slopes. Soils are strongly acidic, 
of low fertility, with moderate to high shrink–swell and plastic 
subsoils. 
Gateshead (9232ga) 
The Gateshead soil landscape comprises undulating to rolling 
rises on Permian conglomerate, shale, and sandstone in the 
Awaba Hills. Elevation reaches up to 130 m, with local relief 
of 60–100 m and slopes of 5–15%. The landscape is 
predominantly cleared woodland and open forest, with broad 
crests (250–500 m) and long slopes (500–1,000 m). Drainage 
lines are narrow and deeply incised at their heads, grading 
into broader flats (up to 5 m wide) downstream. Rock outcrop 
is rare (<2%). 
Soils are moderately deep to deep, ranging from 1 to 4 m, and are 
moderately well to imperfectly drained. Yellow Podzolic Soils and 
yellow Soloths occur on conglomerate crests and sideslopes, with 
localised shallow, rapidly drained Lithosols. On shale parent 
material, Red Podzolic Soils, red Soloths, and some yellow Soloths 
occur, typically with moderate to imperfect drainage. 
Water erosion hazard and Mine Subsidence District, with 
localised steep slopes and shallow soils. High run-on and 
seasonal waterlogging occur on lower slopes. Soils are 
typically acidic and of low fertility. 
Stockrington (9232sn) 
The Stockrington soil landscape comprises steep rises 
developed on conglomerates of the Newcastle Coal 
Measures (Adamstown Subgroup). Elevation ranges from 80 
- 160 m, with local relief up to 180 m. Upper slopes are steep 
(25–>40%) with slope lengths of 200 - 500 m, while colluvial 
benches and lower slopes are gentler (15–20%). The area is 
uncleared tall open forest, with terraced and hummocky 
surfaces common. Rock outcrop is absent, although 
conglomerate boulders may occur on lower slopes and 
benches.  
A landscape variant, Stockrington (9232sna), includes 
sideslopes with lower (<20%) gradients. 
Soils are moderately deep to deep (from 0.7 m to > 3 m). Rapidly 
drained earthy and friable loams occur on upper slopes, while deep 
(>2 m), well-drained podzolic and soloth soils occur on midslopes 
and benches. 
Limitations include steep slopes, mass movement and water 
erosion hazards, and foundation hazard.

3.12 
Mine subsidence 
According to the Mining Exploration and Geoscience Division of Regional NSW (accessed via MinView), the 
Precinct and Teralba Southgate are entirely underlain by the Killingworth-Wallsend and Lake Macquarie 
No.1 Extension Mine Subsidence Districts and bordered by the West Lake & Lake Macquarie Mine 
subsidence Districts, as shown in Figure 3-11. A higher-resolution version of this figure is provided in Figure 
A6.1 of Appendix A – Figures. 
 
Figure 3-11 Mine Subsidence Districts 
Appendix H of the “Mining Operations Plan: Closure of the OCAL Complex” report by SLR on behalf of 
Glencore (SLR, 2016) includes a plan showing the locations of underground mine entry points and extent of 
former underground workings. An extract of this plan is presented in Figure 3-14 and indicates that the 
Precinct and Teralba Southgate are extensively underlain by historical underground bord-and-pillar as well 
as longwall mine workings. It is noted that this report appendix also includes the underground workings, as 
part of Figure 1.2 of the West Wallsend Colliery Continued Operations Project Report (NSW Government 
Planning & Infrastructure, 2012).  
The plan shows several aspects of note: 
 Areas of mining in different coal seams are coloured  
 Some areas of multiple seam workings are shown 
 Areas of Longwall mining are more prevalent in the west of the Precinct 
 Areas of Bord and pillar mining are more prevalent in the east of the Precinct 
 Areas of underground mining do exist below the majority of the Precinct 
As part of the application documents for proposed expanded mine workings at West Wallsend, the data from 
surface monitoring at several regions of the former mine workings is provided in the following reports: 
 Subsidence Predictions and Impact Assessment of the Proposed Western and Southern Domain 
Longwalls, West Wallsend Colliery, Peer Review of Report DGS WWD-012/1, Report No. MSEC433 
(Mine Subsidence Engineering Consultants, 2010).  
 Subsidence Predictions and General Impact Assessment of the Proposed Western and Southern Domain 
Longwalls, West Wallsend Colliery, DGS Report No. WWD-012/1 (Ditton Geotechnical Services, 2010)

The monitoring lines above the Longwalls 11 to 18 in Figure 3-13 show that the maximum record for 
observed surface settlement of 1.0 m was recorded over Longwall 16. The range of total settlements above 
Longwalls 12A to 15 ranges from 0.8 m to 0.9 m, and this variation is driven by the changes in the seam 
height and depth of cover. The depths to underground mine workings typically vary with local topography 
and bedrock geology and therefore the level of subsidence risk is also likely to vary across other areas 
where monitoring has not been completed. But it is noted from this data that the majority of subsidence may 
have already occurred above former Longwalls, which is to be expected as this is part of Longwall mining 
design considerations.  
In addition, Section 3.2.2 of the same report provides summary information on the Historical Mining areas 
across the OCAL complex and refers to a study completed by Ditton Geotechnical Services (DgS) which 
completed a preliminary assessment of the possible long term settlement risks due to instability od the 
historical OCAL workings including those in the West Wallsend No. 2 and Teralba Collieries (circa 1970’s to 
2016)  in the following seams:

The variation in depth in the workings is due to the dip and faulting within the strata as well as the varying 
depth of cover due to hills and valleys at the surface. 
The report notes that the former underground workings consist of first and second working with bord and 
pillar, pillar extraction and longwall panels in regions of each seam, and importantly, that “other non-OCAL 
mine working also exist in higher level seams that may contribute to the long-term subsidence predictions” 
The report makes the following recommendations: 
 Based on the age and the location of the old mine workings, it is considered that the area contains 
several zones in which the risk of post-mining subsidence may be sufficiently ‘low’ for future 
developments to be designed to tolerate relatively small magnitudes of subsidence.  
 Maximum subsidence above the OCAL mine workings due to future instability is estimated to range from 
< 20 mm to < 160 mm, depending on the type of workings and whether they have been flooded. 
 Future structures and infrastructure will probably need to be designed for potential subsidence up to 150 
mm, tilts < 4 mm/m, curvatures < 0.2 km-1 and horizontal strains < 2 mm/m to satisfy SANSW “Safe, 
Serviceable and Repairable’ Design Guidelines in Mine Subsidence Districts.  
 The work by DgS was based on preliminary analysis and further detailed investigations mainly based on 
numerical modelling might be needed to accurately estimate the potential of further post-mining 
subsidence in each sub-area of the site, particularly in areas that contains multi-seam mining or First 
Workings adjacent to Second Workings. 
 Areas where multi-seam mining has accorded with incomplete caving in the lower seam are assessed to 
have a ‘Moderate’ Risk of significant subsidence impact occurring in the future (i.e. subsidence > 150 
mm).  
 The flooding of West Wallsend No 2 Colliery may result in additional subsidence due to strata softening or 
goaf reconsolidation effects. The Teralba Colliery workings are already flooded and have a lower risk of 
additional subsidence than the dry workings do.  

--- Geo Page 40 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Geotechnical Engineering Report Rev B_Clean.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B

 Overall, the study has identified there is ‘low’ risk over the majority of the study area underlain by YW and 
BH Seam mine workings associated with OCAL mining complex, however, further merit based 
assessments of a given site and proposed development may therefore be necessary in Moderate Risk 
Zones (i.e. Multi-seam mining locations).

5 
Geotechnical constraints assessment 
5.1 
Key geotechnical criteria 
The overall site setting, including slope, geology, depth of regolith, soil landscapes, ASS, salinity and mine 
subsidence described in the preceding sections of this Report presents geotechnical constraints that must be 
addressed in infrastructure planning and design, and opportunities that may be optimised from the outset.  
To support the geotechnical constraints assessment, and inform the Master Plan, these constraint categories 
have been defined as key geotechnical criteria for the development of the overall constraint map, using their 
associated primary datasets listed in Table 5-1, and combined risk rankings presented in the subsequent 
sections and Appendix B figures.  
The overall constraints map is provided in Appendix C – Near surface geotechnical constraints map for 
Structure Plan.

5.2 
Data confidence 
 The overall salinity mapping generally correlates with the geological mapping; however, differences in the 
mapped extents may result in local discrepancies in the constraint assessment. The layer is mapped at a 
larger scale across the state and is considered fairly low accuracy in the scale of the Precinct and Teralba 
Southgate but aligns broadly with the underlying geology. 
 No test data available for the materials stored within the TSF. The depth profile is also not available. 
 Rail loop area and anthropogenic fill: limited and incomplete GIS/data coverage. The rail loop is identified 
as a key data gap. At the time of this assessment, anthropogenic fill in this area is treated as moderate 
uncertainty/high risk, unless refined using available Glencore data to better define extent and current 
conditions for improved risk assessment, or through further mapping and site-specific investigation. 
 Input datasets and layer for GIS have been sourced from multiple sources such as MinView, Glencore 
and Lake Macquarie City Council. The level of details and variability of sources / interpretations may 
induce variability in input dataset. The original authors limitation should be referred to if undertaking 
subsequent studies. 
 Due to the Precinct and Teralba Southgate being above a range of historic mining sites the geology 
mapping is considered to be of fair to good quality with faults and local structure well understood 
generally compared to other regions in New South Wales.   

--- Geo Page 52 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Geotechnical Engineering Report Rev B_Clean.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
47 
 
 
 
 
 
 Coal combustion hazard (Sponcom) is not represented as part of the constraint maps as it is not mapped 
or available digitally at the time of writing. The risk is associated with two main forms: existing coal seams 
that remain in the natural geology, and coal materials that remain in mine spoils that have been stockpiled 
or placed as fill across the Precinct and Teralba Southgate. 
 Mine subsidence: all the sub-precincts are underlain by historic underground coal workings, resulting in 
potential subsidence risk that must be considered in land use planning and foundation design. Potential 
subsidence risks are not currently quantified as further studies are required. 
 Limited geotechnical investigation information for strength, consistency or thicknesses of shallow soils 
and rocks. Existing records are generally dated, with incomplete descriptions and limited laboratory 
testing, and in many locations, bedrock was not intersected, meaning soil thickness cannot be confirmed. 
As such, foundation conditions have not been assessed in detail. Slope stability assessment is also 
preliminary and based primarily on available topographic data. 
5.3 
Methodology 
The identified geotechnical criteria were classified into three ranking levels (low, moderate, and high) based 
on their characteristics and relative constraints to development, including foundations, earthworks, and 
excavations. The risk rankings adopted for each geotechnical criterion are presented in Table 5-2. 
Table 5-2 Geotechnical constraints risk ranking criteria 
Risk ranking classification 
Description 
Examples 
Ranking 
Colour code 
Low 
 
Minimal limitations to 
development 
- Sandy soils with no organic or clay content, no 
disturbed terrain recorded  
- Low risk of ASS  
- Low salinity hazard  
Moderate 
 
Some limitations to development 
Combination of low and high risk categories 
and/or inherently moderate-risk categories (e.g. 
mine subsidence hazard). 
High 
 
Multiple limitations to 
development 
- Organic soils (peat), soft or clayey soils 
- Deep soft soils 
- High risk of ASS 
- High salinity   
 
Following assignment of the risk rankings, a multicriteria analysis was undertaken using ArcGIS. Each 
criterion was assigned a numerical value (low = 1, moderate = 2, high = 3) and combined using a weighted 
overlay approach. Equal weighting was applied to all criteria, except slope stability associated with geo 
zones. The Geographic Information System (GIS) layers were then overlaid to generate a composite score, 
which was subsequently colour-coded in accordance with Table 5-2. Higher scores indicate increasingly 
challenging ground conditions for development. 
The risk classification and weighting adopted for each geotechnical criterion are described in the following 
section. It is noted that salinity and slope stability geo zones were not reclassified for this assessment, as 
these datasets already include risk-based classifications. This also generally applies to ASS; however, risk 
classifications have been locally adjusted based on engineering judgement where site conditions in areas of 
disturbed terrain are expected to differ from the mapped classification.

5.3.8 
Mine subsidence criterion 
Given that the entire Precinct is located within a mapped Mine Subsidence District, subsidence risk is 
considered to apply across the entire site. As such, Subsidence Advisory NSW will be the approving 
authority for any future development applications in the districts, regardless of the specific development 
location. It is therefore not treated as a standalone differentiating constraint between sub-precincts at this 
stage. Refer to Sections 7.4.8 and 8 for further details regarding the staged assessment and approval 
process for investigation, design and potential remediation, such as grouting works.

5.5 
TSF area risk ranking 
At the time of the preparation of this Report the TSF area was undergoing placement of capping to achieve 
the final landform. As such, final settlement has not commenced yet. Large settlements are expected and no 
development can occur until such time that the TSF risk rating is reduced sufficiently to allow the structure to 
be de-declared. 
The TSF is constrained by: 
 Dam Safety management requirement 
 Ongoing and historical earthworks 
 Hydraulically placed coal residue   
 Groundwater levels with the storage  
 Underlying natural ground profile that has potential regolith depths of up to 10 m. 
 Steep surrounding slopes 
 Variable storage depth 
The ATC Williams report indicates that the depth of the storage area is variable and is expected to be formed 
of the original valley profile that drains to the original dam wall within the eastern side of the storage. No 
records are available that include estimates of long-term settlement; however, it would be expected to be in 
the order of metres over decades. 
The storage embankments are wider on the eastern slopes and it is understood that this is where the final 
landform capping material is also being won from currently. 
Around the TSF are natural and man-made slopes. Some of which are steep. Along the southern margin is 
an excavated batter.  
These factors result in significant geotechnical constraints to future development, particularly due to 
settlement potential and variable subsurface conditions. 
Given the current earthworks, the existing datasets are considered to provide a limited representation of 
geotechnical risk within the TSF area, as they ground conditions that are unlikely to correspond to the final 
rehabilitated landform. The risk ranking presented in Table 5-18 for the TSF footprint is therefore provided for 
reference only.

7 
Structure plan assessment  
7.1 
Approach 
Reference to the Master Plan identifies the following key principles: 
 Enable transition industries  
 Connect infrastructure and mobility  
 Preserve ecology and water  
 Deliver flexible pathways and resilience  
The Structure Plan has been developed by incorporating the preferred elements of the assessed scenarios, 
further refining areas identified for investigation, and avoiding established no-go zones. Rather than adopting 
a single scenario, the Structure Plan combines the key opportunities identified across all scenarios while 
seeking to minimise known constraints and risks. This approach aims to maximise development outcomes 
while maintaining flexibility for future planning, environmental and engineering requirements. 
7.2 
Proposed Structure Plan 
The Structure Plan has been developed to support the transition of the MCC Precinct and Teralba Southgate 
from a former mining operation to a future employment Precinct. The Structure Plan adopts a staged 
development approach aligned with rehabilitation progress, infrastructure availability and risk reduction. Early 
development is focused on previously disturbed and serviced areas within the Cockle Creek, Killingworth 
and Teralba sub-precincts. Medium-term development is concentrated within Cockle Creek, Killingworth, 
West Lake and Barnsley West, and is dependent on further geotechnical and environmental investigations, 
infrastructure upgrades and utility provision. Long-term development of the TSF and dam break inundation 
areas is contingent on completion of rehabilitation, geotechnical stabilisation and dam safety requirements. 
Land release across all stages will be informed by ongoing geotechnical, environmental, flooding and 
servicing assessments. 
The Precinct and Teralba Southgate benefit from strong regional connectivity, established transport 
infrastructure and its location within the Lower Hunter industrial corridor, supporting a range of future 
employment opportunities. The Killingworth and Barnsley sub-precincts are well suited to early employment 
uses linked to existing residential areas, while Teralba presents opportunities for transport-oriented mixed-
use development due to its proximity to existing rail stations. 
Previously disturbed and rehabilitated land across Cockle Creek, Killingworth and West Lake provide 
suitable areas for staged development, enabling growth to be directed away from higher-value ecological 
corridors. The West Lake sub-precinct also presents opportunities for recreation and nature-based tourism in 
association with surrounding environmentally constrained areas. 
Refer to Figure 2-1 for the MCC Structure Plan Precinct and Teralba Southgate development areas and sub-
precinct layout.

constraints map in Appendix C – Near surface geotechnical constraints map for Structure Plan. The 
map has been developed using the same multi-criteria analysis described in Section 5, based on the key 
datasets outlined in Table 5-1.

sub-precinct are presented in Table 7-1.

7.4 
Constructability 
7.4.1 
Flood management  
Riverine flooding would be expected to induce scour on any developments that border the flood risk areas or 
if developments are planned within these areas. Failing to mitigate flooding may cause excessive total or 
differential settlements in the underlying soft clays soils potentially present in the sub-precincts No.5, 3, 6A, 
6B, 6C and 6D. 
As such, any new development planned in or close to modelled flood regions should be designed to 
incorporate flood resilience features: 
 Scour protection may be necessary for fill embankments or considered in foundation designs of bridges 
or culverts and other structures. 
 New developments, such as ground floor car parking and first floor offices will reduce damage and the 
need for inspections and repair after flood events. 
 Fill embankments should be suitably specified to use free draining materials, adequate erosion control 
measures to avoid fines washout, or incorporate draining base layers. The same is applicable to 
associated structures such as bridge abutments or retaining walls. 
 Levees if required along the proposed boundaries to flood risk areas typically need to be constructed 
using clay rich fill or other less permeable soil material as liner material. 
Reference should be made to the Flooding and Water Cycle Management Engineering Report for details 
related to flood management. 
7.4.2 
Earthworks considerations 
Alluviums and residual soils are generally expected to be readily excavatable using conventional excavator 
equipment (20 tonne mass excavator). Where harder soil consistencies are encountered, the use of a 
toothed bucket / ripper tyne may be required. Suitability for re-use may be limited to general fill depending on 
erosion potential, reactivity, material consistency and presence of organic soils, noting that residual soils are 
expected to be reactive based on the constraints associated with the mapped soil landscapes. Existing fill 
areas may contain contaminants and are therefore considered unsuitable for reuse without further 
assessment.  
Within the Narrabeen Group and Newcastle Coal Measures, excavatability is likely to vary depending on 
rock properties such as strength and degree of natural fracturing. Typically, excavation within the less 
weathered, higher strength and intact sandstone rock may require rock saws and/or hydraulic rock breakers. 
Conglomerate may require more intensive ripping due to its greater strength. Coal and tuff units may present 
excavation challenges and are generally unsuitable for reuse as engineered fill without further assessment.  
Where slopes are greater than 10 degrees, they are generally considered unsuitable for conventional 
industrial and commercial developments that require large, level building pads and hardstand areas. At this 
stage, no preliminary assessment has been undertaken to quantify the extent of cut and fill earthworks, the 
likely need for retaining structures, or the associated impacts on developable land, construction costs, 
drainage, and overall site feasibility. A detailed earthworks assessment, incorporating terrain modelling, 
cut/fill balance, retaining requirements, and optimisation of development platforms, is recommended to better 
understand the site's development constraints and associated costs. 
Where coal seams or coal bearing materials are encountered in cut areas in rock, specific management 
measures may be required due to the potential for spontaneous combustion and long-term geochemical 
instability. In these instances, coal should either be selectively excavated and removed from site or 
alternatively treated through controlled blending with inert materials for reuse as general fill or foundation 
improvement layers.  

--- Geo Page 73 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Geotechnical Engineering Report Rev B_Clean.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
68 
 
 
 
 
 
The risk of spontaneous combustion is also potentially present in reworked fill material that include coal 
material.  
Earthworks planning should incorporate segregation of coal-impacted materials, appropriate stockpile 
management (including temperature and moisture monitoring where required), and controls to prevent 
oxidation and ignition risk. 
Details regarding gas management are provided in the Contamination Engineering Report. 
7.4.3 
Shallow foundations   
Shallow foundations are anticipated across sub-precincts No. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. In sub-precincts No. 1, 2, 3 
and 5, where shallow groundwater conditions are expected, the use of shallow foundation solutions is likely 
to reduce geotechnical challenges. In these areas, founding above typical groundwater levels may minimise 
the need for temporary excavation support and dewatering, thereby reducing construction risk and cost. 
Additionally: 
 The risk of differential and total settlements beneath new structures should be assessed and addressed 
during the design stage. If differential settlement is likely to exceed acceptable limits, foundation 
treatments such as removing reactive soils within the suction zone and replacing them with non-reactive 
engineered granular fill should be considered.  
 Another solution may include surcharge preloading of proposed footprints to improve underlying soils 
(particularly sandy soils) to support fill pads. Preloading is also effective in reducing long-term creep 
deformations for soft to firm clay deposits beneath embankments. The suitability and extents of 
preloading will depend on the proposed infrastructure and underlying ground conditions. Typically, 
cohesive soils (clays) require longer consolidation periods than free draining soils such as sands. Where 
mixed soil profiles are encountered, ground treatment approaches will need to be adapted accordingly.  
 The surcharge period required to achieve acceptable settlement performance in accordance with 
serviceability requirements depends on the thickness of the soft/compressible clay deposits and the 
magnitude of applied preload. While increasing surcharge loads can reduce consolidation timeframes, 
care must be taken to avoid instability in weak ground conditions. Typical preload durations may range 
from 3 to18 months; however, project specific analysis is required to confirm suitable durations. Vertical 
drains may be installed to accelerate consolidation. The use of lightweight fill materials in combination 
with surcharge loading is also an accepted construction approach. Where final levels permit, non-
engineered fill may be used as surcharge material above required grade levels.  
 For light industrial developments such as warehousing and offices buildings, shallow foundations are 
generally expected to be sufficient. However, heavily loaded point structures within warehouses, such as 
gantry cranes, will likely require deep foundation solutions. 
7.4.4 
Deep foundations 
It is recommended that heavy structures requiring deep foundations, such as basement car parks (which 
may be associated with land uses in sub-precincts No. 1 and 2), adopt driven piles or Continuous Flight 
Auger (CFA) pile solutions where practicable. These methods generally reduce the volume of excavated 
material and the need for groundwater management compared to bored piles. Additionally: 
 Pile foundations will need to be designed to account for uplift forces associated with flooding, as well as 
potential negative skin friction in consolidating soils. 
 Where founding conditions extend into rock within a mine impacted strata, rock socketing may be 
suitable; however, localised mine grouting or void treatment may be required. Structural systems should 
also accommodate potential ground variability through appropriate flexibility. 
 Stakeholder requirements, including rail and road authorities, may require additional design constraints 
on foundation selection, construction methodology and allowable movements, which will need to be 
confirmed during design. 

--- Geo Page 74 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Geotechnical Engineering Report Rev B_Clean.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
69 
 
 
 
 
 
7.4.5 
Utilities 
Utilities associated with light industrial, commercial, residential and general industrial development, primarily 
within Sub-precincts No. 1, 2, 4 and 5, should consider the following: 
 Underground services are typically installed within trench excavations. Shallow groundwater conditions, 
together with the potential presence of ASS, may increase construction complexity and cost. 
 Most service trenches are expected to require shoring and dewatering, particularly in areas of shallow 
groundwater. 
 Surficial soils are expected to be easy to excavate. Where shallow rock may be encountered in sub-
precincts No.2, No. 4, and in localised areas of sub-precinct No.1, the excavatability of rock will depend 
on its strength, weathering and degree of fracturing. Excavation of less weathered, higher-strength rock 
may require specialised equipment such as rock saws or hydraulic rock breakers. 
 Above ground utilities such as overhead power lines may require deep foundations to prevent differential 
settlement issues. 
7.4.6 
Pavements and roads  
The surficial soils across much of the Precinct, particularly soft alluvial deposits, are expected to exhibit low 
California Bearing Ratio values and therefore limited subgrade strength.  
Organic soils may be present near Cockle Creek and its tributaries, while highly reactive clays within alluvial 
and residual soils are expected across much of the Precinct. These conditions may require ground treatment 
measures such as removal and replacement or ground improvement. Where road embankments or fill 
platforms are proposed over compressible soils, preloading and/or basal reinforcement may be necessary to 
manage settlement associated with long-term consolidation. 
7.4.7 
Acid Sulfate Soils 
Areas identified as having a higher potential for ASS, particularly within sub-precincts No.2, 6B, 6C and 6D, 
will require ASS testing as part of future site investigations. Where ASS are confirmed, preparation and 
implementation of an ASS management plan is likely to be required during construction. 
7.4.8 
Mine subsidence 
Given the historical mining activities across the entire MCC Precinct and Teralba Southgate and Mine 
Subsidence District zoning, future development applications would trigger a referral to the SA pursuant to the 
Coal Mine Subsidence Compensation Act 2027 (integrated development). 
Initial engagement with Subsidence Advisory NSW has occurred at the time of writing and the advice 
received from the agency with be captured in the finalisation report. 
Optioneering of layouts may potentially reduce subsidence risks and thus approval requirements. 
Development will need to follow Subsidence Advisory NSW procedures and approval conditions, including 
staged review and engagement. 
The proposed development type will govern the approval pathway and may take the form of the guidelines or 
the Merit Assessment Policy (SA NSW version 2 5 April 2023). 
The accuracy of the mapping and precise locations of the historic workings should be assumed to be 
approximate at this stage. To illustrate a typical application process for a mine subsidence affected 
development area the following steps are summarised below: 
1. Identify affected properties on SixMaps – Lot and DP etc. of affected portions or adjacent portions 
where applicable 
2. Search publicly available databases for current mining / exploration leases 

--- Geo Page 75 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Geotechnical Engineering Report Rev B_Clean.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
70 
 
 
 
 
 
3. Meet with SA NSW to get informal advice on classification of site with respect to Mine Subsidence 
conditions 
4. If applicable, lodge RFI with SA NSW to get formal notification of Mine Subsidence requirements (if 
any).  This may include any, or all, of the followings:  
1. Confirmation that the site is in a proclaimed Mine Subsidence district 
2. Prescriptive advice on specific types of development that are allowed / not allowed 
3. Prescriptive advice on the Mine Subsidence Surface Movement Parameters that must be 
applied to development of the site (e.g. Total maximum subsidence, ground tilt, ground 
strain, radius of curvature etc.) 
4. Requirements for additional site investigation (e.g. Drilling to identify existing mine voids in 
the case of existing bord and pillar workings, drilling to identify existing site geology and 
geotechnical conditions etc.) 
5. Requirements for additional analysis and report on predicted mine subsidence induced 
surface movement parameters 
5. Request mining records from the NSW resource regulator (a small payment is often required)  
6. Preparation of a desktop review of historical mine layouts and assessment of the quality of the 
records and associated risk assessment  
7. If applicable, preparation of a pillar stability assessment numerical modelling report  
8. If applicable, geotechnical investigation to confirm extent, depth and condition of workings  
9. If applicable, preparation of a Mine Subsidence Impact Statement (MSIS) for submission with SA 
NSW 
10. Follow up meeting with SA NSW to discuss the recommendations of the MSIS and agree on final 
design requirements 
11. SA NSW issue final conditions for the development 
 
The initial step of the desktop based assessment will provide a better understanding of the  overall mining 
history and associated subsidence risks and as such is a key first step to understand development pathways 
and clarity on require further works for development approval and costs. 
Typically, the following subsidence parameters would be specified in the conditions of approval: 
 Vertical Subsidence (x mm) 
 Compressive Strains (y mm/m) 
 Tensile Strains (z mm/m) 
 Tilts (w mm/m) 
 Radius of Curvature (v km) 
Subsidence Advisory NSW will review the subsidence risk specifically for a proposed development and 
select the requirements based on the policy associated with that type of development. As such, the 
guidelines and polices are tailored to development types, and developments with tighter or lower tolerances 
to settlement types will have more requirements to achieve approval in general. So early engagement can 
help inform options to adjust layouts before progressing to a more developed design stage (e.g. Concept 
Design) 
As a general guide for mitigation measures, elements of any developments should be designed as far as 
practicable and economical, to maintain safe, serviceable operation in the event of subsidence and reduce 
the cost of repair through: 
 Selection of flexible and lightweight materials rather than brittle materials 

--- Geo Page 76 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Geotechnical Engineering Report Rev B_Clean.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
71 
 
 
 
 
 
 Provision for articulation, adjustment and ease of replacement or repair 
 Reducing transfer of ground strains to structure footings 
 Consideration of post-subsidence safety and functionality of drains and surface water storages elements 
such as stormwater detention basins, swales and gravity pipes 
Mine subsidence and design to manage the associated risks is common in the Hunter region and specialist 
firms are available to support development applications and construction work such as grouting of 
underground voids. As the Precinct is located within the Lake Macquarie LGA it is potentially eligible for 
funding assistance through the Lake Macquarie Mines Grouting Fund, with application processes outlined in 
Council guidelines (Program Guideline V1, March 2025) though this would need to be confirmed with LMCC. 
Should geotechnical investigations be deemed necessary to improve the accuracy of mapping of the 
underground layouts or to confirm if workings have already collapsed then these would typically comprise 
boreholes drilled through the seams in question. Whilst the depths of the seams are deep, typical methods 
only retrieve samples or rock core form the zone of interest and as such the upper zone of each borehole is 
typically not sampled and can be drilled quickly. Standard geotechnical methods and testing within the 
boreholes is then complimented by Mine subsidence specific methods which can include: 
• 
Geophysical downhole logging (Density, Neutron and Gamma scanning) 
• 
Downhole camera inspection  
• 
Sonar mapping 
• 
Boreholes installed with high density PVC pipe and capped for future grouting works. 
If mine grouting works are deemed to be required for new developments this is typically completed from the 
surface via grout injection boreholes. Modern techniques include low viscosity grout to create or increase 
pillar sizes within the voids and thus reducing the volumes of grout required and also grouting in flooded 
voids. 
The development designer is required to certify on the drawings that improvements covered by the approval 
will remain safe, serviceable and repairable in the event of the structures being subjected to the specified 
subsidence. 
Across the Precinct, areas above longwall panels would be expected to have already undergone settlement 
associated with mining and, as such, more likely endorsed by SA (subject to conditions). Bord and Pillar 
workings are considered therefore to have a higher likelihood of remaining and potentially more variable 
subsidence risk associate with this older method of mining.  
Some regions have multiple seams already mined and varying methods and are therefore expected to have 
more complicated assessments and development approvals. 
Where significant thick and strong rock units exist above the former working (e.g. Munmorah Conglomerate) 
these may provide better ability to span the ground subsidence and decrease the surface settlement 
amounts. 
Opportunities include: 
 Undertaking a Precinct-wide subsidence risk assessment to support developers’ early investment 
assessments 
 Coordinating with Lake Macquarie Council to simplify or pre-approve selected application stages and 
identify potential funding opportunities. 
7.4.9 
TSF area 
No development can occur on or downstream of the TSF until the TSF is ‘de-declared’. Once the structure is 
de-declared, ground investigations and design considerations will be required.  
Geotechnical investigations are expected to potentially include the following test types: 
 Cone Penetrometer Tests (CPT)

 Oedometer tests 
 Monitoring of phreatic surface 
Reporting may include analysis of total and differential settlements and potential development of 3D 
modelling to understand critical regions and zoning for treatment. 
Design is likely to include: 
 Pre-loading with general fill material (to be designed to suit the underlying fill thicknesses and material 
types) 
 Inclusion of wick drains to allow pore water pressures to dissipate more rapidly 
 Monitoring 
Opportunities may exist to support or accelerate de-declaration of the TSF, including: 
 Dewatering studies, to explore the options to reduce the groundwater levels in the storage and thus the 
risk of dam failure in modelled scenarios. 
 Modifying the embankments to reduce the risk of failure (and increase factors of safety) – this could 
include earthworks such as addition of toe buttressing or general reprofiling of the embankment slope to 
achieve lower Factor of Safety. 
 Adjustments to the agreed final landform (currently being developed by Glencore) to introduce terracing 
or similar developable areas on the eastern embankment, above those regions where fill thickness is 
minimal over the former natural surface and off the dam structure, as shown indicatively in Figure 7-1.

Alluvial sediments area present in the majority of this area and geotechnical investigations to inform design

potential for shallow or perched groundwater would mean that groundwater monitoring would also be

Recommendations  
The majority of the Structure Plan sub-precincts have limited existing geotechnical information available. It is 
therefore strongly recommended that these areas be subject to targeted geotechnical investigations to 
support future development post rezoning. 
The scope of investigations should be proportionate to the proposed land use intensity, sub‑precinct 
characteristics and constraint profile, and structured to inform both precinct-scale planning and site-specific 
development outcomes. 
These should be integrated and applied in conjunction with the Dam, Flooding, Water Cycle Management 
and Contamination Report recommendations.

9 
Conclusion 
The Geotechnical Assessment considers that the Precinct can support future urban and employment uses 
for commercial and industrial uses; however, rezoning must be explicitly aligned with geotechnical 
constraints, risk levels, and rehabilitation. The site is highly heterogeneous, characterised by legacy mining 
impacts, variable fill, alluvial soils, and subsidence risk, meaning that development suitability is location 
dependent.  
Lower-constrained areas such as Teralba Southgate and Killingworth present clear opportunities for urban 
land use such as residential and mixed use, while moderate constraint areas can be progressively released 
subject to detailed investigations and engineered solutions. High constraint areas, including the TSF, 
floodplains, and deep alluvial zones should be reserved for conservation, open space, or deferred long-term 
uses, with development informed by geotechnical investigations. 
The desktop analysis highlights that key geotechnical risks including mine subsidence, settlement, flooding, 
slopes, areas of historic filling, ASS and salinity occur within the Precinct and inform the required site-specific 
detailed investigations infrastructure design following rezoning at the DA stage to support future 
development. Investigations should be tailored to land use intent and constraint profile of the sub-precinct 
outlined in this report. It is considered possible that further subsidence assessment work may indicate that 
development types with low tolerance for ground movement or structural deformation could prove 
uneconomical. 
The Tailings Storage Facility represents a long-term redevelopment constraint, requiring completion of 
rehabilitation, settlement stabilisation and regulatory de‑declaration before any development can be 
contemplated in this area. Similarly, floodplain and estuarine environments which occur within the Precinct 
will remain constrained and are better suited to conservation and recreational land uses that don’t impact 
flood conveyance and increase risk. 
In consideration of the above, future development must be informed by detailed geotechnical assessment 
addressing: 
 Mine subsidence 
 Settlement and fill behaviour 
 Slope stability 
 Ground conditions and rehabilitation status 
 Earthworks  
Overall, the appropriate planning response is to implement a flexible, adaptive rezoning framework that: 
 Prioritises development in low-risk, serviced, and previously disturbed areas 
 Enables conditional development in moderate-risk areas with engineered mitigation 
 Restricts or defers development in high-risk environments 
 Integrates geotechnical constraints into statutory planning controls and staging triggers 
This approach ensures that rezoning balances development potential with physical site limitations, supports 
safe and cost-effective delivery, and aligns with the long-term transformation of the Precinct into a 
sustainable post-mining landscape. 
It is noted that, while additional investigation, design and construction measures may be required beyond 
those typically associated with a greenfield development, these are not expected to present significant 
constraints to development.
