Executive summary 
This Contamination Technical Assessment (CTA) has been prepared by Aurecon Australasia Pty Ltd 
(Aurecon) on behalf of the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) to support the State-
led rezoning of the Macquarie Coal Complex (the Precinct) and Teralba Southgate, located approximately 20 
km southwest of Newcastle within the Lake Macquarie region, NSW. 
The purpose of this CTA is to reinterpret existing contamination data, originally collected to support mine 
closure and rehabilitation, within the context of proposed rezoning and future land use scenarios identified in 
the Structure and Master Plan and Teralba Southgate. The assessment is scoped at the rezoning stage to 
inform land use compatibility and identification of developable land. It does not constitute development 
application (DA) level investigation or detailed remediation design. 
Site Context 
The Precinct comprises four former mining operations: including West Wallsend Colliery, Macquarie Coal, 
Preparation Plant, Westside Mine (open-cut), and Teralba Colliery (Northgate). Teralba Southgate is located 
approximately 2.5 kilometres south of the Precinct and is occupied by former mine infrastructure including 
shafts. Mining activities ceased progressively between 2001 and 2016. Current activities are limited to 
environmental management and rehabilitation in accordance with the Rehabilitation Management Plan (RMP 
2022). The Precinct and Teralba Southgate are surrounded primarily by residential and mixed-use industrial 
areas.  
The rezoning aims to facilitate employment-led development supported by residential, conservation, and 
open space land uses. A figure showing the extent of Teralba Southgate and the current Structure Plan for 
the Precinct is provided in Figure E1. 
 
Figure E1 – Layout and extent of Teralba Southgate and the Structure Plan for the Precinct  

--- Cont Page 4 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
 
 
 
Summary of Contamination Conditions 
The Precinct encompasses five former mining operations: West Wallsend Colliery, Macquarie Coal 
Preparation Plant, Westside Mine (open-cut), and Teralba Colliery (Northgate). Mining operations ceased 
progressively across the Precinct, with Teralba Colliery closing in 2001, Westside Mine ceasing operations in 
2012, and West Wallsend Colliery and Macquarie Coal Preparation Plant concluding operations in 2016. 
Current activities focused on long-term environmental management and rehabilitation in accordance with the 
Rehabilitation Management Plan (RMP 2022). The Precinct and Teralba Southgate is primarily surrounded 
by residential and mixed-use industrial land uses. The proposed rezoning seeks to establish employment-led 
development across multiple sub-precincts, with designated residential, conservation and open space. 
Contamination investigations across the Precinct and Teralba Southgate have been undertaken 
progressively since 2005, involving: 
◼ Approximately 400 soil and sediment sampling locations. 
◼ 17 groundwater monitoring wells. 
◼ Several ground gas monitoring locations.  
These investigations define 16 “Domains” with variable contamination profiles. Key findings from previous 
investigations completed at the Precinct and Teralba Southgate include: 
◼ Soil and sediment contamination - Elevated concentrations of heavy metals (notably zinc), total 
recoverable hydrocarbons (TRH), and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), primarily exceeding 
ecological criteria. 
◼ Human health risks - No exceedances of commercial/industrial human health criteria identified to date. 
◼ Asbestos - Asbestos-containing materials (ACM) confirmed in several domains. 
◼ Acid Sulfate Soils (ASS/PASS) - Actual and potential ASS identified in specific domains at the Precinct 
◼ Salinity - Moderate to high salinity risk across large portions of the Precinct and Teralba Southgate. 
◼ PFAS – Principally PFOS detected above adopted ecological criteria in groundwater and surface water 
across multiple domains, including within the Precinct and Teralba Southgate 
◼ Ground gas - Methane gas concentrations exceeding the lower explosive limit (LEL) identified in 
underground mine workings, posing a potential vapour intrusion risk, including within the Precinct 
(Domain 11) and Teralba Southgate (Domain 13). 
A figure showing the location and extents of domains at the Precinct and Teralba Southgate is provided in 
Figure E2.  

--- Cont Page 5 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
 
 
 
 
Figure E2 – Location and extent of the closure domains at the Precinct and Teralba Southgate 
Data Gaps and Limitations 
Significant data gaps limit ability for full characterisation of contamination and land suitability, including: 
◼ Multiple domains with no intrusive investigation (lacking soil, groundwater, surface water and sediment 
data). 
◼ Incomplete ASS and groundwater characterisation. 
◼ Limited assessment beneath buildings and inaccessible areas/structures. 
◼ Incomplete delineation of buried asbestos materials. 
◼ Limited ground gas assessments. 
Land Use Suitability 
Based on available data and acknowledging limitations: 
◼ Commercial and industrial uses - Generally compatible across most of the Precinct and Teralba 
Southgate, subject to targeted investigation and management. 
◼ Sensitive uses (residential, conservation, recreational) - Require further investigation and risk assessment 
to confirm suitability. 
◼ Key constraint - The Tailings Storage Facility (Domain 7) presents a significant constraint requiring 
detailed, multidisciplinary assessment. 

--- Cont Page 6 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
 
 
 
Implementation Approach and Key Recommendations  
A staged, risk-based approach to investigation and management is recommended to support rezoning and 
future development. With appropriate controls and management (including detailed site investigations and 
appropriate remediation), the Precinct and Teralba Southgate can be made suitable for its intended uses 
while protecting human health and environmental values, including Cockle Creek and Lake Macquarie. 
Based on available data and with consideration to identified data gaps, the assessment concludes that 
known or potential contamination is unlikely to preclude commercial/industrial rezoning for the majority of the 
Precinct and Teralba Southgate, provided that targeted investigation and appropriate management controls 
are implemented during future design and construction phases.  However, suitability determinations vary by 
sub-precinct and proposed land use. Employment-led commercial and industrial uses are generally 
considered compatible with the current contamination profile across most sub-precincts. However, more 
sensitive land uses including medium or high-density residential, conservation, and recreational uses, 
require targeted investigation and risk assessment to confirm suitability. This is particularly important at 
Teralba Southgate where detailed ground gas assessments have not been undertaken. The Tailings Storage 
Facility (Domain 7) also represents a material constraint requiring detailed assessment and integrated 
management across multiple environmental and engineering disciplines. 
Implementation of the management framework and performance criteria outlined in this CTA, combined with 
progressive investigation and remediation through the DA approval process, will enable the Precinct and 
Teralba Southgate to support sustainable post-mining land use while protecting human health and 
environmental values in Cockle Creek and Lake Macquarie.  
Based on the findings of this assessment, and subject to the limitations outlined in Section 11, Aurecon 
presents the following recommendations:  
◼ Implement a risk-based, staged investigation program for all future development proposals, with Detailed 
Site Investigations (DSIs) and Tier 2/3 quantitative risk assessments undertaken where elevated COPC 
concentrations are present or data gaps are identified, ensuring land use suitability is confirmed prior to 
development approval 
◼ Prioritise targeted investigation of Domains 2, 5, 7, 14, and 16 (uninvestigated domains), comprehensive 
groundwater assessment across all domains, ASS characterisation in low-lying areas, and asbestos 
delineation sampling to resolve material data gaps constraining sensitive land use suitability 
determination 
◼ Undertake integrated assessment of the Tailings Storage Facility (TSF) across water management, 
geotechnical stability, dam safety, and regulatory compliance frameworks, including geochemical 
characterisation of tailings materials and assessment of leachate generation and Acid Mine Drainage 
(AMD) pathways to inform remediation and long-term management strategy 
◼ Undertake targeted surface water and sediment quality assessments adjacent to waterway and wetland 
interface zones (including recreational areas within West Lake); and assess PFAS-impacted areas in 
accordance with the PFAS National Environmental Management Plan (NEMP 3.1) 
◼ Undertake comprehensive ground gas assessment in accordance with NSW EPA Assessment and 
management of hazardous ground gases (EPA 2020), with particular focus on Domains 11 and 13 where 
methane concentrations were reported. If required, implement ground gas mitigation measures during 
building design and construction to prevent vapour intrusion risk to future enclosed structures 
◼ Confirm land suitability for more sensitive uses (residential in Teralba Southgate, conservation, and 
recreational uses) through targeted investigation of soil, groundwater, surface water, and ground gas; 
implement PFAS plume delineation, asbestos delineation, and methane management measures; obtain 
Site Audit Statements from NSW EPA-accredited Site Auditors where remediation or management 
measures are implemented 
◼ Implement contamination pathway controls during earthworks and future development to prevent 
migration of identified COPCs to Cockle Creek and Lake Macquarie 
◼ Ensure all contamination assessments comply with NSW EPA Guidelines and are prepared by a suitably 
qualified contaminated land consultant including any review and update of duty to report obligations under 
Section 60 of the Contaminated Land Management Act 1997 at each DA-stage investigation and 

--- Cont Page 7 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
 
 
 
preparation of Long-Term Environmental Management Plans (LTEMPs) where residual contamination 
risks remain. As per Lake Macquarie City Council’s (LMCCs) requirements, an EPA certified consultant 
must be engaged where reports are submitted to the NSW EPA or where required by the consent 
authority 
◼ All future works should be conducted by an appropriately qualified environmental consultant under the 
direction of a CEnvP-SC or equivalent accreditation. An accredited NSW EPA Auditor may be required to 
endorse the investigation, remediation/management and validation works where more sensitive land uses 
are proposed or where there are elevated risks to ecological receptors. 
Pathway for Residential Development (Teralba Southgate) 
Residential development at Teralba Southgate will require a standard but targeted contaminated land 
assessment and approval process, including: 
◼ Detailed Site Investigation (DSI) involving intrusive assessment to fully characterise the nature and extent 
of contamination across the site in potentially affected media (i.e. ground gas and to a lesser extent soil, 
groundwater, surface water, sediment) with data comparison made to applicable land use criteria as per 
the NEPM (e.g. medium to high density residential). 
◼ Remedial Action Plan (RAP) to define extents and media requiring remediation and/or management to 
render the site suitable for the proposed land uses (e.g. residential). 
◼ Validation sampling and reporting to confirm remediation objectives have been achieved. 
◼ Independent Site Audit by an accredited NSW EPA Auditor which is recommended for residential land 
use on a former mine site, to provide independent assurance of site suitability prior to development 
consent being granted. 
This process will demonstrate that the land is suitable, or can be made suitable, for residential use in 
accordance with the NEPM (2013), EP&A Act, State Environmental Planning Policy (SEPP, Resilience and 
Hazards) 2021 and relevant NSW EPA legislation and guidelines.

1 
Introduction 
1.1 
Introduction 
Aurecon Australasia (Aurecon) was engaged by the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure 
(DPHI) for a variety of engineering services to support the State-led rezoning of the Macquarie Coal 
Complex, herein referred to as “the Precinct” and “Teralba Southgate”. The Precinct and Teralba Southgate 
are located approximately 20 kilometres (km) southwest of Newcastle, in the Lake Macquarie region of New 
South Wales (NSW). It is noted that Teralba Southgate has been removed from the scope of the Master Plan 
and will not be pursued under a State Environmental Planning Policy (SEPP) rezoning process. Instead, 
Teralba Southgate is proposed to be rezoned under a Local Environmental Plan (LEP). A figure showing the 
location and extent of the Precinct and Teralba Southgate is provided in Figure 1, Appendix A. 
The Precinct encompasses the former West Wallsend Colliery (WWC), the Macquarie Coal Preparation 
Plant (MCPP), the former open-cut Westside Mine, and the former Teralba Colliery (Northgate site). Mining 
operations ceased progressively across the Precinct, with Teralba Colliery closing in 2001, Westside Mine 
ceasing operations in 2012, and West Wallsend Colliery and Macquarie Coal Preparation Plant concluding 
operations in 2016.Current activities are focused on long-term environmental management and rehabilitation 
in accordance with the Rehabilitation Management Plan (RMP 2022). 
This Contamination Technical Assessment (CTA) builds on the Post Mining Land Use Engineering Analysis 
Report (Aurecon 2026) and has been developed to support refinement of the Master Plan and to inform 
DPHI's decision making as part of the rezoning process. It is noted that environmental and contamination 
investigations completed to date have been undertaken primarily to support mine closure obligations, rather 
than to establish suitability for alternative land uses. Accordingly, this assessment reinterprets existing 
contamination data within the context of the proposed rezoning and future land use scenarios shown in 
Figure 2, Appendix A. 
1.2 
Objectives 
The objective of this CTA is to support refinement of the Master Plan and to inform DPHI's decision making 
as part of the rezoning process. Specifically, the objectives of this CTA are to: 
◼ Provide a precinct-scale contaminated land evidence base to support rezoning and Master Plan land use 
compatibility, building on existing contamination assessments referenced through Enquiry by Design 
(EbD) engineering discussions 
◼ Confirm whether contamination represents a material constraint to developable land verification for 
employment-led uses and identify where more sensitive land uses would require additional evidence and 
management 
◼ Translate contamination findings into Master Plan-ready objectives, performance criteria and a clear 
staged investigation/remediation pathway to be implemented post rezoning.

1.3 
Methodology 
The scope of this CTA comprises five integrated components to achieve the rezoning objectives including: 
◼ Desktop compilation including a review and synthesis of previous investigations and assessment 
documents 
◼ Systematic constraints analysis including the identification of Areas of Environmental Concern (AECs) 
and assessment of remediation implications under different land use scenarios 
◼ Development of a Conceptual Site Model (CSM) to integrate source pathway receptor (SPR) linkages 
across the Precinct and Teralba Southgate 
◼ Identification of data gaps to inform recommendations for future investigation 
◼ Development of a management framework to integrate contamination management into the future 
planning and development approval pathway, including staged investigation triggers, regulatory 
notification protocols, and interfaces with other engineering and environmental disciplines.

Planning context and limitations  
2.1 
Level of detail and exclusions  
This CTA report has been prepared appropriate for a rezoning and Master Plan stage and is structured to 
support precinct-scale land use compatibility decisions and developable land verification for the Precinct and 
Teralba Southgate. This report builds on the existing information mainly from prior investigations undertaken 
across the Precinct and Teralba Southgate at various stages, primarily in support of mine closure obligations 
and reinterprets that data within the context of the proposed rezoning and future land use scenarios. 
This CTA is not intended or scoped to deliver a development application (DA) level investigation, detailed 
remediation design, or construction validation for the Precinct and Teralba Southgate. The assessment has 
been prepared to inform the Structure Plan and development of a Master Plan and to support the DPHI’s 
decision-making as part of the State-led rezoning process. 
Typical items as part of the staged contamination risk assessment and assurance framework are excluded 
from this assessment and would need to be addressed progressively through the DA and approvals process 
as individual proposals are brought forward. These include the following: 
◼ Preliminary Site Investigations (PSIs) 
◼ Detailed site investigations (DSIs) 
◼ Sampling Analysis and Quality Plans (SAQPs) 
◼ Remedial Action Plan (RAP) or management plans relating to contamination including remediation 
costing.

3 
Baseline analysis 
This section presents the baseline environmental and contamination information for the Precinct and Teralba 
Southgate. The baseline analysis draws on a series of previous contamination investigations undertaken 
primarily to support mine closure obligations drawing on the existing evidence base compiled from previous 
investigations and publicly available information. Existing data and available information for the Precinct and 
Teralba Southgate have been reinterpreted within the context of the proposed rezoning and future land use 
scenarios identified in the Structure Plan (Figure 1, Appendix A). This section includes summary of the 
environmental setting information for the Precinct and Teralba Southgate, identifies key AECs and summary 
of previous remediation activities that form the basis for the CSM, and constraint assessment presented in 
Section 4.  
3.1 
Environmental setting  
As outlined in Section 1.1, the Precinct is located approximately 20 kilometres southwest of Newcastle in 
Lake Macquarie, NSW. It comprises four sub-sites (West Wallsend Colliery, Macquarie Coal Preparation 
Plant, Westside Mine, and Teralba Colliery (Northgate) and is currently zoned SP1, Special Activities 
(Mining), C2 Environmental Conservation, C3 Environmental Management and RU2 Rural Landscape 
pursuant to the Lake Macquarie Local Environmental Plan 2014. Teralba Southgate is currently zoned as 
Special Activities (Mining) and occupies an area of approximately 7 hectares (ha). Areas surrounding the 
Precinct and Teralba Southgate generally comprise residential communities and mixed-use industrial land 
uses. A summary of environmental features within the Precinct and Teralba Southgate is provided in Table 
3-1. 
Table 3-1 Summary of Environmental Setting 
Environmental Feature 
Description 
Soil  
A combined review of soil landscape information provided by eSPADE tool hosted by 
the NSW Department of Planning, Industry and Environment (DPE 2025) and previous 
investigations completed at the Precinct and Teralba Southgate indicates that surficial 
soils generally comprise sandy loam topsoil transitioning to sandy clay, with variable fill 
materials (1.9–8.5 m depth) containing coal fragments, concrete, brick and metal. 
Geology 
A review of geological information sourced from NSW Seamless Geology MinView 
(Version 2.5, released May 2025) paired with previous investigations indicates that the 
Precinct and Teralba Southgate is underlain by a mix of sandstone, conglomerate, 
shale, tuff, and coal seams. 
Hydrogeology  
Review of previous investigations indicates that a shallow unconfined groundwater 
underlies the Precinct and Teralba Southgate at approximate depths between 2 m 
below top of casing (btoc) and 15 m btoc. Groundwater quality was reported to be fresh 
to slightly brackish quality (EC 691–1,780 µS/cm) and generally flowed easterly toward 
Cockle Creek and Lake Macquarie.  
Hydrology 
Rainfall is expected to primarily be captured within on-site storage dams or flow to open 
drains in the north-east or south-east of the Precinct and Teralba Southgate. These 
drains eventually discharge to Cockle Creek located approximately 210 metres east of 
the Precinct. During periods of high or prolonged rainfall, it is expected that rainfall 
would flow overland and naturally diffuse to surrounding land.

3.3 
Summary of Previous Investigations  
Contamination investigations across the Precinct and Teralba Southgate have been undertaken 
progressively since 2005 spanning many of the 16 closure Domains. The investigations have been carried 
out by multiple consultants with varying objectives targeting different parts of the Precinct and Teralba 
Southgate. Environmental reports considered as part of this assessment are also listed in Section 1.5. A 
summary of investigations undertaken at each Domain is provided below and discussed further in Appendix 
B. Environmental reports considered as part of this assessment are also listed in Section 1.5. 
RCA Australia (2005) undertook the earliest intrusive investigations across Domains 1 to 4. SLR (2017) 
completed a Precinct-wide assessment across Domains 1, 3, 4, and 6 and did not report human health 
exceedances under a commercial/industrial scenario, however detected ecological exceedances for heavy 
metals and TRH in fill soils. Coffey (2019 to 2020) targeted Domain 6 Catchment Dams, and reported 
additional ecological exceedances for zinc, copper, TRH, PAHs, and PFAS, as well as identified asbestos 
containing material (ACM) in shallow topsoil. 

--- Cont Page 17 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B 
 
8 
 
 
 
Domains 9 and 10 were assessed by SLR (2017) and Coffey (2018–2021). Partial validation of Domain 10 
Maturation Pond remediation identified two residual exceedance locations and heavy metal exceedances 
and ASS were confirmed in Catchment Dam sediments. SLR (2016) identified potential impacts associated 
with slag in the coal stockpile areas of Domain 9. WSP (2025) assessed the Domain 7 TSF for geotechnical 
integrity and closure design only; no intrusive contamination data was included. 
Domains 11 and 13 assessments confirmed ecological exceedances for heavy metals, TRH, PAHs, and 
PFAS in soils and groundwater, methane gas at Domain 11 mine shaft locations, and ACM at both domains. 
Domain 12 assessment by SLR (2017) identified ecological exceedances for zinc and TRH, and elevated 
selenium and uranium concentrations along the Haul Road.

3.5 
Data gaps 
While several investigations have been undertaken at precinct, Aurecon have identified a variety of data 
gaps and uncertainties associated with the level of assessment completed to date. The most common data 
gaps include absence of surface or groundwater data across multiple domains, incomplete or absent ASS 
characterisation across the majority of the Precinct and Teralba Southgate, unassessed building footprints 
and inaccessible structures in Domains 1 and 11, incomplete surface water and sediment quality 
assessment in several domains, and extents of buried asbestos pipework in Domains 6 and 10 has not been 
fully defined. A general data gap across multiple domains is the use of superseded hydrocarbon assessment 
criteria, with hydrocarbon data previously assessed against NEPM 1999 rather than the current NEPM 2013. 
These data gaps are summarised in Appendix C and will need to be progressively resolved through the 
staged DA-stage investigation programs.

4 
Conceptual Site Model 
4.1 
Sources, pathways, and receptors 
Risks associated with potential site contamination are based on evaluating the linkages between sources, 
pathways and receptors (SPRs based) on site specific environmental setting, potential design strategies, and 
proposed land use scenarios. The development of a conceptual site model (CSM) for the Precinct and 
Teralba Southgate facilitates an evaluation of the source-pathway-receptor relationships to assist in 
identifying potential contamination risks based on the nature of the contamination sources, degree of 
exposure of each receptor to a source, and the sensitivity of the likely receptors. A general description of the 
CSM components required to evaluate contamination risk is provided in Table 4-1. 
Table 4-1 Summary of key CSM components 
Term 
Description  
Source 
A substance that has the potential to cause harm to human or environmental receptors. Sources can be 
primary (at the original point of release) or secondary (at a point further down-gradient from the primary 
source following temporary storage and / or transformation) and can be either direct (i.e. emanating 
from a localised area) or diffuse (i.e. widespread) in nature. In a broader sense, sources can also 
include particular ground conditions that may impact on construction materials such as aggressive soils 
(i.e. ASS).   
Pathway 
The route by which the source is brought into contact with the receptor. This can include the transport of 
contamination via water (surface and groundwater), airborne dust, vapours, and particulate-matter 
deposition. It can also include solubility or chemical transformation from a relatively harmless chemical 
species to one that is more toxic. 
Receptor 
Human beings, other living organisms, and built structures that could be affected by the contamination 
source. A receptor will only be affected if an exposure pathway from the source to the receptor is 
complete. 
Groundwater and surface water systems can be considered as receptors as their quality is regulated by 
statutory bodies, as well as being potential pathways for contaminant migration to other receptors. 
In a broader sense, a receptor can be building or construction materials from the presence of 
aggressive soil conditions. 
4.2 
Domain Constraints Analysis  
This section presents a preliminary constraints analysis for each domain presented in Section 3.2. The 
constraints analysis provides a structured, risk-based assessment for each domain based on available data 
and the current structure plan. The analysis is intended to support the rezoning and land use suitability 
assessments at the Precinct and Teralba Southgate and identify where further investigation or remediation is 
required to support or progress the rezoning. The constraint rating for each domain was derived by 
combining a consequence qualification (Section 4.2.1) with a likelihood qualification (Section 4.2.2) using 
the constraint determination matrix (Section 4.2.3).  
4.2.1 
Consequence qualification 
Consequence is defined as the magnitude of potential adverse planning or environmental outcome that 
could result if a constraint were it to materialise in the context of the proposed rezoning strategy. 
Consequences were qualified across three categories that reflect the key considerations relevant to a 
planning proposal and land use suitability assessment under the EP&A Act and CLM Act frameworks. A 
summary of potential consequences and their associated ratings is presented in Table 4-2.

4.2.2 
Likelihood qualification 
Likelihood is defined as the probability that a potential constraint will occur, or be confirmed as present, 
under the proposed land use scenario. Likelihood was qualified based on the weight of available evidence, 
including historical land use data, existing analytical results, site observations, and any identified data gaps. 
A summary of the adopted likelihood ratings is presented below: 
◼ Rare – No credible evidence supports the presence of contamination constraints under the proposed land 
use. Occurrence of elevated contaminants may be present under exceptional circumstances, however is 
not supported by available data 
◼ Unlikely – Available data does not support the presence of contamination constraints. Presence of 
elevated contaminants under proposed land use scenarios is plausible but not expected 
◼ Possible – Contamination constraints may be present or may occur based on identified potential sources 
or pathways 
◼ Likely – Strong evidence or credible site history suggests contamination constraints are present or will 
manifest during redevelopment 
◼ Almost Certain– Contamination constraints are expected to be present based on confirmed site history, 
analytical data, or physical observation. Occurrence is effectively certain under the proposed land use 
and/or development scenario.

4.3 
Constraint determination 
A constraint rating for each domain was determined by combining the consequence and likelihood ratings 
using the matrix in Table 4-3. The matrix applies a conservative approach consistent with the range of 
proposed land uses, with greater weight given to consequence where data gaps exist and receptor 
sensitivity is high (e.g. residential and conservation precincts). Where a domain transects multiple land use 
zones, the more sensitive land use was adopted to derive the constraints rating.

Aurecon has defined the constraints ratings outlined in Error! Reference source not found. as the following: 
◼ Negligible – No known or likely constraint to the proposed rezoning or land use scenario. Contaminant 
concentrations and site conditions are likely consistent with background concentrations or below 
thresholds and do not represent a planning, regulatory, or environmental risk 
◼ Low – Minor or manageable constraint that can be addressed through standard construction and 
environmental management practices. No material impact on rezoning or redevelopment, subject to 
further assessment and standard regulatory compliance 
◼ Moderate – Moderate constraint that warrants further assessment and consideration in future planning, 
design or construction phases. Risk-based management measures, development controls, or targeted 
remediation are likely required 
◼ High – Significant constraint requiring targeted investigation and/or remediation prior to or concurrent with 
rezoning or redevelopment. The proposed land use may be achievable subject to a defined remediation 
or risk management strategy and, where applicable, a Site Audit Statement 
◼ Very High – Fundamental constraint to proposed rezoning or redevelopment program. Contamination or 
environmental conditions are likely incompatible with the proposed land use without significant 
remediation, risk management, or design modification.

5 
Land Use Capability  
The following sections present key findings as they relate to the current structure and master plan, 
interpreting available contamination data and information including analytical results, data gaps, and 
management requirements necessary to support the proposed employment-led uses. Where contamination 
is known or potentially present, recommendations are provided to guide remediation priorities and validation 
requirements prior to development. A figure showing the locations of the domains as they relate to the 
structure plan is provided in Figure 7, Appendix A. 
Throughout the following sections, the term ‘investigation level’ is used which refer to Tier I screening values 
included in the NEPM 2013 (or its preceding version) under commercial industrial land use, or other 
guidance documents such as NEMPv3.1 and ANZG 2018. Tier I screening values are generic 
concentrations, exceedance of which indicate a potential risk could be present in a certain area. Exceedance 
of investigation levels or Tier I screening values do not automatically require remediation or management, 
but rather further investigation and additional tiers of risk assessments are required. It is possible that 
quantitative human health and/or ecological risk assessments can be developed to establish site specific 
levels that inform the necessary extent of remediation/management required to render a particular area as 
suitable for an intended land use. 
5.1 
Sub precinct 1 – Cockle Creek 
Exceedances of investigation levels have been confirmed across multiple contaminants and domains within 
the Cockle Creek sub-precinct. Concentrations of zinc, copper, selenium, uranium, PFAS, nutrients and TRH 
in soil were reported above the ecological assessment criteria adopted during previous investigations. 
Exceedances of human health criteria for industrial/commercial land use were not detected in soil at this sub-
precinct, however fragments of asbestos in fill were identified in fill materials (Domain 11). Detectable 
methane gas emissions were also recorded from mine shafts, indicating a potential ground gas hazard. 
While this sub-precinct has been subject to a variety of previous investigations and localised remediation 
(Domain 10), data gaps and uncertainties exist within this sub-precinct including Domains 7 and 14, ASS 
characterisation, asbestos pipework, and targeted assessment of ground gas, soil/sediment, surface water, 
and groundwater. Domain 7 may represent the most significant constraint on the basis as an intrusive 
investigation has not been undertaken for this domain. These data gaps impact the ability to confidently 
verify land suitability for employment-led uses without additional evidence and management measures.  
Based on available data, and with consideration to identified data gaps, known or potential contamination is 
unlikely to preclude commercial/industrial rezoning but requires targeted investigation of soil, sediment, 
groundwater, surface water and soil vapour/ground gas to confirm land suitability. Heavy industrial uses, as 
currently proposed, are considered compatible with the current understanding of the contamination profile at 
this sub-precinct provided appropriate assessment and management controls are implemented during future 
design and construction phases. Implementation of these management measures will enable the Precinct to 
support employment-led development while protecting environmental values in Cockle Creek and Lake 
Macquarie.

5.2 
Sub precinct 2 – Killingworth 
Exceedances of investigation levels have been confirmed across multiple domains within the Killingworth 
sub-precinct. Concentrations of TRH (C10–C16) in fill were detected above adopted ecological assessment 
criteria in Domain 1 which were associated with historical fuel storage and former UST areas. Exceedances 
of EILs for zinc and TRH were also confirmed in Domain 2, and anomalous enrichment of selenium and 
uranium was identified at a targeted location in Domain 12. Exceedances of human health investigation 
levels were not identified within this sub-precinct. 
Data gaps remain within this sub-precinct including Domains 2 and 14 which have not been subject to 
intrusive investigations. Domain 3 is lacking data outside the borrow pit area, and limited assessment of ASS 
within this sub-precinct. The absence of intrusive data for Domains 2 and 14 represents the most significant 
constraint on land suitability determination. 
Based on available data, known or potential contamination is unlikely to preclude commercial/industrial 
rezoning of the Killingworth sub-precinct but requires targeted investigation of soil, groundwater, surface 
water, soil vapour, and ASS across all domains to confirm land suitability for the proposed light industrial 
use. Previously reported hydrocarbon data also require reassessment against current NEPM 2013 criteria. 
Implementation of appropriate assessment and management measures during future investigation and 
design phases will enable the sub-precinct to support employment-led development. 
5.3 
Sub precinct 3 – West Lake 
Exceedances of ecological assessment criteria have been confirmed at Domain 4 within this sub-precinct. 
Concentrations of zinc and nutrients in surface sediments were recorded above ecological screening levels 
on the north-west margin of the final void of Domain 4. Hydrocarbons and nutrients also exceeded ESLs in 
sediment samples from this domain. Exceedances of ecological or human health assessment criteria were 
not detected in the borrow pit area within Domain 3, indicating that soil conditions in this domain are suitable 
for the proposed commercial-industrial land use based on available data.  
Data gaps constrain land suitability determination across this sub-precinct. Domain 3 lacks intrusive 
investigation data outside the borrow pit area and requires hydrocarbon data reassessment under NEPM 
2013. Domain 4 presents the most significant constraint, with limited available information on bioremediation 
operations and surface water quality retained in the void, insufficiently investigated peripheral areas, and 
submerged sediments inaccessible for assessment. While Domains 14 and 16 are considered to represent 
low risk areas, they have not been subject to intrusive investigations and remain data gaps.  
Based on available data and information, known or potential contamination is unlikely to preclude 
commercial-industrial rezoning of West Lake; however, targeted investigation of soil, sediment, groundwater, 
and surface water is required to confirm land suitability for the proposed tourism and resort uses. The 
ecological exceedances identified in Domain 4 require assessment and management to ensure compatibility 
with the proposed mixed-use development. Additional investigations of all domains within this sub-precinct 
are necessary to address data gaps and verify that these areas do not present unmanageable constraints. 
Surface water within the void (Domain 4) should particularly be subject to detailed assessment given it’s 
proposed to be used for recreational purposes. Implementation of additional assessment programs and 
management controls for this sub-precinct would be necessary to support the proposed rezoning.

5.4 
Teralba Southgate 
Exceedances of investigation levels have been confirmed for multiple contaminants within Teralba 
Southgate. Domain 13 (Teralba Southgate) exhibits confirmed exceedances of ecological criteria for zinc, 
TRH, and benzo(a)pyrene (BaP) in soil, and groundwater exceedances for hexavalent chromium, nickel, 
zinc, and PFAS. Multiple exceedances of sediment criteria have also been recorded for TRH, cadmium, 
copper, lead, mercury, nickel, and zinc. Other identified impacts included the confirmed presence of 
chrysotile asbestos in fill material near the methane plant, and methane gas concentrations exceeding the 
lower explosive limit (LEL) detected during drilling. However, exceedances of human health criteria for 
commercial/industrial land use were not detected during previous investigations, indicating the potential 
suitability of this site for industrial use from a human health perspective. 
Data gaps and uncertainties remain within this site that limit the ability to fully characterise the contamination 
profile and assess suitability for the proposed mixed-use development including high-density residential, 
recreation, and commercial-industrial uses. Further assessment of soil and groundwater is required, 
particularly sampling beneath the workshop, which has not been completed. Asbestos delineation sampling 
has not been undertaken to confirm the full extent of ACM-impacted materials. Surface water sampling has 
not been completed, and detailed ground gas assessments remain outstanding. Additionally, the proposed 
rezoning to high-density residential mixed-use introduces more sensitive land use scenarios than the current 
industrial classification, requiring assessment against residential and public open space criteria rather than 
commercial/industrial for certain exposure pathways.  
Based on available data and with consideration to identified data gaps and limitations, known or potential 
contamination presents a constraint to the proposed high-density residential mixed-use rezoning of this sub-
precinct. While the absence of human health criteria exceedances under commercial/industrial land use 
confirms likely suitability for continued light industrial purposes, the proposed rezoning to include high-
density residential and recreational uses introduces more sensitive exposure scenarios that require targeted 
investigation and risk assessment. The site is likely suitable for the proposed commercial-industrial and 
recreation components of the mixed-use development, provided appropriate assessment and management 
controls are implemented during future design and construction phases. However, the residential component 
requires completion of targeted investigation of ground gas, and to a lesser extent soil, groundwater, and 
surface water to confirm land suitability under residential exposure scenario and to delineate the PFAS 
plume extent. Implementation of management measures including potential capping of PFAS-impacted 
areas, groundwater monitoring, asbestos delineation, and methane management will be necessary to enable 
the this site to support the proposed mixed-use development while protecting environmental values in Cockle 
Bay and Lake Macquarie and ensuring human health protection for future residential occupants. 
As outlined in Section 1.1, through the rezoning process, land at Teralba Southgate is intended for 
residential purpose. For residential development to proceed, targeted contamination investigations will be 
required to demonstrate that Teralba Southgate is suitable, or can be made suitable, for residential land use 
consistent with the requirements of the NEPM 2013, EP&A Act, State Environmental Planning Policy (SEPP, 
Resilience and Hazards) 2021 and relevant NSW EPA legislation and guidelines. This will typically require a 
staged investigation and reporting pathway involving the preparation of the following documents: 
◼ DSI involving intrusive assessment to fully characterise the nature and extent of contamination across the 
site in potentially affected media (i.e. ground gas, soil, groundwater, surface water, sediment) with data 
comparison made to applicable land use criteria as per the NEPM (e.g. medium to high density 
residential). 
◼ RAP to define extents and media requiring remediation and/or management to render the site suitable for 
the proposed land uses (e.g. residential). 
◼ Validation sampling and reporting to confirm remediation objectives have been achieved. 
◼ Site Audit Report by a NSW EPA accredited site auditor, which is recommended for residential land use 
on a former mine site, to provide independent assurance of site suitability prior to development consent 
being granted.

5.5 
Sub precinct 5 – Barnsley West 
Limited exceedances of investigation levels have been detected in domains associated with this sub-
precinct. Domain 12 occupies a small portion of this sub-precinct and is known to contain exceedances of 
ecological criteria for zinc and TRH in fill materials. However, human health criteria exceedances have not 
been recorded for this domain under a commercial/industrial land use. Domain 14 has not been subject to 
intrusive investigations and as such, data and information is not available for interpretation.  
Data gaps limit a detailed understanding of the contamination profile for this sub-precinct. ASS may underlie 
this sub-precinct, and intrusive data is required to determine whether it represents a constraint to future 
development. While this sub-precinct lacks available intrusive data, potential contamination is unlikely to 
preclude commercial and industrial land use given the lower receptor sensitivity associated with this land use 
category. Implementation of a targeted investigation program including soil and groundwater sampling during 
future development applications will enable confirmation of site suitability for commercial/industrial 
development while protecting worker health and environment values.  
5.6 
Sub precinct 6 –Environmentally Sensitive Areas 
5.6.1 
Sub precinct 6a 
Limited exceedances of investigation levels have been confirmed in multiple domains associated with this 
sub-precinct. Domain 3 exhibits no exceedances of human health or ecological investigation levels. Domain 
12 presents confirmed exceedances of ecological criteria for zinc and TRH in fill materials, with anomalous 
enrichment of selenium and uranium identified at a targeted haul road location. Domains 14 and 16 have not 
been subject to intrusive investigations. No human health criteria exceedances have been recorded within 
this sub-precinct based on available data. 
Data gaps constrain full characterisation of the contamination profile across this sub-precinct. Domain 3 
lacks investigation data outside the borrow pit area and requires hydrocarbon data reassessment under 
NEPM 2013. Domain 12 presents minor data gaps including uncharacterised selenium and uranium 
enrichment, and data has not been collected for Domains 14 and 16. 
Known or potential contamination is unlikely to preclude conservation rezoning of Conservation Area 6a. The 
absence of human health exceedances and limited ecological findings confirm broad compatibility with 
conservation land use. Confirmation of suitability requires targeted soil investigation at this sub-precinct to 
close identified data gaps and further evaluate potential ecological risks to enable the Precinct to support 
conservation land use while protecting environmental values and Lake Macquarie. 
5.6.2 
Sub precinct 6b 
Exceedances of investigation levels have been confirmed across multiple contaminants and domains 
associated with this sub-precinct. Domain 1 confirms EIL exceedances for TRH F2 (C10–C16) in fill soils 
associated with fuel and lubricant storage, vehicle refuelling, and former UST areas. Domain 2 presents EIL 
exceedances for zinc and TRH, and Domain 12 confirms ecological exceedances for zinc and TRH F2 in fill 
soils, with anomalous selenium and uranium enrichment at a targeted haul road location. Human health 
criteria exceedances have not been detected during previous investigations.  
A number of data gaps exists within this sub-precinct including Domains 5 and 14 which have not been 
subject to intrusive investigation, and Domain 1 where building footprints and car parks remain 
uninvestigated and no information exists on removal of the Domain 1 fuel storage facility. Domain 2 lacks 
intrusive investigation data. Domain 12 contains uncharacterised selenium and uranium enrichment which is 
considered a lesser constraint. 
Based on available data, known or potential contamination is unlikely to preclude conservation rezoning. The 
absence of human health exceedances and limited ecological findings confirm broad compatibility with 
conservation land use. However, further investigation is needed to address identified data gaps, particularly 
for Domain 1 which represents the highest constraint for this sub-precinct. Additional investigation will 
provide defensible evidence and ensure contamination does not constrain conservation objectives.

5.6.4 
Sub precinct 6d 
Exceedances of investigation levels have been confirmed across multiple domains associated with this sub-
precinct. Domain 9 exhibits confirmed EIL exceedances for TRH and zinc in soils, with fibrous asbestos 
confirmed near former infrastructure. Domain 10 includes ecological exceedances for heavy metals, TRH, 
and PAHs in maturation pond sediments, with PFOS exceeding the 99% species protection criterion in 
surface water. Asbestos was confirmed in surface soils near demolished buildings in Domain 11. However,

Data gaps limit a detailed understanding of the contamination profile for this sub-precinct. Domain 9 presents 
incomplete wastewater cell assessment, absent groundwater data, and incomplete asbestos 
characterisation. Domain 10 presents incomplete maturation pond sediment characterisation, limited

investigations have been undertaken for Domain 14. 
Based on available data and information, known or potential contamination is unlikely to preclude 
conservation rezoning of Conservation Area 6d. However, targeted investigation is required within this sub-
precinct, particularly for sediment and surface water bodies that occupy the northern portion of this sub-
precinct and have not been subject to detailed assessment. Other potential contamination sources 
associated with Domains 9, 10 and 11 are considered less likely to restrict the capacity of this sub-precinct to 
be rezoned for conservation on the basis that many are located external to the zoning boundary (as shown in 
Figure 7, Appendix A). Notwithstanding, targeted site inspections and sediment and surface water 
assessments will enable this area to support conservation land use while protecting environmental values 
and Lake Macquarie.

undertaken within these domains, and consequently no confirmed exceedances of investigation levels have 
been detected in soil, groundwater, surface water, or sediment. Data gaps therefore remain within this sub-
precinct that constrain the ability to confirm land suitability with confidence.  
Domain 14 is unlikely to preclude conservation zoning for this sub-precinct. However, Domain 7 represents a 
material constraint that requires further assessment. Targeted investigations of soil, sediment, surface water, 
and ground gas is required to resolve remaining uncertainties and confirm land use suitability for future use.

5.7 
Interfaces with other constraints  
Management of identified COPCs across the Precinct and Teralba Southgate does not operate in isolation, it 
interacts with a number of other environmental and engineering constraints that must be considered in an 
integrated manner during Master Plan planning, rezoning, and future DA-stage assessments. The following 
section summarises other environmental constraints that require further assessment or consideration at the 
Precinct and Teralba Southgate. 
5.7.1 
Waterways and Wetlands 
The Precinct and Teralba Southgate is surrounded by sensitive water bodies including Cockle Creek, Lake 
Macquarie, and associated wetlands. Several domains contain contaminants, including heavy metals, 
hydrocarbons, nutrients, and PFAS, that may represent a risk of migration to these receiving environments 
via surface water runoff and groundwater discharge pathways, including Domains 4, 6, 9, 10, and 13. 
Surface water and groundwater investigations must be undertaken at the DA stage for proposals adjacent to 
or within the waterway and wetland interface zones, with results assessed against relevant environmental 
legislation and guidance including (but not limited to) the Australian and New Zealand Guidelines for Fresh 
and Marine Water Quality (ANZG 2018). Where PFAS is identified as a COPC, assessment must be 
undertaken in accordance with the PFAS NEMP 3.1. Contamination pathways to these receptors must be 
identified and controlled during earthworks and development consistent the performance criteria outlined in 
Section 6.2. 
5.7.2 
Acid Sulfate Soils 
As shown in Figure 3 (Appendix A), discrete occurrences of potential acid sulfate soils (PASS) have been 
identified across multiple sub-precincts, including Cockle Creek (sub-precinct 1), Killingworth (sub-precinct 
2), Barnsley West (sub-precinct 5), and environmentally constrained sub-precincts 6b, 6c, and 6d. 
Disturbance of ASS during earthworks or dewatering activities can generate acid leachate that mobilises 
heavy metals into groundwater and surface water, presenting a risk to receiving waterways and wetlands. 
While PASS may underlie some areas, it is not expected that this will likely be disturbed based on the 
current zoning plan. However, where PASS may be disturbed, an Acid Sulfate Soil Management Plan 
(ASSMP) must be prepared and implemented prior to earthworks in relevant sub-precincts, consistent with 
the performance criteria outlined in Section 6.2. The ASS risk must be considered in the context of 
geotechnical and dewatering planning at the DA stage to ensure integrated management outcomes. 
 
 

--- Cont Page 31 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B 
 22 
 
 
 
5.7.3 
Salinity 
As shown in Figure 4 (Appendix A), portions of the Precinct and Teralba Southgate are classified as 
moderate to very high salinity hazard zones, associated with low-lying areas, disturbed terrain, and the 
Cockle Creek floodplain interface. Elevated salt concentrations reflect historical mining operations, 
evaporative concentration in surface water structures, and estuarine influence from Lake Macquarie. Salinity 
hazard presents a material constraint to sensitive land use rezoning and may trigger additional assessment 
requirements at the development application stage.  
Within environmentally constrained areas (6a–6f), elevated salinity may preclude low-salinity native 
vegetation establishment, requiring soil remediation, salt-tolerant species selection, or hydrological 
management. In areas where structures are proposed, elevated salinity increases corrosivity risk to buried 
infrastructure and requires assessment of foundation stability where shallow groundwater and high 
evaporative demand may induce heave or differential settlement. Dewatering and excavation require 
management to prevent salt-laden leachate mobilisation.  
Salinity risk should be integrated into site-wide water cycle management and contamination control planning. 
Detailed salinity assessment, including soil and groundwater profiling, should be undertaken for Teralba 
Southgate and all sub-precincts proposed for sensitive land uses prior to development approval. Salinity 
management measures including hydrological controls, soil amendment, or engineered containment should 
be embedded in Environmental Management Plans (EMPs) and validated through post-construction 
monitoring to confirm effectiveness and ongoing compliance with land use suitability criteria. 
5.7.4 
Tailings Storage Facility 
The Tailings Storage Facility (TSF) in Domain 7 represents a discrete and material constraint that operates 
across multiple environmental and engineering disciplines, requiring integrated management during Master 
Plan planning and future development application assessments. Unlike contamination in other domains, the 
TSF presents a fundamental constraint to rezoning and redevelopment that extends beyond standard 
remediation pathways, necessitating coordinated consideration with water management, geotechnical 
stability, dam safety, and regulatory compliance frameworks.  
As outlined in Section 3-4, the TSF is currently being remediated to ensure the final landform is stable and 
environmentally sound, however has not been subject to detailed investigation to inform potential 
contamination risks. TSFs are known to contain tailings materials with unknown geochemical characteristics 
including potential acid-forming materials (PAF), spontaneous combustion potential, and salinity risks. 
Leachate generation and acid mine drainage (AMD) from tailings represent primary contamination pathways 
to downgradient groundwater and surface water environments. These pathways may directly interfere and 
constrain rezoning proposals or development applications, requiring detailed assessment by suitably 
qualified environmental consultants. On this basis, Aurecon recommends that further contamination 
investigations of soil, sediment, groundwater and surface water at and downgradient of the TSF be 
undertaken prior to rezoning and future development applications.   
5.7.5 
Earthworks and Spoil Management 
Significant bulk earthworks are anticipated across the Precinct as part of future development. If offsite 
disposal of material is required during future construction programs, subject material must be classified in 
accordance with the NSW EPA Waste Classification Guidelines, Part 1: Classifying Waste (2014) and PFAS 
Addendum (2016). Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure (TCLP) analysis may also be required for 
soils to confirm final waste categories. Where soils meet the criteria for Virgin Excavated Natural Material 
(VENM) or Excavated Natural Material (ENM), reuse as engineered fill offsite should be considered for 
relevant materials under the Resource Recovery Order or Resource Recovery Exemption (RRO/RRE) to 
minimise disposal costs and waste being sent to landfill. A Spoil Management Plan must be prepared prior to 
bulk earthworks commencing in accordance with the performance criteria outlined in Section 6.2.

contamination across the Precinct through future planning approvals and development stages. They are 
intended to be read in conjunction Sections 4 and 5 of this report. As outlined in Section 1.1, Teralba 
Southgate has been removed from the scope of the Master Plan and is therefore excluded from this section.

8 
Post exhibition management framework and 
approvals pathway  
This section describes how contaminated land will be managed through future planning and development 
approvals, consistent with the master plan objectives and performance criteria outlined in Sections 6 and 7. 
The management framework is structured around the post-exhibition approvals pathway and identifies both 
the obligations and opportunities associated with contamination management across the Precinct and 
Teralba Southgate. 
8.1 
Development application  
Development applications for land within the Precinct and Teralba Southgate must be supported by site 
specific contamination assessments that confirm site suitability for the proposed use, considerate of the 
engineering design, and identify any remediation or management measures required. The nature and extent 
of assessment required at the DA stage will be determined by the land use sensitivity, disturbance footprint, 
and contamination risk profile of identified contamination sources, consistent with performance criteria 1 
(PC1) in Section 6.2.  
Through this approach, contamination risks will be addressed progressively and proportionately, supporting 
the safe and sustainable transformation of the subject site(s) in line with the proposed vision for the Precinct 
and Teralba Southgate. The requirement and triggers for contamination assessment during future DA stages 
are outlined in Section 7. All contamination assessments must be prepared by a suitably qualified 
contaminated land consultant, consistent with LMCCs requirements for development on contaminated land 
and must comply with the NSW EPA Guidelines for Consultants Reporting on Contaminated Sites (2020). 
Where reports are submitted to the NSW EPA or otherwise required by the consent authority, assessments 
must be prepared or reviewed by a consultant certified under an EPA-recognised scheme (CEnvP-SC) or 
equivalent. 
8.2 
Regulatory notifications and duty to report  
Under Section 60 of the Contaminated Land Management Act 1997 (CLM Act), a person who becomes 
aware of contamination of land in NSW must notify the NSW EPA if the contamination is of a type, nature, or 
extent prescribed by the regulations. 
As outlined in this report, several domains contain elevated concentrations of COPCs, however available 
data does not confirm contamination at concentrations or extents sufficient to trigger a notification obligation 
under Section 60 of the CLM Act at this time. Aurecon notes that this conclusion is limited by the data gaps 
identified in Section 3.5, and a number of domains remain largely unassessed or partially investigated. The 
duty to report must therefore be reviewed and updated at each subsequent DA-stage investigation as 
additional intrusive data becomes available. Where future investigations identify contamination that may 
trigger reporting obligations, the relevant landowner or proponent must notify the NSW EPA in accordance 
with the CLM Act and the NSW EPA Guidelines on the Duty to Report Contamination under the CLM Act 
1997 (EPA 2015). 
 
 

--- Cont Page 39 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B 
 30 
 
 
 
8.3 
Opportunities  
The Precinct and Teralba Southgate present a number of opportunities to manage contaminated and 
potentially contaminated materials in a cost-effective and environmentally responsible manner. Identifying 
and pursuing these opportunities at future DA stages can significantly reduce off-site disposal costs and 
minimise the environmental footprint of future development. The following opportunities are identified for 
consideration in future development planning: 
◼ Existing data and information – the contamination investigations completed to date provide a 
substantial and layered evidence base across multiple domains that can be directly built upon for any 
required DSIs. In areas that have already been characterised to an appropriate level, the scope of new 
intrusive investigation can be minimised, reducing both cost and program risk for future development 
proposals 
◼ On-site bioremediation – hydrocarbon impacted soils may be suitable for treatment via an on-site 
bioremediation pad, where excavated material is treated in controlled conditions before being validated 
for reuse or disposal. This approach can significantly reduce off-site disposal volumes and associated 
costs for domains with confirmed hydrocarbon contamination 
◼ Onsite reuse as engineered fill – excavated soils that have been subject to an appropriate level of 
investigation and meets NEPM land use criteria and does not contain indicators of contamination can be 
reused onsite 
◼ Offsite reuse as engineered fill – excavated soils that meet the criteria for VENM or ENM may be 
reused offsite as engineered fill, subject to further classification and validation. RROs/RREs should be 
considered where applicable for aggregates, slag or other eligible materials 
◼ Waste characterisation and soil leachate analysis – TCLP analysis may be undertaken on 
contaminated soils to assess their potential for leaching and determine appropriate waste streams. This is 
particularly relevant for domains with PFAS, hydrocarbon or heavy metal contamination where soils 
require disposal to a licensed waste facility 
◼ Mine water reuse – treated mine water may present an opportunity for reuse in construction activities or 
irrigation across the Precinct and Teralba Southgate, subject to water quality assessment and appropriate 
approvals. This should be considered in the context of integrated water cycle planning for the Precinct 
and Teralba Southgate.

9 
Conclusions and recommendations  
9.1 
Conclusions 
This assessment included a review of publicly available information and previous investigations completed 
progressively at the Precinct and Teralba Southgate since 2005 across several Domains or Areas of 
Environmental Concern. The findings of this assessment confirm that soil, groundwater, surface water quality 
are generally compatible with industrial and commercial land uses through implementation of a staged, risk-
based assessment and remediation pathway. However, more sensitive land uses including residential, 
conservation, and recreational uses require targeted investigation and risk assessment to confirm suitability 
and establish appropriate remediation and management controls. 
Available data and information demonstrate that exceedances of human health investigation levels for 
commercial/industrial land use were not identified during previous investigations. However, ecological 
investigation level exceedances were reported in soil and sediment, reflecting the legacy of coal preparation 
operations. These ecological impacts require management to protect sensitive receptors including Cockle 
Creek and Lake Macquarie, but do not preclude employment-led development provided appropriate 
assessment and management controls are implemented. Contamination sources including asbestos in fill 
materials, PFAS in soil and groundwater, and hazardous ground gases have been confirmed across multiple 
domains and require targeted management consistent with the performance criteria outlined in this 
assessment. 
Significant data gaps constrain the ability to fully characterise the contamination profile across all domains. 
Five domains have not been subject to intrusive investigations, and multiple domains lack groundwater, 
surface water, sediment, or soil vapour/ground gas assessment data. These gaps are most material for 
sensitive land use scenarios including residential, recreation and conservation. The TSF (Domain 7) 
represents a material constraint requiring integrated assessment with water management, geotechnical 
stability, and dam safety considerations. Implementation of the staged investigation program will 
progressively resolve these data gaps through the development application approval process, enabling risk-
based decision-making. 
The management framework established in this assessment provides a clear pathway for contamination 
management through future planning and development approvals. Development applications must be 
supported by site-specific assessments that confirm suitability for the proposed use based on remediation or 
management measures required. Six performance criteria have been established to guide contamination 
management:  
◼ Land Use Suitability,  
◼ Water Quality Protection,  
◼ Validation and Ongoing Monitoring,  
◼ Hazardous Ground Gas Assessment,  
◼ Spoil Management, and  
◼ Waste Characterisation and Management.  
Investigation and remediation triggers have also been defined to ensure that the nature and extent of 
assessment is proportionate to land use sensitivity, disturbance footprint, and contamination risk profile. 
The Precinct and Teralba Southgate present opportunities to manage contaminated materials cost-
effectively, including on-site bioremediation of hydrocarbon-impacted soils, onsite or offsite reuse as 
engineered fill, and mine water reuse in construction activities. Implementation of the management 
framework and performance criteria outlined in this assessment, combined with progressive investigation 
and remediation through the development application approval process, will enable the Precinct and Teralba 
Southgate to support sustainable post-mining land use while protecting human health and environmental 
values in Cockle Creek and Lake Macquarie. The staged, risk-based approach provides regulatory certainty 
and defensible evidence for rezoning decisions while enabling cost-effective contamination management 
aligned with the proposed employment-led vision for the Precinct and Teralba Southgate. 

--- Cont Page 41 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B 
 32 
 
 
 
9.2 
Recommendations  
Based on the conclusions provided above, and subject to the limitations outlined in Section 11, Aurecon 
presents the following recommendations: 
◼ Implement a risk-based, staged investigation program for all future development applications, with 
Detailed Site Investigations (DSIs) and Tier 2/3 quantitative risk assessments undertaken where Tier I 
screening level concentrations exceedances or data gaps are identified, ensuring land use suitability is 
confirmed prior to development approval 
◼ Prioritise targeted investigation of Domains 2, 5, 7, 14, and 16 (uninvestigated domains), comprehensive 
groundwater assessment across all domains, ASS characterisation in low-lying areas, and asbestos 
delineation sampling to resolve material data gaps constraining sensitive land use suitability 
determination. Additionally, it is also recommended that further assessment of the environmentally 
constrained  areas be undertaken, primarily targeting the medium to high-risk domains (1, 7, 9, and 11), 
with lower priority assessment of the low-risk domains to provide broader site coverage where data gaps 
exist. This is to ensure that COPCs from other domains have not migrated into the environmentally 
constrained areas 
◼ Undertake integrated assessment of the TSF across water management, geotechnical stability, dam 
safety, and regulatory compliance frameworks, including geochemical characterisation of tailings 
materials and assessment of leachate generation and AMD pathways to inform remediation and long-
term management strategy 
◼ Undertake targeted surface water and sediment quality assessments adjacent to waterway and wetland 
interface zones (including recreational areas within West Lake); and assess PFAS-impacted areas in 
accordance with the PFAS National Environmental Management Plan (NEMP 3.1) 
◼ Undertake comprehensive ground gas assessment in accordance with NSW EPA Assessment and 
management of hazardous ground gases (EPA 2020), with particular focus on Domains 11 and 13 where 
methane concentrations were reported. If required, implement ground gas mitigation measures during 
building design and construction to prevent vapour intrusion risk to future enclosed structures 
◼ Confirm land suitability for more sensitive uses (residential in Teralba , environmentally constrained 
areas, and recreational uses) through targeted investigation of soil, groundwater, surface water, and 
ground gas; implement PFAS plume delineation, asbestos delineation, and methane management 
measures; obtain Site Audit Statements from NSW EPA-accredited Site Auditors where remediation or 
management measures are implemented 
◼ During construction, implement contamination pathway controls during earthworks and development to 
prevent migration of identified COPCs to Cockle Creek and Lake Macquarie 
◼ Ensure all contamination assessments comply with NSW EPA Guidelines and are prepared by a suitably 
qualified contaminated land consultant including any review and update of duty to report obligations under 
Section 60 of the Contaminated Land Management Act 1997 at each DA-stage investigation and 
preparation of Long-Term Environmental Management Plans (LTEMPs) where residual contamination 
risks remain. As per Lake Macquarie City Council’s (LMCCs) requirements, an EPA certified consultant 
must be engaged where reports are submitted to the NSW EPA or where required by the consent 
authority 
◼ All future works should be conducted by an appropriately qualified environmental consultant under the 
direction of a CEnvP-SC or equivalent accreditation. An accredited NSW EPA Auditor may be required to 
endorse the investigation, remediation/management and validation works where more sensitive land uses 
are proposed or where there are elevated risks to ecological receptors.
