B-1. Detailed summary of investigations undertaken at each 
Domain 
Domain 1 – Westside Administration and Workshop Area 
RCA Australia (2005) — Phase 2 Environmental Site Assessment, Macquarie Coal Preparation Plant, 
Teralba. RCA Australia was engaged by Oceanic Coal Australia Ltd (OCAL) to undertake a Phase 2 
Environmental Site Assessment across the MCPP and associated areas. Assessment criteria were based on 
NEPM 1999 HIL F (Commercial/Industrial). Soil sampling targeted the administration and workshop area, 
former underground storage tank (UST) location, oil lubricant storage area, and vehicle fleet area. No 
exceedances of HIL F criteria were recorded. Hydrocarbon impacts were identified in the vicinity of the 
former UST and oil storage area. Building footprints and the car park area were not investigated due to the 
presence of infrastructure. 
SLR (2017) — Contaminated Site Assessment, OCAL Complex (site-wide) (Rev C, 22 February 2017). 
SLR undertook a site-wide CSA across Domains 1, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 which included soil 
sampling at 250 locations, groundwater sampling at seven locations, and laboratory analysis for heavy 
metals, TRH, BTEXN, PAHs, phenols, OCPs, OPPs, PCBs, ASS (SPOCAS), pH, asbestos, and nutrients. 
No HIL/HSL (NEPM 2013) exceedances were recorded. Exceedance of the ESL criterion for TRH F2 (C10–
C16) was recorded in one fill soil sample indicating limited impacts to the fill/topsoil material across this 
domain. Building footprints and the car park area remain largely uninvestigated. 
Domain 2 – North Rehabilitation Area 
No available investigation data. The domain is identified as a former rehabilitation area associated with the 
Westside Mine. 
Domain 3 – South-West Pit / Borrow Pit Area 
SLR (2017) — Contaminated Site Assessment. Soil sampling was undertaken within the borrow pit area of 
Domain 3. No exceedances of health or ecological investigation criteria were recorded No available 
investigation data for the broader Domain 3 area outside the borrow pit.  
Domain 4 – Westside Final Void / Bioremediation Facility / Sediment Disposal Area 
SLR (2017) — Contaminated Site Assessment. Domain 4 was inspected as part of the pre-work 
assessment. No available intrusive investigation data. SLR noted that no information was available regarding 
the bioremediation facility or the removal of a former fuel storage element. The domain was identified as 
containing a proposed final void, bioremediation facility, and sediment disposal area. 
Domain 5 – Voluntary Conservation Areas 
No available investigation data. The domain is identified as a Voluntary Conservation Area (VCA) partially 
associated with the Westside Mine. 
Domain 6 – West Wallsend Colliery and Pit Top Dam Areas 
SLR (2017) — Contaminated Site Assessment. Domain 6 (WWC Pit Top Facilities) was assessed as part 
of the Precinct and Teralba Southgate CSA. Soil sampling targeted the workshop, laydown yard, coal 
loading facility, explosive magazine, above-ground storage tanks (ASTs), sedimentation dams, and sewage 
treatment facility. Exceedances of ecological criteria were recorded for heavy metals (copper, zinc) and TRH 
in soils. Asbestos was confirmed in soils adjacent to former infrastructure. Buried asbestos cement (AC) 
pipework was also identified but not fully characterised. Groundwater monitoring data was not available for 
Domain 6. 

--- Cont Page 56 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B 
 40 
 
 
 
Coffey (2019) — Contamination Site Assessment – Catchment Dams 1, 2 and 3 (16 April 2019; Rev1, 7 
August 2019). Coffey were engaged to assess three Catchment Dams (Dam 1: ~2.4 ha; Dam 2: ~1.14 ha; 
Dam 3: ~5 ha) located within the MCPP, which received runoff from coal processing areas, coarse rejects 
emplacement, product coal stockpiles, and former site infrastructure. Dam 3 has a licensed discharge point 
(LDP1) to Cockle Creek under EPL No. 1360. The assessment included 81 sediment samples, 6 soil 
samples, and 15 surface water samples, analysed for heavy metals, TRH, BTEX, PAH, PFAS, 
microbiological indicators, ASS (SCR/AVS), EC, pH, CEC, clay content, iron content, and TOC. Assessment 
criteria included both Recreational/Public Open Space and Commercial/Industrial investigation levels. 
Exceedances of ecological criteria were recorded for zinc in Catchment Dams 1, 2, and 4, and for chromium 
in Catchment Dam 4. PFAS was detected in surface water and sediments. PASS was confirmed in sediment 
samples. Statistical appraisal confirmed zinc exceedances above SQGs and EILs in Catchment Dam 1. No 
human health criteria exceedances were recorded. 
Coffey (2020) — Contaminated Site Assessment – Pit Top Catchment Dams, West Wallsend Colliery. 
Additional assessment of the Pit Top Catchment Dams (Dams 1–4) was undertaken in 2020, building on the 
previous assessment completed in 2019 and included additional surface water and groundwater sampling 
around the Catchment Dams including upstream and downstream locations. Results confirmed residual 
heavy metal and PFAS impacts in sediments and surface water. Groundwater data confirmed localised 
impacts in the shallow unconfined aquifer. 
Coffey (2019) — Sediment and Surface Water Sampling for Presence of PFAS within Dam G, 
Westside Mine (11 November 2019) (C105). Targeted PFAS assessment of Dam G (Westside Mine) was 
undertaken following identification of PFAS in the broader MCPP catchment area. Results confirmed PFAS 
detections in sediment and surface water within Dam G. 
SLR (2015) — Hazardous Building Materials Management Survey Report. This HBM survey also 
included Domain 6 area as well as other domains to identify hazardous materials in structures including 
ACM. ACM was confirmed in multiple building components across Domain 6. 
Domain 7 – Tailings Storage Facility (TSF) 
No available investigation data. The TSF is understood to contain tailings from coal processing operations at 
the West Wallsend Colliery and Macquarie Coal Preparation Plant. A Dam Safety Review (DSR) and dam 
break failure impact assessment have been undertaken. The TSF is identified as a major constraint to 
rezoning and redevelopment of the broader Precinct. 
Domain 8 – Rejects Emplacement Area 
No available investigation data. 
Domain 9 – MCPP Surface Facilities 
RCA Australia (2005) — Phase 2 Environmental Site Assessment. RCA Australia undertook Phase 2 
assessment across the MCPP surface facilities area, targeting the workshop, ASTs, former diesel UST, and 
surface bowser. Assessment criteria were based on NEPM 1999 HIL-F. Hydrocarbon impacts were identified 
in the vicinity of the former UST and diesel storage areas. No HIL-F exceedances were recorded. 
SLR (2016) — Report on Intrusive Investigation of Fill Potentially Containing Furnace Slag – Coal 
Product Stockpile Areas (21 December 2016). SLR undertook targeted investigation of fill materials in the 
thermal and coking coal stockpile areas (Domain 9) to assess the presence of furnace slag. Soil sampling 
was undertaken at 17 borehole and test pit locations. Exceedances of Slag Investigation Criteria were 
recorded for arsenic, cadmium, chromium, nickel, selenium, zinc, and pH in both the thermal and coking coal 
stockpile areas. Results indicated that slag materials were present and exhibited geochemical characteristics 
warranting management as potentially reactive fill. 
SLR (2017) — Contaminated Site Assessment. Domain 9 was assessed as part of the Precinct and 
Teralba Southgate CSA. Soil sampling targeted the MCPP surface facilities, rail loop, and coal stockpile 

--- Cont Page 57 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B 
 41 
 
 
 
areas. Exceedances of ecological criteria were recorded for TRH and zinc in soils. Asbestos was confirmed 
near former infrastructure. Five samples were tested for ASS in Domain 9, with four sediment samples from 
Pond 3 and one from the rail loop. ASS testing was deemed inconclusive. Groundwater data was limited to 
the deeper fractured rock aquifer, with limited assessment of the shallow unconfined aquifer. 
Coffey (2018) — Desktop Peer Review of Previous Site Assessment Works, West Wallsend Colliery. 
Coffey undertook a desktop review of the SLR (2017) assessment, identifying data gaps which included: 
inadequate ASS characterisation across closure Domains 9 and 10, absence of shallow groundwater data, 
ecological risk uncertainties and need to compare sediment data against NSW EPA Biosolids Guidelines 
given treated effluent impacts. 
Coffey (2019, 2020) — Catchment Dams Assessment. Catchment Dams 1–3 are located at the Domain 
9/10 interface and receive runoff from Domain 9 surface facilities. Refer to Domain 6 summary above.  
Domain 10 – Maturation Ponds 
SLR (2017) — Contaminated Site Assessment. Domain 10 was assessed as part of the site-wide CSA. 
Soil and sediment sampling targeted the maturation pond areas. Exceedances of ecological criteria were 
recorded for heavy metals, TRH, and PAHs in maturation pond sediments. Two samples were tested for 
ASS in Domain 10, but no sediment samples were tested from the maturation ponds. Available groundwater 
data was limited. 
Coffey (2019) — Maturation Pond Remediation Validation Report (Draft, 1 July 2019). Coffey undertook 
remediation validation of the Maturation Ponds following removal of impacted sediments. Validation sampling 
confirmed that remediation objectives had been achieved across most of the pond areas, with the exception 
of two residual locations which still returned some ecological criteria exceedances. Sediments from 
temporary holding cells were relocated to the Tailings Dam. ASS neutralisation was undertaken and verified. 
ACM was identified and removed during rehabilitation works. 
Coffey (2021) — Maturation Pond Remediation Validation Report (24 February 2021). Updated 
validation reporting confirmed residual exceedances at two locations. Additional groundwater monitoring was 
recommended to assess if heavy metal and PFAS concentrations were declining following remediation. The 
south-eastern corner of Maturation Pond 5 (former pump/pipework area) was not validated at the time of 
reporting. 
Domain 11 – Teralba Northgate 
RCA Australia (2005) — Phase 2 Environmental Site Assessment. RCA Australia undertook Phase 2 
assessment across the Teralba Northgate area, targeting the workshop, ASTs, and former infrastructure. 
Hydrocarbon impacts were identified. ACM was observed in soils. 
SLR (2017) — Contaminated Site Assessment. Domain 11 was assessed as part of the Precinct and 
Teralba Southgate CSA. Soil sampling targeted the Northgate surface facilities, mine shaft locations, and 
former infrastructure areas. Exceedances of ecological criteria were recorded for heavy metals and TRH. 
ACM was confirmed in soils, including fibrous asbestos. Methane gas was detected at mine shaft locations 
(Northgate Shafts 3 and 4). Various buildings and structures were inaccessible during the investigation. SLR 
recommended preparation of a methane management plan. 
SLR (2015) — Hazardous Building Materials Management Survey. ACM confirmed in multiple building 
components across Domain 11. 
Domain 12 – Infrastructure Corridor 
SLR (2017) — Contaminated Site Assessment (as above, C101). Domain 12 was assessed as part of the 
Precinct and Teralba Southgate CSA. Soil sampling targeted the infrastructure corridor and haul road areas. 
Exceedances of ecological criteria were recorded for zinc and TRH in fill materials. Anomalous detections of 

--- Cont Page 58 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU Rezoning_Package B_Contamination Report_Final.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B 
 42 
 
 
 
selenium and uranium were identified at a section of Haul Road. No human health criteria exceedances were 
recorded. PASS was identified in low-lying areas. Groundwater data was not available for Domain 12. 
Domain 13 – Teralba Southgate 
RCA Australia (2005) — Phase 2 Environmental Site Assessment. RCA Australia undertook Phase 2 
assessment across the Teralba Southgate area, targeting the workshop, ASTs, methane plant, and surface 
water storage dam. Hydrocarbon impacts were identified in the vicinity of the workshop and hydrocarbon 
drain facility. Deep ground penetration of hydrocarbons was also observed. 
SLR (2015) — Hazardous Building Materials Management Survey. ACM confirmed in multiple building 
components across Domain 13. 
SLR (2017) — Contaminated Site Assessment. Domain 13 was assessed as part of the Precinct and 
Teralba Southgate CSA. Soil and sediment sampling targeted the Southgate surface facilities, methane plant 
area, and surface water storage dam. Exceedances of ecological criteria were recorded for heavy metals, 
TRH, and PAHs in soils and sediments. Deep hydrocarbon impacts were also identified. Methane gas 
facilities were present. Various buildings and structures were inaccessible during the investigation. 
Groundwater sampling was undertaken at limited locations, with potential for off-site migration of metals 
towards Cockle Bay identified. 
Coffey (2018) — Dam Sediment Assessment, Teralba Southgate. Surface water monitoring identified 
seepage and overflows as potential contaminant pathways. Seven sediment and three surface water 
samples were analysed for COPCs against Australian and New Zealand Guidelines for Fresh and Marine 
Water Quality (2018) criteria. Sediment showed exceedances for TRH (C6–C36) and heavy metals 
(cadmium, copper, nickel, mercury, zinc) above criteria; surface water samples were below criteria. TRH 
concentrations were primarily attributable to coal fines with limited mobility and low subsurface leaching 
potential. Metal concentrations in water were low to non-detectable with minimal bioavailability and toxicity 
risk. The assessment concluded low risk to human health and the environment for current and proposed light 
industrial use; no remedial works required. 
Tetra Tech Coffey (2021) — Contaminated Site Assessment, Teralba Southgate (16 November 2021). 
Soil sampling from 32 locations and groundwater sampling from six existing monitoring wells were 
undertaken to address data gaps and inform future mine closure and rehabilitation planning. No detectable 
methane, health-based risks, or ecological risks were identified. TRH (>C16–C34) exceedances were 
recorded at depth within fill materials and considered acceptable on a qualitative risk basis. Groundwater 
heavy metal exceedances (arsenic, copper, nickel, and zinc) were attributed to regional conditions 
associated with prolonged industrial activity. PFOS exceedances were identified in a down-gradient 
monitoring well, with detectable PFAS analytes in adjacent wells, likely associated with former firefighting 
activities or spills at the site. The site was considered suitable for continued commercial/industrial use, 
subject to appropriate maintenance. Recommendations included a hazardous ground gas assessment within 
enclosed structures prior to reoccupation, and three management options for PFAS: additional assessment 
to define source extent, containment via impervious capping, or a Human Health and Ecological Risk 
Assessment (HHERA) to determine tolerability of reported PFAS levels. Additional assessment would be 
required for any proposed change to a more sensitive land use. 
Tetra Tech Coffey (2022) — Human Health and Environmental Risk Assessment, Teralba Southgate 
(30 August 2022). Tetra Tech Coffey undertook a Human Health and Environmental Risk Assessment 
(HHERA) for Domain 13. This assessment included soil, groundwater, and ground gas sampling. 
Exceedances of ecological criteria were confirmed for heavy metals, TRH, and PAHs. PFAS was detected in 
groundwater. Methane and CO₂ were detected above acceptable thresholds at mine shaft locations. The 
assessment confirmed that the site was not suitable for sensitive land uses without further investigation and 
remediation.

B-2. Summary of Acid Sulfate Soil and Salinity Assessment 
Data 
Acid Sulfate Soils Assessment Data Summary 
Site-specific ASS investigations have been undertaken across several domains, primarily focused on the 
MCPP sediment management areas with key findings summarised below: 
◼ Domain 9 (MCPP Surface Facilities and Catchment Dams 1–3). Tested sediment samples (17 of 20) as 
part of Coffey (2019) assessment returned exceedances of the the SCR action criteria, indicating the 
presence of Actual Acid Sulfate Soils (AASS) and Potential Acid Sulfate Soils (PASS) within dam 
sediments. Samples from Dams 2 and 3 exhibited the highest sulfide concentrations and confirmed active 
acid generation at that time. Presence of monosulfides (AVS) was also confirmed for Dam 3. Coffey 
(2019) recommended preparation of an Acid Sulfate Soil Management Plan (ASSMP) prior to any 
dewatering or sediment disturbance. A subsequent assessment of the Pit Top Catchment Dams (Coffey, 
2020) assessed four dams (Dams 1–4) at WWC. Sulfide concentrations in sediment samples were all 
reported below the ASS action criteria, with the exception of minor detections in Dam 1. No AVS 
exceedances were recorded 
◼ Domain 10 (Maturation Ponds – MCPP). Sediments within five Maturation Ponds at the MCPP tested as 
part of Coffey (2018) were assessed as acid generating once dewatered. Subsequent rehabilitation works 
by KCE which included neutralisation with lime treatment applied to sediments from the five ponds prior to 
relocation to a temporary holding cell and eventual backfill into the Tailings Dam (Domain 7). Validation 
monitoring (Coffey, 2019 — Maturation Ponds Validation Report) recorded pHf values of 6.0–8.1 and 
pHfox values of 2.4–7.7 across treated stockpiles, reflecting the difficulty of achieving uniform lime mixing 
in heavy clay sediments. However, the risk of further acidification of treated material was assessed as low 
given the lined containment cell and lime application records 
◼ Domain 12 (Infrastructure / Haul Road). SLR (2017) identified PASS in underlying natural soils based on 
SPOCAS analysis. An ASS management plan was recommended. ASS characterisation in this domain 
remains incomplete 
◼ Domain 6 (WWC). The domain includes low-lying areas associated with former wastewater management 
cells (North Dam, Old Transpiration Area, Top Dam, Bottom Dam) that have not been assessed for ASS. 
◼ Domain 14. ASS risk is mapped in low-lying areas proximate to Cockle Creek but no intrusive 
investigation have been undertaken at this domain to date. 
SLR (2017) identified the absence of ASS assessment across the majority of the Precinct and Teralba 
Southgate as a data gap. 
Salinity Assessment Data Summary 
Site-specific salinity data across the Precinct and Teralba Southgate is limited. The available data is 
summarised below by domain: 
◼ Domain 9 (MCPP Catchment Dams). Coffey (2019) collected Electrical Conductivity (EC), pH, Cation 
Exchange Capacity (CEC), clay content, iron content, and total organic carbon data from sediment 
samples within Catchment Dams 1–3 as part of the EIL derivation. Specific salinity exceedance results 
were not reported in the available assessment summaries. Groundwater in the vicinity of the Catchment 
Dams was assessed during the Coffey (2019) investigation 
◼ Domain 10 (Maturation Ponds). The Coffey (2018) noted that sediments within the Maturation Ponds 
were highly saline, consistent with the operational history of the ponds receiving process water from coal 
preparation activities. Elevated EC was recorded in groundwater monitoring wells installed in the vicinity 
of the ponds. Post-rehabilitation groundwater monitoring (Coffey, 2019 — Maturation Ponds Validation 
Report) assessed groundwater quality following capping works. Results indicated residual groundwater 
quality concerns, with further monitoring recommended following completion of rehabilitation

Executive summary 
This Dam Engineering Report has been prepared by Aurecon on behalf of the Department of Planning, 
Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) to inform the State-led rezoning of the Macquarie Coal Complex (the 
Precinct) for post-mining land use. The report provides a risk-informed planning framework to guide future 
land use, infrastructure design, and staging decisions relating to the existing Tailings Storage Facility (TSF), 
which remains regulated as declared dam. 
The TSF represents a key constraint to short and medium development, due to the residual risk associated 
with potential dam failure. Dambreak modelling has identified a downstream inundation zone, within which 
development has the potential to increase risk to people (Population at Risk and Potential Loss of Life). 
While current risk levels are well below regulatory thresholds, land use planning must not increase these 
risks, in accordance with NSW dam safety requirements. A staged and adaptive planning approach is 
therefore required. 
Subsequently, post mining land use planning within and downstream of the TSF must adopt a risk-based 
framework that: 
 Avoids increasing population exposure within the dambreak inundation zone 
 Requires periodic reassessment of dambreak risk as site conditions change 
 Aligns developable land to demonstrated risk reduction 
 Ensures compatibility between land use and the evolving residual risk profile of the TSF. 
Key post mining land use implications 
 Development constraints: Land within the dambreak inundation zone is constrained while the TSF 
remains a declared dam. High-intensity or sensitive land uses which increase societal risk (e.g. residential 
and industrial) are not appropriate in the short to medium term. 
 Permissible interim uses: Low-intensity, transient or non-sensitive uses (such as open space, 
conservation or passive recreation) may be considered, subject to maintaining flood conveyance and not 
increasing risk. 
 Infrastructure design: Infrastructure (including roads and utilities) within or crossing the inundation zone 
must be designed above modelled inundation levels and resilient to flood impacts. 
 TSF landform constraints: Development directly on the TSF is limited in the short and medium term due 
to ongoing settlement and geotechnical constraints. Low impact uses that do not compromise the integrity 
of the rehabilitated landform and capping are appropriate. 
Staging and future development potential 
The development potential of the Precinct will increase over time as rehabilitation progresses and dam-
related risks reduce. This is expected to occur through: 
 Progressive lowering of water levels within the TSF (phreatic surface reduction) 
 Completion of capping and landform stabilisation 
 Updated dambreak and consequence assessments demonstrating reduced inundation extent and risk 
As these milestones are achieved, land currently constrained may be progressively released for more 
intensive development, subject to updated technical verification.

1 
Introduction 
This Dam Engineering Report (this Report) has been prepared by Aurecon on behalf of the Department 
Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) to support the State-led rezoning of the Macquarie Coal 
Complex for Post Mining Land Use. The Macquarie Coal Complex Land Transformation Precinct (the 
Precinct) forms part of the NSW Government’s investigation into future land use pathways for mining 
affected land. 
The former operations of the Macquarie Coal Complex have created a legacy Tailings Storage Facility 
(TSF), an engineered structure designed to safely store and manage rejected materials generated from 
operations, including solids and water. Closure of the TSF, including rehabilitation and capping is underway 
however will remain a declared dam until water has been removed from the contained material and the 
structure is stabilised. 
Dambreak modelling has defined inundation extents, flow paths, and level of hazard under a failure scenario. 
These outputs directly inform spatial planning by establishing compatible land use scenarios across the TSF 
areas that would enable flexibility over the period of rehabilitation and closure. Sensitive or high-occupancy 
land uses are avoided in the short to medium term within mapped inundation zones and buffers. Lower-
intensity or transient uses may be considered in the outer zones (such as passive and active recreation, 
storage facilities), subject to appropriate risk mitigation measures. Areas above the TSF could provide land 
uses which do not compromise the capping once rehabilitation is complete and a more stable landform is 
achieved over time.  
New and existing infrastructure, such as roads that traverse the dambreak inundation area and have the 
potential to increase societal risk, must be appropriately designed to ensure they are located above the 
modelled dambreak inundation level whilst the TSF is a declared dam. 
A strategic, risk-informed framework to manage constraints associated with the TSF and the potential for 
dambreak downstream (dambreak inundation area) should therefore be adopted. This ensures that future 
land use is compatible with the residual risk profile of the TSF over its remaining life and following de-
declaration. 
1.1 
Background 
The Macquarie Coal Complex is a decommissioned mining operation previously operated by Glencore, 
which processed coal sourced from the nearby underground West Wallsend Colliery and the Westside open-
cut mining operations. Mining activities at West Wallsend Colliery ceased in 2016. 
The Tailings Storage Facility (TSF), commissioned in 1983, has been the sole tailings storage facility at the 
site. The purpose of the TSF is to provide storage for the disposal of fine reject material (i.e., tailings).  The 
tailings were historically pumped in slurry form to the TSF. Coarse rejects were trucked to the Rejects 
Emplacement Area (REA) situated immediately adjacent to the TSF, on the eastern side.  
While infrastructure rehabilitation has been ongoing, the TSF area has remained largely dormant since 
closure to allow for the drainage and consolidation of the tailings. The only activity undertaken during this 
period has been the placement of fine ash tailings to facilitate site access. Works to achieve the final 
landform of the TSF, including geotechnical stability are currently underway. Capping will be the final stage 
of rehabilitation of the TSF.  
1.2 
Purpose of this report  
The purpose of this Dam Engineering Report is to: 
 Analyse the available information on the existing Tailings Storage Facility (TSF) to better understand the 
annual probability of failure and the dam safety risks associated with the TSF, in particular the northern 
saddle dam (NSD)

2021 
 Provide a rezoning appropriate evidence base to verify developable land and inform land use

 Provide developable land and constraints classification to support the Structure Plan

Site location and context 
Located within the Lake Macquarie Local Government Area, the Precinct comprises approximately 
1160 hectares of land across the suburbs of Killingworth, Wakefield, Barnsley and Teralba. The Precinct 
forms part of the broader Lower Hunter region and is strategically positioned within an established industrial 
and infrastructure corridor, with proximity to key regional centres (Figure 2-1). 
Macquarie Coal Complex is a former mining operation comprising West Wallsend Colliery (underground 
mine), Westside Mine (open cut), the Macquarie Coal Preparation Plant (MCPP), Tailings Storage Facility 
(TSF) and associated infrastructure. Coal mining has been a defining land use in the area since operations 
commenced in 1969, shaping both the physical landscape and the economic profile of surrounding 
communities. The Macquarie Coal Complex site is currently closed and undergoing rehabilitation.

3 
Regulatory Context 
In New South Wales (NSW), dam safety is enforced by the Dams Safety NSW Act 2015 (the Act) and the 
Dams Safety NSW Regulation 2019 (the Regulation). Dams Safety NSW is the state regulator for dam safety 
and responsible for developing and implementing regulations for effective dam safety management to protect 
life, property, and the environment from dam failures. Dam Safety NSW replaces the former Dams Safety 
Committee (DSC).  
Owners of declared dams, and their professional advisors, are accountable to determine and take 
appropriate dam safety management action to prevent the potential failure of their dams and to mitigate 
associated consequences. Responsibility for dam safety obligations remains with the declared dam owner 
unless formally transferred in accordance with the Act, requiring regulatory approval. Dams Safety NSW will 
audit declared dam owners’ policies, processes, and procedures to check compliance with the requirements 
of the Regulation. 
In accordance with the Regulation, declared dam owners must establish, implement and maintain a Dam 
Safety Management System (DSMS) to ensure the ongoing safety of their dam throughout the dam’s 
lifecycle. The DSMS provides a comprehensive and integrated system for the management of all aspects of 
foreseeable risks in relation to the failure of the dam. It provides a structured approach for the development, 
coordination and control of activities undertaken to ensure that these dam failure risks are reduced so far as 
is reasonably practicable (SFAIRP). The DSMS must address the following as set out in the Regulation:  
a. the procedures for managing risks in accordance with Clause 14, 
b. the procedures for reporting incidents in accordance with Clause 19, 
c. 
the procedures for conducting a safety review in accordance with Clause 20, 
d. the procedures for notifying changes to the dam in accordance with Clause 21, 
e. the procedures for ensuring compliance with AS ISO 55001:2014, 
f. 
the procedures for review of the matters in paragraphs (a) to (e), 
g. the resources that will be applied for the effective implementation and use of the DSMS. 
In accordance with the Regulation, Clause 14, the owner of a declared dam must establish a risk 
management framework inclusive of the following components:  
 hazard identification process 
 a risk analysis process 
 a risk evaluation process 
 a risk treatment process. 
Risk in dam safety context is the combination of the probability of dam failure and the resulting 
consequences. The risks posed by a dam involves societal risk, individual risk and financial/economic risk. 
Dam Safety NSW has provided thresholds for societal risk and individual risk as follows: 
 Societal risk rating must be lower than 1E-03 
 Individual risk rating must be lower than 1E-04. 
Societal risk is also presented in societal risk plot, also called F-N plot. Societal safety threshold specified by 
Dam Safety NSW (2022) for an existing dam is presented in Figure 3-1. The societal risk posed by the dam 
must be lower than the safety threshold and so far as is reasonably practicable (SFAIRP).

4 
Baseline analysis 
4.1 
Investigation, design and construction of TSF 
The surveillance report (ATCW, 2024) reports that geotechnical investigations at the TSF were conducted in 
stages. The Phase One Study comprised of a review of existing conditions, embankments, in-situ tailings 
characteristics, capping concept development, and an initial assessment of tailings consolidation to assist 
with final landform design. 
The Phase Two Study was completed in January 2018 and focussed on obtaining additional geotechnical 
data. This included CPTu testing, drilling, sampling, and laboratory testing of the tailings and embankment 
coarse reject materials. It is not clear if the investigations were also conducted at the NSD and eastern 
embankment to establish the material parameters for these embankments and the underlying foundations. 
The Phase Three Study addressed further works, specifically related to the Rejects Emplacement Area 
(REA), that was recommended by ATCW resulting from the Phase Two Study, as well as recommendations 
by a third-party reviewer. 
Tailings 
The fine-grained tailings exhibit compressibility and permeability values ranging from 0.06 to 0.4 m²/year, 
indicating poor consolidation characteristics. Laboratory testing of the clay fraction confirms mineralogy 
dominated by illite, swelling smectite, and kaolin. The in-situ strength profile of the underlying tailings 
(including the capping layer) is not currently available and will require reassessment as part of final landform 
design. For post-seismic assessment, a residual undrained shear strength ratio (Su,res/σ′vo) of 0.04 has 
been adopted for the tailings and fly ash. This value corresponds to the 20th percentile of strengths derived 
from CPT data within the weakest tailings zone adjacent to a hypothetical breach location. 
Embankment Materials 
The embankment materials comprise approximately 85% cobble- and gravel-sized particles, with the 
remaining 15% consisting of sand and fines (silt and clay). For analysis, the embankment has been 
subdivided into ‘new’ and ‘old’ rejects, with drained (effective) strength parameters applied to the new rejects 
and undrained strength parameters applied to the old rejects. Although laboratory testing indicates broadly 
similar particle size distribution and plasticity for both materials, undrained conditions are not considered 
appropriate for the new rejects, as these have historically remained unsaturated. 
The drained shear strength for the REA “new rejects” indicates an effective friction angle (ϕ′) of 
approximately 38°, assuming zero cohesion. The undrained shear strength ratios range from 0.35 to 0.40 for 
REA rejects and from 0.50 to 0.80 for old rejects. CPTu data indicate that the minimum undrained shear 
strength of the coarse rejects consistently exceeds 20 kPa. 
Following completion of the final landform, the phreatic surface within the embankment is expected to 
gradually decline. Seepage modelling undertaken by ATCW in 2020 indicates that the phreatic surface will 
remain within the embankment for approximately 15 years following closure. 
A site-specific seismic hazard assessment completed in February 2017 adopted peak ground accelerations 
of 0.19 g, 0.25 g, 0.43 g, and 0.53 g for return periods of 500, 1,000, 5,000, and 10,000 years respectively. 
Based on ATCW (2024), as part of these studies, the safety, in relation to earthquake loading on the NSD in 
its current condition, was examined and it was concluded that the deformations resulting from the Maximum 
Design Earthquake (now Safety Evaluation Earthquake) would be tolerable and would not result in the 
uncontrolled release of tailings or water from the TSF.  
The current risk assessment reflects the status of capping progress and tailings deposition levels as of 
October 2025. The dam’s risk profile is expected to change following completion of capping, particularly as 
the primary risk driver—overtopping associated with scarp formation and slumping at the buttress toe leading 
to global slope instability (94.68%)—will be reduced over time as stormwater will be diverted away from the 
TSF and there will be natural infiltration.

4.2 
Dambreak & consequence assessments 
This section provides a strategic, desktop-based assessment of existing dam break conditions, constraints 
and opportunities associated with the Tailings Storage Facility (TSF) within the Precinct. It also provides 
recommended actions for the post-rezoning phase. The assessment considers the TSF embankments, 
capping works, potential dam failures, previous dam break assessments and dam safety requirements, and 
included a review of the following documents: 
 Dam break failure impact assessment (ATCW, 2023) 
 West Wallsend Dambreak Presentation Slides (ATCW, 2024) 
 Surveillance review reports (ATCW 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025). 
The TSF has two embankments: the eastern embankment (EE) and northern saddle dam (NSD). Following 
the completion of Stage 1 capping, Stage 2 capping commenced in 2021. Thus far, for Stage 2 capping (29 
June 2021 to November 2024), approximately 435,000 m3 (~356,000 m3 in-situ after initial settlement) of fly 
ash has been hydraulically deposited into the TSF. Stage 2 Phase 3 fly ash deposition has been suspended 
to allow conventional capping. 
Of the two embankments, the eastern embankment has a wide crest and flat downstream slopes as a result 
of the Rejects Emplacement Area (REA) progressively constructed by dumping, spreading and track-rolling 
coarse rejects in lifts to an ultimate surface level to that of the eastern embankment. As such, only the failure 
of the NSD is envisaged. 
The latest dambreak study was undertaken in 2023 (ATCW), which considered three incremental failure 
consequences for the NSD. The population at risk (PAR) was updated in 2024 and potential loss of life (PLL) 
was also estimated in 2024. Incremental Flood Failure (IFF) considered in the dambreak of NSD in 2023 is 
very conservative. A scenario for spillway in operation without obstruction and with downstream concurrent 
inflow during PMF (natural flooding) without dambreak compared with dambreak will be more realistic for 
IFF. 
The dam was re-classified in 2024 as ‘Significant’ consequence category dam for sunny day failure based on 
a PLL of 0.6 and a medium severity of damage and loss. The surveillance report (ATCW, 2024) and the 
presentation slides of the updated consequence assessment do not provide information on flood failure 
related PAR/PLL. TSF is a declared dam under the Dam Safety Act 2015 and the Dam Safety Regulation 
2019. TSF must comply with the requirements of the Dam Safety Act 2015 and the Dam Safety Regulation 
2019.  
Inundation extent during a sunny day failure as shown in the surveillance report (ATCW, 2024) is presented 
below in Figure 4-1.

4.3 
Surveillance and monitoring practice implemented at 
the dam 
The owner of the dam (NSD and TSF) is responsible for operating and maintaining the dam in a safe manner 
until such time that the dam is de-declared, which requires undertaking routine monitoring activities, periodic 
reviews and interpretation of collected data, dam safety surveillance inspections (intermediate, 
comprehensive) and special inspections following an unusual loading at the dam (e.g. flood or seismic). The 
Dam Safety Act 2015 and the Regulation (2019) require that a Dam Safety Management System (DSMS) is 
prepared for all declared dams, including Operation and Maintenance Plan (OMP) and Dam Safety 
Emergency Plan (DSEP).  
Review of previous surveillance and monitoring reports for the TSF reveals that:  
 The TSF has established a Dam Safety Management Plan (DSMS) in 2023 
 There is an Operation and Management Plan for the TSF 
 A Dam Safety Emergency Plan (DSEP) exists for the dam which defines white, amber and red Trigger 
Alert Response Plans (TARPs) 
 The performance of the dam (NSD) is mentioned to be satisfactory per the surveillance report by ATCW 
(2024). It reports a 10-metre-wide scarp and slump associated with it near the downstream toe caused by 
incessant rainfall. This has since been remediated. Minor issues on the capping have been continuously 
monitored and repaired as required 
 The monitoring and surveillance requirements are largely based on the frequencies recommended by 
ANCOLD (2003) or on a risk-based surveillance (RBS) basis. The surveillance report (ATCW, 2024) 
mentions that currently routine visual inspection is undertaken at the dam on a weekly basis and are 
considered to be in compliance with the requirements of ANCOLD (2003) and Dam Safety NSW 

--- Dam Page 14 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU State Led Rezoning_ Dam Report_RevB_CLEAN COPY.docx  2026-07-01
Revision B
9 
 
 
 
 Intermediate surveillance inspections and reporting for the dam are undertaken on an annual basis by 
Engineer of Record. Five yearly comprehensive surveillance inspection and reporting are undertaken 
once every five years by an Independent Dam Specialist 
 Given that the risk assessment was undertaken recently in 2025, the next 5-yearly risk review is due in 
2030 
 The TSF has following instrumentation currently for monitoring of the dam performance: 
− There are ten (10) active standpipe piezometers with real time sensors installed within the NSD which 
extend into the foundation 
− A v-notch weir with automated seepage monitoring installed together with a camera 
− Seven (7) monitoring bores were installed within the Reject Emplacement Area (REA) to establish an 
understanding of phreatic surface levels in the area. REA is situated immediately adjacent to the TSF, 
on the eastern side 
− A v-notch weir also exists in the south-east REA toe drain adjacent to the TSF South Ramp 
− In November 2023, a ground control network to facilitate aerial (photogrammetry) surveys was 
installed. The network consists of thirty-two (32) ground control points and ten (10) check control 
points. Twenty-five (25) survey prisms were also installed across the downstream slope of the NSD to 
monitor embankment movements. 
 The NSD standpipe piezometers and v-notch weir are continuously monitored using eagle.io (with 
assigned trigger levels). Embankment movement is monitored fortnightly using birdi.io (with assigned 
trigger levels). Additionally, storage and ongoing fly ash deposition are monitored regularly via 
photogrammetry processed in the birdi.io platform. The collected data is analysed weekly to understand 
the developing trends. 
4.4 
Dam safety risk 
The following information is gathered from the NSD risk assessment and SFAIRP framework report by 
ATCW (2025). 
Engineering assessment for the dam (embankment and spillway) was undertaken in 2025 following 
engineering standards, guidelines and references. 
Risk assessment was then undertaken in a sequence starting with failure mode and effect analysis (FMEA), 
load partitioning (flood, seismic), event trees (piping and non-piping), estimation of conditional probability of 
failure, consequence of failure, risk integration (annual probability of failure, risk estimates) and risk 
evaluation. 
The annual probability of failure for the dam was estimated to be 1.74E-07. The most significant contributor 
was overtopping due to scarp formation and slump at the buttress toe leading to global slope instability, 
contributing more than 94% of the overall annual probabilities. 
The total societal risk was estimated to be 5.02E-08. It is not clear what the societal risk rating was, yet it 
would still be lower than the total societal risk, the threshold for which is 1E-03. The societal risk (F-N) plots 
four orders of magnitude below the Dam Safety NSW (2022) safety threshold.

Figure 4-2 
NSD societal risk plot (ATCW, 2025) 
 
The total individual risk posed by the dam was estimated to be 3.22E-12. The highest individual risk is not 
clear in the report, yet it will still be lower than the total. The Dam Safety NSW (2022) threshold for individual 
risk rating is 1E-04. 
It should be noted that the safety threshold by Dam Safety NSW (Gazette 113, 2022) states that even if the 
risk plots below the threshold, the risks must be reduced so far as is reasonably practicable (SFAIRP). An 
SFAIRP assessment was undertaken following the risk assessment for NSD in 2024. The outcomes of the 
SFAIRP assessment indicated that the existing control measures were consistent with recognised good 
industry practice. No additional control measures were identified. 
The risk assessment reflects the current condition of the structure, with capping progress and tailings 
deposition levels recorded as of October 2025. It is noted that the post-capping landform is expected to alter 
the risk profile of NSD; however, this has not been considered in the current assessment. 
It should be noted that any development activity implemented downstream of the dam within the current 
inundation area will most likely increase the PAR in the form of itinerant population as well as permanent 
population. In that case, it is highly likely that the PLL will increase as well. 
While the probability under the post-landform condition is expected to decrease, future development on and 
downstream of the dam may increase the Potential Loss of Life (PLL), which is contrary to the Dam Safety 
NSW (2022) directive. Accordingly, the overall societal risk must remain below the prescribed safety 
threshold to maintain compliance. The societal risk estimated in the latest assessment is more than four 
orders of magnitude below the DSNSW safety threshold, and this margin should be maintained under post-
landform conditions.

5 
Structure Plan Assessment  
The Macquarie Coal Complex Land Transformation Precinct Structure Plan (Structure Plan), is the principal 
spatial framework underpinning the Master Plan (Figure 5-1). It provides developable areas, environmentally 
constrained areas, recreation areas, movement networks and key constraints across the Precinct. 
Categories relevant to this Report are as follows: 
 
 Developable areas – Land assessed as most likely to be suitable for development, subject to further 
technical investigation and site-specific assessment at the development application stage. Developable 
areas are concentrated in locations with relative geotechnical stability, accessibility to existing or planned 
transport networks and proximity to utility infrastructure or feasible servicing solutions 
 Environmentally constrained areas – Land identified as having high biodiversity values or where natural 
features (watercourses, wetlands, steep slope, flooding) constrain development for employment uses. 
Detailed environmental investigations are required prior to development or disturbance of vegetation in 
these areas. Environmentally constrained areas form an interconnected network across the Precinct that 
underpins ecological connectivity, water cycle management and landscape identity 
 Recreational areas – Land suitable for active and passive recreation facilities, balanced with protecting 
biodiversity and cultural values. Recreational areas are primarily associated with the West Lake sub-
precinct and the environmentally constrained areas, where the landscape and environmental values 
support nature-based tourism, walking and cycling trails and community recreational facilities 
 Developable land subject to further investigation – Land constrained in the short to medium term by 
geotechnical, dam safety, flood or biodiversity factors requiring resolution before development can 
proceed. Further investigation is required, as described in this Master Plan, prior to development. The 
release of this land for development is contingent upon the completion of relevant technical investigations 
and the achievement of applicable staging triggers 
 Movement network – Existing and proposed road, freight and active transport corridors that structure 
internal and external connectivity 
  Key constraints – Significant infrastructure, environmental or hazard features (e.g. TSF, pipeline, coastal 
wetlands, transmission lines) that influence land use allocation and development design. 
At the time of reporting, the TSF remains a declared dam. Subsequently, development within the dambreak 
inundation zone and above the TSF itself is constrained until the TSF is de-declared. The potential of 
developable land within and adjacent to the inundation zone is contingent upon updated dam break and 
consequence assessments demonstrating a reduction in risk as rehabilitation milestones are achieved. 
The Master Plan provides overarching performance criteria to manage dam risk and support progressive 
development over time. 
 

--- Dam Page 20 ---

5.1 
Downstream dambreak inundation zone 
5.1.1 
Dambreak and consequence assessment 
The update to population at risk (PAR) and potential loss of life (PLL) undertaken in 2024 by ATCW 
considers sunny day failure related PAR and PLL. Flood failure related incremental PAR and PLL is 
calculated based on the dambreak inundation extent for PMF events with and without dam failure. The 
inundation extent for a flood failure may be different to a sunny day failure inundation extent, although the 
incremental PAR/PLL may be insignificant. 
Currently, development  is restricted to areas higher than the maximum inundation levels on the downstream 
side of the dam as it will have potential to increase the PAR/PLL which may increase the baseline dam 
safety risks in contrast to the requirement of Dam Safety NSW (Gazette 113, 2022), which directs that the 
risks must be reduced so far as is reasonably practicable (SFAIRP).  
5.1.2 
Rehabilitation 
The areas downstream of the dam that are impacted by natural flooding should be rehabilitated after each 
flooding event. This might include maintaining the walking tracks, erosion protection works, routine 
vegetation management along the floodplain, construction of flood levees to protect areas of significance 
from the next flooding etc. Severe change to the inundation zone may have significant impact on the 
dambreak inundation flow characteristics (flow depths, velocities and extent) compared to what has been 
estimated in the 2023/2024 dambreak modelling. 
5.1.3 
Development within the inundation zone 
The area downstream of the NSD may be suitable for the development of walking trails, subject to 
appropriate risk management constraints. It may also be utilised for low-impact biodiversity enhancement 
works, provided that such activities do not obstruct potential dam break flood pathways or increase 
inundation levels.  
Following the completion of TSF rehabilitation works, and as the phreatic surface within the TSF 
progressively lowers to a stable condition, updated dam break assessments should be undertaken 
periodically. These assessments will refine the predicted inundation extents over time. 
As inundation extents reduce, portions of land downstream may be progressively released for potential 
development, subject to confirmation of geotechnical stability and safety constraints. Concurrently, land-use 
option studies can be carried out in alignment with the ongoing dam management program, while the dam 
remains declared 
Furthermore, infrastructure such as roads which traverse the dambreak inundation zone and increase 
societal risk will need to be raised above the modelled inundation level and designed to withstand flood 
impacts whilst the dam remains declared. 
5.2 
Northern Saddle Dam (NSD) 
5.2.1 
Dam safety surveillance and monitoring 
Based on the review of the surveillance reports, monitoring and surveillance at the dam shall continue 
following ANCOLD (2003) for a Significant consequence category dam. The evaluation of instrumentation 
data should be undertaken at least quarterly to understand the performance of the dam and early detection 
of any developing trends. 

--- Dam Page 21 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU State Led Rezoning_ Dam Report_RevB_CLEAN COPY.docx  2026-07-01
Revision B
16 
 
 
 
5.2.2 
Dam safety review and risk assessment 
Dam safety reviews are generally undertaken in 10-to-15-year intervals, unless earlier review is warranted 
due to change in loading conditions or deterioration in the condition of the dam. these periodic reviews 
benefit from the availability of additional information over time, including outcomes of investigations and 
studies, as well as updates to hydrological and seismic data. They also take into account any advancements 
in engineering standards, guidelines, and industry best practices. The findings of each dam safety review 
inform updates to the dam’s risk assessment. Following this, a so far as is reasonably practicable (SFAIRP) 
assessment should be carried out to evaluate whether further risk reduction measures are justified and 
proportionate. 
Dam Safety NSW (2022) requires that the risk is reviewed once every 5 years. As such, at the time of 
reporting, the 5-yearly risk review is due in 2030. 
5.2.3 
Upgrade to the dam 
Dam safety risks are fundamentally associated with the potential for dam failure. These risks can only be 
eliminated if all credible failure modes are demonstrably removed, such that no plausible failure scenario can 
be reasonably envisaged. As an example, the TSF is impounded by the NSD and Eastern Embankment. The 
Eastern Embankment has been made significantly wider at crest and flat downstream slopes as a result of 
the Rejects Emplacement Area (REA), progressively constructed by dumping, spreading and track-rolling 
coarse rejects in lifts to an ultimate surface level to that of the eastern embankment. As such, only the failure 
of the NSD is envisaged. If similar buttressing to the NSD can be done with engineered fill sufficiently wide 
enough with flatter slopes, that would eliminate the global failure of the NSD. Practicality of this needs to be 
investigated as this might reduce the duration for de-declaration. 
5.2.4 
Development at the NSD 
The TSF embankment requires ongoing routine monitoring to identify any developing conditions that may 
compromise dam safety. This monitoring is carried out through regular visual inspections by trained 
personnel. Accordingly, key structural components of the embankment, including the upstream and 
downstream faces, crest, groins (both upstream and downstream on the left and right sides), abutments, and 
the embankment toe, collectively define the dam footprint and must be preserved. These areas must not be 
altered, encroached upon, or used for any development activities, as unrestricted access is required for 
inspection, surveillance, and maintenance purposes. 
The dam footprint is also subject to periodic preventative and corrective maintenance. To minimise the risk of 
internal erosion (piping), no vegetation should be permitted to grow, or be planted, within a 10 metre buffer 
zone surrounding the dam footprint. Vegetation root systems can create preferential seepage pathways, 
potentially compromising the structural integrity of the embankment.

Further investigation areas - TSF and reject emplacement area 
5.3 
Tailings Storage Facility (TSF) 
5.3.1 
Investigations, monitoring and surveillance 
The existing seepage modelling is considered conservative due to uncertainties in some of the adopted 
strength parameters. This can be refined through the installation of additional groundwater monitoring wells 
around the tailings storage to better define current water levels and flow directions, as well as through 
targeted testing to improve parameter confidence.  
5.3.2 
Maintenance of final landform 
Once the final landform is established, the tailings material will continue to consolidate, and the capping will 
continue to settle over time. Some ongoing work to rehabilitate impacted areas will be required to maintain 
the designed levels and ensure that the area does not pose safety hazards due to factors such as uneven 
terrain, localised erosion and ponding. 
5.3.3 
Development at the TSF 
On the TSF, the rehabilitated area can be used for recreational facilities; however, due to non-uniform 
settlement over time the surface may become uneven. This will limit the development on the TSF. Subject to 
risk criteria and geotechnical constraints, some low-risk land uses can be considered, such as walking trails 
and passive recreation. Plantation on the TSF shall be avoided. Option studies for land use can be 
undertaken with ongoing dam management programme if the dam remains declared. Once the dam is de-
declared, there may be an opportunity to reuse tailings for industrial use. Whilst the TSF may be de-declared 
there remains an ever-present risk that future development works on the TSF may adversely disrupt the 
stability of the TSF (such as through reintroduction of water to the TSF material). This will also include that 
any investigatory works and ensuring the site is returned to a secure safe state. 

--- Dam Page 23 ---
Project number 531168-000  File MCC PMLU State Led Rezoning_ Dam Report_RevB_CLEAN COPY.docx  2026-07-01
Revision B
18 
 
 
 
5.4 
De-declaration of NSD 
5.4.1 
Natural infiltration 
Currently, the rehabilitation of the TSF is being undertaken, and a final landform will be created which will 
allow channelling run-off from the TSF area to drains on the finished impermeable surface and route the run-
off away from the TSF. This will prevent rainfall infiltration into the TSF. The stored tailings will rely on natural 
infiltration for reduction in the phreatic level. Once the TSF does not have significant volume that can flow 
downstream during a potential dambreak event and that there is no PAR/PLL, the dam will be a candidate 
for de-declaration. Even then, the inundation extent (much reduced compared to the baseline extent) shall 
be avoided for any development that will have the potential to introduce PAR/PLL. 
5.4.2 
Accelerated dewatering 
The de-declaration process may be accelerated by providing additional drainage pathways within the 
tailings, such as through the installation of horizontal or vertical drains. The effectiveness of these measures 
should be assessed during the concept design stage, particularly given the relatively low permeability of the 
tailings. 
The current water level within the tailings is not well defined; therefore, installation of additional groundwater 
monitoring wells is recommended to better characterise groundwater levels and flow directions.  
5.5 
Conclusions and recommendations 
The TSF is a declared dam under the Dam Safety Act 2015 and Dam Safety Regulation 2019. This requires 
complying with the Dam Safety legislation to ensure that the dam is operated and maintained safely, 
required assessments are undertaken from time to time and implementation of remedial or safety measures 
mandated by the authority are undertaken.  
The dam is currently compliant with the recommendations stipulated in various Australian National 
Committee on Large Dams (ANCOLD) guidelines and Dam Safety NSW guidelines based on the 
surveillance report from 2025. Dambreak and consequence assessments were undertaken in 2023 and 
updated in 2024. A safety review of the dam has been undertaken in 2025 followed by risk assessment and 
‘so far as is reasonably practicable’ (SFAIRP) assessment. A staged capping programme is implemented at 
the dam and is still ongoing.  
Until the dam is de-declared, the dam safety monitoring and surveillance activities shall continue to be 
implemented following ANCOLD guidelines and Dam Safety NSW guidelines. The dam (NSD and TSF) shall 
continue to be maintained following the dam safety management system (DSMS). Investigations at the TSF 
shall be undertaken to understand the reduction in phreatic level as well as exact ground water level within 
the tailings. 
New and existing infrastructure, such as roads that traverse the dambreak inundation zone and have the 
potential to increase societal risk, must be appropriately designed to ensure they are located above the 
modelled dambreak inundation level whilst the TSF is a declared dam.The inundation extent will reduce over 
time, with the reduction in phreatic level due to natural infiltration in the TSF, releasing more land 
progressively available for development subject to geotechnical constraints. Areas above the TSF could 
provide land uses which do not compromise the capping once rehabilitation is complete and a more stable 
landform is achieved over time. 
Options for accelerated dewatering the TSF can be explored to reduce the timeframe for revocation of 
declared status. 
A flow chart has been prepared and presented in Figure 5-6 with recommendations to support staged 
development. A list of activities required to be undertaken at the NSD and TSF to continue maintain the 
safety of the dam discussed in this report is compiled and presented in Table 5-1.

The overarching aims of the recommendations to be translated into the Master Plan are as follows: 
 To enable safe, adaptive, and long-term development of the TSF area by embedding a risk-informed 
planning framework that recognises and responds to the Tailings Storage Facility and associated dam 
break hazards over its rehabilitation and post-closure phases until de-declared. 
 To maintain a high level of dam safety by continuing regular inspections, monitoring, and maintenance so 
that any issues are identified early and addressed quickly. 
 To regularly update understanding of flood risk from a potential dam failure as conditions improve over 
time, so that more land can safely be considered for future development. 
 To minimise risk to people by carefully controlling development near the TSF, limiting sensitive land uses 
in affected areas, and ensuring infrastructure is safely designed, until the dam is no longer declared.

=== FLOODING & DRAINAGE ===

Executive summary 
This Flooding and Water Cycle Management Report (This Report) presents a strategic flooding and water 
cycle management (WCM) assessment for the Macquarie Coal Complex Precinct (the Precinct) and Teralba 
Southgate to support a state-led rezoning and Master Plan. The assessment confirms that the Precinct can 
be developed with a coordinated flooding and water cycle management strategy that supports future land 
use while protecting people, property, infrastructure and the surrounding environment.  
The assessment has been undertaken at a master planning scale using available flood studies, water cycle 
data, site investigations and topographic analysis. It focuses on identifying key constraints, opportunities and 
system behaviours rather than detailed design. On this basis, it demonstrates that flooding, stormwater, 
water quality and emergency management outcomes are practically achievable across the Precinct through 
an integrated, precinct-scale approach.  
Flooding Strategy and Precinct Response 
 
Flooding is a defining characteristic of the Precinct, driven predominantly by regional flooding from Cockle 
Creek, supported by local overland flow processes and downstream tidal influences. These mechanisms 
establish the spatial framework for development by identifying where land should be protected, where 
development can occur, and where mitigation is required.  
The Master Plan adopts a fundamental strategy of avoidance first, followed by selective, managed 
encroachment in lower impact areas where development can be supported without increasing risk. This 
approach preserves key floodplain functions while maximising viable development land. 
The recommended flooding strategy is based on several core principles: 
 Preservation of primary floodways and conveyance corridors 
 Retention of flood storage areas and natural drainage pathways 
 Direction of development toward areas of lower flood risk 
 Integration of flood mitigation measures to support safe development 
This approach ensures that development responds to the floodplain rather than working against it, 
maintaining the hydraulic integrity of the system while enabling growth.  
Protection of Surrounding Environment and Property 
A key outcome of the assessment is that the proposed strategy protects both the environmental values of the 
Precinct and the surrounding catchment, while avoiding adverse impacts on adjacent landholdings. 
The Precinct drains to sensitive receiving environments including Cockle Creek, Burkes Creek, Diega Creek 
and Lake Macquarie, which contain important ecological features such as riparian corridors, wetlands and 
key fish habitat.  
The master plan integrates these systems into the development framework by: 
 Maintaining riparian corridors as functional flood conveyance and ecological buffers 
 Protecting water quality through integrated treatment and management measures 
 Avoiding increases in downstream flood risk or changes to flow behaviour 
 Ensuring no material transfer of flood or drainage impacts to neighbouring land 
This ensures that future development does not degrade environmental value or increase risk beyond the 
site, a critical requirement for strategic planning and approval. 
 
 

--- Flood Page 4 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final Flooding & WCM Engineering Report_CLEAN.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
 
 
 
Deliverability of Mitigation Within the Precinct 
A significant finding of the assessment is that the majority of required mitigation measures can be 
accommodated within the Precinct footprint. This includes: 
 Floodway corridors and overland flow paths 
 Regional and local detention systems 
 Stormwater conveyance networks 
 Water quality treatment infrastructure 
 Landform adjustments to manage flow and storage 
These measures can be embedded into the structure of future development, allowing flood risk and water 
cycle objectives to be addressed without reliance on extensive off-site works or unacceptable external 
impacts.  
This outcome demonstrates that the Precinct is not constrained in a way that precludes development, but 
instead requires a coordinated and integrated design response at the master planning level. 
Master Plan Intent and Flexibility 
The master plan establishes a clear, achievable and flexible framework for future development. It defines the 
spatial logic, performance objectives and key principles required to guide design and approvals, rather than 
prescribing a single fixed engineering solution.  
Importantly: 
 The strategy is intended to be implemented progressively 
 Future proponents can refine and adapt solutions 
 Any modifications must remain consistent with the overall objectives 
 All outcomes must comply with relevant legislation, policy and performance criteria 
This ensures the plan remains practical and adaptable to future land use changes, evolving design 
approaches and updated technical standards, while maintaining a consistent approach to flood risk and 
water management. 
Demonstrated Feasibility at Strategic Level 
Based on the site review and strategic assessment, all key aspects of flooding and water cycle management 
are considered feasible across the Precinct. 
This includes: 
 Flood risk management and land use compatibility 
 Stormwater collection, conveyance and discharge 
 Water quality management and protection of receiving environments 
 Emergency access and evacuation planning 
While further modelling and design will be required at later stages, the assessment confirms that there is a 
credible and workable pathway to achieve these outcomes within future development.  
Future Opportunities and Sustainable Water Strategies 
In addition to conventional infrastructure, the Precinct presents opportunities to adopt more sustainable and 
integrated water cycle approaches that reduce reliance on traditional systems. 
 
 

--- Flood Page 5 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final Flooding & WCM Engineering Report_CLEAN.docx  2026-07-01  Revision B
 
 
 
Potential strategies include: 
 Stormwater harvesting for non-potable reuse at lot or precinct scale 
 Rainwater capture systems to reduce runoff volumes 
 Passive irrigation of landscapes and green infrastructure such as through the use of street trees 
 Distributed bioretention, detention and infiltration, where ground conditions allow 
 Integration of water sensitive urban design (WSUD) across the development 
These strategies can: 
 Reduce demand on downstream drainage infrastructure 
 Improve water quality outcomes 
 Enhance resilience to climate variability 
 Support more efficient and sustainable long-term servicing 
Collectively, they represent a pathway toward a lower impact, more adaptive water management system for 
the Precinct.  
Conclusion 
Overall, the flooding and water cycle management assessment supports a master plan that is practical, 
flexible and environmentally responsible. It demonstrates that development within the Precinct can proceed, 
provided that key floodplain functions are maintained and an integrated strategy is implemented. 
The proposed approach protects surrounding communities and environmental systems, accommodates 
required mitigation within the site, and establishes a robust framework to guide future planning, design and 
delivery.

1 
Introduction 
This report confirms that the Precinct can be planned with a practical and achievable flooding and water cycle 
management strategy that supports future development while protecting people, property, infrastructure and the 
surrounding environment. The assessment has been undertaken at a strategic master planning level and is based 
on a review of the site, available flood studies, water cycle management information, topography, waterways, 
receiving environments and existing infrastructure. On that basis, the overall conclusion is that the key flooding, 
stormwater, water quality and evacuation outcomes for the Precinct are capable of being achieved through a 
coordinated precinct-scale approach, subject to detailed design in later phases. 
Flooding is a defining consideration for the Precinct, particularly in relation to Cockle Creek, its tributaries, local 
overland flow paths and downstream tailwater influences. However, the report demonstrates that these constraints 
do not preclude future land use planning. Rather, they establish a clear framework for where development should 
occur, where flood conveyance and storage should be maintained, and where supporting mitigation is required. 
The proposed flooding strategy is built around preserving key floodways, accommodating regional flow paths, 
providing detention and storage where necessary, and locating future development in areas that can achieve an 
acceptable level of flood risk management. This creates a structure for growth that responds to the floodplain rather 
than working against it. 
A key message of the assessment is that the proposed strategy protects the environmental values of the site and 
the surrounding catchment, while also avoiding the transfer of flood impacts to neighbouring landholdings. The 
Precinct contains and drains to sensitive receiving environments, including Cockle Creek, Burkes Creek, Diega 
Creek and Lake Macquarie. It also contains riparian corridors, wetlands, key fish habitat and other ecological 
values that require protection. The recommended approach maintains these systems as important components of 
the masterplan, allowing them to continue functioning as flood conveyance corridors, ecological buffers and water 
quality protection features. In this way, the strategy is not only about making development possible, but about 
ensuring that the surrounding environment and adjoining properties remain protected from increased flood risk, 
water quality decline or inappropriate drainage outcomes. 
Importantly, the report finds that many of the mitigation measures needed to support future development can be 
accommodated within the Precinct footprint. This includes the retention of floodway corridors, provision of regional 
or local detention, integration of stormwater conveyance pathways, on-site detention, water quality treatment 
systems and landform responses that work with the site’s natural drainage patterns. While detailed sizing and 
alignment of infrastructure will need to be resolved by future proponents, the strategic assessment demonstrates 
that sufficient opportunities exist within the Precinct to embed these measures into future development layouts. 
This is a significant outcome because it shows that the masterplan can establish a viable pathway forward without 
relying on unreasonable off-site intervention or unacceptable impacts to external land. 
The intent of the masterplan is therefore to set an achievable and defensible strategy at a precinct scale, rather 
than prescribe a single fixed engineering outcome. The report makes clear that future proponents may modify 
elements of the ultimate flooding and water cycle response as individual development proposals evolve, provided 
the overall objectives of the masterplan are maintained and all relevant legislation, policy and performance criteria 
are met. This is an important distinction. The report does not seek to lock in detailed design at rezoning stage. 
Instead, it establishes the spatial logic, technical principles and performance expectations needed to guide future 
planning, design and approvals in a consistent way. 
Based on the site review and high-level strategic assessment completed for this report, all core aspects of 
stormwater management, flooding response, water quality management and emergency evacuation are considered 
practically achievable across the Precinct. This does not remove the need for future modelling, detailed design, 
staging reviews and approval pathways. However, it does confirm that there is a credible and workable route to 
resolving these matters through later project phases. In particular, the report shows that flood-compatible land use 
planning, structured drainage networks, protection of overland flow paths, water quality treatment trains and future 
emergency access planning can all be integrated into the development of the Precinct in a practical manner. 
Looking ahead, there is also an opportunity to reduce demand on conventional water cycle management 
infrastructure by exploring more sustainable and integrated servicing strategies as the Precinct develops. These 

--- Flood Page 12 ---
 
Project number 531168-000  File Flood & WCM Report  2026-07-01  Revision B           2  
 
may include stormwater harvesting for non-potable reuse, rainwater capture at lot or precinct scale, reuse of 
treated water for landscape irrigation or industrial purposes, passive irrigation of open space, distributed retention 
and infiltration where ground conditions allow, and broader water sensitive urban design initiatives that reduce 
runoff volumes while improving water quality outcomes. Such measures could lessen the burden on downstream 
conveyance and treatment systems, improve resilience and create a more efficient long-term water servicing model 
for the Precinct. Overall, the report supports a masterplan that is practical, flexible and environmentally responsible, 
and which provides a sound basis for future proponents to progress detailed design while meeting flood, water 
cycle and planning objectives. 
1.1 
Site location and context 
Located on Awabakal Country within the Lake Macquarie Local Government Area, the Precinct comprises of 
approximately 1160 hectares of land across the suburbs of Killingworth, Wakefield, Barnsley.and Teralba 
Southgate. The Precinct forms part of the broader Lower Hunter region and is strategically positioned within an 
established industrial and infrastructure corridor, with proximity to key regional centres. Figure 1-1 illustrates the 
regional context of the Precinct. Macquarie Coal Complex is a former mining operation comprising West Wallsend 
Colliery (underground mine), Westside Mine (open cut), the Macquarie Coal Preparation Plant (MCPP), Tailings 
Storage Facility (TSF) and associated infrastructure. Coal mining has been a defining land use in the area since 
operations commenced in 1969, shaping both the physical landscape and the economic profile of surrounding 
communities. The site is currently closed and undergoing rehabilitation, presenting a large, consolidated 
landholding with significant potential for transition to new employment-generating uses.  
At a regional scale, the Precinct is well positioned to leverage existing transport and infrastructure networks that 
have historically supported mining operations, including arterial road connections linking to the Hunter Expressway, 
M1 Pacific Motorway and broader freight networks connecting to the Port of Newcastle. This strategic connectivity 
supports the potential for the site to accommodate a range of employment uses, including advanced 
manufacturing, logistics and emerging industries, consistent with regional economic transition objectives.  
The broader land use context includes a mix of urban residential communities, industrial lands and environmental 
corridors. Similar to other legacy industrial sites transitioning within NSW, the Macquarie Coal Complex site 
represents a significant interface between former heavy industry and surrounding communities, requiring careful 
planning to manage land use compatibility, environmental constraints and future development outcomes.  
The scale, single ownership (Glencore) and relative separation from sensitive urban uses provide a unique 
opportunity to deliver a coordinated, master-planned transition of the site. Large tracts of underutilised and 
rehabilitated land offer flexibility to accommodate new industry typologies, while enabling the retention and 
enhancement of ecological areas and landscape buffers.  
Transition of the Macquarie Coal Complex aligns with the strategic directions of the Hunter Regional Plan 2041, 
which seeks to diversify the regional economy, leverage existing infrastructure and repurpose former mining land to 
support long-term employment growth. At a local level, the Precinct supports the Lake Macquarie Local Strategic 
Planning Statement 2025–2045, particularly in relation to growing and diversifying the economy, protecting 
environmental assets and delivering infrastructure that supports productivity and sustainable growth.  
As with other large-scale industrial transition projects, the evolution of the Precinct from mining to future uses 
represents a complex, long-term process. It requires coordination of mine closure and rehabilitation activities, 
consideration of environmental and physical constraints and alignment of multiple statutory planning pathways. The 
master planning process provides a framework to manage this transition holistically, balancing economic, 
environmental and community outcomes while enabling the site’s progressive transformation into a new 
employment precinct.

use planning, flood planning levels, and long-term flood risk management measures across 
the Lake Macquarie waterway and surrounding foreshore areas.
