6 
Water Cycle Management Assessment 
6.1 
Integrated Water Cycle Management Pathway 
Water cycle management (WCM) is a key consideration for future development within the Precinct. WCM is defined 
as the holistic approach that addresses competing demands placed on a regions water resources whilst optimising 
social benefits and protecting environmental values of receiving waterways.  
Diega Creek and Cockle Creek are the two key waterways located within the Precinct. Burkes Creek is also a 
waterway which is located at the northern side of the Precinct. Existing stormwater management within the 
Precinct is through natural flow paths within the undeveloped areas and via water management infrastructure 
across the disturbed site which includes catchment dams, sediment dams, storage dams, spillways and drainage 
systems. Cockle Creek is the main receiver of stormwater runoff from the Precinct, receiving flows from upstream 
tributaries, natural flow paths and water directed from the disturbed areas via two licenced locations.   
Key variables and interactions associated with groundwater within the Precinct include presence of groundwater 
dependent ecosystems (GDEs), groundwater levels and flow paths, and groundwater quality 
and potential contamination. The Precinct is largely underlain by soils with slow infiltration rates which 
may indicate limited or slow recharge of groundwater aquifers within the Precinct.  
Key sensitive receiving environments that have been considered include:  
 Coastal wetlands, key fish habitat and groundwater dependent ecosystems (GDEs) within the 
Precinct, concentrated largely within the riparian corridor of Diega and Cockle Creeks.   
 Downstream sensitive receiving environments including Lake Macquarie and Cockle Creek estuarine 
environments  
Drainage of stormwater within the Precinct will aim to minimise changes to sub-catchments boundaries and direct 
flows via existing drainage paths where possible. Formalisation of drainage will occur to capture and direct water to 
stormwater treatment prior to discharge to the downstream receiving environment. Onsite stormwater 
detention (OSD) will be required within the Precinct and the stormwater treatment strategy will consider options 
for both on-lot and end-of-pipe treatment to allow for flexibility of development size and staging. Stormwater 
treatment opportunities include rainwater tanks, gross pollutant traps, bioretention, wetlands and street trees.   
For water supply (potable and non-potable), refer to the Utilities report.  
The adoption of an integrated approach to water cycle management prioritises capture, treatment and reuse 
where feasible and aims to minimise water quality and quantity impacts to sensitive receiving environments.   
6.2 
Water Cycle Management Opportunities 
There are various water cycle management opportunities for the Precinct such as utilising existing infrastructure for 
stormwater detention and treatment uses, harvesting rainwater through water tanks and reuse on site and 
integrating stormwater management with landscape design. 
6.2.1 
Existing Infrastructure 
The ‘Discharge Water Management Strategy’ for the Macquarie Coal Preparation Plant (SLR Consulting, 2018) 
indicated that dams at the plant have adequate capacity to contain runoff in accordance with the EPL 1360 and 
Blue Book requirements (Landcom, 2004) for sediment dams.  Pending further investigation, there may be 
opportunities for reuse of existing infrastructure for stormwater detention and treatment uses. For example, the 
MCPP and West Wallsend Colliery ponds could be repurposed for onsite detention. Existing runoff diversions and 
catch drains may be reused depending on final landform and topography changes.  

--- Flood Page 64 ---
 
Project number 531168-000  File Flood & WCM Report  2026-07-01  Revision B           54  
 
6.2.2 
Harvesting and Reuse 
There are opportunities for an integrated water cycle management such as harvesting stormwater and reuse on 
site.  Stormwater can be harvested at an on-lot or precinct scale. At an on-lot scale stormwater from rainwater 
tanks can be used for non-potable re-use such as flushing of toilets and landscape irrigation. At a precinct scale 
stormwater can be used to supply water to local industry, irrigation or for other water uses. Urban development 
typically impacts volume, frequency and quality of stormwater runoff. Harvesting can reduce the volume of water 
flowing into the drainage system and so reduce stream erosion and minimise the impacts of urbanisation on 
aquatic ecosystems. Further, water quality can be improved through re-use by abstracting a proportion of polluted 
stormwater for re-use, trapping pollutants in on-line storages and returning treated stormwater to receiving 
waterways. Finally, stormwater harvesting can also substitute in part for existing mains water uses whilst balancing 
the need to provide flows for urban creeks and rivers (DEC, 2006).  
6.2.3 
Treatment 
Water quality reduction targets can be achieved by using typical Water Sensitive Urban Design (WSUD) treatment 
trains using Stormwater Quality Improvement Devices (SQIDs). Depending on the scale of the development and 
planning agreements, SQIDs can potentially be provided at the lot, street, subdivision or precinct scales. Examples 
of typical treatment trains from the Lake Macquarie City Council SQID Guidelines 2013 (LMCC, 2013) are listed in 
Table 6-1.  
The local constraints may prohibit the implementation of these typical treatment trains in some sections of the 
Precinct. These constraints are discussed in Section 4.5.3.

6.2.4

There may be opportunity to replenish groundwater aquifers through WCM opportunities that promote infiltration of 
soils. This may be particularly beneficial if the Precinct is identified as having depleted aquifers. At this stage due to 
a lack of monitoring and sampling information, groundwater levels and infiltration rates of soils is unknown. As 
mentioned in Section 3.2.5, the soils across the Precinct are anticipated to have slow rates of infiltration due to their 
hydrological soil group. Thus, opportunities for groundwater recharge such as implementation of “leaky” treatment 
trains which utilise infiltration may be limited. Further ground investigations and analysis will determine whether 
groundwater recharge is suitable for the Precinct.

Structure Plan 
7.1 
Proposed Structure Plan 
The proposed structure plan has been developed by GHD and is the principal spatial framework for the Master 
Plan. It identifies the arrangement of developable areas, environmentally constrained areas, recreational areas, 
movement networks and key constraints across the Precinct. The structure plan outlines the spatial logic for future 
development at a precinct scale, providing a framework within which detailed design, subdivision and development 
assessment will occur. The boundaries between land use categories shown on the structure plan are indicative and 
may be refined through detailed technical investigation and assessment at the development application stage. 
The structure plan has five developable sub-precincts with the last sub-precinct consisting of the remaining area 
made up of the environmentally constrained area.  
The following categories are used to describe land within the structure plan as shown in Figure 7-1: 
 Developable areas – Land assessed as most likely to be suitable for development, subject to further technical 
investigation and site-specific assessment at the development application stage. Developable areas are 
concentrated in locations with relative geotechnical stability, accessibility to existing or planned transport 
networks and proximity to utility infrastructure or feasible servicing solutions. 
 Environmentally constrained areas – Land identified as having high biodiversity values or where natural 
features (watercourses, wetlands, steep slope, flooding) constrain development for employment uses. Detailed 
environmental investigations are required prior to development or disturbance of vegetation in these areas. 
Environmentally constrained areas form an interconnected network across the Precinct that underpins 
ecological connectivity, water cycle management and landscape identity. 
 Recreational areas – Land suitable for active and passive recreation facilities, balanced with protecting 
biodiversity and cultural values. Recreational areas are primarily associated with the West Lake sub-precinct 
and the conservation corridor network, where the landscape and environmental values support nature-based 
tourism, walking and cycling trails and community recreational facilities. 
 Further investigation areas – Land constrained in the short to medium term by geotechnical, dam safety, flood 
or biodiversity factors requiring resolution before development can proceed. Further investigation is required, as 
described in this Master Plan, prior to development. The release of this land for development is contingent upon 
the completion of relevant technical investigations and the achievement of applicable staging triggers. These 
areas have been mapped mainly in the Cockle Creek sub-precinct with small areas mapped in the eastern 
section of the Killingworth sub-precinct. 
The rail loop to the northeast has been retained, along with most of the local roads within the Precinct. The six sub-

8 
Flooding and Water Cycle Management Strategy 
8.1 
Flood Management Strategy 
Flooding presents a significant constraint to future development within the Precinct and should be considered as a 
key input to the Structure Plan. The preferred approach is to avoid development within the most flood-sensitive 
areas, including areas defines as floodways and important flood storage areas, wherever practicable. 
Where avoidance is not practical, there may be opportunities for targeted development within lower constraint 
areas of the floodplain, supported by appropriate flood mitigation measures. In practice, a combination of land use 
planning, structural mitigation and non-structural management measures is likely to be required to balance 
development outcomes with acceptable flood risk. The suitability and effectiveness of these measures should be 
confirmed through detailed flood modelling and concept design during subsequent planning stages. 
8.1.1 
Regional Detention Basins 
Regional detention basins may reduce downstream flood levels by temporarily storing runoff during major rainfall 
events and releasing flows at a controlled rate following the flood peak. This approach primarily can mitigate 
increases in peak flow runoff associated with future urban development (refer Section 8.2.1) or it may be used to 
manage the existing catchment flows from Cockle Creek and Diega Creek upstream of the Precinct. Either way, 
the approach manages the flood risk downstream to mitigate impacts of development or potentially unlock areas 
previously at risk of flooding.   
The effectiveness of detention basins depends on their size and location within the catchment. Due to the 
dispersed nature of the proposed development areas and the varying topography, a distributed basin network may 
be more practical than a single regional basin when directly mitigating increases in peak flow from development 
(also refer Section 8.2.1). Where detention basins are used to offset and unlock downstream development, areas 
such as the Final void pit or along (offline) from the main creek lines provide opportunities. 
8.1.2 
Floodway Corridors 
The provision of dedicated floodway corridors may improve flood conveyance through the Precinct and reduce the 
hydraulic impacts associated with future development for local and possibly regional scale flooding. Measures may 
include localised channels, diversion channels or the preservation of broad overland flow corridors through the 
development area. 
Maintaining flood conveyance is particularly important where development may encroach into flood risk areas, as 
reducing the available flow area may increase flood levels in other areas. Future development planning stages 
should therefore consider retaining sufficient floodway corridors through the Precinct to preserve floodplain 
connectivity while balancing development outcomes (refer Figure 8-1). 
 

--- Flood Page 70 ---
 
Project number 531168-000  File Flood & WCM Report  2026-07-01  Revision B           4  
 
Figure 8-1: Typical floodway corridor example 
8.1.3 
Bulk Filling and Flood Storage Offsets 
Bulk filling is the most common approach used to facilitate development within flood-prone land by raising finished 
surface levels above the adopted flood planning level. While this protects development from flooding, it also 
displaces floodwater by reducing the available floodplain storage. 
The magnitude of flood impacts is generally related to the volume of fill placed within the floodplain, although local 
floodplain geometry and hydraulic behaviour also influence the response. Where flooding is predominantly 
characterised by flood storage, the impacts of bulk filling may be partially offset through the creation of 
compensatory flood storage elsewhere within the floodplain (refer Figure 8-2). 
Compensatory flood storage is typically created by excavating an equivalent volume below the design flood level to 
offset the storage lost through filling. However, the effectiveness of this approach depends on the hydraulic 
characteristics of the floodplain and the location of the offset storage. 
There may be limited opportunity to create meaningful compensatory storage where groundwater levels are 
shallow, as excavated areas may become permanently filled with groundwater and provide little additional flood 
storage during flood events. In these circumstances, alternative flood mitigation measures or strategic use of other 
floodplain areas may be required. 
Where development encroaches into floodways, flood storage offsets alone are unlikely to mitigate flood impacts 
as these areas are primarily important for conveying flood flows rather than storing floodwater. In these locations, 
maintaining or replacing flood conveyance through dedicated floodway corridors or diversion channels may provide 
a more appropriate management approach. 
 
 
Figure 8-2: Conceptual Floodplain Filling and Flood Storage Offset Arrangement 
8.1.4 
Non-Structural Management Measures 
In some circumstances, structural mitigation measures alone may not eliminate all flood impacts associated with 
future development. Non-structural measures may therefore form part of an integrated flood management strategy 
where residual impacts remain. 
Such measures may include land use planning controls, restrictions on future development within flood-sensitive 
areas, emergency management planning, or, where justified, compensation arrangements where changes in flood 
behaviour cannot be reasonably avoided. 
Overall, future development within the Precinct is likely to require a combination of flood storage management, 
preservation of flood conveyance, detention basins, careful optimisation of development footprints and appropriate 
non-structural management measures. The final mitigation strategy should be informed by detailed hydraulic 

--- Flood Page 71 ---
 
Project number 531168-000  File Flood & WCM Report  2026-07-01  Revision B           5  
 
modelling to demonstrate that flood impacts can be managed to an acceptable level while maximising development 
opportunities. 
8.2 
Stormwater Management Strategy 
8.2.1 
Stormwater Detention 
Stormwater detention will be required for development within the Precinct, as the increase in impervious surfaces 
will lead to increased runoff being generated under developed conditions. 
As part of the proposed stormwater management approach, stormwater detention will be required to be 
incorporated at either an on-lot or sub-precinct scale to ensure post-development discharge rates do not exceed 
pre-development conditions. Stormwater detention prevents urban flash flooding, protects local infrastructure and 
reduces erosion. Opportunities for detention are to:  
 Provide on-lot on site detention (OSD) through rainwater tanks (or storage tanks for larger allotments) to reduce 
runoff at the source, reducing peak flows entering the downstream network. This also benefits the council piped 
network as it reduces the pipe size show against catchments. On lot OSD design must be in line with Council 
DCP guidelines outlined in Section 3.1.2. Stormwater detention of roads and public infrastructure or open space 
would be required to be managed separately by Council where on-lot detention is provided.  
 Manage detention via a precinct or sub-precinct scale which would involve providing regional basins at the end 
of sub-catchments to provide detention for all upstream development. This type of system would manage 
cumulative catchment flows, providing a centralised detention function that supports efficient conveyance and 
reduces reliance on oversized pipe infrastructure. Refer to Section 8.1.1. Stormwater detention of roads and 
public infrastructure or open space would be incorporated into a regional basin detention strategy.  
The advantages and disadvantages to each detention strategy should be considered when determining the best 
option for development within the Precinct.  
 Rainwater tanks should be chosen when there is limited space available but moderate to low runoff attenuation 
required. Rainwater tanks offer the easiest opportunity for reuse on site and have fairly simple maintenance 
requirements, however they are normally sized for smaller events and may not effectively manage extreme 
storm conditions or large catchment areas.  
 Storage tanks are usually designed for larger runoff volumes than rainwater tanks and can more effectively 
manage higher peak flow reduction. Tanks can be combined with a rainwater harvesting strategy to provide 
reuse on site. Tanks are usually suited to larger development allotments due to high design and cost 
requirements as well as complex maintenance regime.  
 Regional detention basins offer an economical solution to large catchment areas which can achieve high peak 
flow reduction. Regional basins attenuate peak flows but do not largely reduce total runoff volume. Stormwater 
infrastructure also is required to be sized for higher flows up to the detention basin location.  
The suitability of chosen detention infrastructure and management will be dependent on the type and staging of 
development as well as landform and number of discharge locations. It is anticipated that different detention 
options will be suitable for different sub-precincts. There may be alternate uses for water captured onsite such as 
reuse opportunities from rainwater tanks which will further reduce discharge to waterways and be aligned with Lake 
Macquarie City Council’s principle to maximise water reuse. 
Consideration should also be given to ownership and maintenance requirements. Onsite detention options are 
normally owned and maintained privately, whilst regional basins are usually public assets. Maintenance burden of 
these assets should be considered when determining the most suitable option.  
Regardless of detention approach, stormwater quantity will be required to be managed prior to discharge to the 
receiving environment in conjunction with Council.  
When quantifying stormwater detention volumes and identifying potential basin locations, the interaction with the 
mainstream floodplain should also be assessed. As shown in Figure 8-3, most of the 1% AEP flood extent is within 

--- Flood Page 72 ---
 
Project number 531168-000  File Flood & WCM Report  2026-07-01  Revision B           6  
 
Developable Land subject to Further Investigation. Impervious surfaces within West Lake, Cockle Creek, 
Killingworth and Barnsley West sub-precincts encroach small areas of the 1% AEP extent and therefore no 
widespread impacts are expected.  
Further assessment will be required for the West Lake sub-precinct, where an existing lake is located within the 
proposed development footprint. Decisions regarding whether the lake is retained, modified or filled will influence 
both the available floodplain storage and the Water Management Strategy for the site, including the location, 
volume and configuration of any required detention infrastructure. 
The Killingworth sub-precinct also includes areas mapped as floodway, where development is generally 
discouraged due to the need to maintain flood conveyance. Future design stages should therefore seek to avoid or 
minimise encroachment into these areas where practicable. 
No flood modelling has been conducted as part of this assessment, and earthworks volumes are not yet available. 
It is therefore not currently possible to quantify the volume of floodwater displaced or confirm the required size, 
location and configuration of detention basins. These matters should be assessed during subsequent design 
stages once more detailed development layouts, earthworks information and stormwater management strategies 
are available.

8.2.2 
Stormwater Conveyance  
The Stormwater Management Strategy will aim to ensure the protection and function of waterways. The Precinct 
will be designed to work with nature to use the existing landform to dictate the stormwater conveyance network. 

--- Flood Page 73 ---
 
Project number 531168-000  File Flood & WCM Report  2026-07-01  Revision B           7  
 
The minor drainage system should be designed to capture and convey minor system (or nuisance flows) as per the 
LMCC DCP. The minor system flows are defined as localised flowing with an ARI of 2-5 years. The major drainage 
system is part of the public drainage system designed to convey the major storm flows.  
Catchment runoff should be directed through a clearly defined pipe or channel network that conveys flows to 
designated treatment nodes before discharge to receiving environments. Major overland flow paths should be 
preserved if possible, ensuring they remain unobstructed and integrated into the Precinct layout to safely convey 
exceedance flows. 
Drainage of stormwater within the Precinct will aim to minimise changes to sub-catchments boundaries and direct 
flows via existing drainage paths where possible to protect and maintain the hydrological regime of the receiving 
waterways. Formalisation of drainage within the Precinct will capture and direct water to stormwater treatment and 
detention prior to discharge to the natural water systems to mitigate impacts from increased runoff. Scour 
protection and erosion controls should be implemented upstream of discharge locations to natural waterways. 
In addition, if no sub-precinct scale or end of pipe stormwater retention or treatment scheme is developed for a site, 
development should demonstrate that impervious areas are captured for reuse or managed on lot through 
infiltration and retention prior to discharge to the drainage system.  Lake Macquarie City Council DCP indicates that 
only 10% of impervious areas on a site can be discharged directly to the receiving drainage system.  
8.2.3 
Natural Water Systems 
The stormwater strategy recommends development considers natural water systems including those within the 
Precinct and those downstream. In alignment with Section 3.1.3 and the Lake Macquarie City Council DCP, natural 
water systems including waterways and estuaries should be protected and not adversely impacted by 
development. This will be done by retaining creeks and natural drainage pathways within their vegetated riparian 
zone (VRZ). Preliminary mapping of the VRZ for the Precinct is shown in Figure 3-17 and further discussed in 
Section 3.2.9. 
Natural systems including all natural watercourses through the Precinct should be maintained in a natural state in 
alignment with the Controlled Activity Approvals on Waterfront Land. This will require buffer distances from 
waterways to be in place to maintain the riparian vegetation and retain ecological processes. Proactive 
rehabilitation of waterways is also recommended where development has the potential to exacerbate an issue or 
where additional vegetation buffers between development and the waterway is required. 
8.3 
Water Quality Management Strategy  
The Water Management Strategy adopted will be dependent on what targets are required to be achieved based on 
existing/ historical land use. For brownfield development, the strategy will be required to meet best practice 
pollutant load reduction targets. For greenfield development, the strategy will be required to meet no net increase 
to pollutant loads (subsequently referred to as requiring assessment of Neutral or Beneficial Effects (NorBE)). 
Water quality targets are stipulated by the Lake Macquarie City Council DCP and estuary health nutrient loading 
targets outlined in Section  3.1.1. Simple modelling using eWater MUSIC X software was conducted on a number 
of 1 ha MUSIC models to understand preliminary spatial requirements for specific WSUD measures. A more 
detailed MUSIC model and treatment train should be developed for the Precinct to further refine and determine the 
strategy. 
8.3.1 
Water Quality Targets  
Around half of the developable area within the proposed structure plan is stipulated by the Lake Macquarie City 
Council DCP pollutant reduction targets outlined in the second column of Table 3-4. However, there are sections of 
Cockle Creek, Killingworth, West Lake and Barnsley West sub-precincts which are zoned as conservation and rural 
and thus NorBE is required. These areas are marked up in Figure 8-4 and developable areas from the structure 
plan which consist of rural and environmentally constrained land are summarised in Table 8-1.

water quality targets adopted to protect the highly valued environment downstream of the Precinct and respond to 
the local constraints. The key proposed WCM measures are summarised in Table 8-3 and further discussed in 
Sections 8.3.3 to 8.3.5. An indicative treatment train is shown in Figure 8-5. This treatment train has been 
considered suitable for most circumstances but would need to be refined and modelled in detail in subsequent 
planning and design stages.

maintenance requirements for individual trees, preference should be given to consolidated 
biofiltration in place of street trees where possible.

8.3.3 
On-lot Treatment 
Rainwater Tanks 
For the proposed water quality management strategy roof runoff was assumed to be captured in rainwater 
harvesting tanks and reused for non-potable uses such as landscape irrigation and/or toilet flushing.  
Preliminary MUSIC modelling was conducted to model a typical treatment train with rainwater tanks paired with 
biofiltration basins for treatment, see Figure 8-5. The roof area was considered 60% of the developable area which 
was routed to the rainwater tanks with the remaining area going through a GPT. Ultimately, rainwater tank sizing 
would be further informed on an individual lot basis, dependent on the downstream infrastructure and achievement 
of water quality and detention targets for the site and Precinct. Further development of the potential onsite reuse 
will also determine sizing and capture rates for the rainwater tanks. The tanks could be used for irrigation and other 
non-potable uses such as toilet flushing. 
Gross Pollutant Traps 
On lot gross pollutant traps (GPTs) are proposed to be incorporated to provide source-control treatment for 
individual larger allotments. These devices capture coarse sediments, litter, organic debris, and other gross 
pollutants before runoff enters the downstream drainage network, reducing pollutant loads conveyed to 
precinct-scale treatment assets. This helps maintain performance and longevity of downstream end of pipe 
infrastructure. On-lot GPTs also support compliance with water quality objectives by distributing treatment across 
the catchment rather than relying solely on end-of-pipe systems. Their placement within accessible locations 
ensures ongoing maintenance can be undertaken efficiently, preserving treatment effectiveness over the life of the 
development. 
A nominal GPT unit was adopted for the basic modelling conducted for the removal of gross pollutants, sediment 
and some nutrients. If other units are proposed at a later stage, then analysis to confirm equivalent performance 
would be required. While on-lot measures support flexible delivery time frames, there is a high risk of on-lot 
measures failing due to poor management and maintenance practices in private ownership. 
8.3.4 
Road Treatment 
If no end of pipe treatment is available and water quality is being managed on lot, public roads should have an 
independent treatment management approach.  The approach to on street treatment would be via bioretention 
basins where size and routing of flows to larger downstream locations is possible. Where space is not available or 
for smaller portions of roads, street trees could be considered for implementation along public roads in the Precinct. 
The replacement of natural vegetated landscape with impervious areas increases urban temperatures and 
stormwater runoff. Street trees will be passively irrigated by directing stormwater into their tree pits, allowing them 
to naturally absorb moisture and helping to create a cooler, greener streetscape. Figure 8-7 is an example of a 
biofiltration street tree.   
Preliminary MUSIC modelling assumed biofiltration street trees were assumed to be incorporated at a ratio of 
approximately 16 trees per hectare of development.

Figure 8-6 Example of bioretention street tree (Blacktown City Council, 2026) 
8.3.5 
End of Pipe Treatment 
The preferred approach to achieving the required pollutant reduction targets is through an end-of-pipe treatment 
train incorporating a biofiltration basin and GPT or a constructed wetland and GPT. The suitability of these systems 
will be dependent on catchment characteristics, potential of inundation from flooding or tidal flows, available land 
and integration with landscape design. As part of the proposed strategy, wetlands and larger biofiltration basins will 
be located within public open space areas adjacent to the riparian corridors and positioned at local catchment low 
points. These end-of-pipe systems provide robust treatment of sediments, nutrients, and gross pollutants while also 
offering opportunities for habitat creation and landscape amenity. Where these assets are intended to become 
Council-owned infrastructure, appropriate drainage and access easements will be required to ensure long-term 
maintenance and operational functionality.  
Preliminary MUSIC model has been undertaken to size bioretention basins and wetlands. To achieve council 
pollutant reduction targets and nutrient reduction targets the bioretention basins need to be at least 1% per hectare 
of development and wetlands will need to be 5% per hectare of development footprint when paired with end of pipe 
GPTs. These GPTs work in the same way as on lot GPTs but are bigger for higher flows.

9 
Integrated Spatial Planning Implications 
9.1 
Flooding Constraint Classification Framework 
The Precinct has been classified into high, moderate and lower flood constraint areas based on the strategic flood 
assessment undertaken for the Precinct. The classification provides a framework for identifying areas where 
flooding is likely to constrain future development and where additional investigation may be required. 
The flood constraint classification is summarised in Table 9-1 and spatially presented in Figure 9-1. The framework 
supports an avoidance-first approach, directing future development towards lower constraint areas while 
recognising that targeted encroachment into parts of the floodplain may be feasible where supported by 
appropriate flood mitigation measures and detailed assessment. This approach seeks to balance development 
opportunities with the need to preserve floodplain function and manage flood risk. 
The characteristics and planning implications of each flood constraint category are discussed in the following 
sections.

9.1.1 
High Flood Constraint Areas 
The Cockle Creek, Burkes Creek and Diega Creek floodplain corridors represent the primary flood constraints 
within the Precinct. These waterways and their associated floodplains perform important flood conveyance and 
flood storage functions and accommodate significant flood flows during regional flood events. 
Development within these corridors has the potential to: 
 increase flood levels and flood risk to surrounding land; 
 reduce available flood storage; 
 obstruct flood conveyance pathways; 
 increase flood isolation and evacuation risk; and 
 require substantial flood mitigation measures and associated infrastructure upgrades. 
The confluence of Cockle Creek, Burkes Creek and Diega Creek is of particular importance, as it represents a 
hydraulically complex area where multiple flood mechanisms interact and floodplain connectivity is critical to the 
overall performance of the catchment. Development within these areas should be minimised unless supported by 
detailed flood investigations demonstrating that flood behaviour and flood risk can be appropriately managed. 
Accordingly, these areas are generally better suited to land uses that are compatible with periodic inundation, 
including drainage functions, open space, environmental conservation, utility corridors and other low-intensity uses 
that do not significantly alter floodplain behaviour. 

--- Flood Page 80 ---
 
Project number 531168-000  File Flood & WCM Report  2026-07-01  Revision B           14  
 
9.1.2 
Moderate Flood Constraint Areas (Further Investigation Areas) 
Moderate constraint areas generally include land adjacent to high hazard floodplain corridors, consist of low hazard 
flooding, low-lying drainage depressions, and areas with poor drainage gradients. 
While these areas may ultimately be suitable for development, they are likely to require further investigation such 
as detailed flood assessment, drainage investigations and potentially additional engineering measures to 
demonstrate that flood risk and drainage constraints can be appropriately managed. Development within these 
areas should carefully consider flood immunity, drainage feasibility, emergency access and the potential impacts of 
earthworks on flood behaviour. 
9.1.3 
Lower Constraint Areas 
Areas located outside the mapped flood extent and away from major drainage corridors generally represent lower 
flood-related constraints and potentially are subject to more local flooding and drainage issues and may provide 
greater opportunities for future development. These areas are likely to require less extensive flood mitigation 
infrastructure and may be more suitable for early activation within the Master Plan. 
Notwithstanding their comparatively lower flood risk, future development should still be supported by detailed flood 
assessment, drainage feasibility assessment and access and evacuation assessment to confirm development 
suitability. The identification of lower constraint land through the Master Plan should therefore be regarded as 
indicative only and does not remove the requirement for subsequent flood and drainage investigations during future 
planning and development approval processes. 
9.1.4 
Master Plan Implications 
The flood constraint classification has been compared with the draft Master Plan to identify areas where flooding 
may influence future development and where additional investigations are required. The assessment is intended to 
guide strategic planning and should not be interpreted as confirming or preventing development within any 
particular area. 
The review indicates that some development areas in the Master Plan extend into land identified as having 
moderate or high flood constraints. These areas will require further flood assessment to demonstrate that flood risk, 
drainage, emergency access and evacuation can be appropriately managed. 
Conversely, some flood-constrained land may have the potential to support future development where appropriate 
flood mitigation measures are implemented. Measures such as detention basins, floodway corridors, channel 
improvements and flood storage management may reduce flood impacts and increase the amount of developable 
land, subject to detailed investigation.   
One key aspect of the areas identified for further investigation is the encroachment into the dam failure inundation 
area. The concept is that the existing failure flood inundation area is based on current landform. Given the low risk 
of failure there is opportunity to control the failure pathway. This allows for the opportunity to reclaim a portion of 
the at risk area through an engineering mechanism. 
Figure 9-2 presents the flood constraint classification overlaid on the Master Plan and identifies areas where further 
flood investigations may either support future development opportunities or confirm that existing flood constraints 
should be retained within the final Master Plan.

10 
Master Plan Objectives and Performance Criteria 
The objectives and performance criteria in this section have been developed to guide future land use planning, 
infrastructure provision and development within the Precinct. They are informed by the flooding and water cycle 
management investigations and seek to ensure that future development responds appropriately to flood risk, 
drainage constraints, water quality considerations and broader water management outcomes. The objectives 
establish the desired strategic outcomes for the Precinct, while the performance criteria provide a framework for 
assessing future development proposals and identifying where further investigation or management measures may 
be required. 
10.1 
Proposed Objectives 
The proposed objectives establish the desired outcomes for flooding and water cycle management within the 
Precinct, having regard to the opportunities and constraints identified through the technical investigations.  
 Direct future development towards areas with comparatively lower flood risk and drainage constraints. 
 Protect the floodway and flood storage functions of the waterways and associated floodplain areas. 
 Avoid intensification of development within areas subject to significant flood hazard or life safety risk. 
 Support a movement network that considers flood resilience to future climate risk, emergency access and flood 
isolation risks. 
 Ensure future development is compatible with the flood risk (hazard, function) and does not increase flood risk 
to surrounding land, infrastructure or communities. 
 Establish a framework for future detailed flood risk, drainage and emergency management assessments to 
demonstrate any management and mitigation measures are suitable for developing in areas of the floodplain. 
 Recognise drainage feasibility as a key consideration in determining developable land and future staging. 
 Ensure future development incorporates drainage infrastructure that is compatible with downstream hydraulic 
controls, including flood and tidal influences. 
 Implement Water Sensitive Urban Design (WSUD) measures to achieve urban water cycle management 
objectives  
 Minimise water quality and quantity impacts from surface water runoff to waterways and sensitive receiving 
environments including GDEs, sensitive wetlands and downstream estuarine environments  
 Ensure compliance with Lake Macquarie Council Development Control Plan including OSD and stormwater 
pollution reduction targets  
 Ensure compliance with NSW Estuary Health Risk Dataset which defines nutrient load targets for estuary 
catchments  
 Preserve groundwater recharge where feasible and minimise impacts to groundwater levels and quality  
 Implement proactive construction phase sediment and erosion control measures are implemented to protect 
downstream sensitive receptors.  
10.2 
Proposed Performance Criteria 
The proposed performance criteria provide guidance for future planning and development assessment and identify 
the matters that should be addressed to achieve the intended outcomes for the Precinct. 
 
 Flood planning levels (including freeboard) are to be as per Council requirements and include allowance 
Climate Change to year 2100. 

--- Flood Page 86 ---
 
Project number 531168-000  File Flood & WCM Report  2026-07-01  Revision B           20  
 
 Development is to demonstrate that it will not unreasonably increase flood levels, flood extents, flow velocities 
or flood hazard on surrounding land outside of the precinct. 
 Development within flood-affected or drainage-constrained land is to demonstrate that flood risk and drainage 
constraints are acceptable for the development type or have been mitigated to achieve an acceptable level of 
impact. 
 Future road, access and movement network planning is to consider flood risk, flood immunity to align with level 
of service required and flood isolation risks. 
 Flood-constrained land identified through the Master Plan is generally not intended for intensive and/or sensitive 
development, evacuation-sensitive land uses or critical infrastructure unless supported by a detailed 
assessment and suitable management measures are implemented. 
 Future development applications undertake detailed flood, drainage and emergency management 
investigations. 
 Development must achieve applicable stormwater quality targets including pollutant load reduction and nutrient 
load limits relevant to the Lake Macquarie catchment.  
 High-priority groundwater dependent ecosystems must be protected in accordance with the applicable policy 
framework.  
 Development must demonstrate an integrated water cycle and WSUD response that minimises hydrological and 
water quality impacts on downstream sensitive receivers. 
 WSUD measures must be designed to treat frequent storm events, including flows up to and including the three-
month ARI event 
 Development must maintain, to the extent practicable, natural flow paths, sub-catchment function and flow 
direction and must not rely solely on piped or heavily engineered stormwater systems where this would increase 
erosion, scour or downstream impacts.  
 Public domain, landscape and street design must integrate WSUD assets to support urban cooling, biodiversity, 
amenity and place identity.  
 Construction-phase sediment and erosion controls must be implemented in accordance with the Blue Book 
11 
Staging Triggers and Later-Stage Investigations 
The flooding and water cycle management investigations undertaken for the Master Plan have identified a range of 
opportunities, constraints and areas requiring further investigation. Given the strategic nature of the Master Plan, 
detailed engineering investigations have not been undertaken at this stage. 
Future planning, subdivision and development proposals will require progressively more detailed investigations to 
demonstrate that flooding, drainage, water quality, groundwater and related environmental constraints have been 
appropriately considered. The staging triggers outlined below identify the circumstances under which additional 
investigations, modelling, design development and consultation with relevant authorities may be required. 
11.1 
Triggers Table 
The Master Plan has identified a number of flooding and water cycle management matters that will require further 
investigation as planning and development progresses. The trigger framework presented in Table 11-1 identifies 
the circumstances under which additional technical assessment, modelling, design development or authority 
consultation may be required. The framework is intended to guide future planning and development assessment 
processes and ensure that investigations are undertaken at a level of detail commensurate with the scale, location 
and risk profile of the proposed development.

11.2 
Exclusions and Deferred Items 
The purpose of this Master Plan assessment is to identify flooding and water cycle management constraints 
relevant to strategic land use planning. The assessment is not intended to replace the detailed investigations and 
design processes that will be required to support future development applications and infrastructure delivery. 
Accordingly, the following matters have been deferred to subsequent planning, design and approval stages unless 
specifically required to resolve a critical Master Plan decision: 
 Catchment-wide hydrologic and hydraulic model development or major updates to existing flood models. 
 Two-dimensional hydraulic modelling of flood risk. 
 Flood impact assessments associated with final landform designs, filling strategies or infrastructure layouts. 
 Stormwater network design, including pipe sizing, drainage layouts and operational design. 
 Stormwater detention and water quality treatment system design. 
 Detailed water sensitive urban design (WSUD) sizing and performance modelling. 
 Detailed receiving water quality modelling and compliance assessment. 
 Emergency management planning and evacuation procedures. 
 Authority consultation and approval processes associated with future development applications. 
These investigations should be undertaken progressively as future land use layouts, infrastructure requirements 
and development staging are refined. The need for any investigation should be commensurate with the scale, 
location and risk profile of the proposed development and informed by the staging triggers identified in Section 9.1.

12 
Conclusions and Recommendations 
The flooding and drainage assessment has identified that flood risk is a key consideration for future planning and 
development within the Precinct. Regional flooding from Cockle Creek, local overland flow paths and downstream 
tailwater influences create varying levels of flood constraint across the site, influencing land use suitability, 
infrastructure planning and development staging. 
While significant flood-prone areas exist, the assessment indicates that opportunities may be available to facilitate 
future development through appropriate land use planning, flood mitigation measures and detailed flood and 
drainage investigations. The findings provide a strategic framework to guide refinement of the Master Plan and 
support future planning decisions. 
Water cycle management is a key consideration for future development within the Precinct. Diega Creek, Cockle 
Creek and Burkes Creek are the key waterways located within the Precinct. Existing stormwater management 
within the Precinct is through natural flow paths within the undeveloped areas and via water management 
infrastructure across the disturbed site which includes catchment dams, sediment dams, storage 
dams, spillways and drainage systems. The adoption of an integrated approach to water cycle management 
prioritises capture, treatment and reuse where feasible and aims to minimise water quality and quantity impacts to 
sensitive receiving environments. 
12.1 
Summary of Findings 
The following lists the key findings of the assessment: 
 Flooding within the Precinct is primarily influenced by regional flooding from Cockle Creek, together with local 
flooding, drainage and downstream tidal influences. 
 Flood constraints vary across the Precinct and have been classified into high, moderate and lower constraint 
areas to assist future planning and Master Plan refinement. 
 Floodways and major flood storage areas should generally be retained to preserve floodplain function and 
minimise increases in flood risk. 
 Several proposed development areas intersect flood-constrained land and will require further flood and drainage 
investigations to demonstrate development feasibility and identify appropriate mitigation measures. 
 Emergency management should adopt evacuation as the preferred strategy, with future transport planning 
considering flood resilience and flood isolation risks. 
 Flood mitigation measures, including detention basins, floodway corridors, flood storage management and 
development footprint optimisation, may provide opportunities to increase developable land, subject to detailed 
investigation and hydraulic modelling. 
 The assessment has been undertaken at a strategic Master Plan level using the latest available flood studies 
and supporting information at a desktop level and therefore provides a suitable level of confidence for identifying 
broad flooding constraints and opportunities across the Precinct. 
 The assessment is not intended to confirm development suitability or mitigation feasibility at individual sites. 
Detailed flood modelling, drainage investigations and emergency management assessments will be required 
during subsequent planning and design stages to refine flood constraints, assess climate change impacts and 
confirm the feasibility of proposed development and mitigation measures. 
 Diega Creek, Cockle Creek and Burkes Creek are the key waterways located within the Precinct. Lake 
Macquarie is a sensitive receiving waterway for the project. 
 Stormwater quality targets from the DCP and nutrient load limits (kg/ha) outlined in the NSW Estuary Health 
Risk Dataset (NSW Department of Planning, Industry and Environment, 2019) for Lake Macquarie Estuary are 
the key targets for water quality. 

--- Flood Page 90 ---
 
Project number 531168-000  File Flood & WCM Report  2026-07-01  Revision B           24  
 
 The Water Management Strategy adopted will be dependent on what targets are required to be achieved based 
on existing/ historical land use. For brownfield development, the strategy will be required to meet best practice 
pollutant load reduction targets. For greenfield development, the strategy will be required to meet no net 
increase to pollutant loads (considered NorBE). 
12.2 
Recommendations for the Master Plan  
A site-wide integrated Flood and Stormwater Management Strategy should be prepared following exhibition and 
prior to finalisation of development footprints, staging and infrastructure planning. The strategy should assess the 
cumulative impact of the proposed development across the wider catchment in greater detail, including changes to 
impervious area, runoff volumes and peak flows, floodplain storage, flood conveyance, flood levels and emergency 
access. This should be supported by detailed flood modelling, hydraulic modelling and MUSIC modelling 
undertaken post-exhibition, including testing of future development layouts, earthworks assumptions and 
stormwater management options. 
The current assessment is considered suitable to support exhibition of the Master Plan, noting that further detailed 
assessment will be required to inform subsequent planning, design and development application stages. The 
following recommendations are therefore provided to guide the next stages of planning and development of the 
Precinct: 
 Use the flood constraint mapping to guide refinement of the Master Plan and future development staging. 
 Direct future development towards areas of comparatively lower flood risk where practicable. 
 Preserve key flood conveyance corridors and flood storage areas within future land use planning. 
 Undertake detailed flood modelling, drainage investigations and emergency management assessments for 
areas proposed for future development within or adjacent to flood-prone land. 
 Investigate flood mitigation measures, including detention basins, floodway corridors, flood storage offsets and 
development footprint optimisation, to maximise development opportunities while maintaining acceptable flood 
risk outcomes. 
 Review flood planning assumptions against the latest Australian Rainfall and Runoff (ARR2019) climate change 
guidance during subsequent planning and design stages. 
 Ensure future development demonstrates appropriate flood immunity, drainage performance, emergency 
access and evacuation arrangements consistent with Council requirements and contemporary flood risk 
management practice. 
 Utilise a whole of catchment approach coordinating surface water management across all sub-precincts while 
responding to local topography, land use, and hydrological characteristics.  
 Adopt a Stormwater Management Strategy which considers stormwater detention, stormwater conveyance and 
natural water systems. 
 Adopt a water quality management strategy that achieves water quality targets and WSUD measures (on-lot, 
end of pipe and/or road treatment). 
 A surface water quality monitoring program should be developed to further understand and quantify the water 
quality within and downstream of the Precinct. 
 Comprehensive hydrogeological, ASS and salinity investigation and risk assessment will be essential to identify 
groundwater constraints, inform design modifications, and establish long-term management protocols that 
protect both development viability and water resource sustainability.

Executive summary 
This Traffic and Transport Report has been prepared to support the State led rezoning and associated 
master planning of the Macquarie Coal Complex (the Precinct) and Teralba South Gate sub-precinct 
(collectively referred to as the Site), a large post mining landholding west of Cockle Creek in the Lake 
Macquarie Local Government Area. The Site would be located between Teralba and Barnsley, framed by the 
M1 Pacific Motorway to the west, the B89 George Booth Drive and Main Road corridor to the north and the 
B53 arterial to the east. Wakefield Road is the key north-south spine through the area. 
The Site would comprise approximately 211,100 m2 of large format warehousing across the Cockle Creek 
and Killingworth employment cores, and a mixed-use core of around 18,100 m2 at West Lake. At full 
development, the Site is anticipated to generate in the order of 12,470 daily trips of which 1,030 trips are 
expected to be heavy vehicles and 300 RAV 19 metre B-doubles. Peak hour volumes are expected to be in 
the order of 1,400 vehicles in the AM peak and 1,300 in the PM peak. 
Midblock and intersection performance was reviewed across the base year and the short, medium and long 
term, with and without the Precinct and a new Cockle Creek crossing. In the base year the network is 
expected to operate at Level of Service (LoS) A to B, with only the Northville Drive corridor toward the B89 
approaching LoS C to D.  
Background growth is expected to drive the Northville Drive corridor to LoS E by the long term. The southern 
and western network would remain at LoS A to C with the Precinct throughout. The Northville Drive and The 
Weir Road intersections on the northern approach to the B89, would have adjoining links reaching LoS D in 
the short term and level of service F by the long term and consequently have been identified for potential 
upgrade, with proportionate contributions where they reach capacity under background growth.  
Cockle Creek is a major line of severance for access in the wider area resulting in an already congested 
network to the southeast of the precinct. Reducing future vehicle demands on existing creek crossings 
through traffic management, mode shift, infrastructure upgrades and potential new infrastructure will be 
appropriately incorporated within the onward planning for the precinct. 
Three structural findings drive the network strategy: 
◼ The approved RAV B-double network does not extend into the Precinct, and heavy vehicle access would 
need to be newly established. Upgrading The Weir Road would provide the first compliant RAV route in 
the short term, the Wakefield Road route to the M1 would follow in the medium term as the principal 
freight route avoiding Barnsley, Holmesville and nearby schools. RAV access from the east through 
Teralba could be considered in the long term but would likely require a new road and creek crossing to 
bypass the grade constrained Rhondda Road 
◼ Rhondda Road climbs features a sustained uphill climb of approximately 1 km for eastbound traffic with 
grades ranging from 5 to 10%, followed by a sustained downhill descent of over 1 km at similar grades 
with localised slopes over 12 per cent, beyond the Austroads limit for heavy vehicles, so the Precinct is 
not accessible for freight from Teralba by the existing Rhondda Road alignment. Alternative eastern 
access to the Precinct suitable for RAV would be a key part of the strategy, this could be a new Cockle 
Creek crossing or upgrades to other infrastructure that currently restricts RAV access. 
◼ The Five Islands Road crossing of Cockle Creek is the only principal crossing and already operates at or 
near capacity. Therefore, the potential for a second crossing is a consideration in managing Precinct 
traffic in the long term. 
A staged upgrade program has been identified: 
◼ Short term (0 to 10 years). Establish The Weir Road as a RAV 19 metre B-double route to the northern 
access, deliver sub-precinct access intersections, and signalise and upgrade the Northville Drive 
intersections at The Weir Road and the B89 as well as the Northville Drive / Appletree Road / Wakefield 
Road intersection. Establish active transport links and extend public transport connections into the sub-
precincts 
◼ Medium term (10 to 20 years). Upgrade and approve Wakefield Road as the principal RAV 19 metre B-
double route to the M1, upgrade the bridge over the railway in Teralba, deliver improved east-west 

--- Traffic Page 4 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C
 
 
 
connectivity via a new internal road connecting to Wakefield Road, and provide internal spine duplication 
of the Northville Drive corridor. 
◼ Long term (20 plus years). Protect and progress a direct M1 connection, potential reactivation of the 
colliery rail loop with a south facing junction connecting to the Main North Rail Line, railway overpass over 
Racecourse Road upgrade, and integration with the Lower Hunter Freight Corridor and High Speed Rail. 
The assessment concludes that the proposed rezoning is not expected to be the sole contributor to future 
constraints on the surrounding road network, with background growth of local traffic being a key driver of the 
degradation in performance at the key intersections and corridors. Subject to the staged upgrade program 
identified in this report, there are no presently known transport issues that would make the rezoning 
inherently unfeasible.

1 
Introduction 
1.1 
Introduction 
This Traffic and Transport Report (this Report) has been prepared by Aurecon on behalf of the Department 
Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) to support the State-led rezoning of the Macquarie Coal 
Complex (the Precinct).  This Report assesses the proposed rezoning and accompanying Master Plan in 
relation to traffic engineering and transport planning related matters. 
This Report is structured as set out in Table 1-1. 
Table 1-1: Report structure 
Chapter 
Description 
Chapter 1 – Introduction 
Explains the report's purpose and the methodology used to assess the rezoning. Covers 
the baseline and future horizons, trip generation and distribution, network performance 
approach, and data reliance. 
Chapter 2 – Strategic 
Context 
Sets out the federal, state and local policy and planning framework the report responds 
to. Includes freight, Movement and Place, regional plans and the local LEP, LSPS and 
DCP. 
Chapter 3 – Baseline 
Analysis 
Describes existing conditions across the road, active transport, bus, rail and freight 
networks. Covers crash history, traffic growth, trip patterns, existing midblock 
performance and the key existing traffic issues such as the Rhondda Road gradient and 
severance features for future traffic connectivity such as Cockle Creek and the Main 
Northern railway line. 
Chapter 4 – Structure 
Plan 
Presents the proposed structure plan, transport network and traffic generation, then 
assesses midblock and intersection performance across the horizons. Sets out the freight 
and RAV route strategy, the integration of transport opportunities and the staged required 
upgrades. 
Chapter 5 – Conclusion 
Summarises the baseline results against Precinct findings, a Cockle Creek crossing 
benefit and the staged upgrade program. Concludes the rezoning is feasible subject to 
staged delivery. 
Appendices 
Detailed midblock assessment results supporting the performance analysis. 
1.2 
Purpose of this report 
This Report establishes an evidence based foundation to inform land use planning and infrastructure 
decision making for the Precinct to support the rezoning. The Report has been prepared to: 
◼ Support the development of the Master Plan including the establishment of the movement network 
objectives, access arrangements and connectivity principles, and transport performance outcomes criteria 
aligned with intended land uses. 
◼ Inform State-led rezoning by demonstrating that proposed land use allocations are supported by feasible 
and appropriate access arrangements, and that key transport opportunities and constraints are properly 
integrated into land use planning and staging. 
◼ Identify and prioritise transport infrastructure requirements necessary to enable development, including 
key upgrades and new connections, and to establish indicative timing triggers across short, medium, and 
long-term horizons (0-10, 10-20, and 20+ years respectively), supporting an orderly and coordinated 
delivery of land use outcomes.

1.3 
Methodology 
The assessment follows the TfNSW Guide to Transport Impact Assessment (GTIA) (TS00085 v1.1, 2024), 
and the principles of the TfNSW Transport Management and Accessibility Plan, supported by the Austroads 
Guide to Traffic Management (Parts 3 and 12) and the Austroads Guide to Road Design. The methodology 
applied to each component of the assessment and is set out in the following sections. 
1.3.1 
Baseline and Future horizons 
The baseline and future horizons adopted are as follows: 
Horizon 
Description 
Base year (2026) 
The existing network with current background traffic and no Precinct development. This 
establishes the baseline against which each future horizon is compared. 
Short term (+5 years) 
Background traffic is grown to 2031 and the Precinct is partially developed. Full build 
out is not expected within this horizon and a development reduction factor of 
50 per cent is applied to the generated traffic.  
The key road network connectivity links, being a new Cockle Creek crossing, the 
railway overpass upgrade in Teralba and the proposed internal local road facilitating 
east-west access to the site, are assumed not yet to developed, as well as the 
formalisation of Wakefield Road, south of Rhondda Road as an approved RAV B-
double route. This results in site access to Area 1 being primarily from the northern and 
southern access points via B89. 
Medium term (+15 years) 
Background traffic is further projected to 2041 and the Precinct is assumed to be at full 
build out, with full generation applied (no reduction factor). The connectivity links, 
including a new Cockle Creek crossing, the completion of upgrades to the railway 
overpass, development of the internal east-west local road and approval of Wakefield 
Road, south of Rhondda Road as a RAV B-double route, are assumed to have been 
established, activating the eastern access point to the Precinct.  
Long term (+20 years) 
Full build out and the connectivity links in place, with background traffic further projected 
to 2051. 
1.3.2 
Existing trip patterns 
Existing travel behaviour is established from ABS Census data for 2016 and 2021. Vehicle ownership trends 
are assessed at the Bolton Point to Teralba SA2 level by comparing the distribution of motor vehicles per 
dwelling between the two census years and against the NSW average, indicating the degree of car 
dependency that new land uses must plan around.  
Journey to work (JTW) patterns are assessed from ABS 2021 Census data tabulating place of usual residence 
by place of work at the SA2 level, for the suburbs in and around the master plan area (Teralba, West Wallsend, 
Barnsley, Holmesville, Edgeworth, Fassifern and Wakefield), identifying the dominant modes, the share of 
public and active transport and the principal origin and destination markets. These patterns inform both the 
mode share assumptions and the geographic distribution of light vehicle trips. 
1.3.3 
Background traffic growth 
Background traffic data was drawn from several sources, each covering a different part of the network and 
period. The sources are as follows: 
◼ Draft West Wallsend Rezoning TIA (GHD, 2025), providing 2024 survey volumes at a number of key 
intersections and the STFM (TZP22STMV3.93) growth rates. 
◼ TfNSW permanent classifier stations on the corridors surrounding the study area. Annual Average Daily 
Traffic (AADT) is compiled for each station over the available data periods providing a long‑term dataset 
suitable for understanding historic traffic patterns. with the 2020 and 2021 COVID-19 affected years 

--- Traffic Page 10 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 
3 
 
 
 
identified separately so that they do not distort the trend. Data from the following permanent TfNSW traffic 
counters were utilised: 
− Lake Road, 130 metres north of T C Frith Avenue (Station ID: 05208), providing coverage from 2008 
to 2023 
− M1 Pacific Motorway northbound off-ramp to B89, 250 metres West of George Booth Drive (Station 
ID: 050995), providing coverage from 2007 to 2016 
− Main Road on B89, 70 metres east of Fairleigh Street (Station ID: 05571), providing coverage from 
2009 to 2020. 
A global background growth rate of 1.2 per cent per annum, derived from the STFM approach rates, was 
adopted and applied linearly to forecast all source data to the common 2026 base year. The basis for this 
rate, and why the STFM data was preferred over the classifier trends for the lower order roads through the 
Precinct, is set out in the historical traffic growth section of the baseline analysis.

application of rates also does not consider any discounts to account for trip-chaining and/or self-containment 
within the Site given the early stage of planning. This further supports that the assessment is conservative.

The rates above give the trip generation at full development. A development reduction factor is also adopted 
to represent the short term, when the Precinct is only partially built out during the short term: 
◼ A factor of 50 per cent is applied for the short term, reducing all generated trips to 50 per cent of the full 
development total 
◼ This recognises that the rezoned land uses will not be established or fully tenanted in the short term, and 
that demand accrues progressively as parcels are released and occupied 
◼ The factor is applied uniformly across all land uses and vehicle classes and flows through to the 
distributions and the network assessment. As such, both the residential and the employment demand 
reduce proportionately 
◼ The factor is adjustable and is to be refined as the staging plan and release sequence are confirmed. 
1.3.5

Directional splits consistent with the surveyed entry and exit splits in the TfNSW GTIA were adopted to 
determine trip entry and exit movements throughout the Precinct and are summarised in Table 1-4. The 
residential entry and exit distributions are not provided in the GTIA, the adopted values align with: 
◼ The commuter based nature of residential travel, where trips are predominantly exiting movements in the 
AM peak (journey to work or education) and entering in the PM peak 
◼ Standard practice in NSW traffic and transport assessments, where residential areas exhibit a strong 
directional bias during peak periods.

Light vehicle trip distribution 
Light vehicle trips are distributed using ABS 2021 Census JTW desire lines (place of usual residence by place 
of work at SA2 level) for the suburbs in and around the Precinct, with each area assigned to its logical corridor 
of approach. The tabulation of around 1,600 resident workers shows that for the nearer destinations: 
◼ North (38 per cent) to the Edgeworth and Cameron Park SA2 
◼ South (24 per cent combined) to the Toronto, Morisset and western lake SA2s 
◼ Local west (23 per cent) within the West Wallsend, Barnsley and Killingworth area 
◼ East (16 per cent) to the Bolton Point and Teralba SA2, across Cockle Creek via Five Islands Road. 
The adopted shares combine this local pattern with the longer distance commute to central Newcastle and the 
Central Coast recorded in the wider Census data, which adds weight to the B53 and B89 corridors and the 
M1.  
Heavy vehicle trip distribution 
Heavy vehicle trips are distributed by freight market analysis, identifying the long haul, port, regional industrial 
and local markets the employment land would serve and assigning each to the route it would use under the 
heavy vehicle access strategy. The market identification draws on: 
◼ NSW Freight and Ports Plan 2018 to 2023 (TfNSW, 2018), forecasting the NSW freight task to grow 
28 per cent to 618 million tonnes by 2036 and identifying the M1 as the principal road freight corridor 
between Greater Sydney, the Hunter and Queensland 
◼ Lower Hunter Freight Corridor Strategic Environmental Assessment (TfNSW, 2021), describing the 
Hunter freight task as movements within the region and between Greater Sydney, northern NSW and 
Queensland 
◼ Port of Newcastle trade data, recording more than 160 million tonnes of total trade and a record 
11.1 million tonnes of diversified non-coal cargo across 25 cargo types in 2025 
◼ Greater Newcastle Metropolitan Plan (DPE, 2018), assigning the strategic freight and logistics role to this 
catalyst area. 
The heavy vehicle share of employment trips and the B-double share of heavy vehicles are benchmarked 
against the vehicle classification splits in the TfNSW Large Format Warehousing – Data and Analysis note 
(2024). The combined light and heavy vehicle distributions are then assigned to the external network to 
produce corridor volumes for the midblock and intersection assessments. 
1.3.6 
Road network performance 
An assessment of the performance of the road network under the future traffic demands has been 
undertaken. This includes evaluating the quantum of increase in average daily traffic on relevant roads and a 
Level of Service (LoS) review at key intersections or midblock sections and comparing these to established 
thresholds for LoS. The assessment also considered critical volumes as the maximum experienced flows in 

--- Traffic Page 13 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 
6 
 
 
 
AM and PM peaks for each midblock or intersection location. A midblock refers to a section of road located 
between two intersections. 
Given the expedited nature of the assessment required to support the state-led rezoning, this analysis has 
been undertaken using available information and in line with methodologies adopted for other rapid precinct 
rezoning projects. 
Midblock assessment 
Midblock performance is assessed using volume to capacity ratios (VCR) consistent with the Austroads 
Guide to Traffic Management Part 3. One-way lane capacities at level of service E are adopted by functional 
class, being 1,400 vehicles per hour per lane for arterials, 1,200 for sub arterials, 1,000 for collectors and 
900 for local streets. This methodology and the associated capacity parameters are consistent with those 
adopted for the adjacent West Wallsend rezoning, ensuring a uniform assessment criterion. The LoS traffic 
flow descriptions are provided in Table 1-5. 
Table 1-5: LoS traffic flow descriptions 
LOS 
Traffic flow description 
A 
Free flow conditions with unimpeded manoeuvrability and minimal delay 
B 
Stable flow with some restriction on manoeuvrability and acceptable delay 
C 
Stable but constrained flow, speeds and lane changing more restricted 
D 
Approaching unstable flow, limited gaps, speeds declining with little headroom 
E 
Operating at capacity, unstable flow with queues forming on any disruption 
F 
Demand exceeds capacity, forced flow, breakdown conditions and persistent queuing 
 
Conversion between VCR and LoS is speed dependent and based on methodologies outlined in Austroads 
guidelines. With regards to lane capacity, the following assumptions have been made based on the 
functional hierarchy of road as per Austroads Guide to Traffic Management Part 3: Transport Study and 
Analysis Methods: 
◼ Arterial road (typically regional roads or state roads in urban areas) represents interrupted road conditions 
with access to some properties and streets with operation speed of 70 km/hr to 90 km/hr 
◼ Collector roads (typically regional roads and some Local roads) are similar to arterial roads with speed 
limit less than or equal to 60 km/hr 
◼ Local roads represent interrupted conditions with access to properties, parking lanes and posted speed of 
50 km/hr. 
Table 1-6 provides the reference for conversion of VCR and LoS and lists the lane capacity based on 
functional classification of roads based on Austroads (2020) Guide to Traffic Management Part 3: Transport

Intersection performance 
Intersection modelling was not undertaken for this assessment as base traffic volumes and performance was 
not available, therefore only qualitative assessment was undertaken. For the qualitative assessment, 
approaching midblock LoS were adopted as a guide to suggest intersection performance, as follows: 
◼ Intersections between midblock segments with reserve capacity (LoS C or better) would generally 
operate with reasonable levels of services 
◼ Intersections with any adjoining approach midblock capacity of LoS D or above may be subject to poorer 
LoS D and therefore may require upgrades

1.3.7 
Traffic Assessment Assumptions 
The following assumptions were adopted for this traffic assessment: 
◼ A gross floor area to gross leasable area efficiency factor of 80 per cent is adopted for the commercial 
floorspace, accounting for common areas, circulation, amenities and back of house space that are not 
leasable 
◼ The commercial mixed-use rate of 31 daily and 4.29 peak hour trips per 100 m2 GLA is a blended 
average of component retail and commercial rates, as the GTIA does not publish a rate for this composite 
use 
◼ A 50 per cent development reduction factor represents partial build out and occupancy in the short term 
(0 to 10 years). The factor is applied uniformly across all land uses and vehicle classes, a simplification to 
be refined against the staging plan 
◼ AM and PM inbound and outbound splits adopted from GTIA guidance (employment 62 per cent inbound 
AM, 34.5 per cent inbound PM, residential 20 per cent inbound AM, 80 per cent inbound PM 
◼ PM trips assumed to be the reverse leg of AM trips, with origin and destination reversed 
◼ Site peak hour rates are adopted and the full site peak is assigned to the network peak hour, which is 
conservative 
◼ Highest order vehicle assumed to be the 19 metre B-double over 50 tonnes 
◼ Freight market shares are professional judgement informed by freight strategy, not a surveyed origin 
destination matrix, supporting the market hierarchy rather than precise percentages 
◼ A new Cockle Creek crossing is assumed, for the purposes of the with-Crossing scenario only and is 
assumed to be delivered during the medium term horizon 
◼ A heavy vehicle share of 15 per cent of employment trips and a B-double share of 3 per cent of heavy 
vehicles are adopted, benchmarked against the TfNSW September 2024 large format warehousing 
surveys 
◼ Light vehicle trips are distributed on ABS 2021 Census journey to work patterns and heavy vehicle trips 
on a freight market analysis, with the same corridor and market shares applied in every scenario 
◼ The M1 (Central Coast and Sydney) and Teralba local shares are professional judgement, not direct 
Census outputs, pending an extended journey to work extraction 
◼ Industrial light vehicle distribution assumed to mirror the residential corridor split 
◼ Distribution assumed constant across all horizons, with only volume scaling 
◼ Background traffic is grown from a 2026 base year at a single global linear rate of 1.2 per cent per 
annum, derived from the Draft West Wallsend Rezoning Traffic and Transport Assessment (GHD, 2025), 
STFM data and applied uniformly to all corridors 
◼ Survey volumes and turning counts adopted from the Draft West Wallsend Rezoning Traffic and 
Transport Assessment (GHD, 2025), pending updated surveys for the Precinct 
◼ Passenger car equivalents of 8.0 for B-doubles and 3.0 on general heavy vehicles 
◼ Intersection performance is not assessed quantitatively at the rezoning stage. It is inferred qualitatively 
from the adjoining midblock level of service 
◼ Any intersection whose adjoining midblock approaches reach level of service D or worse is flagged for 
mitigation consideration and detailed SIDRA modelling at the development application stage 
◼ The assessment is a strategic, rezoning stage analysis to establish structure plan feasibility and the order 
of upgrades, not design stage performance.
