2 
Strategic Context 
The planning policy documents in the following sections establish the strategic context that the transport 
response considers.  
2.1 
Regional Context and Connectivity  
The Precinct is located between Teralba and Barnsley, framed by the M1 Pacific Motorway to the west, the 
B89 George Booth Drive and Main Road corridor to the north, and the B53 arterial route to the east. 
Wakefield Road forms the primary north–south spine through the area, providing key internal connectivity. 
At a regional scale, the Precinct is well positioned to leverage established transport and infrastructure 
networks that have historically supported mining operations. These include direct access to the Hunter 
Expressway, the M1 Pacific Motorway, and broader freight corridors connecting to the Port of Newcastle. 
This strategic connectivity underpins the Precinct’s capacity to accommodate a diverse range of employment 
uses, including advanced manufacturing, logistics, and emerging industries, aligning with broader regional 
economic transition objectives. The regional context and connectivity are shown in Figure 2-1. 
 
Figure 2-1 Regional context and connectivity (PMLU Master Plan, 2026) 

--- Traffic Page 18 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 11 
 
 
 
2.2 
Federal 
2.2.1 
National Freight and Supply Chain Strategy 
The National Freight and Supply Chain Strategy is the Commonwealth framework for improving the 
efficiency, safety and resilience of the national freight task, supported by national action plans for heavy 
vehicle productivity and access. It is relevant as the employment cores are positioned as freight and logistics 
land served by the M1 national corridor and the Port of Newcastle, and the strategy direction toward high 
productivity vehicle access and harmonised heavy vehicle regulation under the Heavy Vehicle National Law 
underpins the RAV route approach taken in this report. 
2.2.2 
Sydney to Newcastle High Speed Rail 
The Sydney to Newcastle High Speed Rail program, progressed by the Commonwealth High Speed Rail 
Authority, is developing a preferred scheme with stations proposed at Broadmeadow and at Morisset in the 
Lake Macquarie local government area, with the alignment still being finalised. It is relevant as development 
within the Precinct must not prejudice the corridor or preclude any future desire to incorporate a tie into its 
infrastructure, and as even without a local stop the project would materially improve regional accessibility 
through interchange via the Northern line and could release capacity on the existing line for additional local 
passenger and freight services. 
2.3 
State 
2.3.1 
Future Transport Strategy  
The Future Transport Strategy is the NSW Government framework for transport planning and investment, 
directing a multi modal and place-based approach, successful places, net zero emissions and resilient 
networks. It is relevant as the Precinct creates an entirely new movement network, so every new road can be 
designed from the outset as a complete street with walking, cycling and public transport provision, and due 
to the strategy elevates network resilience. 
2.3.2 
NSW Movement and Place Framework 
The Movement and Place Framework is the NSW Government approach to planning, designing and 
operating roads and streets, prepared jointly by TfNSW and the Government Architect NSW and embedded 
in the Future Transport Strategy, supported by the Practitioners Guide to Movement and Place and the 
Design of Roads and Streets guideline. It classifies every road by two, its movement function for people and 
goods and its place intensity as a destination in its own right, producing street types that range from 
movement corridors with high movement and low place significance through main streets where both are 
high to local streets and places for people where place dominates. It is relevant for two reasons: 
◼ The Precinct creates a new network on a largely blank canvas, so every street can be assigned its 
movement and place street type from the outset and designed to it, rather than retrofitting place outcomes 
onto roads built only for movement 
◼ The framework gives the master plan its sharpest tool for resolving the central tension in this Precinct, 
being a substantial freight task passing close to the high place value Teralba centre, by concentrating 
freight on movement corridors that bypass the centre and protecting the centre streets as places for 
people.  
2.3.3 
Hunter Regional Plan 2041 
The Hunter Regional Plan 2041 sets the land use vision for the region, promoting sustainable growth, 15-
minute neighbourhoods and the global gateway roles of the Port of Newcastle and Newcastle Airport. It is 
relevant as the Precinct contributes regionally significant employment land within the fastest growing corridor 

--- Traffic Page 19 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 12 
 
 
 
in the State, and the plan requires everyday needs to be met close to home, which shapes the residential 
components at West Lake, Teralba and Barnsley West and their walking and cycling connections to the 
Teralba centre and the rail stations. 
2.3.4 
Greater Newcastle Metropolitan Plan 
The Greater Newcastle Metropolitan Plan identifies North West Lake Macquarie as a gateway to Greater 
Newcastle with a strategic freight and rail position. It is relevant as the employment cores at Cockle Creek 
and Killingworth give effect to that gateway role, and the plan therefore requires the Precinct to be served by 
a purpose built restricted access vehicle network, protection of the West Wallsend Colliery rail loop and 
consistency with the Lower Hunter Freight Corridor alignment. 
 
2.3.5 
NSW Freight Policy Reform and the Lower Hunter Freight Corridor 
The NSW freight policy reform program and the protected Lower Hunter Freight Corridor between Fassifern 
and Hexham preserve a future dedicated freight rail bypass of the Newcastle passenger network, with no 
committed delivery timeframe. They are relevant as the corridor passes the western side of the study area 
and strengthens the long term case for freight oriented land uses, while the absence of a committed 
timeframe means land uses relying on the corridor must be treated as a longer term proposition and local 
freight planning must remain consistent with the corridor in the interim. 
2.3.6 
Speers Point Transport Improvements (TfNSW) 
The Speers Point Transport Improvements are committed TfNSW works on the B53 at the Five Islands Road 
roundabout, forecast to reduce travel times by up to 50 per cent. They are relevant as the assessment 
assumes this short-term relief at the only existing Cockle Creek crossing, while identifying that residual 
capacity works will be required in the medium term as background growth and development demand 
continue. 
2.3.7 
West Wallsend Rezoning 
The Hunter and Central Coast Development Corporation (HCCDC) owns more than 1,500 hectares of former 
BHP Steelworks land at West Wallsend, immediately adjoining the Precinct, which planning strategies 
including the Hunter Regional Plan 2041 have identified as a potential site for environmental, economic and 
community benefits.  
HCCDC is undertaking technical investigations to inform a future rezoning expected to deliver a mix of 
conservation, residential, employment and recreation land uses. Of particular relevance to this assessment, 
HCCDC will work with TNSW to preserve land for the future Lower Hunter Freight Corridor in West Wallsend. 
Given its scale, adjacency and shared freight corridor, the West Wallsend rezoning is a key cumulative 
development context for the Precinct, requiring coordination of access, network upgrades and staging as 
both progress. 
2.4 
Local 
2.4.1 
Lake Macquarie Local Strategic Planning Statement and Imagine 
Lake Mac Community Strategy 
The Local Strategic Planning Statement (LSPS) and the Imagine Lake Mac community strategy set Council 
direction for jobs growth and 15-minute neighbourhoods. They are relevant as the structure plan gives effect 
to that direction, delivering regionally significant employment land and walkable residential neighbourhoods 
served by an integrated movement network.

2.4.2 
Walking, Cycling and Better Streets Strategy 
The Walking, Cycling and Better Streets Strategy sets Council direction for active transport across the local 
government area and identifies a rail trail from Cockle Creek to West Wallsend along the colliery rail corridor 
crossing the creek in the north east of the precinct and running along the northern boundary to Barnsley. 
This is a key link to Cockle Creek Station and also would be a safe attractive link between the precinct and 
key areas of population that may well work in the precinct. It is also relevant as the rail loop corridor is 
protected for the rail trail should freight reactivation not proceed, and the active transport network within the 
Precinct is designed to connect to this strategic route. 
2.4.3 
North West Lake Macquarie Catalyst Area Place Strategy 
The Place Strategy is the most location specific document, setting place outcomes for Teralba, Boolaroo and 
the surrounding centres. It identifies a walkable Teralba centre, improved station access at Teralba and 
Booragul (items S13 and S16), an active transport crossing of Five Islands Road from Lake Crescent (items 
S12 and S15), the Pitt Street intersection upgrade (item L19) and the Munibung Road multi modal freight 
corridor treatment in the Cardiff Advanced Industry Precinct. The North West Catalyst Area is shown in

3.1.1 
State Roads 
M1 Pacific Motorway 
The M1 Pacific Motorway is a major motorway running north to south that forms part of the Sydney to 
Brisbane transport corridor. The motorway provides a key connection between Sydney, the Central Coast, 
Newcastle and the hunter region. Near the study area, the motorway is a divided multi-laned road with a 
posted speed limit of 100km/hr or 110km/hr. T Access between the M1 and the study area is provided via 
the Newcastle Link (for south bound) or the B89 Route (for north bound). From this point the study area can 
be accessed via regional roads such as Northville Drive. The route accommodates significant commuter, 
freight, and tourist traffic volumes and is approved for use by heavy vehicles, including B-doubles and carries 
approximately 80,000 vehicles per day.  
B89 Route – George Booth Drive and Main Road 
The B89 route of George Booth Drive and Main Road form a regional arterial connection linking the north 
bound M1 Pacific Motorway with suburbs surrounding Lake Macquarie and western Newcastle. George 
Booth Drive serves as a commuter and freight movements between the industrial precinct and motorway 
network whilst Main Road provides access to urban centres. West of Edgeworth the B89 typically operates 
as a two-lane undivided road with wider carriageways at key intersections. East of Edgeworth the route B89 
has a shoulder lane mostly used for unrestricted parking with a cycle lane. The B89 route connects with 
Northville Drive via a two-laned roundabout then a single-laned roundabout to Wakefield Road into the study 
area. The route is also connected to the B53 via a multilane signalised intersection. The route is approved 
for use by heavy vehicles and accommodates regular bus services and has a posted speed limit between 
50km/hr and 80km/hr depending on the surrounding land use.  
B57 Route – The Esplanade 
The Esplanade (B57 route) is an arterial road providing access along Lake Macquarie and connecting 
residential and commercial areas. The route comprises a single laned urban road with a cycle lane and 
signalised intersections. It provides direct property access and accommodates local traffic movements, 
transport services and cyclists’ movements. The route to the west connects to the B53 at Speers point at a 
two-laned roundabout and the connects to the A37 east of Hillsborough. Parking is prohibited along its 
length. The posted speed limit ranges between 50km/hr and 60km/hr. Although not a primary freight corridor 
the route is approved for heavy vehicle use and accommodates approximately 22,000 vehicles per day.  
B53 Route – Lake Road | T C Frith | Five Islands Road | Toronto Road 
The B53 route comprises of Lake Road, T C Frith Avenue, Five Islands Road and Toronto Road. The route 
is a major arterial corridor connecting western Lake Macquarie with the M1 Pacific Motorway (via the B89) 
and surrounding regional road network. The route consists of a two-lane urban road with additional turning 
lanes at major intersections including the B89 signalised intersection and the two-laned roundabout 
connecting to the B57. The B53 does not have any existing links over Cockle Creek to access the study area 
except using single laned regional roads through Teralba. Posted speed limits vary between 50km/hr and 
80km/hr depending on the surrounding land use and road environment. The corridor supports a mix of 
commuter, freight, commercial, and public transport movements and is approved for heavy vehicle 
movements.

3.1.2 
Regional Roads 
Cameron Park Drive 
Cameron Park Drive is a regional collector road allowing south bound vehicles from the M1 to access the 
B89 Route from the Newcastle Link. The road generally operates as a two-lane urban carriageway with 
signalised intersections and turning lanes provided at key intersections. The road connects to the B89 at a 
two-laned roundabout and the Newcastle link at a signalised intersection. The road has a posted speed limit 
of 80 km/hr and parking is not permitted. The route accommodates regular heavy vehicle and service vehicle 
movements associated with residential construction, commercial activity, and regional freight access. Due to 
significant residential growth in the western Newcastle corridor, the surrounding road network experiences 
notable peak period congestion, particularly near the Newcastle Link intersection. 
3.1.3 
Local Roads 
Carrington Street 
Carrington Street is a sealed, two-way local road that connects to the B89. It carries a posted speed limit of 
50 km/hr and traverses a residential area, with on-street parking lanes provided on both sides. The road 
intersects Withers Street at an unsignalised junction. Carrington Street forms part of the local school bus 
network. 
Withers Street 
Withers Street is a sealed, two-way local road with a posted speed limit of 50 km/hr through a residential 
area. On-street parking lanes are provided on both sides. The road meets Appletree Road at an unsignalised 
T-junction and forms part of the local school bus network. 
Appletree Road 
Appletree Road is a sealed, two-way local road with on-street parking lanes on both sides. It passes through 
a residential area and a school zone associated with West Wallsend High School, with a posted speed limit 
of 60 km/hr which decreases to 50 km/hr on the approach to Holmesville. The road crosses Slatey Creek via 
a small bridge. Appletree Road terminates at a single-lane roundabout in Barnsley at its intersection with 
Northville Drive and Wakefield Road, and forms part of the local school bus network. 
Northville Drive 
Northville Drive is a sealed, two-way local road connecting to the B89. It passes through a school zone 
associated with Edgeworth Heights Public School and provides on-street parking lanes within residential 
areas, with a posted speed limit of 50 km/hr. The road crosses Slatey Creek via a small bridge and meets 
Wakefield Road at a single-lane roundabout. Northville Drive forms part of the local school bus network. 
Wakefield Road 
Wakefield Road is a sealed, two-way local road with a posted speed limit of 80 km/hr, reflecting its function 
as a connecting route between the Barnsley roundabout and the M1 Pacific Motorway at its southern extent.  
Rhondda Road 
Rhondda Road is a sealed, two-way local road serving an area of mixed residential and industrial land use in 
Teralba, including established industrial operations. The posted speed limit is 80 km/hr which decreases to 
50 km/hr on the approach to Teralba. The road runs broadly parallel to the rail corridor and the Cockle Creek 
floodplain. The steep descent into Teralba at its eastern end is a significant constraint on heavy vehicle 

--- Traffic Page 28 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C

movement, so in practice Rhondda Road is only readily traversable by larger vehicles toward its western 
end, with the grade limiting its suitability as a heavy vehicle route into Teralba. Further detail on the Rhondda 
Road gradient is provided in Section 3.10.5. 
Railway Street 
Railway Street is a sealed, two-way local road within a predominantly residential area of Teralba, with a 
posted speed limit of 50 km/hr. The road aligns with the rail corridor and provides local access to adjoining 
properties, with on-street parking available along the frontages. The road connects to the surrounding local 
road network at each end. The connecting roads and their intersection control types should be confirmed 
against the design base. 
3.2 
Crash statistics 
A review of the crash history within the study area was undertaken utilising the publicly available data from 
the TfNSW Centre for Road Safety. This tool captures recorded crash history in the 5 year period between 
2020 and 2024. The analysis breaks down the crash history to outline the trends in the crashes, accident 
prone areas, the type, severity, and number of crashes, categorised by natural lighting conditions. The crash 
degree definitions adopted for this analysis are outlined in Table 3-3 below. 
Table 3-3: Crash degree definitions 
Term 
Definition 
Fatal 
A crash in which a person dies within 30 days form injuries received in a road traffic crash. 
Serious 
A crash in which a person is admitted to hospital as a result of injuries sustained in a road 
traffic crash. 
Moderate injury 
crash 
A crash in which a person attends an emergency department following a crash but is not 
admitted to hospital. 
Minor / other injury 
crash 
A crash in which a person identified as injured in police crash data who did not attend an 
emergency department and was not admitted to hospital. 
Non-casualty 
(towaway) 
A crash in which at least one vehicle is towed away where there's no death and no person 
injured. 
 
The crash history of the Precinct road network and its surrounding corridors recorded 235 crashes. The 
records confirm that the existing network already carries a measurable safety burden, concentrated on the 
higher order corridors that the Precinct traffic would use. Accordingly, upgrades proposed as part of the 
Precinct may help with addressing the safety burdens currently present. The crashes are summarised below 
by severity, by the most frequent Road User Movement (RUM) types and by location. The locations of the 
recorded crashes are shown in Figure 3-2. Summaries of the recorded crash data along the Precinct road 
network are provided in Table 3-4 to Table 3-7. 
The records establish three points relevant to the rezoning being: 
◼ The existing network already carries a measurable safety burden, with around 29 per cent of all crashes 
resulting in death or serious injury 
◼ The crashes are concentrated on the higher order corridors and at a small number of intersections rather 
than spread evenly across the network, which means the safety risk is location specific and can be 
targeted by treatments at defined points 
◼ The dominant crash types, being rear-end, run-off-road movements and cross traffic, would be the most 
responsive to the proposed intersection upgrades proposed in this report.

Across the fatal crashes the common factors are higher speed environments and a mix of run-off-road, head-
on and sideswipe movements rather than intersection conflicts, with two of the three occurring in adverse 
conditions (overcast or raining) or in darkness.  
The serious injury crashes follow a broader pattern, dominated by intersection movements (right near, cross 
traffic and right through together accounting for around a third) and run-off-road events. Most serious 
crashes occurred in fine weather (~68 per cent) and in daylight (~57 per cent), as such the safety burden 
reflects the volume and geometry of the network rather than being driven by weather or lighting.  
Heavy vehicles were involved in a small number of serious crashes, including rear-end and sideswipe events 
on Rhondda Road, Cessnock Road and the Newcastle Expressway, and a notable share of serious crashes 
involved vulnerable road users, with pedal cyclists, motorcyclists and pedestrians appearing across Main 
Road, Lake Road, The Esplanade, T C Frith Avenue, Appletree Road, Racecourse Road and Railway 
Street. 
3.3 
Traffic Growth 
Historical traffic growth on the higher-order corridors framing the Precinct (the M1, the B53 and the B89) 
shows modest long term background growth, broadly in the order of 0.5 to 1 per cent per annum, with further 
detail provided in Appendix A.  

--- Traffic Page 31 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 24 
 
 
 
A global background traffic growth rate of 1.2 per cent per annum has been adopted for the assessment, 
based on the STFM growth rates documented in the Draft West Wallsend Rezoning TIA (GHD, 2025). The 
available traffic count stations are located on surrounding arterial roads rather than lower-order local roads 
within the Precinct; therefore, the STFM growth profile was considered a suitable basis for applying a 
consistent background growth allowance. 
Review of the STFM data indicates that the highest forecast growth occurred during the 2021–2026 period, 
with annual growth rates of approximately 1.9 to 2.0 per cent. This period also aligns with substantial recent 
development activity evident from historical satellite imagery, with much of the surrounding area now 
appearing largely built out. For the subsequent five-year periods from 2026 to 2041, the STFM indicates 
lower annual growth rates, generally ranging from approximately 1.0 to 1.59 per cent. As most base traffic 
volumes used in the assessment are from 2024, an adopted growth rate of 1.2 per cent per annum, rounded 
for assessment and reporting purposes, is considered to appropriately reflect the forecast growth profile 
beyond the initial high-growth period. 
3.4 
Existing Trip Patterns 
Existing trip patterns confirm a strongly car dependent baseline, with private vehicles accounting for around 
63 to 66 per cent of journeys to work and only 0 to 1 per cent by public transport and 1 to 2 per cent by 
active transport.  
This reflects the current regional, lower density context and limited public and active transport connectivity 
rather than a desired end state. Consistent with the mode shift sought by NSW Future Transport, the 
Movement and Place framework and Council's active transport strategies, the Precinct is planned to improve 
on this baseline rather than perpetuate it, through land use, density and connectivity that support higher 
walking, cycling and public transport mode share over time. As such the car-based trip generation adopted in 
this assessment represents a conservative approach pending the delivery of those improvements. 
3.5 
Existing Midblock Performance Results 
The 2026 baseline AM and PM Peak hour midblock performance assessment was undertaken for locations 
illustrated in Figure 3-3. The 2026 baseline indicates how the network performs in its present state, before 
any Precinct demand, and identifies where the spare capacity sits and where it does not. LoS A to C 
indicates free to stable flow with little delay, LoS D indicates the onset of congestion where flow becomes 
sensitive to small increases in demand, level of service E indicates operation at or near capacity, and level of 
service F indicates demand exceeding capacity with queuing and breakdown. 
◼ The Wakefield Road spine operates at LoS A to B in both directions and both peaks, the strongest result 
in the network. The northbound (inbound to the employment cores) direction carries marginally more than 
the southbound, but both sit well within capacity, confirming the spine has the potential to absorb some 
level of additional freight tasks prior to any upgrades. 
◼ Rhondda Road, The Broadway, Appletree Road, Racecourse Road and Charlton Street all operate at 
LoS A to B in both directions, reflecting their current role as lightly utilised local and collector roads. 
◼ Northville Drive is the exception. The segment north of The Weir Road already runs at LoS C to D and the 
segment between Wakefield Road and The Weir Road at LoS C during AM peak and Los D during PM 
peak. The eastbound and northbound toward the B89 direction is the more loaded in the AM and the 
pattern reverses in the PM, consistent with a commuter tidal flow to and from Newcastle. 
The 2026 baseline therefore frames the assessment. The Wakefield Road, Rhondda Road and western local 
corridors have ample capacity, while the Northville Drive corridor toward the B89 is the part of the network 
closest to its limit based on current traffic volumes and patterns, making it the corridor to monitor as demand 
grows. The 2026 baseline AM and PM Peak hour midblock performance are summarised in Table 3-8.

3.6 
Active Transport Network 
The existing active transport network within and surrounding the Precinct is limited and fragmented, 
reflecting the area's historical industrial and mining land uses. Within the study area itself, there is currently 
no formal active transport infrastructure no dedicated pedestrian paths, shared use paths, or cycling facilities 
exist internal to the site. 
In the broader locality, active transport infrastructure is generally concentrated along the surrounding arterial 
road network as show in Figure 3-4. The most significant facility in the immediate area is a shared use path 
running along The Esplanade and T C Frith Avenue on the eastern fringe of the study area, providing a 
north-south connection toward Speers Point. Beyond this, cycling is largely accommodated via mixed traffic 
arrangements on local roads, with a dedicated bicycle path present along the M1 Pacific Motorway corridor 
further to the west. There are no dedicated separated cycling facilities directly serving the study area. 
Connectivity across Cockle Creek is a significant constraint. Five Islands Road provides the only crossing 
point available to pedestrians and cyclists within the immediate area, limiting direct active transport access 
between the study area, Cockle Creek Station, and the residential areas to the east. 
Pedestrian and cycling access to the nearest rail stations is provided via the local road and footpath network. 
A shared use path runs along the rail corridor in the vicinity of both Teralba and Booragul stations, providing 
a degree of active transport connectivity between the two stations and the study area boundaries. Cockle 
Creek Station is accessible primarily via footpaths and the shared use path along Five Islands Road, though 
no dedicated cycling infrastructure connects directly to the station from the study area. 
Overall, the existing active transport network provides limited connectivity to surrounding public transport 
services, with significant gaps in infrastructure continuity both within the study area and across the broader 
locality. These key gaps are constraints to achieving the shift to more sustainable travel modes sought by 
the strategy for the Precinct. Addressing these gaps through a connected walking and cycling network linking 
the developable areas to the nearby train stations, local centres and bus services will be necessary to 
support higher active and public transport mode share over time. 
 
 

--- Traffic Page 35 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 28 
 
 
 
3.7 
Bus Network 
The Precinct has limited access to the general public bus network, with the Hunter Buses Network providing 
service along the northern edge of the study area. Bus stops are present at or near the northern boundary, 
associated with services connecting Killingworth and Glendale via the local road network. Most of the study 
area, including its central and southern portions, remains beyond walkable distance of any regular route bus 
service, as shown in Figure 3-5.  
More broadly, bus services are concentrated along the Five Islands Road, Seventh Street, Lake Road and 
Main Road corridor to the east, forming the primary bus route serving the immediate locality under the 
Hunter Buses Network, operated under the TfNSW public transport network. Services provide connections to 
surrounding suburban centres including Speers Point and broader regional destinations including Newcastle 
CBD. 
School bus services operate through the Precinct along Wakefield Road, routing between Wakefield and 
Barnsley Public School via Killingworth during the morning and afternoon school peaks. These services do 
not form part of the general public bus network and are not available for general passenger use. However, 
they are recognised as it could be expected that bus stops on these routes would likely attract 
concentrations of vulnerable users, particularly children walking during the school start and finish periods 
coinciding with peak times, which represents a road safety consideration where these routes coincide with 
proposed heavy vehicle and RAV movements. This reinforces the strategy of routing heavy vehicle 
movements away from sensitive areas where possible, and of providing safe crossing points and separation 
between heavy vehicles and pedestrians at the respective intersections. 
In terms of network capacity, bus services along the Five Islands Road, Seventh Street, Lake Road and 
Main Road corridor operate at a combined peak frequency of approximately 4 services during the AM peak 
hour (8:00 am to 9:00 am) and approximately two services per hour during the PM peak (4:00 pm to 6:00 
pm). Based on an assumed seated capacity of approximately 45 passengers per service, this equates to a 
theoretical capacity of approximately 180 passengers per hour in the AM peak and 90 passengers per hour 
in the PM peak direction.  
 
 

--- Traffic Page 37 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 30 
 
 
 
3.8 
Rail Network 
The Precinct is served by the Central Coast & Newcastle Line (CCN), which provides intercity rail 
connections between Newcastle Interchange and Sydney Central via the Central Coast. The line serves as 
the primary heavy rail corridor for the region, providing connections to major destinations including 
Newcastle CBD, Gosford, and Sydney, with broader interchange opportunities available at key nodes along 
the corridor. 
Four stations are located in the surrounding area particularly on the eastern side, as shown in Figure 3-5. 
Teralba Station is located east of the Precinct providing the most direct rail access. The southern parcel of 
the Precinct sits between Teralba Station to the north and Booragul Station to the south, affording this 
portion of the site particularly strong access to the rail network. Cockle Creek Station, located to the north, 
serves as a broader interchange station and key public transport node for the locality. Fassifern Station, 
located further south beyond the study area boundary, serves as the most significant station in the broader 
locality, accommodating CCN services as well as intercity and regional services to Brisbane, Casino, Grafton 
and Armidale. 
CCN services at Teralba, Booragul and Cockle Creek stations operate at a frequency of approximately 2 
services per hour in each direction during the AM peak (7:00 am 8:00 am) and PM peak (5:00 pm 6:00 pm) 
periods, resulting in a combined frequency of approximately 4 services per hour across both directions. 
Services are operated by the Mariyung (D-Set) fleet, which operates in configurations of 4 to 10 cars with a 
seated capacity ranging from 325 passengers (4-car) to 1,312 passengers (10-car) per service. Based on a 
conservative assumed 4-car consist, this equates to a theoretical capacity of approximately 650 passengers 
per hour in the peak direction. 
3.9 
Freight Network 
3.9.1 
Road freight network  
The road freight network in the vicinity of the Precinct is served by multiple approved heavy vehicle routes. 
B-double approved routes, as identified on the National Heavy Vehicle Regulator (NHVR) network, in the 
immediate area include the Pacific Motorway (M1), the B53 arterial corridor (Five Islands Road and The 
Esplanade), the B89 arterial route, Northville Drive and TC Frith Avenue. These routes are approved for B-
double vehicles up to 19m, 23m and 25/26m configurations. 
Within and immediately adjacent to the Precinct, Rhonda Road along the southern boundary, a section of 
Wakefield Road within the western portion of the study area, and York Street east of the southern parcel are 
also B-double approved for the same vehicle configurations. These routes provide connectivity between the 
study area and the broader regional road freight network, including access to the M1 Pacific Motorway. 
3.9.2 
Rail freight network 
The existing and planned freight network in the surrounding area is shown in Figure 3-6. The Precinct 
currently has no active rail freight operations. The only rail freight infrastructure within the Precinct is the 
disused internal rail loop associated with the former Macquarie Coal Complex, which is currently in a 
dilapidated and unusable state. The disused West Wallsend Colliery rail loop formerly carried coal to the Port 
of Newcastle but is dilapidated, and its junction with the Main Northern line near Cockle Creek faces north 
only, therefore, trains cannot turn directly south toward Teralba without a reversing movement via Port 
Waratah.  
This loop historically connected the site to the broader rail network and the Port of Newcastle for coal export 
purposes but no longer functions in this capacity. The disused rail loop also presents a separate long-term 
opportunity for adaptive reuse as a rail trail connecting Cockle Creek to West Wallsend, as identified in the 
Lake Macquarie City Council Walking and Cycling Strategy. 
The Main Northern Line passes adjacent to the study area via Teralba and Cockle Creek stations, managed 
by the Australian Rail Track Corporation (ARTC) and carrying both passenger and freight services 
connecting the Hunter Valley to the Port of Newcastle. While this provides a degree of proximity to the active 

--- Traffic Page 38 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 31 
 
 
 
freight network, there is currently no operational connection between the study area's internal rail 
infrastructure and the Main Northern Line. 
The proposed Lower Hunter Freight Corridor (LHFC), shown as a key planned rail freight route in Figure 3-6, 
is a TfNSW initiative to provide a dedicated freight rail line between Fassifern and Hexham station (located 
further up north of the Precinct The corridor alignment was protected in 2022, though no construction 
timeline has been committed to. Subject to its delivery, the LHFC may present a long-term freight 
connectivity opportunity that could strengthen the case for freight-based land uses on the site, and this 
potential should be protected through the structure plan.

3.10 
Existing Traffic Issues 
The existing road network in the vicinity of the study area is subject to areas of known performance and 
connectivity constraints, which are summarised below. 
3.10.1 
Roundabout Congestion (Five Islands Road / The Esplanade / TC 
Frith Avenue) 
The roundabout at the intersection of Five Islands Road, The Esplanade and TC Frith Avenue on the B53 
arterial corridor is a known congested location, experiencing significant queuing and delays during AM, PM 
and Saturday peak periods. As at May 2024, the average daily traffic volumes of approximately 40,000 
vehicles on Five Islands Road south of The Esplanade, 26,000 vehicles on The Esplanade between TC Frith 
Avenue and Park Road, and 22,000 vehicles on TC Frith Avenue between Munibung Road and Seventh 
Street reflect the considerable demand pressure on this intersection.  
Live traffic conditions illustrating stop-and-go and slow traffic on the Five Islands Road approach are shown 
in Figure 3-7. The Speers Point Transport Improvements project is planned to address this existing 
congestion and delays along the B53 corridor and is forecast to reduce travel times by up to 50% (TfNSW, 
Speers Point Transport Improvements). 
 
Figure 3-7 Five Islands Road / The Esplanade / TC Frith Avenue Roundabout traffic conditions (Source: ArcGIS 
Online Live Traffic Services, 9:30 am to 10:00 am) 
3.10.2 
Connectivity over Cockle Creek 
East West connectivity across Cockle Creek is limited to the B53 Five Islands Road corridor, with no 
alternative crossing available in the immediate area. This constraint concentrates traffic demand onto a 
single crossing point, contributing to and exacerbating the congestion issues at the Five Islands Road / The 
Esplanade / TC Frith Avenue roundabout described above.

3.10.3 
Connectivity to the M1 Pacific Motorway 
Direct connectivity between the study area and the M1 Pacific Motorway is limited. The absence of a direct 
arterial connection requires traffic to navigate the local road network, reducing the efficiency and reliability of 
freight and general vehicle movements to and from the motorway network. 
3.10.4 
Limited road connectivity - Teralba   
Teralba has poor connectivity to the broader road network, with traffic concentrated through the William 
Street bridge over the rail line north of Teralba Station, as shown in Figure 3-8. This bridge represents a 
significant pinch point, limiting access from the western portions of the study area to the broader Teralba 
road network via a single narrow crossing. 
 
Figure 3-8 William Street Bridge - Single Rail Crossing Point, Teralba 
3.10.5 
Rhondda Road Gradient  
Connectivity between Wakefield Road and Teralba is limited to Rhondda Road. Rhondda Road presents 
significant challenges for heavy vehicle movements due to its vertical alignment. As illustrated in Figure 3-9, 
the road features a sustained uphill climb of approximately 1 km for eastbound traffic with grades ranging 
from 5 to 10%, followed by a sustained downhill descent of over 1 km at similar grades. 

--- Traffic Page 42 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C

Figure 3-9 Rhondda Road Elevation Profile (Source: Google Earth) 
Assessed against Table 8.2 of the Austroads Guide to Road Design Part 3,reproduced in Table 3-9, the 
sustained grades sit in the 9 to 12 per cent band, where heavy vehicles are significantly slower uphill with 
substantial downhill reductions on winding alignments, while the localised slopes approaching over 12 per 
cent which Austroads classifies as not negotiable by heavy vehicles. Rhondda Road therefore is not 
recommended for heavy vehicle access from Teralba.

Rhondda Road is also the main sealed connection between Teralba and the interior of the Precinct. The only 
other sealed connecting, Powerhouse Road, has access through Teralba as it geometrically constrained by 
a narrow bridge over the railway that limits its suitability for larger vehicles. With both eastern approaches 
constrained, the issue is not an inconvenience of one of severable viable routes, but a structural barrier on 
the eastern side of the Precinct. Access to the Precinct from Teralba is accordingly difficult for all vehicles 
and unsuitable for heavy vehicles, which underpins strategy adopted in this report.  

--- Traffic Page 43 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 36 
 
 
 
Freight access is established from the south via Wakefield Road and the north via Northville Drive rather 
than from the east. The east access through Teralba is limited to general heavy vehicles for local servicing 
and is not available for the RAV access strategy in the short term.  
A potential future crossing of Cockle Creek linking The Weir Road and Racecourse Road could improve 
connectivity between Teralba, the B53 corridor and the interior of the Precinct, offering a more direct eastern 
connection than Rhondda Road. If delivered, such a connection has the potential to support heavy vehicle 
access via the B53, which could help divert freight away from residential catchments such as Barnsley and 
reduce demand on Northville Drive. The crossing is identified as an opportunity to enhance connectivity 
rather than a prerequisite for the Precinct, and its delivery, timing and form would be subject to further 
investigation. 
3.10.6 
Racecourse Road and The Weir Road 
Travel on this route is currently limited to smaller vehicles due to a rail overpass which restricts vertical 
clearance to 4.2 metres. This overpass supporting structure also introduces width constraints with a 
structural wall dividing the traffic lanes. More broadly, the active rail line presents three compounding 
constraints:  
◼ The limited clearance beneath the existing road-under-rail bridge 
◼ The restricted capacity and geometry of the existing road-over-rail bridge 
◼ The significant cost and complexity of crossing an active rail line to establish any additional crossing 
point.  
Together these limit the practical options for improving eastern access and are a key consideration in the 
connectivity and freight routing strategy for the Precinct.

4 
Structure Plan 
4.1 
Proposed Structure Plan 
The Structure Plan (GHD, 2026) organises the Macquarie Coal Complex into a series of sub-precincts set 
within a framework of conservation lands, creek corridors and the existing rail and road network. The 
developable areas are concentrated in the centre and east of the site and are separated from one another by 
extensive conservation areas, such that the transport network must connect a set of discrete parcels rather 
than a single contiguous landholding. The Structure Plan distinguishes developable areas, conservation 
areas, recreation areas, and further investigation areas, and identifies the indicative road hierarchy and 
connectivity links that the transport assessment tests. 
The principal sub precincts and their transport roles are: 
◼ Areas 1 forms the central and eastern employment core around the former Cockle Creek workings, the 
largest developable holdings, accessed from The Weir Road, Northville Drive with a potential future 
Cockle Creek crossing to the B53 identified as an opportunity to improve eastern connectivity 
◼ Area 2 is the northern developable area between The Broadway and Wakefield Road, accessed from the 
Wakefield Road spine and The Broadway 
◼ Area 4 is the western developable area south of Wakefield Road around the water body, accessed from 
Wakefield Road and Rhondda Road 
◼ Area 5 is a small developable and consideration areas on the northern and eastern fringes, accessed 
from Appletree Road, Northville Drive and the local road network 
◼ Area 6 is largely conservation and recreation areas to the west and south-west, framed by the Sugarloaf 
Conservation Area, with limited or no developable yield. 
Wakefield Road, collector roads distributing through the developable areas, and a network of existing and 
proposed local roads. The Structure Plan is shown below Figure 4-1. 

--- Traffic Page 45 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 38 
 
 
 
 
 
Figure 4-1: Structure Plan (GHD, 2026) 
4.2 
Transport Network 
4.2.1 
Overview 
The road network is organised as a clear hierarchy connecting the developable land to the regional network, 
consistent with the master plan. Three corridors frame the area, being the B53 along the eastern edge, the 
B89 to the north and the M1 to the west. A sub arterial road enters off Wakefield Road and the western 
connections to carry the main internal movement, while collector and local roads distribute traffic to the 
developable parcels.  
Access to the developable parcels is taken from defined points on Rhondda Road, Wakefield Road, The 
Broadway, Charlton Street, The Weir Road and Powerhouse Road. A new local road connection across the 
centre of the area is contingent on declassification of the tailings storage facility and an interim connection 
arrangement is to be provided. The short-term and long-term road networks are shown below in Figure 4-2 
and Figure 4-3 respectively. 
 
 
 
 
 
 

--- Traffic Page 47 ---
Project number 531168-000  File Final_Traffic & Transport_Engineering Report Structure.docx  2026-07-13  Revision C 
 40 
 
 
 
4.2.2 
Benefits of the proposed road network 
For general vehicles the proposed network delivers three principal benefits: 
◼ Demand is distributed across three to four directions of approach rather than loading a single access, 
keeping every access within a manageable range so all internal corridors are expected to operate at LoS 
C or better at full development once appropriate upgrades to the surrounding network have been 
delivered 
◼ The hierarchy is legible, with a single sub arterial spine collecting from collectors and locals, so through 
movements and freight stay on the roads designed for them and the residential streets are protected from 
intrusion 
◼ Resilience is built in, with multiple accesses and internal connections forming a connected network that 
offers alternative paths when an access is closed by incident, flood or maintenance. Future connectivity 
improvements, including a potential Cockle Creek crossing, would further strengthen this network over 
time. 
The Wakefield Road spine gives the employment cores a direct, sensitive receiver free run to the M1 Pacific 
Motorway, the highest capability freight corridor in the region, while Northville Drive provides a second 
classified route to the B89 for the port and Newcastle industrial markets.  
Significant or major freight generating lots front the spine and the principal collectors, allowing heavy 
vehicles to navigate without traversing local streets. The separation of the residential sub-precincts from the 
employment cores by the conservation lands and the creek corridors allows freight amenity impacts to be 
managed by geography as much as by regulation. The deferred central link, contingent on declassification of 
the tailings storage facility, will shorten internal freight paths between Cockle Creek and Killingworth and 
remove circuitous routing via the external network. 
4.2.3 
Freight access points 
The Precinct has three defined freight access points, each with a distinct role: 
◼ South Access from Wakefield Road. The primary RAV gateway to the M1 Pacific Motorway, carrying the 
Sydney, Central Coast long haul markets. Its upgrade and NHVR approval are the critical enabling aspect 
◼ North Access from Northville Drive and the B89. Serves the Port of Newcastle, Newcastle industrial and 
Hunter Valley markets and long haul routes on the M1 Pacific Motorway to northern regions 
◼ East Access from Powerhouse Road, Teralba. Limited to general heavy vehicles for local servicing in the 
short term and enabled for RAV access in the long term. A potential new Cockle Creek crossing is one 
option that could alleviate heavy vehicle traffic through Teralba and improve connection to the eastern 
regions, though it may not be required if other upgrades deliver improved conditions through to the east. 
4.2.4 
Transport Authority Engagement 
Engagement with TfNSW, Lake Macquarie City Council, the NHVR and ARTC is to continue through the 
rezoning. The traffic modelling methodology, including assessment intersections, horizons and assumptions, 
are to be confirmed with TfNSW.

The heavy vehicle task is derived from the employment land component. The heavy vehicle share is taken 
as 15 per cent of both daily and peak hour employment trips, being the average of the medium (class 2 to 5, 
21 per cent) and long (class 6 to 9, 7 per cent) class shares observed in the TfNSW September 2024 
surveys, and the B-double share is taken as 3 per cent of heavy vehicles consistent with the double 
combination class observed at the surveyed estates.  
On this basis the Precinct is expected to generate approximately 1,030 heavy vehicles per day (two way), 
around 108 in the AM peak hour and 96 in the PM peak hour, of which approximately 30 daily movements 
are RAV 19 metre B-doubles (over 50 tonnes). The Precinct is anticipated to generate approximately 11,450 
daily light vehicles trips, comprising around 1,320 in the AM peak hour and 1,250 in the PM peak hour.

The M1 Pacific Motorway captures 50 per cent of the heavy vehicle task (Sydney, Brisbane and Hunter

Heavy vehicle peak flows follow the warehousing entry and exit profile of the GTIA, with around 67 of the

outbound distribution run.

business day on the combined route set, with the Wakefield Road routes to the M1 Pacific Motorway 
carrying around 12 per day, RAV movements typically occur throughout the outside of the AM and PM peak 
periods. The broader heavy vehicle task on Wakefield Road of around 410 movements per day equates to 
roughly 28 per hour two way across the business day.  
4.3.3 
Distribution summary by scenario 
The same corridor and market shares are applied in every scenario, therefore, the difference between the 
short term and the medium and long term distributions is due to volume rather than direction. The short term 
applies the 50 per cent development reduction factor, while the medium and long term apply full 
development generation.  
Table 4-5 and Table 4-6 summarises the two distributions for light vehicle and heavy vehicles respectively 
and the share applied to each location. Light vehicle volumes combine the West Lake, Teralba and Barnsley 
West residential trips with the employment light vehicles, and heavy vehicle volumes are the employment 
freight task. As noted in the previous section, RAV movements typically occur throughout the outside of the 
AM and PM peak periods and therefore are not considered in the assessment of the AM and PM peak 
periods.

4.4 
Transport Performance Analysis 
4.4.1 
Midblock Performance 
Midblock performance is assessed using volume to capacity ratios (VCR) against lane capacities as set out 
in Section 1.3.6.Given the uncertainty in both the existing traffic baseline and the ultimate development 
detail, this assessment adopts a conservative LoS D as the criterion for identifying where upgrades may be 
warranted, with confirmed upgrade requirements to be assessed through more detailed modelling as more 
definitive information becomes available. 
The assessment is structured around the staging of the Precinct rather than a single full development case, 
so that the network response can be tied to demand staging and to the potential upgrades that unlock the 
network to support this demand. Three development horizons are tested, being: 
◼ Short term 2031 - 5 years 
◼ Medium term 2041 - 15 years 
◼ Long term 2051 - 25 years. 
Background traffic is grown linearly at 1.2 per cent per annum. Within each horizon the network is tested 
without the Precinct (background growth only) and with the Precinct. The medium and long term the with-
Precinct case is run both with and without a potential Cockle Creek crossing in place. This allows for the 
impacts to be identified from background growth, the Precinct traffic generation and the relief provided by a 
new Cockle Creek crossing, allowing each upgrade trigger to be attributed targeted issues. 
To represent the short term, when the Precinct is only partially developed and occupied, a development 
reduction factor of 50 per cent is applied to all generated trips, reducing them to 50 per cent of the full 
development total for the short-term scenario.  
This recognises that the rezoned land uses will not be established or fully tenanted in the short-term horizon, 
that demand accrues progressively as parcels are released and occupied, and that the warehousing and 
commercial floorspace in particular will fill over a period of years rather than on opening. The factor is 
applied uniformly across all land uses and vehicle classes and flows through to the distributions and the 
network assessment. Therefore, short term scenario reflects a proportionate reduction in both the residential 
and the employment generated demand. The factor is adjustable and is to be refined as the staging plan and 
release sequence are confirmed. 
The medium and long term results show the with-Precinct cases at full generation, with and without a 
potential Cockle Creek crossing. A potential Cockle Creek crossing (Corridor 14) is only present in the 
medium and long term scenarios, accordingly, no results are presented for this corridor in the base year or 
short term. The AM and PM Peak hour midblock performance assessment for development scenarios was 
undertaken for the locations illustrated in Figure 4-4.

Midblock Performance Results – Short Term 
The short term compares the 2031 network with and without the partially developed Precinct (80 per cent 
generation), which isolates the traffic the Precinct itself adds in this period. A new Cockle Creek crossing and 
the Teralba rail overpass upgrade are assumed not to be in place, therefore, all Precinct traffic enters and 
leaves through the northern and southern access points for Area 1, concentrating the load on The Weir 
Road, Northville Drive and Rhondda Road. 
◼ Without the Precinct, every corridor stays at or close to its base year LoS except for  Northville Drive 
north of The Weir Road  where LoS in base year changes from LoS C to D, with the increase in 
background traffic. 
◼ Adding the Precinct is clearly visible on the northern access corridors.  
◼ During AM peak, eastbound section of Northville Drive, between Wakefield Road and The Weir Road is 
expected to operate at LoS D with precinct in comparison to LoS C without precinct and Westbound 
section is expected to operate at LoS C with precinct in comparison to LoS B without precinct. During PM 
peak the midblock performance of this section in eastbound is expected at LoS C and in westbound 
section at LoS D in both with precinct and without precinct scenarios.   
◼ The eastbound section of Weir Road west of the northern access is expected to operate at LoS B during 
both the AM and PM peak without precinct, with precinct this section is expected to operate at LoS D in 
the AM peak and LoS C in the PM peak. The performance of westbound section is expected to change 
from LoS B to LOS C in the AM peak and from LoS C to LoS D in the PM peak under with precinct 
scenario when compared to without precinct. 
◼ The southern access performs better than the northern access. Rhondda Road east and west of the 
southern access stays at LoS A in both directions even with the Precinct, confirming the southern 
connections have substantial spare capacity to carry early employment demand and that the constraint is 
specific to the northern corridors, not to Precinct access generally.

In performance terms the short term shows that the Precinct could be established and partially built without 
triggering a duplication anywhere, however, that the northern access corridors including The Weir Road and 
Northville Drive would be the corridors most affected by Precinct related traffic as all site traffic is funnelled 
north and south while the eastern access is absent.

Midblock Performance Results – Medium Term 
The medium term applies full Precinct generation against background growth to 2041 and is the first horizon 
to test the network both with and without a potential Cockle Creek crossing. Comparing these two cases 
isolates the benefit the crossing provides. 
◼ Without the Precinct, the background growth alone pushes Northville Drive and The Weir Road to level of 
service D, confirming these corridors are on a congestion path independent of the Precinct. 
◼ With the Precinct but without the crossing, the northern corridors are expected to deteriorate further. 
Northville Drive north of The Weir Road is expected to reach a VCR of around 0.96 (LoS E) during the 
AM peak and PM peak in both directions of travel. The westbound section of Weir Road west of the 
northern access is expected to reach LoS Eat a VCR of 0.89 during PM peak, as the full eastern 
employment demand would still need to access and exit to the north to and from these roads. 
◼ Under the with-precinct scenario, provision of the crossing is expected to improve operations on the same 
corridors by reducing the VCR and improving performance from LoS E to LoS D. This indicates the 
potential benefit of the crossing, with an improvement of one LoS band on the constrained corridor under 
the same precinct traffic demand. 
◼ A new Cockle Creek crossing is expected to operate at level of service A in both directions and both 
peaks, with a very low VCR.   
◼ Charlton Street, Racecourse Road and Appletree Road all remain at LoS A, and the Wakefield Road 
spine and southern corridors operate at LoS B or better. 
The medium term therefore shows that full build out is expected to be achievable without the northern 
corridors failing, and that some alleviated corridor performance could be achieved if a Cockle Creek crossing 
or other improvements to the east were delivered. Improving connections to the east would have dual 
benefits, providing direct eastern access to the site and relieving the northern collectors by giving the B53 
bound traffic a route that would not pass through the Northville Drive and The Weir Road intersections. 
Further investigation is needed into wider network distribution impacts of a potential crossing, including the 
potential for rat-running to avoid congestion on the B53 corridor. 
The medium term midblock performance results without the Precinct, with the Precinct and without a new 
Cockle Creek crossing, and with the Precinct and new Cockle Creek crossing during the AM and PM peak 
are summarised in Table 4-8.

Midblock Performance Results – Long Term 
The long term applies full Precinct generation against background growth to 2051. With background growth 
dominating by this horizon, the with and without crossing comparison shows that a Cockle Creek crossing 
does not fully address the constraints on the northern corridors and is not the full solution to the longer term 
access constraints to the north, which would require separate upgrades to the Northville Drive corridor 
toward the B89. 
◼ Northville Drive reaches LoS E in both segments and both directions under background growth without 
the Precinct. The segment north of The Weir Road is expected to operate at LoS E  both directions of 
travel during the AM and PM peak, meaning operation is at capacity and unstable flow and queuing is 
expected without duplication. 
◼ With precinct and without crossing, the performance is expected to deteriorate with the addition of 
precinct traffic demand, is expected to lead to LoS F for eastbound and westbound section of Northville 
Drive, north of The Weir Road during AM and PM peak. 
◼ The crossing is expected to provide some relief to the northern corridor and result in a level of service 
broadly comparable to the background-growth scenario without precinct traffic. With the crossing, 
Northville Drive north of The Weir Road is expected to operate at LoS E, compared with LoS F without 
the crossing. Similarly, The Weir Road west of the northern access is expected to operate at LoS E or 
better in both directions with the crossing, compared with LoS F ( Westbound PM peak) without the 
crossing. 
◼ Charlton Street and Racecourse Road remain at LoS A or better, and Appletree Road is expected to 
operate at LoS C and the Wakefield Road segments at LoS C or better, therefore, these collector and 
local roads are identified for monitoring as background growth accumulates even though they sit below a 
duplication trigger. 
◼ The crossing operates at level of service A with very low VCR ratios in both directions, which suggests it 
could carry additional diverted demand if required, though it would have limited ability to provide long term 
relief to the northern corridor on its own. 
In performance terms the long term confirms that the primary constraint would be the Northville Drive 
corridor to the B89, which is expected to reach capacity under cumulative background growth regardless of 
the Precinct. The Precinct would contribute to the timing, and as such duplication of Northville Drive may 
need to be considered and could be progressed alongside eastern connectivity improvements such as a 
Cockle Creek crossing, with the development contributing proportionately to works that would serve both the 
Precinct and the wider catchment. 
Across the horizons, the results show consistent trend. The Wakefield Road spine, the southern Rhondda 
Road access and the western local roads carry the Precinct comfortably in every scenario, and the south 
and west corridors are not constraints. The northern access corridors, being Northville Drive and The Weir 
Road, are the corridors that carry the Precinct traffic toward the B89 and they begin the assessment at LoS 
C to D but are expected to reach a duplication trigger under cumulative background growth in the long term 
rather than purely due to the traffic generated by the Precinct.  
Improving connectivity to the east to reduce reliance on Northville Drive would be important for the precinct, 
and the wider community however whether this is via a new crossing of the creek or improvements to the 
existing network will require further investigation. Whether the Precinct significantly uses the northern 
corridor or not, it is apparent that this corridor may struggle in the long term without some forms of 
intervention to either reduce demands or increase capacity.  
The long term midblock performance results without the Precinct, with the Precinct and without the new 
Cockle Creek crossing, and with the Precinct and new Cockle Creek crossing during the AM and PM peak 
are summarised in Table 4-9.

4.4.2 
Intersection Performance 
As detailed in Section 1.3.6, intersection performance is not assessed quantitatively at this stage but is 
inferred from the LoS of the adjoining midblock segments. Any intersection whose approaches reach LoS D 
or worse is identified as a potential intersection that may require improvements subject to further 
investigation as development is defined and progresses.  
In the short term the intersections that may require early consideration and potential mitigation works are: 
◼ Northville Drive / Appletree Road / Wakefield Road intersection 
◼ Northville Drive intersections at The Weir Road and at George Booth Drive and Main Road (the B89) 
◼ Northern access on The Weir Road 
The Northville Drive / The Broadway and Rhondda Road accesses are not considered candidates for early 
capacity upgrade considerations as their adjoining links remain at level of service C however spatial and 
geometrical works may be required in the form of access treatments, turn lanes to accommodate RAV swept 
paths. 
By the medium term the same Northville Drive and The Weir Road intersections remain the binding 
constraints, now reaching level of service E on several approaches assuming no short term works are 
undertaken, and The Weir Road at Racecourse Road is added as the east-west movements grow.  
By the long term the most of Northville Drive approaches reach level of service E (assuming works have not 
been completed) irrespective of whether the Precinct is developed or not, confirming Northville Drive, and 
the Appletree Road approaches to the Northville Drive / Appletree Road / Wakefield Road intersection will 
require considerations in relation to increasing capacity. 
Detailed SIDRA network modelling will be required to confirm capacity constraints and potential opportunities 
or requirements for specific treatment for each identified intersection at the development application or 
subdivision stage, consistent with the master plan performance criteria.  
The indicative intersection performance based on the LoS of adjoining midblock segments are summarised 
in Table 4-10 to Table 4-12 for short, medium and long term horizons respectively.
