There are also extensive areas identified as ‘environmentally constrained areas’ in the 
Structure Plan (Figure 2), mainly due to the presence of high biodiversity values as well as 
other natural features that constrain future development. The environmentally constrained 
areas identified in the Structure Plan also provide for continued fauna movement within and 
beyond the subject land, by retaining substantial key wildlife corridors. 
Further details of the project are included in the Master Plan and the Explanation of Intended 
Effect that are submitted with the rezoning proposal.  
1.2.2 
Location 
Located on Awabakal Country within the Lake Macquarie Local Government Area (LGA), the 
subject land comprises approximately 1,159 hectares of land across the suburbs of 
Killingworth, Wakefield, Barnsley and Teralba. The subject land forms part of the broader 
Lower Hunter region and is strategically positioned within an established industrial and 
infrastructure corridor, with proximity to key regional centres.  
The subject land is generally bounded by residential areas and remnant vegetation to the 
north, Racecourse Road and Cockle Creek to the east, residential areas, a Black Rock 
Motor Resort, and remnant vegetation to the south, and the M1 Pacific Motorway to the west 
(Figure 1). The broader surrounding land use includes a mix of urban residential 
communities, industrial land, and remnant bushland that creates a network of habitat 
corridors.  
The subject land is characterised by a diverse post-mining landscape that includes 
rehabilitating landforms, residual industrial infrastructure, water management features and 
areas of ecological regeneration. These attributes create a complex but opportunity rich 
setting, where extensive brownfield areas with existing access and servicing potential are 
complemented by areas of environmental value requiring protection and integration into 
future land use outcomes.   
Most of the subject land is currently zoned C2 Environmental Conservation, C3 
Environmental Management, SP1 Special Activities and RU2 Rural Landscape. A number of 
existing smaller roads as well as utility easements bisect the subject land, whilst the western 
extent of the subject land borders the M1 Pacific Motorway.  
A site map and location map have been prepared in accordance with the BAM and are 
presented in Figure 3 and Figure 4, respectively. 
1.2.3 
General Description of the Subject land 
The subject land has been extensively cleared and modified in the past in association with 
the historical disturbance of the mining operations, with the progression of the disturbance 
visible in historical aerial photographs (Figures 5-7). Mining operations at the subject land 
are no longer active, however rehabilitation and long-term environmental management 
activities are currently ongoing. Nonetheless, large parts of the subject land still comprise 
relatively undisturbed, remnant native vegetation that is largely contiguous with large tracts 
of bushland to the south and west, which subsequently connects with the Sugarloaf State 
Conservation Area west of the M1 Pacific Motorway. 
Several existing watercourses that are tributaries to Cockle Creek flow through the central 
and western portions of the subject land, including Burkes Creek and Diega Creek. Several 
human-made waterbodies/dams also occur, mainly in the central/western portion of the 
subject land. A relatively large portion of the subject land is also identified as ‘coastal

The areas identified as coastal wetlands under the Resilience and Hazards SEPP are also

addition to the mapped Key Fish Habitat, there are also smaller areas mapped as

the potential presence of saltmarsh (Figure 9). 
The subject land also comprises areas that are identified as high biodiversity values in the 
NSW Biodiversity Values Map, as shown in Figure 10, which overlaps with the previous

Fish Habitat (refer to Figures 8 and 9). 
There are three existing offset areas within the central and western parts of the subject land, 
which are subject to Voluntary Conservation Agreements (VCA) for the former mining 
operation of the Macquarie Coal Complex (Figure 10).

1.4 
Relevant Legislation 
1.4.1 
Commonwealth Environment Protection and Biodiversity 
Conservation Act 1999  
The EPBC Act is the Commonwealth Government’s central piece of environmental 
legislation.  It provides a legal framework to protect and manage nationally and 
internationally important flora, fauna, ecological communities and heritage places – defined 
in the EPBC Act as Matters of National Environmental Significance (MNES).  Under the 
EPBC Act, any action (which includes a development, project or activity) that is considered 
likely to have a significant impact on MNES (including nationally listed threated communities 
and species and listed migratory species) must be referred to the Australian Government 
Minister for the Environment.  The purpose of the referral is to allow a decision to be made 
about whether an action requires approval on a Commonwealth level. If an action is declared 
a “controlled action”, then Commonwealth approval is required. 
This report considers the potential for MNES to occur within the subject land. 
1.4.2 
NSW Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 
The NSW Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979 (EP&A Act) is the overarching 
planning legislation in NSW that provides for the creation of planning instruments that guide 
land use. The EP&A Act also provides for the protection of the environment, including the 
protection and conservation of native fauna and flora species.  This includes threatened 
species, populations and ecological communities, and their habitats, as listed under the BC 
Act and FM Act. 
1.4.3 
NSW Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016  
The BC Act is the key piece of legislation in NSW relating to the protection and management 
of biodiversity and threatened species. The purpose of the BC Act is to maintain a healthy, 
productive and resilient environment for the greatest well-being of the community, now and 
into the future, consistent with the principles of ecologically sustainable development. The 
BC Act is supported by regulations, including the Biodiversity Conservation Regulation 2019 
(BC Regulation). 
The BC Act requires consideration of whether a development or an activity is likely to 
significantly affect threatened species and as a result trigger entry into the Biodiversity Offset 
Scheme (BOS). The BOS is intended to simplify biodiversity assessment and improve 
biodiversity outcomes by creating consistent assessment requirements to measure the likely 
biodiversity loss of development proposals and gains in biodiversity value achieved at offset 
sites through active management. The BOS requires an assessment following the BAM by 
an accredited BAM assessor and the preparation of either a Biodiversity Development 
Assessment Report (BDAR) or Biodiversity Certification Assessment Report. 
The preparation of a BDAR is not required at this stage, as a DA is not being submitted. 
However, this assessment generally follows the Stage 1 of the BAM to identify the 
assessment requirements for future developments.

1.4.7 
Fisheries Management Act 1994 
The FM Act protects threatened fish species and marine vegetation and identifies associated 
threatening processes and is administered by the Department of Primary Industries 
(Fisheries).  The FM Act has the objective to conserve, develop and share the fishery 
resources of NSW for the benefit of present and future generations. In particular, this Act 
includes measures to conserve fish stocks and key fish habitats, to conserve threatened 
species, populations and ecological communities of fish and marine vegetation, and to 
promote ecologically sustainable development, including the conservation of biological 
diversity.   
Assessments under the FM Act are required to assess potential impacts to areas mapped as 
Key Fish Habitat and/or indicative distributions of threatened freshwater species. The subject 
land includes large areas mapped as Key Fish Habitat, which coincides with the locations of 
the mapped Coastal Wetlands.

2.0 
Methodology 
2.1 
Desktop Assessment 
2.1.1 
Database Analysis 
A database analysis was conducted for the locality of the subject land using the BioNet Atlas 
(DCCEEW (NSW), 2026b) and the EPBC Protected Matters Search Tool (PMST) 
(DCCEEW, 2026). The locality is defined as the area within a 5 km buffer from the boundary 
of the subject land. The BioNet Atlas search facility was used to generate records of 
threatened flora and fauna species and populations listed under the BC Act and/or EPBC 
Act within the locality of the subject land. The abundance, distribution and age of records 
generated within the search areas provided supplementary information for the assessment 
of occurrence of those threatened species within the subject land. The PMST generated a 
list of potentially occurring EPBC Act listed entities within the locality of the subject land. 
The following databases and map tools were also interrogated: 
• 
BioNet Vegetation Classification database (DCCEEW (NSW), 2026c); 
• 
NSW Threatened Biodiversity Data Collection (DCCEEW (NSW), 2026e); 
• 
Biodiversity Values Map (DCCEEW (NSW), 2026a); 
• 
NSW Historical Imagery Viewer (NSW Spatial Services, 2026a); 
• 
ePlanning Spatial Viewer – Land Zoning Maps (DPHI, 2026); and 
• 
Hydrological datasets. 
In addition to the database analysis, a review of relevant literature was undertaken, focusing 
on relevant technical reports for the subject land as well as relevant sections of NSW and 
Commonwealth legislation and guidelines.  
This existing information was considered and included, where appropriate, into survey 
design, vegetation mapping and reporting. 
2.1.2 
Identification of Ecosystem and Species Credit Species 
In addition to the database analysis, the Biodiversity Assessment Method Calculator (BAM-
C) was used to generate a list of threatened flora and fauna species for the developable 
areas of the subject land, known as ecosystem credit species and species credit species 
according to the BAM. These ecosystem credit species and species credit species are 
indicative of the type of threatened flora and fauna that have the potential to occur within the 
developable areas, and which will require further assessment at the DA stage of future 
developments in the subject land. 
A likelihood of occurrence assessment was also completed for the subject land, which was 
used to supplement the lists of predicted ecosystem and species credits species derived 
from the BAM-C, to assist in the prediction of potential impacts associated with future 
developments that will need to be assessed in detail at a future DA stage. 
2.2 
Site Context Methods 
2.2.1 
Landscape Features 
Desktop searches were completed throughout the assessment process to confirm currency 
of data and to ensure ongoing changes to the project layout were captured in desktop

2.5 
Survey Limitations 
Coverage of the entire subject land during field surveys was not possible due to constraints 
associated with timing of this assessment in combination with safety hazards in some 
sections of the subject land where existing mining rehabilitation works is ongoing. Based on 
instructions from DPHI, the focus of the surveys was therefore on the potential developable 
areas of the subject land, as shown on the Structure Plan. Based on the results from the 
desktop assessment, it is considered that the areas identified as environmentally 
constrained areas in the Structure Plan are highly likely to comprise the biodiversity values 
identified in this assessment and would therefore restrict the potential for future 
development. Nonetheless, where time permitted, parts of the environmentally constrained 
areas were also subject to surveys. 
Due to the restricted timing for this assessment, the entirety of the rehabilitated vegetation in 
the western parts of the subject land were not subject to field traverses. However, 
representative areas were surveyed along the boundaries of the rehabilitated areas. In 
combination with the flora planting list that SLR was provided, which details the flora species 
planted within the rehabilitation areas, the assessment of PCTs and associated TECs in 
these areas are considered sufficient for this BAR. Nonetheless, future detailed 
assessments at the DA stage will need to further assess the vegetation mapping in the 
rehabilitation areas, as well as all other areas of the subject land subject to a future DA.  
Although condition states for PCTs were mapped where time permitted, in line with the 
mapping of vegetation zones under the BAM, further refinement of vegetation zones is 
required at the DA stage for relevant technical assessments. 
The weather conditions at the time of the flora surveys were generally favourable for plant 
growth and production of features required for identification of most species. Shrubs, 
grasses, herbs and creepers were readily identifiable in most instances. Despite this, it is 
expected that not all flora species present within the subject land would have been recorded 
during surveys as no floristic BAM plot surveys were undertaken in the subject land. 
However, it is considered that sufficient information has been collected during the vegetation 
mapping verification surveys to satisfactorily assess issues including conservation 
significance of the PCTs and associated TECs, condition and viability of bushland and likely 
impact on native vegetation for the purpose of the rezoning proposal and this BAR.  
No targeted flora or fauna surveys were undertaken for this assessment, which relied on 
database analysis, preliminary fauna habitat assessment and incidental observations. In 
general, opportunistic observations of threatened flora and fauna provide a “snapshot” of 
some of the threatened species present on site. However, database analysis including a 
likelihood of occurrence assessment and identification of ecosystem and species credits 
species predicted for the PCTs mapped in the developable areas are considered to provide 
sufficient information for this assessment, in relation to potential impacts on threatened 
species from future developments. Nonetheless, targeted surveys for threatened flora and 
fauna species potentially occurring within the subject land will need to be undertaken for 
future DAs in accordance with the BAM.

4.2.2.4 Alignment with Threatened Ecological Communities 
BC Act Status: Not listed 
EPBC Act Status: Not listed 
This PCT is associated with the TEC Pittwater and Wagstaffe Spotted Gum Forest in the 
Sydney Basin Bioregion, which is listed as an Endangered Ecological Community (EEC) 
under the BC Act. However, the vegetation within the subject land does not conform to the 
TEC, as the TEC is only known to occur within the Gosford and Pittwater LGAs (NSW 
Scientific Committee, 2008). The TEC is also stated as occurring on shale derived soils of 
the Narrabeen Group, whereas the soils supporting PCT 3234 within the subject land are 
derived from Permian sediments (NSW DPIRD, 2026). 
4.2.2.5 Justification of PCT Selection 
PCT 3234 was assigned to these areas in the subject land due to the dominance of 
Corymbia maculata in the canopy, along with other associated canopy species including 
Eucalyptus piperita and Eucalyptus umbra, along with a subcanopy of Allocasuarina 
torulosa. The shrub layer matches PCT 3234 by having dense occurrences of Pittosporum 
undulatum. Additionally, the ground layer dominated by Imperata cylindrica is a good match 
for the PCT.  
A review of regional mapping shows that the entirety of the southern parts of the subject land 
where this PCT occurs was mapped as PCT 3244 on the SVTM (DCCEEW (NSW), 2020). 
However, PCT 3244 does not match these areas of vegetation as it is described as a less 
mesic community, whilst  the vegetation present in this area of the subject land is a Spotted 
Gum assemblage typified by a dense, mesic understorey.  
The Lake Macquarie City Council (LMCC) vegetation mapping maps these areas as M 15 
Coastal Foothills Spotted Gum – Ironbark Forest. This is likely the most closely matching 
LMCC community, though the description of that community does not mention the 
dominance of Pittosporum undulatum. However, it does mention other species such as 
Backhousia myrtifolia, which were present in some small areas. 
4.2.3 
PCT 3244: Lower North Spotted Gum-Mahogany-Ironbark Sheltered 
Forest 
Vegetation Formation: Wet Sclerophyll Forests (Grassy sub-formation)  
Vegetation Class: Northern Hinterland Wet Sclerophyll Forests  
Percentage cleared: 39.18 
4.2.3.1 BioNet Description  
A tall to very tall sclerophyll open forest with a mid-stratum of dry and soft-leaved shrubs or 
small trees and a ground cover of grasses and graminoids on lower slopes in the 
escarpment foothills of the lower north coast. The canopy includes a diverse mix of trees, 
which very frequently includes Corymbia maculata, and a suite of other eucalypts which 
individually occur occasionally or rarely. Collectively, mahoganies and ironbarks are almost 
always present and grey gums are common. The more frequent mahoganies, ironbarks and 
grey gums are Eucalyptus siderophloia, Eucalyptus acmenoides, Eucalyptus umbra and

occurs closest to the coast, and the damper understorey is likely a reflection of near coastal

4.2.4 
PCT 3258 Sydney Basin Creekflat Blue Gum-Apple Forest 
Vegetation Formation: Wet Sclerophyll Forests (Grassy sub-formation)  
Vegetation Class: Northern Hinterland Wet Sclerophyll Forests  
Percentage cleared: 13.68 
4.2.4.1 BioNet Description  
A very tall to extremely tall open sclerophyll forest with a sparse mid-stratum of tall acacias 
and a ground layer of grasses and ferns found on sandy alluvial creek flats in dissected 
sandstone plateaus mainly in the greater Blue Mountains. The tree canopy is variable 
however very frequently includes Angophora floribunda in the canopy or as a small tree. 
Common eucalypts with a high foliage cover are species from the blue gum eucalypt group, 
Eucalyptus deanei or Eucalyptus saligna, occasionally in association with stringybark 
eucalypts including Eucalyptus eugenioides. Isolated occurrences of Eucalyptus baueriana, 
Eucalyptus elata and Eucalyptus amplifolia occur in the Putty and Macdonald River 
catchments.  
The mid-stratum is layered, commonly with taller Acacia parramattensis or rarely Melaleuca 
linariifolia, and a sparse lower shrub layer which commonly includes Breynia oblongifolia, 
occasionally with Bursaria spinosa and Persoonia linearis. The mid-dense to dense ground 
layer almost always includes Pteridium esculentum, very frequently with Microlaena 
stipoides, often with a high cover, and Adiantum aethiopicum. Common ground layer species 
include Entolasia marginata, Oplismenus imbecillis and Doodia aspera.  
This PCT is widespread throughout dry mid-elevations of Wollemi and Yengo national parks 
in the northern Sydney Basin, however, is restricted to small and medium sized narrow creek 
flats and colluvial infill gullies. Stands may be discontinuous along creeks that pass through 
narrow pinches, bends and accumulated boulders. This community is also recorded in the 
hinterland plateaus of the Hawkesbury and Burragorang districts north and south-west of 
Sydney. Southern outliers are recorded on creek flats in tributaries of the Shoalhaven River 
west of Nowra. It grades into tall grassy eucalypt forest PCT 4058 on larger creeks and river 
flats with richer soils across the Sydney hinterland catchments. There is also spatial overlap 
with PCT 4058, particularly across lower elevations shared between both PCTs, although 
that PCT may be distinguishable by the frequency of Eucalyptus tereticornis or Eucalyptus 
amplifolia amongst the tallest stratum.

4.2.4.5 Alignment with Threatened Ecological Communities

EPBC Act Status: Critically Endangered Ecological Community (CEEC) 
This PCT is associated with the River-flat Eucalypt Forest (RFEF) TEC, which is listed as an 
EEC under the BC Act as River-Flat Eucalypt Forest on Coastal Floodplains of the New 
South Wales North Coast, Sydney Basin and South East Corner Bioregions, and as a CEEC 
under the EPBC Act as River-flat eucalypt forest on coastal floodplains of southern New 
South Wales and eastern Victoria. 
An assessment has not been made against the condition criteria for the EPBC Listed TEC, 
however based on the observations from the field surveys, the vegetation in the subject land 
generally matches the BC Act and EPBC Act listed TECs (NSW Scientific Committee, 
2011a; Threatened Species Scientific Committee, 2020) due to: 
• 
Occurring on periodically inundated alluvial flats and drainage lines associated with 
coastal floodplains; 
• 
Having a canopy dominated by Eucalyptus saligna and Angophora floribunda, and 
understorey dominated by Melaleuca styphelioides and/or Melaleuca linariifolia; 
• 
Having a shrub layer including species such as Breynia oblongifolia, Acmena smithii, 
Phyllanthus gunnii, Rubus parvifolius, and Trema aspera;  
• 
Having a ground layer including species such as Oplismenus aemulus, Microlaena 
stipoides var. Stipoides, Eustrephus latifolius, Imperata cylindrica, and Hypolepis 
muelleri; and  
• 
Occurring in the Lake Macquarie LGA and Sydney Basin Bioregion.

A tall to very tall sclerophyll open forest with a sparse dry shrub layer and grassy ground

costata is very frequently recorded, commonly in association with Corymbia gummifera,

PCT 3433: Hunter Coast Foothills Spotted Gum-Ironbark Grassy 
Forest 
Vegetation Formation: Dry Sclerophyll Forests (Shrub/grass sub-formation)  
Vegetation Class: Hunter-Macleay Dry Sclerophyll Forests

4.2.6.1 BioNet Description  
A tall to very tall sclerophyll open forest with dry and soft-leaved shrubs and a grassy ground 
cover on undulating foothills of the Hunter coast hinterland from Tuggerah to Stratford, and 
the lower Hunter valley around Cessnock. The canopy almost always includes Corymbia 
maculata accompanied by one or more ironbarks (Eucalyptus fibrosa or Eucalyptus 
siderophloia). Mahoganies (Eucalyptus umbra or Eucalyptus acmenoides) are also 
commonly present in the canopy.  
The sparse mid-stratum almost always includes one or more Acacia species, of which 
Acacia falcata and Acacia ulicifolia are the most frequent and abundant. The shrubs and 
small trees that complete the mid-stratum very frequently include Daviesia ulicifolia, 
commonly Bursaria spinosa, Persoonia linearis and rarely Pultenaea villosa, Leucopogon 
juniperinus or patches of Melaleuca nodosa. The mid-dense ground layer typically includes 
graminoids, forbs, twiners and a hardy fern. Entolasia stricta is almost always present, with 
Themeda triandra, Lobelia purpurascens, Microlaena stipoides, Aristida vagans, Lomandra

4.2.6.5 Alignment with Threatened Ecological Communities 
BC Act Status: Not listed 
EPBC Act Status: Not listed 
This PCT is associated with the BC Act listed TEC Lower Hunter Spotted Gum Ironbark 
Forest (LHSGIF). BioNet (DCCEEW (NSW), 2026c) states the PCT is only the listed TEC 
where it occurs within the Lower Hunter Valley as defined in Paragraph 4.1 of the final 
determination (NSW Scientific Committee, 2019). Paragraph 4.1 states: “Cessnock-
Beresfield area and approximately bounded by the towns of Paxton, Branxton, Clarence 
Town, Beresfield, Mt Vincent and the northern boundary of Watagans National Park”. The 
subject land is not situated in this location, which describes an area with the eastern extent 
consistent with the Mount Sugarloaf range.  
PCT 3433 is one of a number of PCTs associated with LHSGIF. The data analyses 
undertaken as part of the development of the revised east coast PCTs (Connolly et al., 
2022) shows by grouped primary reference plots, and the distribution of them (NSW 
Government, 2026), that PCT 3433 is a wider ranging PCT than the Lower Hunter Spotted 
Gum Ironbark Forest TEC. It is included as LHSGIF only in the area covered by the final 
determination because in this area it is closer in species composition to the described 
LHSGIF TEC. However, the PCT differs in composition closer to the coast in higher rainfall 
areas. Nonetheless, primary reference plots across the range remain close enough in 
species composition to be grouped as the one PCT. 
PCT 3433 includes vegetation described by Stephen Bell in the LMCC mapping as MU 17o 
Hinterland Spotted Gum – Red Ironbark Forest, but has a larger range than that community. 
Within the LMCC vegetation mapping project, Stephen Bell considers MU 17o to be LHSGIF 
(S. A. J. Bell, 2016), but this is an erroneous contention. Like all TECs, the legally defensible 
description of the LHSGIF TEC is defined in the final determination. The final determination 
states that the unit Hinterland Spotted Gum Ironbark Forest from Stephen Bell’s thesis (S. 
Bell, 2013) is not LHSGIF in Paragraph 4.6. This unit from Bell’s thesis is the equivalent 
community to MU 17o of the LMCC mapping, which therefore is not LHSGIF. Paragraph 4.6 
of the final determination also lists the species that are more likely to occur in Hinterland 
Spotted Gum Ironbark Forest than in LHSGIF. The vegetation within the subject land 
contains more species that are associated with the Hinterland Spotteg Gum Ironbark Forest 
map unit, such as Eucalyptus umbra, Goodenia heterophylla, Breynia oblongifolia, 
Eustrephus latifolius, and Imperata cylindrica, than species that are considered more likely to 
occur in LHSGIF such as Grevillea montana, Pultenaea spinosa, and Goodenia rotundifolia. 
Further reasons vegetation within the subject land mapped as PCT 3433 is more consistent 
with Hinterland Spotted Gum Ironbark Forest than LHSGIF by definition in the final 
determination are: 
• 
It occurs to the east of the Mount Sugarloaf rain shadow, with the Mount Sugarloaf 
Range being the easternmost limit of the 700-1000mm rainfall band supporting the 
TEC, and therefore within areas of higher coastal rainfall (>1000mm) than supports 
the more inland LHSGIF (Paragraph 4.5); 
• 
It is not on any of the Permian substrates (NSW DPIRD, 2026) or soil landscapes 
(DCCEEW (NSW), 2026d) described as most likely to support the TEC (Paragraph 
4.2); and

A defining characteristic is the presence of a sub-canopy of taller Melaleuca spp., mostly 
Melaleuca decora or Melaleuca sieberi, coupled with a moderately dense understorey of

3436 have a unique canopy dominated nearly entirely by hybrids of the threatened species 
Angophora inopina and Angophora floribunda. These trees are generally taller than 
Angophora inopina and often have leaf petioles greater than 8mm (petioles less than 8mm in 
length is one of the defining features of Angophora inopina). Leaves however are thicker, 
shorter, and narrower than is typical for Angophora inopina. This situation is not mentioned 
in the LMCC mapping (S. A. J. Bell, 2016), but is mentioned in (S. Bell, 2004), where it is 
described as: 
In addition, representation of Angophora inopina in other geographically 
restricted vegetation types not described here may also have significant 
conservation value. These include an Angophora inopina x Angophora floribunda 
– Melaleuca Thicket Forest from the northern Lake Macquarie area, where 
hybrid zones of Angophora inopina x Angophora floribunda occur with Melaleuca 
linariifolia, Melaleuca nodosa, Melaleuca decora and Eucalyptus resinifera, 
generally on the Cockle Creek (cc) soil landscape of Matthei (1995).

4.2.7.4 Justification of PCT Selection 
A review of regional mapping (DCCEEW (NSW), 2020) shows the areas mapped by SLR as 
PCT 3435 have been frequently mapped as PCT 3998 by the SVTM, along with various drier 
PCTs that were mapped elsewhere by SLR within the subject land. PCT 3998 is present 
within the subject land, but PCT 3435 is a better fit for these areas, due to generally lacking 
the ground layer of semi-aquatic species described as common in the ground layer of PCT 
3998 such as Gahnia clarkii (which is present, but scattered), and Lepyrodia scariosa, 
Chorizandra cymbaria, and Hemarthria uncinata, Empodisma minus, and Schoenus 
brevifolius, species which have been recorded in more than 45% of PCT primary reference 
plots for the PCT or more (DCCEEW (NSW), 2026c). 
The combination of common occurrences of Angophora costata and Eucalyptus resinifera 
subsp. resinifera, vegetation occurring on or fringing alluvial soils, having a sub-canopy and 
shrub layer characterised by Melaleuca spp., and having a grassy ground layer, generally 
not including aquatic and semi-aquatic species makes PCT 3435 the best fit for these areas 
of vegetation.  
This vegetation is associated with the LMCC MU 42 Red Mahogany – Apple – Paperbark 
Forest, which broadly covers vegetation which would fit with PCT 3435 and PCT 3998.

BC Act Status: Not listed 
EPBC Act Status: Not listed 
This PCT is associated with the EPBC listed endangered Subtropical eucalypt floodplain 
forest and woodland TEC. However, this TEC does not occur as far south as the subject 
land and is limited to the NSW Nort Coast and Southeast Queensland IBRA regions.  
 
4.2.8 
PCT 3436: Hunter Coast Sandy Creekflat Low Paperbark Scrub 
Vegetation Formation: Dry Sclerophyll Forests (Shrub/Grass Formation)

Percentage cleared: 51.82 
4.2.8.1 Bionet Description 
A mid-high to tall Melaleuca closed forest or tall to very tall sclerophyll open forest with a 
very dense mid-stratum of Melaleuca trees found on lowlands between Gosford and Port 
Macquarie, lower north and Hunter coasts. This PCT is strongly associated with low-lying 
sandy clay alluviums at elevations of below 40 metres asl. A sparse to mid-dense cover of 
eucalypts is occasionally present as the tallest layer however no single species dominates. 
Species include Eucalyptus resinifera and Angophora costata however these are commonly

absent and replaced by a wide variety of other coastal eucalypt species including Eucalyptus

The main diagnostic attribute is the closed canopy of the mid-stratum that almost always is 
completely dominated by Melaleuca nodosa. Other Melaleucas are occasionally present 
such as Melaleuca sieberi and Melaleuca decora, however only as scattered individuals. The 
dense mid-stratum shades much of the light and sclerophyll shrubs are sparse and only

juniperinum. The ground layer is a mid-dense to dense cover of grasses, mainly dominated 
by two species, Entolasia stricta and Microlaena stipoides, with other species such Imperata 
cylindrica less abundant. Other very frequent species are graminoids and forbs including 
Dianella caerulea, Lomandra longifolia and Lobelia purpurascens.  
This PCT is recorded on alluviums, fine grained Permo-Triassic and Carboniferous 
sediment, typically on flats and depressions, occasionally also found on adjoining gentle 
gradient hill slopes that retain soil moisture from subsurface water. It grades into PCT 3435 
with gradual increase in elevation or improved soil drainage. 
4.2.8.2 Subject Land Description  
PCT 3436 occurs in areas of alluvial flats, broadly across the north of the subject land on the 
fringes of floodplains associated with Burkes Creek and Cockle Creek. PCT 3436 occupies 
similar areas of habitat to PCT 3435, though often occurs in slightly lower areas where soils 
are more likely to be more frequently waterlogged.  
Canopy species are similar to PCT 3435, with Angophora costata and Eucalyptus resinifera 
subsp. resinifera the most likely generally to be present and together have most fidelity to 
the PCT. However, in this PCT, eucalypts mostly occur as scattered emergents over a 
dense scrub of Melaleuca nodosa. Other Melaleuca spp. occur as juveniles in the scrubby 
understorey, or as more mature emergents with eucalypts, and include Melaleuca decora 
and Melaleuca sieberi.  
The shrub and ground layer besides denser occurrences of Melaleuca nodosa are similar to 
PCT 3435. Other shrub species can be common, with Leptospermum polygalifolium subsp. 
cismontanum frequently present, along with Acacia longifolia subsp. longifolia and Banksia 
collina.  
The ground layer is frequently dominated by Entolasia stricta, Microlaena stipoides var. 
stipoides, and Ptilothrix deusta, with Entolasia marginata common. Gonocarpus tetragynus 
and Dianella caerulea subsp. producta are forbs that are often present.  
In the north of the subject land as with PCT 3435, some occurrences of this PCT include 
hybrids of the threatened species Angophora inopina and Angophora floribunda.

PCT 3581: Hunter Coast Foothills Apple Forest 
Vegetation Formation: Dry Sclerophyll Forests (Shrub/grass sub-formation)  
Vegetation Class: Hunter-Macleay Dry Sclerophyll Forests  
Percentage cleared: 26.09 
4.2.9.1 BioNet Description  
A tall to very tall sclerophyll open forest with dry shrub layer and a grassy ground cover 
mainly found on enriched sedimentary hills and rises on the coastal plains between Gosford 
and Wallis Lake on the Lower North and Hunter coasts. The tree canopy almost always 
includes a high cover of Angophora costata, very frequently with Corymbia gummifera and 
commonly Eucalyptus piperita. Occasionally other eucalypts may be associated with or 
replace these species including Eucalyptus umbra or Eucalyptus pilularis.  
The mid-stratum is layered with a very frequent tall sparse layer of Allocasuarina littoralis or 
Allocasuarina torulosa. Lower dry shrubs are also typically sparse with Persoonia linearis, 
Podolobium ilicifolium commonly recorded, occasionally with Persoonia levis, Breynia 
oblongifolia, Leptospermum polygalifolium or a range of Acacia spp. The ground layer is 
mid-dense to dense and is comprised of grasses of which Entolasia stricta, Themeda 
australis and Imperata cylindrica are the most frequently recorded. Graminoid species are 
also very frequent and add to the grass like appearance of the ground layer. Dianella 
caerulea, Lepidosperma laterale and Lomandra longifolia are the most common examples. 
The fern Pteridium esculentum is almost always present however generally a low cover.  
Very common on Narrabeen sandstone, including a southern outlier in Pittwater and 
extending north through Kincumber, Gosford and western Lake Macquarie and the foothills 
of the Watagan Escarpment. Mainly occurs below 160 metres asl, however may reach over 
350 metres on highest peaks. Found on Permian sandstones north and north-east of Lake 
Macquarie, Carboniferous sandstone in the Medowie and Karuah districts and a small area 
on Nerong Volcanics either side of the Karuah River. This PCT grades into PCT 3582 and

PCT 3975: Southern Lower Floodplain Freshwater Wetland 
Vegetation Formation: Freshwater Wetlands 
Vegetation Class: Coastal Freshwater Lagoons 
Percentage cleared: 92.99 
4.2.11.1 BioNet Description  
A tall to very tall freshwater sedgeland or forbland occurring in depressions on Quaternary 
alluvial deposits (primarily backswamps with organic-rich mud, silt or clay soils) on coastal 
floodplains of the Central Coast and South Coast botanical divisions. Almost all known 
locations occur at elevations of below 10 metres asl, however this PCT can occur at higher 
elevations in lagoons that have prolonged inundation, such as Ellalong Lagoon south-west of 
Cessnock which is just over 100 metres asl.  
This PCT describes non-woody freshwater wetlands on Quaternary alluvium south from the 
Hunter valley that are not dominated by Phragmites australis or Eleocharis equisetina and 
are either on low coastal floodplains or at the edges of more elevated lagoons that have 
prolonged inundation. Within these environmental and floristic parameters this PCT can 
encompass a range of sedgeland and aquatic forb assemblages. On presently available 
information the aquatic forb Persicaria decipiens is very frequently present with very sparse 
cover.  
The grasses Cynodon dactylon and Paspalum distichum and the reed Typha orientalis 
commonly occur with sparse cover, while the sedge Eleocharis sphacelata is occasionally 
present however where it does occur tends to have mid-dense cover. A diversity of other 
sedges, rushes and aquatic forbs are occasionally or rarely recorded, such as Persicaria 
hydropiper, Cycnogeton microtuberosum, Ludwigia peploides subsp. montevidensis, 
Alternanthera denticulata and species of Juncus. Rarely, a very sparse emergent tree layer 
is present, which may include Casuarina glauca, melaleucas or, very rarely, overhanging 
Eucalypts. Some sedges such as Machaerina articulata, Fimbristylis velata, Eleocharis acuta

This PCT relates to the BC Act listed Freshwater Wetlands on Coastal Floodplains of the 
New South Wales North Coast, Sydney Basin and South East Corner Bioregions TEC. 
Paragraph 4 of the final determination (NSW Scientific Committee, 2011c) for this TEC 
states “Artificial wetlands created on previously dry land specifically for purposes such as 
sewerage treatment, stormwater management and farm production, are not regarded as part 
of this community, although they may provide habitat for threatened species”. The TEC 
occurs in a number of artificial waterbodies within the subject land, and in some natural 
areas. Many of the artificial waterbodies in the east of the subject land appear to be in areas 
that would have historically been floodplains and swamps, and therefore not previously dry 
land. As a precautionary approach all areas have been considered to conform to the TEC, 
pending future detailed consideration of all evidence of historical water bodies and water 
courses.

4.2.12.5 Alignment with Threatened Ecological Communities 
BC Act Status: EEC 
EPBC Act Status: EEC 
This PCT is associated with the BC Act listed EEC Swamp Sclerophyll Forest on Coastal 
Floodplains of the New South Wales North Coast, Sydney Basin and South East Corner 
Bioregions, and the EPBC Act listed EEC Coastal Swamp Sclerophyll Forest of New South 
Wales and South East Queensland ecological community. Areas fit the TEC (DAWE, 2022; 
NSW Scientific Committee, 2011b) because they: 
• 
Occur on coastal floodplains in alluvial flats sand drainage lines, that are waterlogged 
or periodically inundated; 
• 
Are dominated by Eucalyptus robusta and/or characteristic Melaleuca spp. including 
Melaleuca linariifolia and Melaleuca styphelioides; and 
• 
Include characteristic shrub species such as Acacia longifolia subsp. longifolia and 
Melaleuca nodosa; 
• 
Have a ground layer dominated by characteristic species including Gahnia clarkei, 
Entolasia stricta and Entolasia marginata, and Oplismenus imbecillis.  
Some areas that are dominated by Angophora costata and Eucalyptus resinifera subsp. 
resinifera (not subsp. hemilampra which is associated with the TEC), including areas that 
floristically best fit with PCT 3435 and PCT 3436, are considered to conform to the TEC 
despite the general lack of Eucalyptus robusta and Melaleuca quinquenervia in the canopy, 
and a relatively dry ground layer. The final determination states “The combination of features 
that distinguish Swamp Sclerophyll Forest on Coastal Floodplains from other endangered 
ecological communities on the coastal floodplains include: its relatively dense tree canopy 
dominated by Eucalyptus robusta, Melaleuca quinquenervia or  E. botryoides,   the   relatively 
infrequent occurrence of other eucalypts,  Casuarina glauca or  Lophostemon suaveolens; 
the occasional presence of rainforest elements as scattered trees or understorey plants; and 
the prominence of large sedges and ferns in the groundcover”. However, the final 
determination also states that: “In the lower Hunter district, this community includes ‘Swamp 
Mahogany-Paperbark Swamp Forest’ (map unit 37), Riparian Melaleuca Swamp Woodland 
(map unit 42) and Melaleuca Scrub (map unit 42a) of NPWS (2000)”. These vegetation units 
describe vegetation dominated by Angophora costata, Eucalyptus resinifera subsp. 
resinifera, and Melaleuca nodosa, which are consisted with the descriptions of PCT 3435, 
PCT 3436, and PCT 3998. Therefore, areas within flood plains that were consistent with 
PCT 3435 and PCT 3436, were remapped as PCT 3998, as the former PCTs cannot be 
associated with Swamp Sclerophyll Forest TEC in the BAM-C.  
The final determination, which states the ground layer is generally dominated by tall sedges 
and ferns, which fits PCT 3998 and PCT 4020, but not PCT 3435 and PCT 3436, also states 
“On sites downslope of lithic substrates or with soils of clay-loam texture, species such as 
Allocasuarina littoralis (black she-oak) , Banksia oblongifolia, B. spinulosa (var.  collina or var. 
 spinulosa) (hairpin banksia),  Ptilothrix deusta and Themeda australis (kangaroo grass), may 
also be present in the understorey ”. This description of shrubs and ground layer species 
also fits the occurrences of PCT 3435 and PCT 3436 within the subject land. Therefore, only 
areas of PCT 3435 and PCT 3436 that do not occur on floodplains (and therefore are not the

4.2.14 
PCT 4038: Hunter Estuarine Melaleuca nodosa Scrub 
Vegetation Formation: Forested Wetlands 
Vegetation Class: Coastal Floodplain Wetlands 
Percentage cleared: 50.58 
4.2.14.1 BioNet Description  
A mid-high Melaleuca closed forest or mid-high to tall open forest dominated by casuarinas 
and eucalypts with a dense mid-stratum of Melaleuca and a sedge ground cover on 
estuarine creek flats, Hunter coast between Gosford and Karuah. A taller tree canopy is 
commonly present either as an emergent layer or a sparse to mid-dense cover of Casuarina 
glauca, occasionally with Eucalyptus robusta or Eucalyptus resinifera. Melaleuca nodosa 
almost always dominates the mid-stratum or the upper strata where taller species are 
absent, commonly with other Melaleucas such as Melaleuca ericifolia or Melaleuca 
styphelioides. Other shrubs or small trees include Dodonaea triquetra Pittosporum 
undulatum and Acacia longifolia.  
The ground layer comprises species tolerant of the estuarine influences, including very 
frequent high cover of Machaerina juncea and occasionally Juncus kraussii subsp. 
australiensis or Phragmites australis. Other species include Lomandra longifolia, Entolasia 
marginata and Gahnia clarkei. This PCT has a very low species richness relative to other

4.2.14.4 Justification of PCT Selection 
A review of regional mapping shows the areas mapped by SLR as PCT 4038 have been 
mapped as cleared on the SVTM (DCCEEW (NSW), 2020), or as PCT 4036. PCT 4036 is a 
community dominated by Angophora floribunda or Eucalyptus tereticornis, whereas these 
areas have a canopy strongly dominated by Casuarina glauca. PCT 4038 is evidently the 
best match of the local PCTs due to the prominence of Casuarina glauca and Melaleuca 
nodosa which is common in the northeast of the subject land, however more detailed 
investigation of patches is needed to confidently assign PCT.  
This vegetation is likely best associated with the LMCC MU 40 Swamp Oak – Rushland 
Forest, but these areas were not surveyed in enough detail to comment on the ground layer 
to confirm the presence of the sedges, rushes, and salt-tolerant grasses that define MU 40.  
4.2.14.5 Alignment with Threatened Ecological Communities 
BC Act Status: EEC 
EPBC Act Status: EEC 
This PCT is associated with the BC Act listed EEC Swamp Sclerophyll Forest on Coastal 
Floodplains of the New South Wales North Coast, Sydney Basin and South East Corner 
Bioregions. This community is also listed as an EEC under the EPBC Act as Coastal Swamp 
Oak (Casuarina glauca) Forest of New South Wales and South East Queensland ecological 
community.  
Areas mapped as the Rehabilitation Plantings condition do not meet the listed community 
under the BC Act or the EPBC Act. This is because they comprise Casuarina glauca 
plantings only, on artificial topography, and there has been no attempt to replicate any other 
strata of the vegetation community, with the exception of planting the trees. Other vegetation 
in these areas comprises predominately exotic grasses only, of species such as Chloris 
gayana and Hyparrhenia rufa.

4.2.15.4 Justification of PCT Selection 
A review of regional mapping shows the areas of 4042 have been mapped generally as PCT 
4042, with some areas mapped as PCT 3583 (DCCEEW (NSW), 2020). PCT 3583 is a dry 
sclerophyll forest PCT areas dominated by Eucalyptus haemastoma, which does not match 
these wetland areas dominated by Eucalyptus amplifolia and Angophora floribunda.  
PCT 4042 fits these areas well as it is described as being dominated by the red gums 
Eucalyptus amplifolia and Eucalyptus tereticornis with Angophora floribunda, and matches 
the River-flat Eucalypt Forest  (RFEF) TEC. There is no other coastal PCT from the Wyong 
IBRA subregion dominated by red gums that is also associated with the RFEF TEC.  
These areas are consistent with the MU 38a Floodplain Redgum – Rough-barked Apple 
Forest from the LMCC Mapping. Stephen Bell notes Eucalyptus tereticornis as the dominant 
red gum, however Eucalyptus amplifolia is mostly dominant in the community between the 
subject land and West Wallsend, with Eucalyptus tereticornis occurring occasionally. 
Sporadic individuals with large buds and more than 7 buds in an umbellaster indicate there 
is hybridisation between the species in the locality.

and eastern Victoria.

4.2.16.2 Subject Land Description  
PCT 4044 occurs in one riparian area in the north-west of the subject land, and is associated 
with the floodplain of an unmapped tributary of Burkes Creek.  
The PCT is associated with quaternary alluviums within the subject land (NSW DPIRD, 
2026).  
The canopy of vegetation within the subject land dominated by Melaleuca styphelioides, with 
Melaleuca nodosa also occurring, and a ground layer is present that includes Gahnia clarkei, 
Entolasia marginata, Microlaena stipoides var. stipoides, and Oplismenus imbecillis.   
4.2.16.3 Condition States 
Within the subject land PCT 4044 occurs in one condition state.   
Intact 
The Intact form of PCT 4044 comprises the entirety of the occurrence in the subject land. 
Vegetation is as described above in the subject land description. This condition is dominated 
by native species in all strata. 
4.2.16.4 Justification of PCT Selection 
A review of regional mapping shows the area of 4044 has been mapped as the PCT 3583 
SVTM (DCCEEW (NSW), 2020). This PCT is not a riparian community, and the dominant 
species such as Eucalyptus haemastoma and Angophora costata described for that 
community are not dominant/present. PCT 4044 is a good fit for areas on alluvium 
dominated by Melaleuca styphelioides with a ground layer including species such as Gahnia 
clarkei and Oplismenus imbecillis.  
These areas are most consistent with the Alluvial Tall Moist Forest community from NPWS 
2000 and the LMCC Mapping, but lacking the canopy of Eucalyptus saligna/Angophora 
floribunda. However, these species are present downstream where the PCT develops into 
PCT 3258. Stephen Bell considers this community to be RFEF, but specific areas dominated 
by Melaleuca styphelioides and Melaleuca linariifolia rather than Eucalyptus saligna and 
Angophora floribunda, are a slightly better fit for the SSF TEC.

5.0 
Threatened Species 
No targeted threatened species surveys were undertaken for this BAR. However, this 
chapter provides an assessment of the threatened flora and fauna species that are likely to 
require further assessment at the DA stage for a future development in the in the 
developable areas of the subject land, in accordance with the BAM. 
5.1 
Identifying Threatened Species 
The BAM-C generates a list of threatened species requiring assessment utilising a number 
of variables. The following criteria have been utilised to predict the threatened species 
requiring further assessment for a future development: 
• 
IBRA Subregion: Wyong; 
• 
Associated PCTs (limited to PCTs in the developable area only):  
• 
Percent native vegetation cover in the assessment area: 60%; 
• 
Patch size: ≥100 ha; and 
• 
Credit type: Ecosystem and/or species. 
Based on the above variables, the BAM-C generated a list of ecosystem credit species and 
species credit species. Ecosystem credit species and species credit species are assessed 
further in Section 5.2 and Section 5.3, respectively. 
In addition to the species predicted by the BAM-C, species that occur in the subject land or 
are likely to occur in the subject land, based on a likelihood of occurrence assessment 
(Appendix A) of previous records held in BioNet and species generated by a PMST search, 
have been added to the relevant lists of ecosystem credit species and species credits 
species, where indicated in subsequent sections. Threatened flora and fauna species 
recorded in the locality of the subject land are shown in Figures 16 and 17, respectively. 
5.1.1 
Threatened Species Habitat 
5.1.1.1 Threatened Flora 
Threatened flora habitat is primarily represented by the relatively undisturbed, remnant 
native vegetation across the developable areas of the subject land. All threatened flora 
species are listed as species credit species, and their habitat constraints are discussed 
further in Section 5.3. 
5.1.1.2 Threatened Fauna 
The developable areas of the subject land contain areas of both intact and modified/planted 
vegetation as well as disturbed areas that contain potential foraging, shelter and breeding 
opportunities for native fauna species. Key habitat features within the subject land include: 
• 
Riparian environments suitable for fauna species dependent on these habitats such 
as amphibians, birds, mammals and reptiles; 
• 
Terrestrial habitat features such as ground and shrub layer vegetation, leaf litter and 
coarse woody debris as shelter for small terrestrial fauna species; 
• 
Hollow-bearing trees and stags suitable as shelter and breeding habitat for a range of 
hollow-dependent fauna; and 
• 
Blossom-producing trees and shrubs suitable as forage for a range of nectarivores.  

--- Bio Page 78 ---
Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure 
Biodiversity Assessment Report 
1 July 2026
SLR Project No.: 610.033744.00001
SLR Ref No.: 610.033744.00001-R02-BAR-
v1.0 20260701.docx
 
 
69 
 
These fauna habitats are described further below. 
Riparian Environments and Dams 
Several existing watercourses that are tributaries to Cockle Creek flow through the central 
and western portion of the subject land, including Burkes Creek. These watercourses range 
from first to fourth order streams. Some of these watercourses and associated riparian 
corridors occurs within or adjacent to the developable areas. 
The riparian corridors within the subject land provide suitable foraging and breeding habitat 
for a number of fauna species, including amphibians, birds, mammals and reptiles. Pools of 
water in the drainage lines would provide a valuable drinking water source in hot and dry 
periods. 
Terrestrial Habitat Features 
Terrestrial habitat features occur in the vegetated areas of the subject land. Features such 
as fallen logs, debris and leaf litter provide shelter for small to medium sized terrestrial fauna 
species known from the locality of the subject land. In addition to providing habitat for 
terrestrial fauna, fallen logs and shrub vegetation provide foraging perches and calling 
locations for small birds. 
Stick Nests 
Stick nests were recorded in the subject land during field surveys that provide breeding 
habitat for native bird species. Stick nests were categorised in terms of size, to determine 
their suitability for threatened species. Only small and medium stick nests were recorded. 
Hollow-bearing Trees and Stags 
Tree hollows are an essential resource for a number of fauna species that rely on them for 
refuge and nesting (Newton 1994, Gibbons and Lindenmayer 2002, Heinsohn et al. 2003, 
Cockle et al. 2010). A number of hollow-bearing trees were observed within the developable 
areas, which mainly comprised small hollows (<10cm diameter) in mature living trees and 
stags. Due to the relatively young age of the rehabilitation areas, these areas are not 
expected to comprise many tree hollows. The tree hollows and stags within the developable 
areas and wider subject land provide shelter, roosting and nesting habitat for arboreal fauna 
species, including microchiropteran bats (microbats), gliders, diurnal and nocturnal birds, 
and some reptiles. 
Blossom-producing Trees and Shrubs 
The treed vegetation within the subject land would provide suitable foraging habitat for a 
range of nectivorous birds and arboreal mammals during blossom periods. It is expected that 
nectar-dependent species would be attracted to the subject land and wider locality during the 
blossoming period of dominant trees. In addition to providing direct resources to birds and 
arboreal mammals, the blossom-producing trees would also attract insects. Microbats known 
from the locality are insectivorous and would feed on moths, beetles and other insects.

subject land based on the results of the BAM-C and the Likelihood of Occurrence 
assessment (Appendix A), including 19 dual credit species which are considered as 
ecosystem credit species for their foraging habitat and species credit species for their 
breeding habitat.

6.0 
Constraints and Opportunities Assessment 
This chapter provides a discussion of the existing biodiversity constraints that are present 
within the subject land, based on the result from the desktop assessment and field surveys. 
It also includes a justification around the selection of potential developable areas as well as 
environmentally constrained areas as part of the Structure Plan, based on existing 
biodiversity values. The findings of this assessment have informed and shaped the Master 
Plan in relation to general areas that could have potential future development outcomes. 
6.1 
Constraints Classes 
The subject land has been subject to wide-spread disturbance from the previous mining 
operations. Nonetheless, there are parts of the subject land that comprises biodiversity 
values that would, or have the potential to, constrain future development in relevant areas of 
the subject land.  
Key biodiversity constraints identified within the subject land in this assessment include: 
• 
Presence of native vegetation, including TECs and rehabilitation areas; 
• 
Known and potential habitat for threatened species, including habitat features;  
• 
Land mapped as Coastal Wetlands, Key Fish Habitat, and land within riparian 
corridors; and 
• 
Land subject to existing VCAs. 
This assessment has identified five constraint classes relevant to the above listed 
biodiversity constraints, based on how likely they are to restrict future development: very 
high, high, moderate-remnant native vegetation, moderate-rehabilitation areas, and low 
ecological constraint.  The definition for each constraint class is provided below in Table 7.  
The location of these constraints is shown in Figure 18.

6.2 
Potential Developable Areas and Environmentally 
Constrained Areas 
Based on the assessment of biodiversity values in the subject land, there are areas of the 
subject land that provide potentially developable land, whilst other areas provide potential 
constraints to future development due to their high intrinsic biodiversity values. The Structure 
Plan (Figure 2) of the proposal attempts to achieve a balanced outcome in the subject land 
that provides both potential opportunities for development, whilst retaining the areas of 
highest biodiversity values in the subject land. 
As shown in Figure 19, the Structure Plan proposes an extensive network of retained areas 
throughout the subject land, which are shown as ‘environmentally constrained areas’. These 
comprise the highest biodiversity values mapped in the subject land, including the Coastal 
Wetlands and associated proximity areas, existing VCA sites, riparian corridors, and larger 
tracts of confirmed and potential TECs. The proposed retained areas continue to provide key 
wildlife corridors within the subject land, that will facilitate movement in both north-south and 
east-west direction. The key wildlife corridors will ensure the high biodiversity values within 
the subject land will provide for movement within and beyond the subject land. 
Land identified in the Structure Plan as potential developable areas and recreation areas are 
mainly limited to areas of moderate and low biodiversity constraints (Figure 20). All land 
identified as comprising ‘very high’ biodiversity constraints have been avoided in the 
Structure Plan. As shown in Figure 20, the smaller areas of high biodiversity that occur in the 
potential development site occur as either small, isolated patches of TECs within previously 
disturbed areas associated with the mining operations, or on the edges of patches of 
remnant vegetation. These areas will be subject to further detailed assessment as part of the 
DA stage for future developments.  
It is acknowledged that as targeted threatened species surveys have not been conducted for 
this assessment, there may be further areas of high constraint within the subject land 
beyond what is captured in this assessment. Future detailed assessments at the DA stage 
will be required to assess all impact areas and implement further avoidance and 
minimisation measures as required, in accordance with the requirements of the BC Act and 
EPBC Act.  
6.3 
Biodiversity Offset Opportunity Areas  
This assessment has identified two key areas within the subject land as biodiversity offset 
opportunity areas. As acknowledged in previous chapters of this report, there are currently 
three VCA sites within the subject land, as shown in Figure 21. In addition to the VCA sites, 
there are two large parcels of land along the western boundary of the subject land that are 
identified as potentially suitable for future offset outcomes, under a Biodiversity Stewardship 
Agreement (BSA) or similar conservation mechanism.  
Future assessment should assess the potential for these areas to be established as formal 
offset sites.

There are no direct impacts resulting from the proposed rezoning; however, this BAR has

Direct Impacts 
7.1.1.1 Impacts to Native Vegetation and Threatened Species 
The primary impact of a future development is the loss of vegetation and associated habitat 
within the developable areas. Table 8 identifies the potential extent of impacts to vegetation 
within the development site, including TECs, based on the assumption of complete 
clearance, noting that any future DA will need to demonstrate sufficient avoidance (i.e. it is

the land identified as environmentally constrained areas in the Master Plan. 
Approximately 58% of the native vegetation in the subject land occurs in areas mapped as 
environmentally constrained land, whilst approximately 42% of the native vegetation 
(including rehabilitation plantings) in the subject land occurs in areas that have been 
identified as having development potential. 
Additional targeted threatened species surveys are required to determine the presence of 
threatened species within the developable areas and calculate offsetting requirements which 
will need to be undertaken at the DA stage for future developments once exact impact 
footprints are known. Nonetheless, based on previous records within or adjacent to the 
developable areas and the subject land, it is likely that a number of threatened flora species 
such as Tetratheca juncea and Callistemon linerifolis, and a number of threatened and 
migratory fauna species, such as the Koala (Phascolarctos cinereus), large forest owls, and 
the South-eastern Glossy Black-cockatoo (Calyptorhynchus lathami lathami) have the 
potential to be impacted by a future development. The potential impacted flora and fauna 
species include both species listed under the BC Act and EPBC Act.

7.1.1.2 Impacts to Koala Habitat 
The development site contains vegetation that comprise tree species that are listed as a 
Koala Use Trees as listed in Schedule 1 of the BC SEPP. Based on the large number of 
Koala records that occur to the north-west, west and south of the subject land, it is likely that 
Koalas also use parts of the subject land. The extent of impact on Koalas and their habitat 
will need to be assessed at the DA stage for future developments once exact impact 
footprints are known.   
7.1.1.3 Impacts to Coastal Wetlands 
Land mapped as Coastal Wetlands under the Resilience and Hazards SEPP occur across 
large parts of the subject land, as shown in Figure 8. Based on the Structure Plan, all areas 
of Coastal Wetlands will be avoided by future developments and as a result there will be no 
direct impact from the project on the Coastal Wetlands. However, there is potential for some 
indirect impacts to occur to Coastal Wetlands depending on the nature and extent of future 
developments. Potential indirect impacts will be addressed in a future detailed assessment 
at the DA stage. 
Most of the Proximity Areas for Coastal Wetlands, as per the SEPP mapping, will also be 
avoided by future developments based on the Structure Plan apart from a small area in the 
central portion of the subject land. Any potential impacts on proximity areas must be 
assessed in future detailed assessment during the DA stage, and must satisfy the relevant 
objectives of the Resilience and Hazards SEPP and CM Act. 
7.1.1.4 Impact to Riparian Land and Mapped Watercourses 
The development site mostly avoids riparian corridors, however they include some direct 
impacts to riparian land and mapped watercourses in the north-western and central portions 
of the subject land. 
Riparian corridors consist of the following components (DPI 2018): 
• 
The channel which comprises the bed and banks of the watercourse (to the highest 
bank); and 
• 
The vegetated riparian zone (VRZ) adjoining the channel. 
The width of the VRZ is required to be measured from the top of the highest bank on both 
sides of the watercourse (DPI, 2018). The exact impact to each mapped watercourse and its 
associated VRZs will need to be assessed at the DA stage for future developments once 
exact impact footprints are known. NRAR may also need to be consulted and additional 
approvals sought under the WM Act for any impacts proposed on waterfront land (areas with 
40m of a watercourse). 
7.1.1.5 Impact to Biodiversity Corridors 
Direct impacts to existing biodiversity/wildlife corridors are mainly limited to narrowing the 
width of existing key corridors in the subject land. Based on the existing Structure Plan, the 
subject land will continue to provide key wildlife corridors that will facilitate movement in a 
north-south and east-west direction throughout and beyond the subject land. Regardless, a 
future detailed assessment will need to assess the impacts on threatened species based on 
the narrowing of wildlife corridors in the subject land as part of any future DA. These 
assessments should also consider any species-specific guidance or requirements for 
corridor widths.

Although the existing biodiversity values within the subject land is already likely to have been 
subject to indirect impacts from dust from the mining operations, future developments will 
need to assess potential indirect impacts from dust at the DA stage. 
Light 
Future development has the potential to increase the level of artificial light in the natural 
environment.  Increased light levels may adversely impact wildlife by direct glare, chronic or 
periodic increased illumination and temporary unexpected fluctuations in light levels (Saleh, 
2007) (Longcore & Rich, 2010).   
While future development will have some effect on the surrounding environment, the impacts 
from light pollution are likely to be minimal compared to current conditions. Any increase in 
light levels is expected to be localised to the developable areas and immediate surrounds. 
Future developments will need to assess potential indirect impacts from light pollution at the 
DA stage. 
Sedimentation and Erosion 
During the construction and earthworks phase of a future development, the retained 
vegetation and vegetation occurring directly adjacent but outside of the developable areas 
has potential to be impacted by sedimentation and erosion. Eroded sediment can smother 
retained vegetation if appropriate control measures are not implemented. Smothering can 
reduce regeneration of groundcover species and enter drainage lines. Sediment and eroded 
material can also contain weed matter and nutrients, and movement of this material into the 
retained vegetation can facilitate the spread of weeds which can result in changes to 
community composition. However, it is considered that with the implementation of 
appropriate sediment control methods, the risk of sedimentation is considered to be minor 
and manageable. 
Future developments will need to assess potential indirect impacts from light pollution at the 
DA stage. 
7.1.3 
Prescribed Impacts 
Prescribed impacts are identified in Clause 6.1 of the BC Regulation.  Prescribed impacts 
are those that are additional to the clearing of native vegetation and associated habitat.  
These include: 
• 
Development on the habitat of threatened species or ecological communities 
associated with: 
o karst, caves, crevices, cliffs, rock outcrops and other geological features of 
significance; 
o human-made structures; 
o non-native vegetation; 
• 
Development on areas connecting threatened species habitat, such as movement 
corridors; 
• 
Development on water quality, water bodies and hydrological processes that sustain 
threatened species and TECs (including from subsidence or upsidence from 
underground mining); 
• 
Wind turbine strikes on protected animals; and 
• 
Vehicle strikes on threatened species or on animals that are part of a TEC.

7.2 
Recommendations for Avoidance, Mitigation, and Offsetting 
Under the BAM, there is a requirement to consider potential impacts from a proposed 
development and to then apply the following assessment hierarchy: 
• 
Avoid or minimise: consideration should first be given to designing to avoid or 
minimise potential development impacts on biodiversity values. 
• 
Mitigate: mitigation measures should be formulated to ameliorate the impacts 
remaining after avoidance has been implemented. 
• 
Offset: biodiversity offsetting should be implemented in order to compensate for any 
residual impacts that cannot be avoided or mitigated. 
The findings of this BAR have informed and shaped the Master Plan for the Precinct. The 
Master Plan seeks to avoid and minimise future impacts on high biodiversity values. 
Nonetheless, future development applications in the subject land will need to prepare 
detailed technical assessments in accordance with the requirements under the BC Act and 
EPBC Act, and will be subject to the requirement to apply the avoid, minimise and offset 
hierarchy for each DA. 
This section provides recommendations for measures that should be implemented to avoid, 
mitigate and offset the impacts of a future development in the subject land. 
7.2.1 
Avoidance and Minimisation Measures 
The BAM requires proponents to demonstrate how impacts on biodiversity values have been 
avoided and minimised through project development and design, including during the 
process of selecting the project location. All projects must demonstrate that that reasonable 
steps to avoid and minimise impacts to biodiversity values have been carried out as part of 
project development. Impacts must be avoided and minimised before offsets are proposed to 
compensate for any residual impacts.   
It is recommended the following measures are considered at the DA stage for future 
developments within the developable areas, to ensure native vegetation and threatened 
species habitat can be avoided or minimised: 
• 
Locating future developments within previously disturbed areas and/or areas with low 
biodiversity values; 
• 
Situating a development within areas where the native vegetation and threatened 
species habitat is in the poorest condition (i.e. low vegetation integrity scores); 
• 
Locating future developments in areas that avoid direct impacts to mapped TECs and 
threatened species habitats; 
• 
Designing the development in a manner that avoids fragmentation and/or isolation of 
remnant native vegetation and threatened species habitats; 
• 
Designing future developments to reuse existing infrastructure to the greatest extent 
possible; and 
• 
Locating future developments to include setbacks and relevant buffers to areas of 
high biodiversity values, such as TECs, existing locations of threatened flora, and 
wetlands. 
Where impacts to biodiversity values cannot be avoided by future developments, the 
potential mitigation measures proposed in Section 7.2.2 should be considered, prior to the 
implementation of offsetting.

7.2.2 
Mitigation Measures 
As demonstrated in previous chapters, the subject land comprises large areas of high 
biodiversity values including areas of TECs, Coastal Wetlands, threatened species habitats, 
and riparian corridors. As a result, there will be a need to implement measures to minimise 
and mitigate impacts to these entities. This section outlines recommended mitigation 
measures for future developments in the subject land.  These measures will be described in 
further detail within the relevant biodiversity assessment at the DA stage. Construction 
related mitigation measures will be detailed in separate Construction Environmental 
Management Plan (CEMP).  
7.2.2.1 Inductions 
Site inductions should be given by the civil contractor to ensure all site workers and visitors 
are aware of ecological issues associated with the subject land and the location of any 
restricted access areas. 
7.2.2.2 Access Restrictions 
To avoid unnecessary removal or damage to vegetation to be retained adjacent to the 
subject land, the clearing area should be clearly demarcated and signed to ensure no 
vegetation beyond these boundaries is removed. Clearing works and equipment should be 
excluded from areas outside the clearing area. 
7.2.2.3 Traffic Management 
In order to reduce the risk to fauna from vehicle strike, traffic management will be 
implemented during construction to maintain slow vehicle speeds. Traffic management 
measures will be developed as part of a CEMP.  
Post construction, speed signage will be installed on internal roads, and traffic calming 
measures installed, where required (subject to Council approval). 
7.2.2.4 Erosion, Sedimentation and Pollution Control 
To reduce sedimentation on the construction site, erosion control measures should be 
implemented. This includes minimising the amount of exposed soils on the site at any given 
time. All soil stockpiles should be adequately covered when not in use to prevent erosion 
through heavy rainfall. 
Sediment fences should be established around the perimeter of the development area to 
prevent the impacts of sedimentation on adjoining vegetation and the adjacent drainage line. 
During development, precautions should be taken to ensure that no pollution, such as 
petrochemical substances or water containing suspended solids, escapes the construction 
site. Pollution traps and efficient removal of pollution to an off-site location would help to 
minimise pollution impacts. 
7.2.2.5 Weed Management 
In order to minimise the spread of weeds throughout the subject land, appropriate weed 
control activities will be undertaken prior to vegetation clearing in accordance with the North 
Coast Regional Strategic Weed Management Plan 2023 – 2027 (LLS, 2022) under the NSW 
Biosecurity Act 2015.  
The Biosecurity Act 2015 and regulations provide specific legal requirements for state level 
priority weeds and high risk activities, as provided in the Appendices of the North Coast 
Regional Strategic Weed Management Plan 2023 – 2027 (LLS, 2022). In order to comply 

--- Bio Page 98 ---
Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure 
Biodiversity Assessment Report 
1 July 2026
SLR Project No.: 610.033744.00001
SLR Ref No.: 610.033744.00001-R02-BAR-
v1.0 20260701.docx
 
 
89 
 
with the objectives of the plan, it is recommended the following measures be implemented 
as part of weed management for the subject land. 
Prevention 
Appropriate construction site hygiene measures will be implemented to prevent entry of new 
weeds to the area such as the cleaning of equipment prior to entering the subject land.   
Eradication 
Initial weed management will be carried out within the subject land according to best-practice 
methods.  The targeted species will be those listed under Appendix 1 of the North Coast 
Regional Strategic Weed Management Plan 2023 – 2027 (LLS, 2022) under which have 
been recorded from the subject land.  Initial weed treatment will include eliminating woody 
species and targeting large dominant infestations of exotic herbs.  This may be achieved via 
a combination of manual weed removal and herbicide use. 
Weed management measures should avoid adverse impacts to retained vegetation within 
the subject land, including not over clearing (remove only targeted species), employment of 
minimal disturbance techniques to avoid soil and surrounding vegetation disturbance. 
Containment 
Follow-up monitoring and maintenance should be undertaken in the subject land following 
vegetation clearing activities, to contain any re-emergence of weed species.  
7.2.2.6 Biodiversity Management Plan 
Due to the potential for future development to impact on areas of potential habitat for 
threatened species, including the Koala, in the subject land, a Biodiversity Management Plan 
(BMP) should be prepared for any future DAs within the subject land. A future BMP should 
also cover any environmentally constrained areas proposed to be retained by a future DA. 
The overall objectives of the BMP will be to minimise impacts to biodiversity as a result of 
development by prescribing a range of management measures that will be implemented both 
during construction and in the long-term.   
Specific management measures that should be detailed in the BMP include the following: 
• 
Pre-clearance surveys and clearance supervision during construction to minimise 
impacts of construction; 
• 
Delineation of clearing boundaries and the installation of sediment fences and erosion 
control measures; 
• 
Retention and management for biodiversity of all wooded habitat that is outside of the 
development areas; 
• 
Implementation of weed control measures, both during construction and in areas of 
retained vegetation in the long-term; 
• 
Implementation of measures to avoid and minimise sedimentation and erosion; 
• 
Undertake a monitoring programme, including water quality, weeds and threatened 
species; and 
• 
Rehabilitation/revegetation of treed habitat in areas outside of the development footprint. 
The implementation of the BMP will enable the minimisation of impacts to biodiversity and 
the appropriate mitigation of potential impacts.

7.3 
Future Assessment Requirements 
7.3.1 
EPBC Act Requirements 
Threatened species, populations and communities listed under the EPBC Act that are 
considered to be directly or indirectly impacted by future proposed development should be 
assessed in accordance with the Matters of National Environmental Significance Significant 
Impact Guidelines 1.1 (DoE, 2013).  If a development is considered to significantly impact 
any MNES, then a referral would be required to be submitted to the Commonwealth 
Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (Cth DCCEEW). 
Three TECs that are listed under the EPBC Act occurs in the developable areas and have 
the potential to be impacted by future developments: Swamp Oak Floodplain Forest, River-
flat Eucalypt Forest, and Swamp Sclerophyll Forest. Additionally, several threatened flora 
and fauna species, as well as migratory species, have been recording or have the potential 
to occur in the developable area. As such, any future DAs will need to consider impacts to 
threatened species and populations listed under the EPBC Act if recorded as present within 
the subject land. A referral to the Cth DCCEEW should be prepared if impacts on MNES are 
considered to be significant, in accordance with the Commonwealth Significant Impact 
Assessment Guidelines (DotE, 2013). 
7.3.2 
BC Act Requirements 
To determine the type of assessment required for a future development under the EP&A Act, 
it is necessary to determine whether the proposed development triggers the Biodiversity 
Offset Scheme (BOS). If the project is a State Significant Development, the BOS is 
automatically triggered and a BDAR is required, unless a BDAR Waiver is granted. 
For a local development to trigger the BOS, it would need to be considered as likely to 
significantly affect threatened species, which could occur as follows: 
• 
It is likely to significantly affect threatened species or ecological communities, or their 
habitats, according to the test of significance in Section 7.3 of the BC Act; 
• 
It exceeds the biodiversity offsets scheme threshold according to Clause 7.1 of the 
BC Regulation, with the thresholds being: 
o The clearing of native vegetation of an area above a prescribed threshold based 
on the minimum lot size; or 
o The clearing of native vegetation, or other prescribed action, on land included on 
the Biodiversity Values Map. 
• 
It is carried out in a declared area of outstanding biodiversity value (AOBV).

7.3.2.1 Offsetting Requirements 
The BOS provides a framework to avoid, minimise and offset impacts on biodiversity from 
development and clearing, and to ensure land that is used to offset impacts is secured in-
perpetuity. Developers and landholders who undertake development or clearing, generating 
a credit obligation that must be retired to offset their activity following approval by the 
consent authority. Under the BAM, there are two types of credits on development sites: 
• 
Ecosystem credits, which measure the offset requirement for impacts on threatened 
ecological communities, threatened species habitat for species that can be reliably 
predicted to occur with a plant community type, and other plant community types 
generally; and 
• 
Species credits, which measure the offset requirement for impacts on threatened 
species individuals or area of habitat. 
Once the consent authority has issued the approval or consent that includes the final credit 
obligation of ecosystem and/or species credits, the obligation can be satisfied as follows: 
• 
The retirement of the required number and class of like-for-like biodiversity credits; 
• 
The retirement of the required biodiversity credits in accordance with the variation 
rules; 
• 
The funding of a biodiversity conservation action that would benefit the relevant 
threatened species or ecological community and that is equivalent to the cost of

payment calculator referred to in Section 6.32 of the BC Act; and 
•
