7.3.3 
WM Act Requirements 
Under the WM Act, a 'controlled activity approval' is required to carry out activities in, on or 
under waterfront land, which includes the bed and a distance of 40 metres from any river, 
lake or estuary. An application for a ‘controlled activity approval’ will be refused if adequate 
arrangements are not in force to ensure that no more than minimal harm will be done to any 
waterfront land as a consequence of the carrying out of the proposed controlled activity.   
As land proposed to be developed in the subject land includes impacts to selected 
watercourses, the WM Act is relevant to the project due to the proposed activities taking 
place within waterfront land and a controlled activity approval will need to be obtained prior 
to the commencement of works. 
The Guidelines for controlled activities on waterfront land (DPI, 2018)permits non-riparian 
corridor works or development within the outer 50% of the VRZ if deemed suitable.  Non-
riparian uses, such as Asset Protection Zones (APZs) are allowed within the outer 50% of 
the VRZ, so long as offsets are provided in accordance with the averaging rule (DPI, 2018). 
Non-riparian corridor works or development is considered suitable for cleared land, where an 
averaging rule is applied to ensure no net reduction in corridor width.  However, 
developments that contain existing native vegetation along the riparian corridor should seek 
to maintain the required VRZ width in accordance with the minimum requirements. 
Therefore, future DAs will be required to consider the VRZ of impacted watercourses, and 
the project will likely require a Controlled Activity Approval from NRAR.   
7.3.4 
State Environmental Planning Policy (Biodiversity Conservation) 2021 
As explained previously, the Lake Macquarie LGA is included in Schedule 2 of the BC 
SEPP, and therefore it applies to the subject land.   
Under the BC SEPP, ‘core koala habitat’ is defined as: 
a) an area of land which has been assessed by a suitably qualified and 
experienced person as being highly suitable koala habitat and where koalas 
are recorded as being present at the time of assessment of the land as highly 
suitable koala habitat, OR 
b) an area of land which has been assessed by a suitably qualified and 
experienced person as being highly suitable koala habitat and where koalas 
have been recorded as being present in the previous 18 years. 
The subject land contains PCTs which comprises trees that are listed as a Koala Use Tree 
species under Schedule 1 of the BC SEPP 2021.  Therefore, according to the BC SEPP the 
subject land is determined to be ‘highly suitable koala habitat’. Additionally, several historic 
and recent Koala records occur on land directly adjacent to the subject land, and as a result 
the subject land would likely be considered to include ‘Core Koala habitat’, as defined under 
the BC SEPP. For land under which BC SEPP 2021 applies, DAs impacting Koalas or Koala 
Habitat must be accompanied by a Koala Assessment Report (KAR). Additionally, Koala 
Plans of Management (KPoM) are likely to be required for sites impacting core Koala habitat.

7.4 
Recommended Master Plan Aims and Performance Criteria 
As detailed in this BAR, parts of the subject land have been subject to a high degree of 
previous disturbance, including vegetation clearing, from the former mining operations. 
Nonetheless, large areas of the subject land also comprise high biodiversity values including 
TECs listed under the BC Act and EPBC Act, Coastal Wetlands, and Key Fish Habitat. The 
subject land also includes a number of key wildlife corridors that facilitate movement through 
the subject land and within the wider landscape for several threatened and non-threatened 
species.  
In recognition of the development potential of parts of the subject land, as well as the 
existing high biodiversity values within other parts of the subject land, a number of 
performance criteria have been developed for the Master Plan. These performance criteria 
will guide and control future development within the Precinct, to achieve a set of biodiversity 
related aims. 
The intent of the aims and associated performance criteria is to protect the highest 
biodiversity values in the subject land, whilst still allowing for development to occur in areas 
with lower biodiversity values. The performance criteria recognise the limitations of this BAR, 
in terms of targeted threatened species surveys, and acknowledges the need for detailed 
biodiversity assessments for future DAs. It is also recognised within the performance criteria 
that the avoid, minimise and offset hierarchy will need to be applied for all future DAs. 
The relevant  aims and performance criteria that are recommended to be incorporated in the 
Master Plan for the rezoning proposal are detailed in Section 7.4.1 and 7.4.2, respectively. 
7.4.1 
Aims 
• 
Protect areas of high biodiversity values from development to avoid serious and 
irreversible impacts on TECs and threatened species. 
• 
Promote a development outcome that is consistent with the requirements of the 
avoid, minimise and offset hierarchy of applicable NSW and Commonwealth 
biodiversity legislation. 
• 
Maintain the function of key linkages that facilitate wildlife movement within the 
subject land and the wider landscape. 
• 
Identify and secure environmentally constrained areas with an appropriate size and 
configuration to be protected under suitable conservation mechanisms.  
• 
Protect wetlands, watercourses, and associated riparian corridors and aquatic 
habitats from development.  
• 
Implement ecological restoration or rehabilitation measures on residual land or buffer 
zones to achieve a net positive biodiversity outcome. 
• 
Apply ecologically sustainable development principles for future land use and 
development. 
• 
Respond and adapt to future environmental changes to avoid adverse impacts on 
high biodiversity values.  
7.4.2 
Performance Criteria 
• 
Development footprints must be located to avoid and minimise impacts on areas of 
high biodiversity values that could result in a serious and irreversible impact on TECs 
or threatened species.

8.0 
Conclusion  
This BAR has been prepared by SLR to accompany a rezoning proposal for the subject land 
in support of a proposed amendment to the Regional Precincts SEPP. The proposed 
amendments to the Regional Precincts SEPP are intended to give effect to a Master Plan 
that will facilitate future development and conservation of the Precinct.  
The vegetation within the subject land has been subject to previous disturbance from the 
former mining operations. Despite the previous disturbance, large areas of relatively 
undisturbed, remnant vegetation still occurs across the subject land. This includes four TECs 
that are listed under the BC Act and/or EPBC Act, as well as the presence of potential 
habitat for threatened species. As it was not possible to undertake targeted threatened 
species surveys for this assessment, further field surveys are required to be undertaken at 
the DA stage for a future development to verify the extent of threatened species habitat 
within the subject land. 
The Structure Plan for the project identifies a large network of environmentally constrained 
areas that are suitable for long-term conservation due to the high biodiversity values present. 
The environmentally constrained areas will continue to provide key wildlife corridors in the 
subject land, which will facilitate movement within and beyond the subject land. Identification 
of potential developable areas has focused on largely avoiding areas of known high 
biodiversity values in the subject land, with a focus on situating future developments within 
previously disturbed areas that likely comprise lower biodiversity values. Regardless, future 
detailed assessments under the BAM are required at the DA stage for future developments 
to further verify the biodiversity in the developable areas. 
The BAM sets a standard that will result in no net loss of biodiversity values where the 
impacts on biodiversity values are avoided, minimised and mitigated, and all residual 
impacts are offset by the retirement of the required number of biodiversity credits. Any 
clearing of native vegetation and threatened species habitat facilitated by the project will be 
subject to further assessment at the DA stage but is expected to result in the requirement of 
offsets in the form of ecosystem credits and species credits. Although targeted threatened 
flora and fauna species surveys have not been conducted at this stage, the results of the 
database analysis and habitat assessments indicate that several species credit species are 
likely to occur on the subject land. Hence, credit calculations will need be conducted for 
these species credits species (if impacted by a DA) to determine the offset liability at the DA 
stage of the project. Further to this, a future DA will also need to complete an assessment of 
potential Serious and Irreversible Impact to a threatened species. 
The project has sought to avoid impacts to key biodiversity values at the rezoning stage, and 
it is recommended that a suite of mitigation measures will be implemented for the project 
including weed management, delineation of clearing limits, sedimentation control measures 
and landscaping utilising native species. It is also recommended that a BMP is prepared for 
the subject land to minimise impacts to biodiversity as far as practicable. 
It is further recommended that future assessments have regard to the additional avoidance 
and mitigation measures recommended in this report. Additionally, future offsetting should 
consider the potential for establishing onsite offset sites under a Biodiversity Stewardship 
Agreement. 
With the implementation of the recommended avoidance, mitigation and compensation 
measures, and the adherence to relevant proposed performance criteria, it is expected that 
future impacts on TECs and/or threatened flora and fauna species can be appropriately 
managed.

Acacia bynoeana

E 
V 
Found in central eastern NSW, from the 
Hunter District (Morisset) south to the 
Southern Highlands and west to the Blue 
Mountains. Occurs in heath or dry 
sclerophyll forest on sandy soils. The 
species apparently prefers open, 
sometimes slightly disturbed sites such

mounds and in recently burnt patches. 
Unlikely to occur. Although suitable habitat is

Thismia clavarioides 
Fairy Lantern 
E 
Rare, subterranean plant endemic to 
NSW. It relies on a specialized, dark, and 
damp habitat to complete its lifecycle 
completely out of the sun. Known 
populations in Morton National Park and 
Barrington Tops National Park. 
Unlikely to occur. Subject land is not within the 
Morton or Barrington Tops National Parks.

Neophema chrysostoma 
Blue-winged 
Parrot 
Inhabit a range of habitats from coastal, sub-
coastal and inland areas, through to semi-arid 
zones. They tend to favour grasslands and grassy 
woodlands and are often found near wetlands 
both near the coast and in semi-arid zones. Pairs 
or small parties of blue-winged parrots forage 
mainly near or on the ground for seeds of a wide 
range of native and introduced grasses, herbs and 
shrubs.  
Unlikely to occur. Although potential 
habitat is present in the subject land, 
there are no records of this species 
within the locality. 
Hoplocephalus bungaroides 
Broad-headed 
Snake 
E 
V 
Shelters in rock crevices and under flat sandstone 
rocks on exposed cliff edges during autumn, 
winter and spring. Moves from the sandstone 
rocks to shelters in crevices or hollows in large 
trees within 500m of escarpments in summer. 
Unlikely to occur. Although potential 
habitat is present in the subject land, 
there are no records of this species 
within the locality. 
Climacteris picumnus victoriae 
Brown 
Treecreeper 
(eastern 
subspecies) 
V 
Found in eucalypt woodlands and dry open forest 
of the inland slopes and plains inland of the Great 
Dividing Range. The species favours woodlands 
dominated by stringybarks or other rough-barked 
eucalypts, usually with an open grassy 
understorey, sometimes with one or more shrub 
Potential to occur. The species may 
utilise the subject land as part of an 
extended foraging range.

Phascolarctos cinereus 
Koala 
V 
V 
Inhabit eucalypt woodlands and forests.  Feed on 
the foliage of more than 70 eucalypt species and 
30 non-eucalypt species, but in any one area will 
select preferred feed species.  Home range size 
varies with quality of habitat, ranging from less 
than two ha to several hundred hectares in size. 
Potential to occur. Suitable foraging 
and breeding habitat is present within 
the subject land.
